Leave was granted to consider the submissions that admittedly the writ-petitioners having not made any construction on the case plot and thereby violated the provision of clause 3 of the lease deed, the lease of the writ-petitioners was liable to be cancelled for which notice dated 2-9-1990 was served and thereupon the lease was cancelled on 29-5-1994 and, as such, the High Court Division was in error in making the Rule absolute upon observing since cancellation was made after expiry of 4 years Government ought to have issued fresh show cause notice, that once a lease is liable to be cancelled there is no further requirement that the order of cancellation has to be passed within a certain period of time and, as such, the High Court Division was in error in finding the order of cancellation of lease on 29-5-1994 illegal simply because the show cause notice was issued on 2-9-1990, particularly when there is no assertion in the writ petition that the writ-petitioners changed their position by making construction or otherwise between the date of issuance of the show cause notice and the date of cancellation of the lease, that the High Court Division failed to appreciate properly the decision of Moni Begum vs RAJUK, 46 DLR (AD) 154 and wrongly held that in writ jurisdiction review application is not maintainable, that new relevant facts having bearing on the case having been discovered and a review having been sought on that ground, the High Court Division was wrong in summarily dismissing the review application without applying its judicial mind to the new evidence placed before it.</u>

<u>10. The learned Counsels appearing for the appellants in Appeal Nos. 152 and 155 have submitted that the proceeding initiated upon a writ petition before the constitution Bench of the High Court Division is undoubtedly being civil proceeding and there being nothing in Article 102(2) of the Constitution to preclude the High Court Division from exercising the power of review which inheres in every court of plenary jurisdiction to prevent miscarriage of justice or to correct grave and palpable errors committed by it, the High Court Division was in error in rejecting the review application holding the same not maintainable and it has also been submitted that the High Court Division failed to appreciate the decision reported in 46 DLR (AD) 154 and thereupon wrongly held that in writ jurisdiction review application is not maintaihable.</u>

<u>11. In the case of Moni Begum vs Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakha this Division while considering the question of application of the provision of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the proceedings in writ in the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution observed that the provision of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure "does not in terms apply to proceedings in writ in the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. But the Court in its discretion can apply the principles as distinguished from the technical provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure to meet the exigencies of the situation in appropriate cases on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience. In what situations the principles of the Code of Civil Procedure will be applied and to what extent may perhaps be left to the wise discretion of the Court itself. In other words, barring what is specifically provided for in the Rules themselves, the Court is the master of its own procedure and it will exercise both its procedural and substantive discretions only on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience." In the said case Mr Latifur Rahman, J, (as he then was) has observed that the Writ Court being a civil Court though does not possess specifically powers as are in Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Writ Court must possess this power of doing justice in a case and whether Court will exercise such power is a matter of judicial discretion for that Court.</u>

12. The learned Counsel for the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 152 of 2000 has submitted that proceedings before the Writ Court are undoubtedly proceedings of a civil nature and that being so review as provided by section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure is very much available in the writ jurisdiction. 	.

<u>13. In support of the said submission the learned Counsel has referred to a decision in the case of Hussain Bakhsh vs Settlement Commissioner and another reported in 21 DLR (SC) 456 wherein it has been observed, "A review of such an order is therefore, competent under clause (b) of section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure". A review under section 114(b) CPC lies in case of decree or order from which no appeal was allowed by the CPC. In the background of the decision referred to above it has been submitted by the learned Counsel that it is not correct that review is at all available before the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction. The learned Counsel has also referred to the case of Khadomul Islam Chowdhury vs Bangladesh and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 111 wherein it has been observed "the question involved, no doubt, is of great public importance, but none of the Counsels appearing for the parties challenged the power of the High Court Division to review its order made under Article 102 of the Constitution". The fact of the aforesaid case is that a writ petition was heard in the absence of one of the respondents and the Rule was made absolute. Thereupon, respondent in whose absence the writ petition was disposed of filed an application before the same very Bench with the prayer for re-hearing of the writ petition and the High Court Division allowed the same and restored the writ petition to its file and number. As against the order of the High Court Division restoring the writ petition for fresh hearing the appeal was filed. The learned Counsel in support of his contention since there is nothing in Article 102 precluding the High Court Division from reviewing its order and, as such, the said Division in the exigency of a case or to correct palpable error as well as to prevent miscarriage of justice is very much competent to exercise power of review in writ jurisdiction has referred to the case of Ariban Tuleshwar Sharma vs Ariban Pishak Sharma and others reported in AIR 1979 SC 1047 wherein it has been observed "It is true as observed by this Court in Shivdeo Singh vs State of Punjab (AIR 1963 SC 1909) there is nothing in Article 226 of the Constitution to preclude a High Court from exercising the power of review which inheres in every Court of plenary jurisdiction to prevent miscarriage of justice or to correct grave and palpable errors committed by it. But, there are definitive limits to the exercise of the power of review. The power of review may be exercised on the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence was not within the knowledge of the person seeking the review or could not be produced by him at the time when the order was made; it may be exercised where some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record is found; it may also be exercised on any analogous ground. But it may not be exercised on the ground that the decision was erroneous on merits. That would be the province of a Court of appeal". The learned Counsel has also referred to the case of State of Kerala vs PK Syed Akbar Sahib, reported in AIR 1988 SC 702 wherein it has been observed "in our considered opinion the High Court should have entertained the application for review". It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division in Review Petition Nos. 10 and 11, as against which Civil Appeal Nos. 152 and 153 have been filed, the said Division has placed reliance in holding that review application in writ jurisdiction is not maintainable on the decision in the case of Azra Zaman Chowdhury vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 34 DLR 247 wherein it has been observed "that the High Court Division is not empowered under the Constitution of Bangladesh or under any other law to review its judgment made in an application under Article 102 of the Constitution". The High Court Division held the same on the view that in a proceeding under Article 102 of the Constitution, there is no provision either in the Constitution itself or in any other law providing for any such review of any judgment passed by the High Court Division in exercising its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution and also, upon referring to Article 105 of the Constitution, has observed that the provision of the said Article empowered the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court to review any judgment pronounced by it and such specific power of reviewing its judgment or order is conspicuously absent so far as the High Court Division is concerned. The High Court Division has also referred to the case of Omar Faruk (Md) and others vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 51 DLR 118 (same has also been reported in 1999 BLD 70 wherein it has been observed that the jurisdiction is the creation of the statute and as the Constitution is silent as to power of the High Court Division to review its judgment and order passed in writ jurisdiction there is no scope for entertaining the application for review and to review the judgment or order passed by the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction. The view expressed in the case reported 21 DLR (SC) 456 and 46 DLR (AD) 154 as to power to the High Court Division to exercise the power of review and as to application of the provision as in sections 114 and 141 of the Civil Procedure Code has already been quoted hereinabove.</u>

<u>14. The learned Counsel for the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 152 of 2000 has submitted that the Court exercises its power, either in the writ jurisdiction or in the ordinary civil jurisdiction, for dispensation of justice and in doing so the Court is competent to exercise its discretion in the background of the materials brought before it in one form or other or, in other words, while seeks exercise of discretion either by way of review or re-hearing or reconsideration of its judgment earlier made in the background of the fresh material(s) brought before it. The learned Counsel has also submitted that in Moni Begum's case this Division has in no way precluded the High Court Division from exercising its discretion either recoursing to review, or re-hearing to revise the decision already made in a case upon placement of the materials which earlier could not be placed after due diligence before it and if the same would have been placed before the Writ Court the judgment already delivered would not have been one made, but would have been otherwise. In the case reported in 46 DLR (AD) 154 this Division has observed that High Court Division in its discretion can "apply the principles as distinguished from the technical provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure to meet  the exigencies of the situation in appropriate cases on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience." It is true in the Constitution there is no provision empowering the High Court Division to review its judgment and order, but it is also true that there was no provision precluding the High Court Division from exercising power of review. The Court's inherent power to do justice to the parties before it is an accepted one and for that the form in which the Court shall dispense justice is a matter for the Court or, in other words, it may either by way of review of its judgment or upon revising its judgment in the background of the material(s) brought before it subsequent to the pronouncement of the judgment since "the Court is the master of its own procedure and it will exercise both its procedural and substantive discretions only on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience."</u>

15. The leaned Counsel appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-4 in all the appeals has submitted that the question whether High Court Division while exercising writ jurisdiction is empowered to exercise the power to review its judgment or order since is a question of great public importance this Division is required to give its decision finally, in either of the ways.

<u>16. There being no dispute that the Court is for dispensation of justice and in doing so is competent to exercise its discretion to advance the cause of justice upon resorting to the procedure that would advance the cause of justice, equity and good conscience and as there is nothing in Article 102 of the Constitution to preclude the High Court Division from exercising the power of review we are of the view that the High Court Division is very much competent to entertain an application for review and to revise its judgment if a case for review is made out or, in other words, the material(s), which if would have been before the Court the judgment already made would not have been the one but different is placed before the High Court Division then the said Division to advance cause of action is not precluded from reviewing its judgment.</u>

17. The High Court Division primarily made the Rule absolute upon declaring the order of cancellation of allotment of the plot in question of the respondent Nos. 1-4 and the subsequent allotment to the writ-respondent Nos. 6-9 on the ground of malafide. The materials and the circumstances that mainly weighed with the High Court Division in arriving at the finding of malafide have already been stated hereinbefore.

18. The learned Counsels for the appellants have submitted that the respondent Nos. 1-4 did not make out any case of malafide or non-transparency as regard cancellation of their allotment of the plot in question and allotment of the said plot to the appellants in appeal No. 155 of 2000 (the writ respondent Nos. 6-9). The learned Counsel appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-4 has submitted that the elements highlighting malafide are very much on record and the said elements are primarily, the decision to cancel the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 was taken in hot haste. In elaborating the same he has submitted that the allotment was cancelled on the very day on which notings were made for the purpose of taking decision as regard cancellation of the plot allotted to the respondent Nos. 1-4 and that policy decision that was taken in the meeting held on 25-10-93 was in respect of all the affected persons and the policy decision so taken though was of generai nature but allotment was made only to 2 affected persons from amongst the affected persons and the decision to cancel allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 was taken after lapse of more or less 4 years from the date of service of 2nd show cause notice.

<u>19. In refutal of the aforesaid contentions of the respondents it has been submitted by the learned Counsels for the appellants that materials on record, particularly from the decision No.2 of the meeting held on 28-2-94, it would clearly be seen what prompted the authority to make the allotment in question avoiding procrastination. It is seen from the materials on record that the matter of allotment of plot to the affected persons was pending for sufficiently long time and thereupon there was agitation by the affected person for finalisation of allotment of plot to the affected person without further procrastination. The learned Counsel for the respondents heavily relied on the fact that matter of cancellation of the plot allotted to the respondent Nos. 1-4 was taken in the course of the day although 2nd notice for cancellation was issued about 4 years back. We have already observed that there are materials on the record that prompted the authority to take decision relating to the matter of cancellation of the allotment without sitting over the same any further. The learned Counsel for the appellants in appeal No. 155 of 2000 has submitted that merely for the delay in taking decision in a matter no bad motive can be ascribed to the decision taken and, in that respect, has referred to the observation made in the case of Chairman, BCSIR vs Abdul Khaleque reported in 43 DLR 209, and, as such, the learned Counsel submitted conversely, in view of the materials on record, bad motive cannot be ascribed to the decision taken by the authority for the cancellation of the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 avoiding procrastination.</u>

20. The contention of mala fide either on the ground of delay in taking decision or for taking decision avoiding procrastination in a given case is to be considered in the context of facts and circumstances of the same as well as on consideration of the tangible material(s) in the background whereof reasonable deduction can be made or conclusion can be arrived at as regard contention of malafide.

21. From the materials on record it is seen that process of cancellation was initiated by serving show cause notice in September 1989 and thereafter in September 1990. The authority allowed time to the respondent Nos. 1-4 as prayed in their reply to the 2nd show cause notice up to June 30, 1991. It was the contention of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that they prayed for extension of time up to December 31, 1994 by their letter dated October 14, 1993. In respect of this letter it has been stated by the writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 ie appellants in Civil Appeal Nos. 153 and 154 of 2000, that the said letter was not received by the Office of the Assistant Commissioner, Settlement, Ministry of Housing and Public Works. The respondent Nos. 1-4 have not taken step to establish that the letter dated 14-10-93 was received by the appellant No.2 in Civil Appeal Nos. 153 and 154 of 2000 i.e. by the Office of the Assistant Commissioner. That being the position the contention of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that they applied for further extension of time after expiry of the time earlier extended up to June 30, 1991 remained unestablished. The order of cancellation was issued on May 29, 1994 and till that date the respondent Nos. 1-4 did not take any step for making construction in the plot in question although they got the plan approved in August, 1990.

22. It has been contended by the learned Counsel for the respondent Nos. 1-4 that 2nd show cause notice was issued in September 1990 and to the same they replied and prayed for time and the authority extended time as prayed for up to June 30, 1991 and after the expiry of the same since no step was taken for cancellation of the allotment till 28-5-1994 and consequently the 2nd show cause notice as became stale the authority ought to have initiated fresh proceeding for cancellation of the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4. The submission that the earlier show cause notices became stale and fresh show cause notice ought to have been issued for cancellation of the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4, in our view, is not legally well founded, since lapse of some time in making the decision after initiation of proceeding therefor does in no way make the proceeding stale or requires initiation of fresh proceeding for the validity or legality of the decision made in respect of the matter in the light of the proceeding earlier was initiated and at no point of point of time was dropped.

23. Since there is no time-frame for taking decision within specified time after issuance of show cause notice to an allottee to show cause why his allotment should not be cancelled and as there is nothing in law that precludes from taking decision by the authority in the light of the show cause notice that was issued some time back, as such, it cannot be said the action of the authority as regard cancellation of the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 was made on stale material or proceeding. It may be mentioned in the period between the issuance of 2nd show cause notice and the date on which letter of cancellation was issued the respondent Nos. 1-4 did not take any step causing change in the state of the matter in the background whereof show cause notices for cancellation of allotment of the said respondents were issued. Moreover, from the file, which was placed before the High Court Division at the time of hearing of the writ petition by the appellant in Civil Appeal Nos. 153 and 154, it is seen that respondent Nos. 1-4 were served with the show cause notice lastly, on February 17, 1994. It has been contended on behalf of the respondents that the said notice was a manufactured one as because the same was not referred to in the affidavit-in-opposition nor was placed before the High Court Division at the time of hearing of the writ petition, but brought before the Court while review application was filed. Since earlier show cause notices, were received by the respondent Nos. 1-4 at their addresses as mentioned in the 1 st and 2nd show cause notice, and, as such, there was no reason for non-receiving of 3rd show cause notice addressed to the respondent Nos. 1-4 to their addressees in which earlier 2 show cause notices were served. It may be mentioned show cause notice dated 17-2-94 was sent through registered post. The contention of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that the 3rd show cause notice was a manufactured one is not well founded. So, in the background of the discussions made hereinabove it cannot be said that allotment of the said respondents was cancelled on the basis of the show cause notice which became stale.

24. The High Court Division while declaring the order of cancellation as not legal observed that there was no policy decision on 25-10-93 although in the allotment letter it was mentioned that allotment to the appellant Nos. 1-4 in appeal No. 155 of 2000 (writ-respondent Nos. 5-9) was made pursuant to the decision taken in the meeting of the allotment committee held on 25-10-93. In fact, in the said meeting policy decision was taken how quantity of land would be allotted to the much different categories of affected people and also the list of effected persons was prepared and decision was taken to make allotment in future to the listed affected persons and in the background of the decision of the said meeting while allotment was made to the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 (in Appeal No. 155 of 2000) being  the affected persons, from the list of the affected  persons so finalised in the meeting of 25-10-93, as such, in the allotment letter the said date was mentioned. The High Court Division took exception for allotting the plot in question to the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 on the view that the said plot in pursuance to the policy of the Government was meant for allotment to a group of 4 or 6 persons. As seen from the materials on record that the allotment committee in its meeting held on 28-2-94 upon taking into consideration prevalent situation took decision to allot to the affected person vacant land/residential cancelled plot/less developed plot available in the residential or rehabilitation area of Mohammadpur and Mirpur Housing Estate in the light of the decision taken in the meeting held on 25-10-93. Thus the High Court Division was in error in taking exception to the allotment made to respondents to get the allotment of the same.

25. The High Court Division while holding that in canceling the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 there was discrimination or, in other words, they were not treated at par with the other allottee i.e. allottees similar to the category of the respondents, in that their allotments were not cancelled. The High Court Division in this respect was very much in error in that materials on record show that allotment of other allottees similarly placed to the position of respondent Nos. 1-4 were cancelled. The High Court Division in view of the materials on record was also in error in holding that although in the letter of allotment it was mentioned decision for making allotment to the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 was taken on 25-10-93 but there was no such decision in the file placed before it by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2, ie appellants in Civil Appeal Nos. 153 and 154 of 2000, on being directed by the said Division in that it was in the allotment letter that allotment to the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 was made in pursuant to the decision taken in the meeting of the Allotment Committee held on 25-10-93 as because the said respondents were the affected persons and they were listed as affected persons in the list that was made final in the meeting held on 25-10-93. It may be mentioned decision was made on 29-5-1994 for making allotment to the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 and thereupon allotment letter was issued to the said respondents on June 6, 1994. The High Court Division. in declaring the order of cancellation to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the order of cancellation as  malafide and the same to have been passed without jurisdiction and the subsequent actions had no legal validity, held that the order of cancellation was not made on the basis of 2nd show cause notice. The file upon looking into which the High Court Division took the aforesaid view was also fi led before us and therefrom it is seen, in fact, decision was taken in the background of the show cause notices issued on three occasions. Although the respondent Nos. 1 to 4 tried to make out a case that they on October 14, 1993 filed an application addressed to Assistant Commissioner, Settlement, Directorate of Housing seeking extension of time up to December 31, 1994 and the same as was not replied to in the negative they were in genuine belief that time was extended to the date prayed for. The writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 denied addressing any such letter to the writ-respondent No. 2 and receiving of the same. The respondent Nos. 1-4 in the background of the said denial by the writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 has not placed any reliable material before the Court to establish the fact of receiving of the letter dated 14-10-93 by the authority.

<u>26. It has been contended by the appellants that High Court Division resorted to unsafe course as well as to a mode almost susceptible to falling into serious error or arriving at fallacious opinion or decision for ascertainment of similarity of the thumb impressions in the petition seeking allotment filed by the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 with the signatures appearing in the power of attorney executed by the said respondents in favour of respondent No.9 (in Appeal No. 155 of 2000) and thus the High Court Division erred in holding upon re-coursing to the said course or mode that signatures appearing in the petition seeking allotment and in the power of attorney were not similar or same. In our view High Court Division working on ascertainment of similarity of the thumb impressions by itself went for an hazardous enquiry risking the susceptibility of falling into error in reaching at the decision intended to and arrived at. It has been submitted on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that as the law very much empowers the Court to examine the signature including thumb impression by itself and to arrive at a decision, as such, no error has been committed by the High Court Division in comparing the thumb impressions appearing in the petition seeking allotment and in the power of attorney and thereupon in taking the view that the thumb impressions appearing in the said documents are not similar. The law permits the Court to compare signature of a person with his admitted signature, but still then superior Courts have sounded caution to avoid the course of comparing the signature thumb impression by the Court itself. Since by scientific process or method examination of signature, particularly thumb impression, has developed much and, as such, it is safe and sound to leave the matter of exam ination of signature including thumb impression as well as hand writing to the expert or to the person specialised in the examination of writing including thumb impression for avoiding possibility or probability of falling very much in error in arriving at an opinion by the Court upon resorting to comparison for ascertainment of similarity or dissimilarity of writing or thumb impression.</u>

27. It has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the respondents that in the letter of cancellation there is no mention that respondent Nos. 1-4's allotment was cancelled after serving show cause notice and, as such, the same was not a letter of cancellation as per law. In the letter of cancellation it has been mentioned that the lease of the respondent Nos. 1-4 has been cancelled pursuant to the provision of Clause 23 of the lease deed for violation of clause 3 of the leased deed. The undenied  position is that show cause notice, in all 3 (three), of which receipt of first and second admitted but disputed receipt of the 3rd show cause notice, and in all the show cause notices the respondent Nos. 1-4 were asked to show cause why their lease shall not be cancelled as per provision of clause 23 of the lease deed for violation of clause 3 of the lease deed. So, the submissions  so made is not well founded and merited. It has also been submitted on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that cancellation of their allotment lacked transparency as well as there was absence of fairness on the part of the authority in cancelling their allotment. As it appears contention of lack of transparency has been made in the background of the fact that the 2nd show cause notice was issued on September 2, 1990 and on receipt whereof respondents prayed for extension of time up to June 30, 1991 and thereafter allotment was cancelled on May 29, 1994 and the letter of cancellation was issued on that very date. In our view of being somewhat late in taking decision as well as in the communication of decision as regard cancellation of allotment for violation of condition in the lease deed, in all cases, as is the instant case, cannot be considered lacks transparency. In the facts and circumstances of each individual case matter of transparency in decision making and communication thereof is to be considered. The contention of absence of fairness in the background of the facts and circumstances of the matter is also not well merited. It was also the contention of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that as the authority did not reply to their prayer for extension of time till June 30, 1991 and thereafter, as no action was taken they were definite as they had got the plan approved from the RAJUK for making construction and had taken steps for making construction the authority has dropped the matter of cancellation of their allotment after lapse of so many years since September 1990, but suddenly, the authority initiated the proposal for cancellation in May 1994 and made the decision final for cancellation in the course of a day and the said hot-haste step clearly shows lack of fairness. It is seen from the file, which was produced before the High Court Division also, that 3 show cause notices were issued to the respondent Nos. 1-4 of which the said respondents disputed receipt of the last one, and also made the allegation that the same was manufactured for the purpose of filing review before the High Court Division. Since respondents' allotment has been cancelled after serving show cause notices and because of undisputed position no construction was made as required by the terms of lease deed within the specified time as well as within the extended period, absence of fairness can hardly be attributed to the action of cancellation of allotment of the respondents. The allegation of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that the fact of issuance of 3rd show cause notice is a manufactured one, in ourview, in the background of the materials placed by the authority, said allegation to have been made without any basis as well as the same has been made for allegation's sake and we are of the view that the allegation so made as against the issuance of the 3rd show cause notice is not well founded and the said allegation has been made to cover up the lapse on the part of respondents in making construction in the plot so cancelled as per provision of their lease deed. It is difficult to accept the contention of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that there was absence of fairness on the part of the authority in cancelling their allotment since issuance of the 2nd show cause notice and giving reply thereof by them there was lapse of sufficient period, which the respondents contended sufficiently long, and only in May 1994 proposal was initiated for cancellation and was made final in one day and thereupon the letter of cancellation was issued on that very date as, in our view, prompt decision in the background of the materials on record taken cannot be considered to have lacked fairness or transparency on the part of the authority since first, there is no time limit for taking decision for cancelling allotment like the one as of the respondent Nos. 1-4 within a specified time after issuance of the show cause notice, second, the authority was not precluded from taking decision in the light of the show cause notice issued to the respondent Nos. 1-4 after lapse of 3 years and a little more time. In view of our discussions made hereinabove we are of the view the action of the Writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 i.e. appellants in Civil Appeal Nos. 153 and 154 of 2000, in the matter of cancellation of the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 cannot be considered malafide or, in other words, it can also be not said that the action of the said authority lacked fairness and transparency and, as such, the High Court Division was in error in holding that the action of the Writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in cancelling the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 and making allotment of the said land to the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 was not legally valid and was made without lawful authority.

<u>28. In our view, High Court Division was in error in rejecting the application filed by the Writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 as well as by the Writ respondent Nos. 6-9 seeking review of its judgment since the Court is for dispensation of justice and in doing so the Court is competent to exercise its discretion in a case where party seeking review/reconsideration of the judgment of a particular Court upon placing material(s), which if would have been before the Court, the same would have not been the one the Court has made and, in such a situation, the Court for dispensation of justice is quite competent to recourse to a procedure, of which the same is the master, to advance the cause of justice as wel1 as on the ground of equity and good conscience. The procedure that the Court is quite competent to recourse may either be by review or some other suitable procedure. Moreover, provision of Article 102(2) or any other provision of the Constitution do not preclude the High Court Division either to reconsider or to review or to see the correctness or its judgment earlier made on furnishing of fresh material(s) by a party to the case which, according to him, if were before the Court the judgment would have been otherwise than the one made.</u>

29. In the background of the discussions made hereinbefore, we are of the view that the High Court Division is competent to resort to the procedure. either by the same review or reconsideration or re-examining of its judgment, of which it is the master, and thereupon would be competent to exercise "both its procedural and substantive discretions only on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience."

30. In the background of the discussions made hereinbefore we find merit in the appeals.

Accordingly, the appeals are allowed with costs in two appeals.

End.

caseno: Income Tax Reference Application No. 23 of 2000.
lawyer:
Altaf Hossain, Advocate------ For the Applicant. 
Mosharraf Hossain, Deputy Attorney-General with Kazi Waliul Islam, Assistant Attorney-General------ For the Respondent.
parties:
Eskayef Bangladesh Ltd ------ Appellant
vs
Commissioner of Taxes ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J: This reference application under section 160 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984, (hereinafter referred to as the Ordinance 1984) at the instance of the assessee has arisen out of the order dated 6-12-1999 passed by the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Division Bench No.3, Dhaka in Income Tax Appeal No. 558 of 1998-99 (assessment year 1993-94), allowing the appeal in part.

2. Short facts necessary for the disposal of the reference application are as follows:

3. The assessee-applicant, a private limited company, submitted its income tax return for the assessment year 1993-94. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, Intelligence & Investigation Circle-4, Dhaka, now Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, Circle-75, Zone-7, Dhaka (hereinafter referred to as the DCT) assessed the total income of the assessee at Taka 1,04,13,331 against the disclosed profit of Taka 23,27,338 during the said financial year.

4. The applicant being aggrieved by the assessment order of the DCT preferred an appeal being Income Tax Appeal No.72/Coy-20/Z-7/96-97 before the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeals) Taxes Appeal Zone-3, Dhaka (hereinafter referred to as the CT, Appeals) challenging the various disallowances and additions made by the DCT. The CT (Appeals) by his order dated 30-6-98 allowed the appeal in part by granting some reliefs to the assessee. The assessee applicant being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said first appellate order, preferred a second appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal. The Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Division Bench-3, Dhaka which heard the said appeal by the impugned order allowed the appeal in part deleting the disallowances made under the head (a) Automobile expenses, (b) Printing and Stationery expenses (c) Medical expenses, (d) Uniform and Clearing expenses, (e) Carriage outward and also reducing the order disallowances from other heads. It also deleted the disallowance from miscellaneous expenses under the broad head advertisement and promotional expenses. The Tribunal also reduced the disallowance of excess perquisite under section 30(e) of the Ordinance, 1984 from Taka 8,55,078 to Taka 3,49,539. The Tribunal also confirmed the disallowance of Taka 45,94,005 from the head "Sample expenses". Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order of the Tribunal the assessee has filed the instant reference application contending, inter alia, that the DCT, the CT (Appeals) and the Tribunal having found no defect in the entries in the books of accounts and the method of accounting, the books of accounts of the Company should have been accepted. The DCT, the CT (Appeals) and the Tribunal failed to consider that the account of the assessee has been duly audited by a Chartered Accountant in compliance with the provisions of section 35 of the Ordinance 1984 and duly certified the accounts are true and correct. The following questions have been formulated in this reference for our answer:

"(i) Whether the accounts duly audited by a chartered accountant in compliance with the provision of section 35 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 be rejected when the chartered accountant had certified the petitioner's accounts to be true and correct as per statute?

(ii) Whether the accounts duly audited and certified by the Chartered Accountant under statute as per Companies Act 1913, and Chartered Accountant Ordinance, 1973 is liable to be rejected?

(iii) Whether the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes can disallow carrying cost, printing material cost, packing cost and VAT relating to the sample in addition to the value of sample under rule 65 (c) of ITO, 1984 ?

(iv) Whether the Tribunal was right in holding that the allowances and benefit paid to the employees in case and as per agreement attracts the provisions of section 30(e) of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984?

(v) Whether the Tribunal can tax (sic) the excess perquisites without ascertaining the actual benefits given to each individual employee as defined in section 30(e) of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984?"

5. No affidavit-in-reply has been filed by the respondent.

6. Mr Altaf Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the applicant, strenuously argues that section 35 of the Ordinance, 1984 has made it mandatory upon the DCT to accept the accounts if it is found that the assessee regularly maintains the accounts under a system either it be mercantile or other system. He further submits that the assessing officer could ignore the audited accounts only when he could point out specific defect in it; but in the instant case no such defect having been pointed out he was legally obliged to accept the audited accounts. Mr Altaf Hossain further submits that the Chartered Accountant having been appointed under the Companies Act to examine the applicant's books of accounts and also under the provisions of the Ordinance, 1984, and if after examining the books of accounts having certified that it reflects a clear picture of the state of affairs of the company, both the DCT and the Appellate Tribunal acted illegally in not accepting the same as a whole. Mr Altaf Hossain lastly submits that the Appellate Tribunal committed error of law in not allowing the entire amount of perquisites paid to the employees of the company, and, as such, the questions formulated in the reference applications be answered in the negative and in favour of the assessee. In support of his submissions, Mr Altaf Hossain has referred to many cases being the case of Titas Gas Transmissions and Distribution Co Lid vs Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 2000 BTD 27 = 53 DLR 209; Sagorika and Co (Pvt) vs Commissioner of Taxes reported in 1999 BTD 87 = 52 DLR 484: Mohd Engineering Industries Ltd vs Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 2000 BTD 29 = 54 DLR 132; Hotel Samrat vs Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 2000 BTD 50; Abdul Monem Limited vs Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 2001 BTD 77 = 6 BLC 574; No.1 0 Biri Company Limited vs Commissioner of Taxes, Chiuagong, reported in 2001 BTD 157 = 6 BLC 540; Friends Corporation Ltd vs Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 1975 BTD 221 = 27 DLR 566; CIT, API vs Warmer Hindustan Ltd. reported in ITR, 24, 145, CIT West Bengal-II vs Kanan Devan Hills Product Company Ltd reported in ITR, 119, 431; CIT vs Tecalmit (Hind) Ltd reported in ITR, 137,285; United Commercial Bank Ltd vs Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 2002 BTD 73; Pfizer Laboratories (Bangladesh) Ltd vs Commissioner of Taxes, reported in 2002 BTD 57 = 9 BLC 674; Commissioner of Taxes vs Mysore Commercial Union Ltd reported in ITR. 126. 340 and Subramanian ITO and another vs Siemens India Ltd. and another, reported in ITR 156,11.

7. Mr Mosharraf Hossain Khan, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing along with Mr Kazi Waliul Islam, the learned Assistant Attorney. General on behalf of the respondent, on the other hand, submits that although the PCT disallowed the expenditure on some heads of the accounts, yet the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeals) as well as the Appellate Tribunal after considering the materials on record almost gave full relief to the assessee and the disallowances which have been affirmed by the Tribunal were done rightly as the assessee could not produce relevant vouchers in respect of its said heads of expenditure. He further submits that the questions formulated in the reference applications are purely questions of fact which cannot be reopened by this court in exercising jurisdiction under section 160 of the Ordinance, 1984 and, as such, the questions be answered in the affirmative.

<u>8. So far as the submission of Mr Altaf Hossain that section 35 of the Ordinance, 1984 has made it mandatory upon the DCT to accept the audited accounts if the same is found to have been maintained in a particular method is concerned, we are of the view that merely because a particular method of accounting was not followed and was audited by a chartered accountant firm the same could not be said to be sacrosanct when the expenditures were not verifiable. From the order of the DCT, it is clear that he specified the heads of expenditure which were not verifiable and accordingly, he disallowed some expenses. Thus, defects in the account of the assessee having been clearly pointed out in the assessment order of the DCT, he as well as the Tribunal did not commit any illegality in not accepting the audited account as a whole. We have also perused the decision cited by Mr Altaf Hossain, as mentioned hereinbefore; we do not dispute the proposition of law as enunciated in the cited cases that if the assessee follows a particular method of accounts regularly and unless any defect in the accounts is specifically pointed out by the assessing authority he is to accept the accounting, The accounts maintained by the assessee having not been totally verifiable, that is, supported by vouchers as pointed out by the DCT, is definitely a defect and, therefore, we do not find any substance in the submission of Mr Altaf Hossain as to the mandate of law to accept an audited account even when the expenditures are not verifiable. It is to be noted that though some of the expenses were not verifiable as specifically pointed out by the DCT, yet the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeals) after considering the materials on record reduced the amount of disallowances and also deleted some of the disallowances altogether which were made by the DCT. The Taxes Appellate Tribunal on consideration of the materials on record maintained the said disallowances. Thus, we do not see any reasons on the part of the assessee to be aggrieved by the impugned order. Moreso, these are all questions of fact which cannot be re-opened in exercising jurisdiction under section 160 of the Ordinance, 1984. However, in paragraph 12 of the reference application, it has been specifically stated that a sum of Taka 7,36,007.94 was paid as VAT under the head of the expenditure on distribution of free sample and this assertion has not been denied by the Department by filing any affidavit-in-reply. But none of the authorities namely, the DCT, the 1st appellate authority and the Appellate Tribunal considered this amount of VAT paid by the assessee while considering the disallowances on account of sample expenses. We are of the view that the amount of VAT paid to the government cannot form part of the disallowance and that be added to the expenditure of the assessee under the said head, Accordingly, we direct the DCT to add the amount of Taka 7,36,007.94 paid as VAT by the assessee as expenditure on account of sample expenses and revise the assessment of income accordingly.</u>

9. So far as the perquisites are concerned, it appears that the Tribunal on consideration of the detailed statements of salary and allowances furnished by the Authorised Representative found that excess perquisites paid to the employees were to the tune of Taka 3,49,539 and accordingly, it vacated the impugned order in that respect and reduced the disallowance to Taka 3,49,539.

10. For the discussions made above, question Nos. (i)(ii) and (iv) are answered in the affirmative and against the assessee and question No. (iii), so far as it relates to VAT, is answered in the negative and against the Department but other costs mentioned in the said question are answered in the affirmative.

No order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Md Zahirul Haque Zahir with AKM Enayet Hossain and KM Jabir; Advocates------ For the Petitioner. 
Md Badruddoza, Advocate------ For Respondent No, 1.
parties:
Anwara Begum ------ Petitioner
vs
Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Tariq-ul-Hakim J: This Rule Nisi has been issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned decision dated 24-10-2001 (Annexure-F to the Writ Petition) passed by the First Court of Settlement, Bangladesh Abandoned Buildings, Segunbagicha, Dhaka in Case No. 2 of 2000 (Kha 36, Second Colon/Mirpur) dismissing the case and thereby refusing to exclude House No. 29-A/A Second Colony/Mirpur), Dhaka (Kha 36) from the list of Abandoned Buildings as published in the Ka list dated 28-4-1986 should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. It has been stated that House No. 29-A/A Second Colony/Mirpur), Dhaka (Kha 36) measuring an area of 5 kathas of land along with pucca structures was given allotment to one Md Younus Ali, son of late Md Yusuf Ali of the same address by registered agreement dated 29-7-1963 followed by possession and thereby the said Md Younus Ali became the owner of the house in question, The said Md Younus Ali while possessing the property had obtained loan for construction of his house with prior permission of the concerned authority and mortgaged the said property as security against the loan to the House Building Finance Corporation by registered mortgage deed dated 23-12-1965. It is further stated that while the said Md Younus Ali had been in possession in the aforesaid land measuring an area of 5 kathas, he transferred the same along with pucca structures to the petitioner by registered kabala dated 3-1-1977 after obtaining due permission from the then Authorised Officer i.e. the Assistant Commissioner of Settlement, Housing and Public Works Town Improvement, Dhaka vide his Memo No. 1603 dated 13-7-1976 on receipt of the consideration of Taka 19,500. The petitioner after purchasing the aforesaid property possessed the same and has been exercising her own right, title and interest openly and thereafter obtained permission for mutating her name with the office of the Assistant Commissioner, Settlement, Dhaka and duly mutated the same vide No. 3704 dated 9-5-1979 and also mutated her name with the CO Revenue as well as Dhaka Municipal Corporation and has been paying rent to the said authorities regularly. The petitioner also took gas, water and electricity connection in her name in the said property and has been duly paying the requisite charges. It is further stated that the house in question was never treated or listed as Abandoned Property and the sameal through remained in possession of the petitioner and said Md Younus Ali supervised, managed and occupied the same during the past years including 'the relevant time i.e. from 25th March, 1971 to 28th February, 1912 and therefore the property does not answer the description of Abandoned Property. It is further stated that the Government never took over possession of the house in question at any point of time, It is further stated that the Government promulgated the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985) making provisions for publishing a list of the abandoned buildings and the petitioner, to her utter surpris, found that the house in question has been included in the Kha list at serial No. 36 published in the Gazette dated 28-4-1986. Thereafter, the petitioner as per provisions of the said Ordinance filed an application before the Court of Settlement praying for exclusion of the property in question from the 'Kha' list of the Abandoned Buildings and the said application was registered as Case No. 2 of 2000 (Kha-36, Second Colony/Mirpur).

3. The Government did not file any written objection against the said application but contested the said case during hearing by making verbal submissions contending, inter alia. that the land comprising an area of 5 kathas was given lease to a refugee Md Younus Ali and that he left this country  without making any transfer and his whereabouts were not known and, as such, the Government rightly enlisted the property as Abandoned Buildings under the provision of President's Order 16 of 1972. The Court of Settlement on conclusion of the hearing of the case by its judgment and order dated 24-10-2001 dismissed the case and thereby refused to exclude, the aforesaid property from the Ka list of Abandoned Buildings on the ground that the petitioner has not been able to prove that the said property is not an abandoned property within the meaning of PO 16 of 1972. The Court of Settlement further held that the signature of the vendor Md Younus Ali does not match the signature of the said person as apparent on the mortgage deed. The Court of Settlement also agreed with the submissions of the Government side that the sale permission and other documents obtained from the Ministry of Housing and Settlement were forged and created by the petitioner with the help of unscrupulous and dishonest officers.

4. Being aggrieved, the petitioner has come to this Court and obtained the present Rule along with an interim order of stay of the operation of the impugned order passed by the First Court of Settlement.

5. The respondent No.1, Ministry of Housing and Public Works, is contesting this Rule by filing Affidavit-in-Opposition, wherein it has been stated that the petitioner with the help of some corrupt officers of the concerned Department obtained sale permission and got the sale deed registered in her favour on 2-1-1977 by getting someone to impersonate Md Younus AIi since the said Md Younus Ali, the original allottee of the case land, left the said house during the War of Liberation. It is further alleged that the petitioner thereafter with the help of same corrupt officers managed to mutate her name in the office of the Housing and Settlement. It is further alleged that during the war of liberation the Non-Bengali allottees of the case house left the house uncared for and after the war of liberation the whereabouts of the original allottees were not known and hence the case house came under the mischief of PO 16 of 1972 and was duly published in the official Gazette as per provisions of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. The Court of Settlement in case No. 2 of 2000 examined the petitioner and all her papers and documents and compared the signature of the Non Bengali original allottee Md Younus Ali apparent in the mortgage deed of the House Building Finance Corporation and found that it does not tally with the signature in the sale deed dated 3-1-1977 in favour of the petitioner. It is further stated that the petitioner failed to prove the presence of Md Younus Ali, original allot tee of the case house, in Bangladesh during the period 26th March, 1971 to 3rd January, 1977 and, as such, the Court of Settlement lawfully and rightly dismissed the case of the petitioner and that the petitioner has no cause to be aggrieved and that the grounds taken in the Writ Petition not being tenable in law, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

6. Mr Zahirul Haque Zahir, the learned Advocate along with Mr AKM Enayet Hossain and Mr KM Jaber, the learned Advocates, appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that Md Younus Ali, original allottee, executed and registered a sale deed in favour of the petitioner on 3-1-1977 after obtaining permission at the time when the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance. 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985) was not even promulgated and the Court of Settlement acted illegally and arbitrarily in disbelieving the registered deed without considering that under the law there is a presumption of genuineness of a registered document. The learned Advocate further submits that the Government failed to produce a scrap of paper to show that the Government or its agent has been in possession of the case house during the relevant time or thereafter. The learned Advocate also, submits that no notice as contemplated under section 7 of the PO 16 of 1972 and sections 4 and 5 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 was served upon the petitioner requiring her to surrender possession of the property and, as such, the publication of the said property in the list of the Abandoned Buildings is illegal and the Court of Settlement not having addressed this point the impugned order is not sustainable in law. In this connection, the learned Advocate relies upon a number of decisions those reported in 53 DLR (AD) 55, 4 MLR (AD) 140, 56 DLR (AD) 1 as well as 57 DLR 332. The learned Advocate further submits that the possession of the property in question was never taken by the Government although the same was listed under Ka list of the Abandoned Buildings and this being an admitted fact, no mention of the matter was made by the Court of Settlement which prejudiced the petitioner and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the Court of Settlement is not tenable in law. In this respect, the learned Advocate relies upon the decision reported in 5 BLC (AD) 25.

7. As against this, Mr Md Badruddoza, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the Government, submits that the Court of Settlement is the only authority to decide whether a property is abandoned property or not and in the instant case, by the impugned judgment and order the Court of Settlement having decided that the property in question is an abandoned property due to the inability of the petitioner to prove otherwise, calls for no interference by this Court. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that the onus is upon the petitioner to prove that the original allottee/owner was in Bangladesh at the relevant time and that the property is not an abandoned property and, in the instant case the petitioner failed to prove the same before the Court of Settlement and, as such, the impugned order calls for no interference by this Court. The learned Deputy Attorney- General further submits that since the petitioner failed to prove that the original owner of the property was not in Bangladesh it is immaterial whether the same was in the Ka list or Kha list and whether the possession of the same was with the Government or not. In this connection, he relies upon the decisions reported in 3 BLC (AD) 42 and 48 DLR (AD) 10. The learned Deputy Attorney- General further submits that the service of notice is not mandatory even if the property is listed as an abandoned property provided the Government does not wish to take over possession thereof and in this case non service of notice cannot be said to have caused any illegality enlisting the property as an abandoned property.

8. Heard the learned Advocates, perused the Writ Petition, Supplementary Affidavit, Affidavit-in- Opposition and their annexures and the impugned judgment and order of the Court of Settlement.

9. It has been alleged that the petitioner purchased the aforesaid property from one Md Younus Ali by registered kabala deed dated 3-1-1977 and has been residing therein after mutating her name with the concerned authorities including the Housing and Settlement Office. Her predecessor-in- interest was one Md Younus Ali who was the original allottee of the said land. The said property was listed as an abandoned property in the Ka list of the Abandoned Buildings as published on 28-4-1986 by the Ministry of Housing and Public Works. Section 5(1 )(a) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 authorises the Government to publish in the official Gazette the list of the buildings, the possession of which was taken over as an abandoned property under the provision of PO 16 of 1972. The Ordinance had made provision in section 5(1) that any abandoned property in the possession of the Government will be enlisted in a list to be maintained under section 5(1)a) of the Ordinance, 1985 which is termed as Ka list and those not in possession of the Government but notice for surrendering them has been issued are to be maintained under section 5(b) of the Ordinance, 1985 which would be treated as Kha list.

Section 5 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions), Ordinance, 1985 is as follows:

"5. Publication of lists of buildings. (1) The Government shall, after the [commencement of this Ordinance and before the [31st day of December, 1988] publish, from time to time, in the official Gazette], (a) lists of buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property under the President's Order; (b) [lists of buildings in respect of which notices for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under the said Order have been issued: Provided that.................. 	.

(b) .....................................................................................................................

The property, in the instant case, has been listed in the Ka list of the Abandoned Buildings indicating that the Government is in possession of the same although it has been admitted that the Government has never been in possession of the same through a tenant or otherwise.

10. The Gazette Notification dated 23rd September. 1986 reads as follows:

ঢাকা, ২৩ শে সেপ্টেমবর, ১৯৮৬ নং এস,আর,ও ৩৬৪-এল/৮৬-১৯৮৫ সনের পরিত্যক্ত ইমারত (সম্পূরক বিধান) অধ্যাদেশ (১৯৮৫ সনের ৫৪ নং অধ্যাদেশ) পত্র ৫(১) (ক) ধারা অনুযায়ী এবং অত্র মন্ত্রণালয়ের বিজ্ঞপ্তি নং এস,আর,ও ১৪১-এল/৮৬ শাখা-৯/১ এম-৭২/৮৫/৪১৬, তারিখ ২৮ শে এপ্রিল ১৯৮৬ বতিল ক্রমে সরকার ১৯৭২ সনের বাংলাদেশ পরিত্যক্ত সম্পত্তি (নিয়ন্ত্রণ, ব্যবস্থাপনা ও হস্তান্তর) আদেশ (১৯৭২ সনের রাষ্টপতির ১৬নং আদেশ) এর অধীনে পরিত্যক্ত সম্পত্তি হিসেবে দখল নেওয়া হইয়াছে এমন সমস্ত ইমারতের তালিকা এতদসংগে প্রকাশ করিতেছেন।

11. The Court of Settlement came to the finding that the petitioner was not able to prove that the property was not abandoned property on the ground that the petitioner was unable to prove that his vendor was in Bangladesh at the relevant time. It was also of the view that the signature of the vendor as given on the sale deed did not match the signature of the original owner on the mortgage deed. The Court of Settlement, however, did not make any finding as to how the said property was in the Ka list of the Abandoned. Buildings even though the government was not in its possession.

12. It is stated in section 7(3) of the PO 16 of 1972 that where a person in possession of any abandoned property fails to surrender such property the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate shall serve a notice on him in the prescribed manner requiring him to surrender possession of the property, within seven days of the service of notice, to the person mentioned in the notice or to show cause against such surrender within the said period and, if he fails to do so, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate shall take possession of the property in such manner as may be prescribed. Although under section 5(1)(a) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 the Government is to publish in the official Gazette a list of buildings which are claimed as abandoned property under PO 16 of 1972, the minimum the Government must show is that the property has at some point of time been taken possession of as an abandoned property. The process of service of notice of surrender upon the occupants to take over possession upon enquiry or investigation forming opinion whether the property is an abandoned property or not and, in the final stage, the formation of opinion for taking over possession of the property must be exhausted before a property can be listed in the official Gazette under Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. This has been the consistent view in a number of decisions of this court including the case of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and others vs Helaluddin Ahmed reported in 4 MLR (AD) 140 and the case of Begum Lutfunnessa vs Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and others reported in 42 DLR (AD) 86. In the instant case, it is admitted that no notice was served upon the petitioner and the learned Deputy Attorney-General wants to say that no such notice is required for enlisting the property as an abandoned property unless the Government wants to take over actual possession. This appears to be a misconception since Gazette Notification as well as the contemplation of section 5 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 as well as Article 7 of the PO 16 of 1972 requires service of notice before categorising property as an abandoned property, and particularly before listing it under Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 under the Ka list. In the instant case, the Government neither took over possession of the said property from the petitioner by evicting them nor served notice on them under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972. The facts of this case appear to be similar to that of the case of Amir Hossain vs Government of' Bangladesh reported in 57 DLR 332 wherein it has been held that-

"The Court of Settlement had also fallen in error in failing to consider the legal position that the Government was not competent to take over possession and enlist the said house property in the Ka list under section 5(1)(a) of the Ordinance No.LIV of 1985 without issuing any notice under section 4 of the said Ordinance 1985 asking the petitioner to surrender possession of the said house.

13. In that case also it has been said that the respondents in their. Affidavit-in-Opposition has not stated anything about taking over of possession of the said house property at any time between 28-2-70 and the date of inclusion of the same in the Ka list. The Government was under legal obligation to establish that it formed an opinion that the said house was lying vacant and uncared for as its  owners were not present in Bangladesh from before 28-2-1972 and it took it over as an abandoned property and subsequently, the Government being in possession enlisted the said house in the Ka list. But the Government has failed to do so. Mere saying that whereabouts of the original lessee is unknown or that they were not present in Bangladesh from 28-2-1972 will not absolve the Government in law for not complying with other appropriate steps as required, particularly service of notice under Article 7(2) and (3) of the President's Order 16 of 1972 and under sections 4 and 5(1)(a) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. In the case of Bangladesh vs Md Shahjahan reported in 5 BLC (AD) 25, the High Court Division on consideration of the material facts found that since the possession of the building was not taken over by the Government but the said matter received no consideration by the Court of Settlement, it prejudiced the respondent. In the instant case therefore, the Court of Settlement not having considered the fact that possession of the building was never taken over by the Government prior to listing the said property in the 'Ka' list as an abandoned property appears to have prejudiced the petitioner.

14. In the case of Bangladesh vs Amela Khatun and others reported in 53 DLR (AD) 55, it has been stated that since no notice as contemplated under section 5(1)(a) of the Ordinance was issued to the respondents or any other person inclusion of disputed property in the Ka list of the abandoned buildings is without lawful authority.

15. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has drawn our attention to the case of Hazerullah and another vs Chairman, 1st Court of Settlement and another reported in 3 BLC (AD) 42 wherein it has been held that

"the house in question having not been in the possession of the Government, section 5 of the Ordinance did not authorise the Government to enlist the same in the Ka list. This contention will stand only when the claimant can prove that the disputed building was not an abandoned property"

16. It was further held that on consideration or the materials on record the Court or Settlement has held that the original lessee and his heirs at the relevant time were not traceable in Bangladesh and that the appellants have unauthorisedly been occupying the property in question since 28-2-72 which having been affirmed by the High Court Division, it is immaterial, so far as the appellants are concerned, whether the disputed property was published in the "Ka" list or "Kha" list. Although in the said decision it has been stated that a person claiming that a particular property is not abandoned property, is required to prove the same in the Court of Settlement and not being able to do so, it will be immaterial whether the said property is published in the Ka or Kha list, in our opinion, the aforesaid decision is confined to its particular facts and will not be applicable in the instant case, particularly in view of the recent decisions of the Appellate Division in the ease of Bangladesh vs Rehana Kamal and others reported in 56 DLR (AD) 1 and Bangladesh vs Amela Khatun and others reported in 53 DLR (AD) 55. In the said decision no reference has been made as to whether notice as contemplated under section 7 of the Presidents Order No. 16 of 1972 and under sections 4 and 5(1)(a) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 was served upon the petitioner or not. Although the onus lies upon the petitioner to prove that at the relevant time the property was not an abandoned property, nevertheless, the Government cannot absolve its laches of not serving  appropriate notice as contemplated under the aforesaid law, by saying that the petitioner was unable to prove that the property was not an abandoned property and the petitioner made her best efforts to discharge her onus cast on her to prove that the property is not an abandoned property.

17. In the case of Bangladesh vs Rehana Kamal and others reported in 56 DLR (AD) 1, it has been held as follows:

"Similarly, no notice which is a mandatory requirement under section 5(b) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, was served on the person in possession of the abandoned building requiring him to surrender possession so as to make the listing of the property as abandoned in schedule 'Ka' and publication in the Gazette in respect of which the notice has not been issued making the listing illegal. Similarly, although the property has been listed in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned buildings, admittedly no possession of the building has been taken treating the same as abandoned property, Admittedly, the American Embassy as the tenant of the owner had' been in possession, but no attempt was taken by the Government to recover possession of the case building so as to entitle the authority to list the same in Ka list rendering the said listing per se illegal".

18. The learned Deputy Attorney-General's submission that the High Court Division cannot sit as a Court of Appeal, as was held in the case of Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary Ministry of Works vs Md Jalil and others, reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10, is no doubt true but the fact is, that the High Court Division always retains its jurisdiction to intervene in, the Court of Settlement in passing its judgment does not take into account- the facts causing prejudice to the parties in dispute. It is clearly stated even in the said decision that the High Court Division although not a court of appeal it can interfere with the findings of a tribunal of fact under its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102, if it can be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence/facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it had acted malafide or in violation of any of the principles of natural justice. Thus in our opinion the Court of Settlement appears to have approached this matter wrongly. As stated in the case of Shamsul Haque vs Court of Settlement and others reported in 49 DLR 469 that

"the lease deed together with other documents showing the continuity of petitioner's possession and the fail lire of the Government to show any basis of the owner of the property in dispute leaving the country and acquiring citizenship of other country go to show the title of the petitioner in the property and renders its enlistment in the Ka list denude of any legal authority"

<u>19. Thus section 7(1)(3) of the, Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 requires the Government to take over possession of Abandoned Property not in possession of any person and to issue notice of surrender of possession of other properties in possession of any person. Section 5(1)(a)(b) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. LlV of 1985) requires the Government to make two types of lists of abandoned properties. One list known as Ka list is to consist of Abandoned Properties of which possession has been taken over by the Government and another list known as Kba list, is to consist of abandoned properties of which possession has not been taken over by the Government but notice to hand over possession has been issued. Both lists are to be published in the official Gazette. In view of the decisions of this Court and the Appellate Division cited above as well as the aforesaid statutory provisions for an abandoned property to be listed in the Ka list pursuant to section 5 of the Ordiriance No. LlV of 1985 the Government must be in possession of the same. For a property in the Kha list notice to surrender must have been issued. The submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General that service of notice is not mandatory if the Government does not wish to take over possession of an Abandoned Property is misconceived. In the instant case, it is admitted that the Government never took possession of the case property or even served a notice to surrender its possession, therefore, its listing as an abandoned property, either in Ka or Kha list, cannot be sustained in law.</u>

<u>20. It may be mentioned here that the petitioner in the Court of Settlement submitted a series of papers and documents from various Government offices in support of her possession of the property but the Court of Settlement outright rejected the same as being the product of collusion with some dishonest officers of the Ministry of Housing and Settlement. Such outright rejection without any cogent reasons and subsequent action by the concerned Department against the alleged corrupt officers cannot be a ground for totally disregarding such papers and documents. Although it is accepted that in certain cases documents are forged and manufactured to file fictitious suit but if weight is to be given to such claim, then the Government must act its part by making enquiry to find the responsible persons and taking appropriate action against them for such dishonesty to avoid the recurrence of such incident. Merely saying that they are spurious documents given by dishonest officers is not sufficient.</u>

21. In the facts and circumstances discussed above, we are of the opinion that the Court of Settlement acted without lawful authority in dismissing the petitioner's case. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order dated 24-10-2001 (Annexure F to the Writ Petition) passed by the First Court of Settlement, Bangladesh Abandoned Buildings, Segunbagicha, Dhaka in Case No.2 of 2000 (Kha 36, Second Colony/Mirpur) is declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

The respondents are directed to exclude House No. 29-A/A Second Colony/Mirpur), Dhaka (Kha 36) from the list of Abandoned Buildings as published in Ka list dated 28-4-1986 within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of this order.

End.

lawyer:
Khan Saifur Rahman, Senior Advocate, instructed by ASM Khalequzzaman, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Appellants, 
Rafique-ul-Huq, Senior Advocate, Ahsanul Karim, Advocate with him instructed by Md Wahidullah, Advocate-on-Record ------- For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Anti- Corruption Commission and others ------- Appellant. (In both the cases)
Vs.
Mahmud Hossain and others ------- Respondents (In both the cases)
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 13th day of December, 2007 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 10844 and 10845 of 2007).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin CJ: I have read the judgments by my brothers Mohammad Fazlul Karim, J and Md Joynul Abedin, J. I agree with the result of the appeals reached by my brother Md Joynul Abedin, J. But my, approach to the point of law involved in the appeals is somewhat, different from that of my brother Md Joynul Abedin, In the totality of the facts of the case I am of the view the writ petitioner was neither in abscondence nor a fugitive while moving the writ petition, since he was, in any respect, not fleeing or running away from the law or the Court, or avoiding process of the Court.

2. It was contended from the side of the appellants that in the first information report offence alleged against the writ petitioner is a cognizable one and, as such, being liable to be taken into custody or of being apprehended by the police or any other competent body or authority; the writ petition could only be filed on surrendering before the appropriate Court and having had not done so the writ petition ought not to have been entertained by the High Court Division, or, in other words, the writ petition was incompetent one.

3. The sum total of the contention of the appellants, as it appears to me, is that the writ petitioner being an accused of alleged cognizable offence having of his own had not appeared before the Court and obtained bail prior to the filing of the writ petition he was a fugitive from the law, or a person who has been fleeing away from the Court, or, in other words, the writ petitioner is in abscondence.

<u>4. There is no material on the record to show that in the backdrop of the filing of the first information report alleging alleged cognizable offence against the writ petitioner any process from the Court has been issued either directing the writ petitioner to appear before the Court or directing the law enforcing agency to take the writ petitioner into its custody and to produce him before the Court. No material has also been brought on record from the side of the appellants to show that after lodging of the first information report alleging commission of alleged cognizable offence by the writ petitioner police looked for him but did not find him as to avoid apprehension by the law enforcing agency the writ petitioner has left his residence where he stays or, in other words, left the address as given in the first information report and thereon hiding. There is no such situation in the instant appeals.</u>

<u>5. Before arriving at the decision/conclusion as to whether a person whose appearance before the Court in compliance of the process is wanted in connection with an offence of which Court has taken cognizance or that law enforcing agency is looking for or taking steps for apprehension of a person on lodging of first information report alleging alleged cognizable offence is fugitive from law or is in abscondence, the Court or that the law enforcing agency would be required to exhaust the process as in the Code of Criminal Procedure to make known such person that his appearance is wanted before the Court or that the law enforcing agency is looking for his apprehension on the lodging of first information report alleging cognizable offence. In the absence of exhaustion of the procedure relating to apprehension of a person by the law enforcing agency either at its level or in compliance of the process of the Court or that without exhaustion of the procedure by public notification/publication of notice in the newspaper, the person whose presence is wanted before the Court in compliance of the process of the Court or that law enforcing agency is looking for apprehension in connection with a cognizable offence or in execution of the process from the Court, it would not be legally well founded to consider such person fugitive from Court or law, or that in abscondence.</u>

6. In the background of the discussion I am of the view the writ petitioner was not a fugitive while moving the High Court Division under Article 102(2) of the Constitution.

<u>7.
