It is pertinent and would not be out of context to mention that when an alleged accused or a convict by a duly constituted Court or a Court of competent jurisdiction gets himself temporarily released from custody on execution of bail bond, the law enjoins upon him to be present before the Court on the date fixed for his presence and that to keep himself at his level aware of up-to-date position/ stage of the proceeding and to take step(s) required by the law in the proceeding wherein he has obtained his temporary release or, in other words, bail. Default on his part in the aforementioned situation/stage would make him a fugitive from law/ Court and that would disentitle him from complaining that proceeding against him has been concluded in his absence. Same would also be the case in respect of an alleged accused or convict for whose appearance before the Court the procedure in the Code of Criminal Procedure has been exhausted, but he remained absent from the Court without plausible/legally tenable excuse.</u>

Md Fazlul Karim J : These two appeals, by leave, are directed against the judgment and order dated 13-12-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 10844 of 2007 and 10845 of 2007 issuing Rule Nisi staying further proceeding in ACC GR Case Nos. 67 of 2007 and 68 of 2007 corresponding to Shahbag Police Station Case No. 50 dated 25-7-2007 and Dhanmondi Police Station Case No. 79 dated 25-7-2007 now pending in the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka.

8. The common facts of the cases, in short, are that the respondent is an Executive Director and a shareholder of Aegis Textile Mills Limited, a Private Limited Company, incorporated under the laws of Bangladesh having its place of business at 9/A, Motijheel C/A Dhaka and is alleged to have committed acts of corruption along with other accused. The said respondent by filing the aforesaid writ petitions has challenged the initiation and continuation of the proceedings of the ACC GR Case Nos. 67 and 68 of 2007 arising out of Shahbag Police Station Case No. 50 dated 25-7-2007 and Dhanmondi Police Station Case No. 79 dated 25-7- 2007 under sections 161 and 109 of the Penal «ode read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and Rule 15 of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 now pending in the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. Since the offences alleged against the respondent are schedule offences under the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 the cases initiated against the respondent were required to be filed after due inquiry and investigation as contemplated under section 17(Kha) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. But the Commission has initiated these two cases without conducting any investigation in clear violation of section 17(Kha) of the said Act. Further, since the offence mentioned in the said two cases are allegedly committed before the Emergency Power Rules came into existence, the application of the said Rules in these two cases is unwarranted and not tenable in law. Hence the, initiation and continuation of the proceedings in these two cases under the Emergency Power Rules are unauthorised and without lawful authority.

9. In this backdrop of the case, the High Court Division having heard the writ petitions, issued Rule Nisi and stayed further proceedings in ACC GR Case Nos. 67 and 68 of 2007 by the judgment and order dated 13-12-2007. Being dissatisfied with the said judgment and order of the high Court Division the petitioners have filed the above petitions for leave to appeal.

10. Leave was granted to consider the submission of the learned advocate for the petitioners that since the writ petitions are silent about the stage of the proceedings in the Court below and since the offences disclosed in the aforesaid two first information reports are cognizable under the provisions of section 28(Ka) of the Anti Corruption Commission Act, 2004, the filing of the writ petitions as well as the issuance of the Rule thereon lacked legal sanction and are therefore not tenable in law. The learned Counsel further submits that since the respondent being a named accused in the first information report has not surrendered in the Court and is a fugitive from justice, the writ petitions filed by him were not entertainable and the Rule issued therein by the High Court Division is not sustainable in law and in this view of the matter the impugned judgment and order issuing Rule and staying the proceedings in the aforesaid two cases are illegal and without jurisdiction.

11. Mr Khan Saifur Rahman learned Counsel appearing for the Appellants submitted that the writ petitions are silent about the stage of the proceedings in the Court below and since the offences disclosed in the aforesaid two first information reports are cognizable under the provisions of section 28 Ka of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, the filing of the writ petitions as well as the issuance of the Rule thereon lacked legal sanction and are therefore not tenable in law; that the respondent being a named accused in the first information report has not surrendered in the Court and is a fugitive from justice, the Writ Petitions filed by him were not entertainable and the Rule issued therein by the High Court Division is not sustainable in law and in this view of the matter the impugned judgment and order issuing Rule and staying the proceedings in the aforesaid two cases are illegal and without jurisdiction.

<u>12. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, learned Counsel appearing for the respondent No. 1 submits that the High Court Division issued Rule Nisi and stayed further proceedings as complained of because the alleged offence occurred during the period of 20-2-2000 and 23-2-2000 which is before the promulgation of emergency and does not come within the purview of Emergency Ordinance, 2007 and the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 and' the learned Judges of the High Court Division considering the facts in issue and law involved in the case, rightly and lawfully issued Rule Nisi in the writ petition invoking original jurisdiction and stayed further proceedings of the case as complained of. The learned Counsel further submitted that under Rule 24 of the ACC Rules, it is mandatory provision that enquiry (অনুসন্ধান) and investigation (তদন্ত) must be conducted by two different officers of the said Commission. Thereafter, the case on the basis of the enquiry and investigation has to be filed with prior sanction of the said Commission. There being no investigation before filing the said case, the proceeding of the said case has been initiated and is being continued without lawful authority. The learned Counsel finally submitted that the President of the Republic of Bangladesh promulgated Ordinance No. 6 of 2007 dated 16-4-2007 amending the said Ordinance by inserting a new section as sub-section 3Ka of section 3 of the said Ordinance that (৩ক। এই ধারার আইন প্রণীত বিধি দ্বারা জরুরী অবস্থা ঘোষনার কার্যকরতাকালে যে কোন আইনের অধীন সংঘটিত অপরাধের অনুসন্ধান, তদন্ত, বিচার, আপীল বা তৎসংশ্লিষ্ট অন্য কোন বিষয়  দ্রুত ও কার্যকরভাবে সম্পন্ন করিবার জন্য বিশেষ বিধান প্রণয়ন করা যাইবে। So, under section 3(3Ka) of the said Ordinance, the said Rules can be made applicable for any offence which had occurred during the subsistence (কার্যকরতাকালে) of the Emergency.</u>

<u>13. Cardinal principle of the criminal jurisprudence is that the person concerned should submit to the process of justice before he can claim the right of audience provided in law as well as the judicial convention, which is very much effective in the Court of law, Enunciating the age-old maxim that a man who seeks justice from the Court of the law must come before the Court to agitate his grievance and must surrender first to the process of justice, otherwise he remains to be fugitive from justice and could not seek aid or assistance of the process of justice in order to claim right of audience against the process of the Court issued against him.</u>

14. This view is-the age-old judicial norm and convention in our Court from the time immemorial and this view finds support in the decision in the case of Chand Shah vs Crown reported in PLD 1956 FC 43 = 8 DLR (FC) 24 as under.

"The present is an individual case and, in our opinion, it is an essential condition of the administration of justice, in a case affecting an individual or individuals, that the persons concerned should submit to the due process of justice. We cannot conceive of a more flagrant violation of this condition that a case-like the present-where the individual seeks the interference of the Sovereign to obtain revision of a judicial order, when he is himself engaged in setting that judicial order at naught. We accordingly, dismiss this .petition, by reason of its being, in the existing circumstances, wholly unsuitable for the exercise of this Court's special jurisdiction in criminal cases.

....... Attorneys and Advocates who appear to present petitions, on the criminal side other than those which lie as of right-are under a duty to see that they are acting in furtherance of justice. It seems to us that this duty is clearly violated when aid; for securing interference by this Court with a judicial order, is given by these officers of the Court to persons who, in their knowledge, are in contempt, i.e. as fugitives from justice, without at the same time ensuring that such persons conform to the judicial orders applicable to them.

We fully subscribe to this view and reiterate that the attorneys and members of the bar will bear in mind the serious consequence of committing contempt of this Court in moving on behalf of a prisoner who is a fugitive from law. The appeal filed by the Counsel on the basis of the power-of-attorney executed by Gul Hassan in favour of Khawaja Muhammad Khan before his absconsion was thus not properly constituted and should have been dismissed by the High Court Division on that ground alone.

In this view, Gul Hassan being a fugitive from law and a contemner was not entitled to hearing and leave granted to him on limited questions of law was liable to be rescinded. As to the proceedings under section 374, CrPC, we endorse the view adopted by the learned Judges in the High Court Division that if a prisoner de- camps and thereby forfeits the right of audience, the sentence of death may be confirmed in his absence.

On merits Mr Manzur Qadir took us through the evidence on the record, but failed to make out a case for interference with the conviction and sentence of Bahadur Khan, appellant Karim Khan, deceased, was shot dead on 1-7-1965 during day light as a result of blood-feud within the sight of Mir Muhammad, Sarbaz and Yaqub Khan, PW'S."

15. The said view has further been reiterated in the case of Gut Hassan vs State reported in PLD 1969 SC 89 = 21 DLR (SC) 109.

<u>16. Even in our jurisdiction this principle is always adhered to and was never deviated from, as because this convention or principle has been a norm maintained in our criminal jurisprudence to affect the audience or appearance of the accused in reply to any process of the Court. This has become very much a practice and procedure in our Criminal Jurisprudence that a persons in obedience to a process of the Court must surrender before the Court and challenge the alleged action against him. In the instant case, the petitioner having not surrendered to the process of the Court could not file any application or put his grievance before a Court of law, far less before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. Thus, in the absence of any surrender before the process of law, the Court of law is incompetent to issue any order or stay any process at its behest and if done so that would be illegal and without jurisdiction and, as such, this petition is not maintainable.</u>

17. Suffice it to mention in respect of the merit of the case that the subject matter of challenge has been dealt with by this Division in other cases of similar nature and held that the proceeding could be continued and that the accused respondent may challenge any illegality in the judicial proceeding pending in a Court of law as and when occasion shall arise.

18. These appeals are, accordingly, allowed and the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 10844 and 10845 of 2007 including the issuance of Rule Nisi staying further proceedings in ACC GR Case Nos. 67 and 68 of 2007 corresponding to Shahbagh Police Station Case No. 50 dated 25-7-2007 and Dhanmondi Police Station Case No. 79 dated 25-7-2007 now pending in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, are, hereby, set aside.

MM Ruhul Amin J: I agree with my learned brother Mohammad Fazlul Karim, J that the appeals should be allowed.

Md Joynul Abedin J: I have gone through the judgment delivered by my learned brother Mr Justice Mohammad Fazlul Karim allowing the appeals on the ground that the respondent No. 1 , Mahmud Hossain, being fugitive from justice the writ petitions filed by him are not maintainable. I regret I cannot agree with the same and intend to deliver a dissenting judgment as under.

19. As the relevant fact is already stated in the main judgment only reiterate such fact as is relevant for recording dissenting judgment. The prosecution case against respondent No.1 in both the Anti-Corruption cases is that Anwar Hossain Manju as Communication Minister obtained two pay orders for Taka 1,00,00,200 from AI-Amin Construction Limited by way of illegal gratification for awarding contract for carrying on construction works of 648 metres long Pre Stressed Concrete Girder Bridge over Dharla river including River Training and Approach Road works and caused said amount to be deposited in the account of Aegis Textile Mills Limited. Since the respondent No.1 as an executive director of the said Textile Mill also looks after the bank account of the said Textile Mill along with the wife and a daughter of Anwar Hossain Manju, Mrs. Tasmima Hossain and Sima Hossain, as the Managing Director and a director respectively, he is also an accused as an abettor of the principal accused Anwar Hossain Manju in committing the offence under sections 161/109 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and Rule 15 of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007.

20. In this background of the case, the respondent No.1 filed Writ Petition Nos. 10844 and 10845 of 2007 challenging the aforesaid two Anti-Corruption cases as without lawful authority stating that no process in the aforesaid two criminal cases were issued against him till then.

21. In both the writ petitions rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents, Anti-Corruption Commission and the Government of Bangladesh in the Ministry of Home Affairs, to show cause why initiation and continuation of proceedings in the aforesaid two Anti-Corruption cases pending before the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka under the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority. The High Court Division also stayed further proceedings of the aforesaid two criminal cases by order dated 13-12-2007.

22. The only question that falls for our consideration is, whether the respondent No.1 was fugitive from justice when he moved the aforesaid writ petitions and obtained Rule Nisi therein and thus forfeited his right to any relief in the aforesaid writ petitions pending in the High Court Division.

<u>23. The word "fugitive" is not defined anywhere in our law. The expression "fugitive offender" is however defined in section 2(1)( d) in the Extradition Act, 1974 and means the person who, being accused or convicted of an extradition offence is, or is suspected to be, in any part of Bangladesh. The expression "fugitive from justice" is defined in Black's Law Dictionary, 7th Edition, page 680 as "A criminal suspect who flees, evades or escapes arrest, prosecution, or imprisonment, especially by fleeing the jurisdiction or by hiding".</u>

<u>24. The word "abscond" as a verb and "absconder" as a noun are however known in our criminal justice system but it is also not defined anywhere in our law. This word "abscond" is used as a synonym to the word "fugitive" in section 339B of the Code of Criminal Procedure to mean an accused avoiding service of process or concealing himself to avoid arrest and prosecution. Our Courts have consistently denied relief to an accused who is either regarded as fugitive or absconder. Careful and critical analysis of a few decided cases of the superior Courts of the Sub-continent will reveal that mere absence or failure to surrender to the jurisdiction of criminal Courts at any stage of any criminal case initiated and pending against him will not make him a fugitive or absconder.</u>

25. In the case of Khalilur Rahman vs State, 33 DLR 12, accused Khalilur Rahman and Atiqulla were convicted under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code and sentenced to undergo transportation for life by the Additional Sessions Judge, First Court, Dacca in Sessions Case No.113 of 1968 on 31-8- 1968. Both the convicts filed Criminal Appeal No.35 of 1968 before the High Court, Dhaka. The report dated 25-4-1973 of the DIG Prisons, Dacca showed that accused appellant Atiqulla died on 13- 5-1971 in the Mitford Hospital, Dacca and his appeal accordingly abated. But the accused appellant Khalilur Rahman escaped from the jail custody on 17-12-1971 and he was absconding. In this background of the case a Division Bench of the High Court, Dacca denied any relief to the accused appellant Khalilur Rahman treating his appeal as dismissed on account of his being a fugitive relying on a decision dated 13-4-1978 of the Special Bench of the Dacca High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 472 of 1968 in the case of Nirmal Krishna Chanda and another vs State.

26. In the case of Chand Shah vs Crown. 8 DLR (FC) 24, the accused Chand Shah was acquitted by the Sessions Judge of the charge of murder and subsequently the Lahore High Court on appeal filed by the Provincial Government against his acquittal and Chand Shah being brought before the Court on execution of a warrant for his arrest issued by the High Court admitted his appeal and enlarged him on bail. He was on bail when his conviction and sentence were pronounced by the Lahore High Court but he neither surrendered himself to the authorities nor it was possible for the authorities to secure his arrest. In that situation, Chand Shah presented a petition for special leave to appeal before the Federal Court of Pakistan through his Attorney. But the Federal Court dismissed his petition refusing to grant him any relief considering him a fugitive in the following terms:

"The statutory provisions relating to this Court do not provide any "inherent powers" of the kind necessary for the entertainment of the present petition. The principles upon which this Court acts to revise the decisions of subordinate tribunals in criminal cases have been exhaustively considered in a number of pronouncements by the Court itself, as well as its predecessor, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. Its functions are confined to the limits of the sovereign's prerogative in the sphere of the administration of justice, which are succinctly stated in the judgment of the Privy Council in the case R vs. Bertrand as follows:

" the inherent prerogative right and on all proper occasions, the duty of the Queen in Council to exercise an appellate jurisdiction, with a view not only to ensure, so far as may be, the due administration of justice in the individual case but also to preserve the due course of procedure generally.

The present is an "individual case", and in our opinion, it is an essential condition of the administration of justice, in a case affecting an individual or individuals, that the persons concerned should submit to the due process of justice. We cannot conceive of a more flagrant violation of this condition than a case-like the present-where the individual seeks the interference of the Sovereign to obtain revision of a judicial order, when he is himself engaged in setting that judicial order at naught. We accordingly dismiss this petition, by reason of its being, in existing circumstances, wholly unsuitable for the exercise of this Court's special jurisdiction in criminal cases;"

27. In the case of Mansur Ali vs State 55 DLR (AD) 131, the convicted accused appealed before the Additional Sessions Judge, Gaibandha against their conviction and sentence by the Additional District Magistrate which was dismissed. They then preferred criminal revision before the High Court Division and obtained Rule and also bail for 6(six) months but no step was taken to extend their bail. In this situation the High Court Division discharged the Rule without entering into the merit of the Rule. The convict accused then filed criminal petition for leave to appeal before the Appellate Division and the Appellate Division dismissed the same stating that the fugitive has no right to seek any redress.

28. However, in the facts and circumstances of the following cases superior Courts have not regarded the absent accused as fugitive or absconder and granted relief.

29. In the case of Md Sabuj vs State, 1988 BLD 251 = 40 DLR 150, accused Md Sabuj along with co-accused Md Alai Miah were tried by Assistant Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal Judge in absentia and convicted and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 10(ten) years and to pay a fine of Taka 100 in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 1 (one) year more under section 156(8) of the Customs Act read with section 25(B) of the Special Powers Act. Before they were tried by the Assistant Sessions Judge and the Special Tribunal Judge, the Additional District Magistrate granted them bail. At the time of framing charge both the accused were absent and the trial was held in absentia and they were convicted and sentenced as above. Against the aforesaid, conviction and sentence accused Md Sabuj only filed Criminal Appeal No. 491 of 1986. A Division Bench of the High Court Division allowed the appeal and set aside the aforesaid order of conviction and sentence holding that the accused could not be regarded as having absconded, because they were on bail and summons and warrants were directed to be issued but there was neither any service of summons nor any execution of the warrants nor any return or report in that regard.

30. In the case of Saidur Rahman vs State, 40 DLR (AD) 281, the accused appellants were tried for an offence under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code by the learned Sessions Judge, Netrokona but were found guilty only under section 147 of the Penal Code and accordingly Sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for 2(two) years and a fine of Taka 1000. On an application filed by the accused appellants on the same day the Sessions Judge granted them interim bail pending filing of appeal before the High Court Division and confirmation of bail. The accused appellants thereafter filed criminal appeal before the High Court Division but the learned Judge of the High Court Division summarily rejected the petition of appeal on the ground that the appellants did not surrender before the High Court Division before moving their petition of appeal and they being fugitive from law "fugitive cannot get protection."

<u>31. In this backdrop, the accused appellants surrendered before moving the leave petition and were subsequently released on bail by the Appellate Division. The Appellate Division granted leave to consider whether the aforesaid order of the High Court Division was a just and proper order. The Appellate Division allowed the appeal in the following terms:</u>

<u>"There was nothing in the conduct of the accused appellants to show that they were running away from the jurisdiction of the Court or avoiding its process. It is true that there is a long established practice since the days of the Dhaka High Court nay from before, that the Court will refuse to entertain or hear an appeal when the appellant docs not surrender in accordance with the sentence passed on him (vide 13 DLR 1). In the present case the appellants surrendered before the Sessions Judge upon conviction and obtained an order of interim bail. It is true that the Sessions Judge was not competent to grant such bail under section 426 of the Code of Criminal Procedure since the sentence was in excess of one year. The order was, therefore. illegal but the fact remains that the appellants submitted themselves to the sentence passed and obtained an interim order of bail in their favour albeit wrongly. In the facts of the case it will be less than charitable to attribute to the appellants that they were "fugitive from law". There was nothing in their conduct to show that they were running away from the jurisdiction of the Court or avoiding its process. Since, however, the appellants were not covered by a legal order of interim bail, the proper order the learned Judge ought to have passed and which is always usually passed in such cases was to direct the appellants to surrender within a certain time before taking up the petition of appeal for hearing. If after grant of reasonable time for the said purpose, the appellants failed to surrender then, of course, the Court could dismiss the appeal but the circumstances and manner in which the impugned order has been passed are such that it cannot be said that the order was a just and proper one."</u>

32. In the case of Nesar Ahmed vs Bangladesh, 49 DLR (AD) 111, appellant Nesar Ahmed filed Writ Petition No.720 of 1994 on the averments that Begumganj PS Case No. 20 dated 19-9-1991 was started against him and one Anwarullah under section 19(F) of the Arms Act read with section 26 of the Special Powers Act on the allegation that a rope and electrically-charged torch-light were recovered from the person of the accused appellant Nesar Ahmed and a knife measuring 11 inches was recovered from the possession of Anwarullah. The police submitted charge-sheet against them on 3-12- 1991 and thereafter the accused appellant obtained bail from the Thana Magistrate, Begumgonj. The case was then sent to the Court of Senior Special Tribunal and Sessions Judge, Noakhali for trial and they were then tried by the Assistant Sessions Judge, Noakhali for committing offence under the aforesaid sections. The Special Tribunal thereafter by its judgment and order dated 14-2-1993 convicted the accused appellant and Anwarullah under the a foresaid sections of the Arms Act and section 26 of the Special Powers Act and they were sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 10(ten) years and also to pay a fine of Taka 500 in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 1(one) year more. The accused appellant was not at all aware of the trial, conviction and sentence before his arrest. He obtained certified copy of the relevant papers and filed an application under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the High Court Division against. the aforesaid judgment and order of conviction and sentence. But the learned Judges of the High Court Division observed that the said application was not maintainable and the learned Advocate for the accused appellant took it back and filed the aforesaid writ petition. The learned Judges of the High Court Division having summarily rejected the writ petition held that there was an alternative remedy of appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act and the writ petitioner n01 having availed of it was not entitled to any relief under Article 102 of the Constitution. The accused appellant thereupon tiled a leave petition and the leave was granted, among others, to consider his submission that the order of conviction and sentence of the accused appellant being without jurisdiction the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the application under Article 102 of the Constitution was not maintainable.

<u>33. Appellate Division held that an absent person should not be too readily assumed to be an absconder without fixing a date for his appearance and without directing his sureties to produce him, inasmuch as it was found that the appellant made out his case that although he was found to be absconding after obtaining bail from the Thana Magistrate, Begumgonj he was not aware of the subsequent developments leading to the trial and conviction by the Special Tribunal after he obtained bail, inasmuch as neither he was informed of the development by his Advocate as to the transmission of the case record to the Special Tribunal for trial nor any date was fixed for his appearance nor there was any direction on his sureties by the Special Tribunal to produce him for the trial.</u>

34. In the case of Jahangir Hossain Howlader vs CMM, Dhaka 58 DLR 106, FIR (first information report) was filed and warrant of arrest was yet to be issued by the Magistrate. The accused named in the first information report approached the High Court Division and filed a writ petition for quashing BACGR Case No. 9 of 2002 arising out of Subujbagh, PS Case No.27 dated 16-1-2002 pending before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate. The accused petitioner in this case invoked writ jurisdiction before the warrant of arrest was issued against him. A Division Bench of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute and quashed the aforesaid case pending before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate on the ground that the allegations contained in the first information report did not constitute any criminal offence. The learned Judges of the High Court Division entertained the writ petition and granted the relief saying that the accused petitioner was before the Court by filing the writ petition and he could not be termed fugitive from justice.

35. In the case of Messrs Pepsi Food Ltd is Special Judicial Magistrate AIR 1998 (SC) 128, accused filed a writ petition notwithstanding the fact that they did not surrender before the Court of Magistrate. The Supreme Court of India even then found that the writ petition was maintainable and thus set aside the impugned judgment of the High Court and quashed the proceeding in the complaint case filed against the petitioner. In this case the Magistrate took cognizance on the complaint case and issued summons but the accused petitioner without surrendering before the Court of Magistrate moved the High Court by filing writ petition but the High Court declined to interfere in the case. The Supreme Court of India while setting aside the judgment of the High Court held that despite the summons was served the accused Was entitled to invoke writ jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 or for quashing of the first information report case under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure when the complainant did not make out any case against him and it was not necessary for the accused to surrender before the Criminal Court to undergo an agony of the criminal trial when the complaint itself did not make out any case against him. In this ease the Supreme Court of India not only found the writ petition to be maintainable but also observed as under:

"It is no comfortable thought for the appellants to be told that they could appear before the Court which is at a far off place in Gazipur in the State of Uttar Pradesh, seek their release on bail and then to either move an application under section 245(2) of the Code or to face trial when the complaint and the preliminary evidence recorded makes out no case against them. It is certainly one of those cases where is an abuse of the process of the law and the Courts and the High Court should not have shied away in exercising its jurisdiction. Provisions of Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution and section 482 of the Code are devised to advance justice and not to frustrate it. In our view, High Court should riot have adopted such a rigid approach which certainly has led to miscarriage of justice in the case. Power of judicial review is discretionary but this was a case where the High Court should have exercised it."

<u>36. There is yet another category of cases where first information report is lodged but no process is issued by the Court. An accused named in the first information report can approach the High Court Division for quashing the first. information report without surrendering before the Criminal Court where the first information report case is pending. Because the accused is under no obligation to surrender before the criminal Court till the process is issued. The High Court Division is competent to quash the first information report cases where the allegations -contained in the first information report (FIR) even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not constitute offence alleged. Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts no case can stand against the, accused and that a further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to harassment to an innocent party and abuse of the process of the Court.</u>

<u>37. In the case in hand, only first information report was lodged against the respondent No. 1, no warrant of arrest or any other process was issued. In view of the principle deduced and expounded in the aforesaid judicial pronouncements, I am of the view, that the respondent No. 1 was not a fugitive from justice and the High Court Division committed no illegality in entertaining the writ petitions of the respondent No. 1 and issuing Rule Nisi on the appellants. Hence the points raised in the Rules issued in the aforesaid two writ petitions must be left to be determined by the High Court Division and any contrary view would render the jurisdiction of the writ Court nugatory.</u>

38. In the light of the foregoing discussions both the appeals are dismissed without any order as to costs.

Md Hassan Ameen J: I agree with the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother Mohammad Fazlul Karim J.

Md Abdul Matin J: I agree with the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother Md Fazlul Karim J.

Order of the Court

The appeals are allowed without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider  J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 23-9- 2008, passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 40 of 2005 (Originally Title Suit No. 135 of2003) decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff-landlord, holding that the defendant tenant is a defaulter and, as such, he is liable to be evicted and was also directed the defendant-tenant to vacate the suit premises upon removing all the structures constructed by him from the suit premises and handover the vacant possession of the same to the plaintiff landlord within 30 days.

2. The predecessor of the plaintiff-landlords and the predecessor of the defendant tenant entered into two lease agreements in respect of the suit premises on 12-1-1988 upon creating a monthly tenancy in the suit premises which were, subsequently, renewed from time to time on mutual consent. Lastly, on 22-1-1995 the predecessor of the plaintiff-landlords and the present defendant-appellant- tenant entered into two agreements for monthly tenancy in respect of the same for a period of two years ending on 31-12-1996 at a monthly rent of Taka 12,000 for the building situated therein and Taka 40,000 for the vacant place of the suit premises in total Taka 52,000 to be paid by the first week of every month. In the said agreement it was contemplated that the agreement would expire on 31-12- 1996 determining the landlord tenant relationship and the same will not be extended or renewed any further under any circumstances. It was also contended that the 2nd party tenant would hand over the vacant possession of the suit premises to the landlords on 1-1-1997 without fail upon removing all structures constructed by the tenant therein. It was further agreed by the tenant that in case he fails to handover the vacant possession of the suit premises to the landlords after 31-12-1996 then the tenant would pay Taka 1,000 for each agreement i.e. Taka 2,000 for each day's possession of the same. He further agreed that all the temporary structures constructed in the suit premises will be removed immediately on the expiry of the said agreements. According to one of the clauses of the said agreements the tenant deposited Taka 1,60,000, equivalent to four month's rent for the vacant space in one deed and Taka 48,000, equivalent to four month's rent for the building in another deed as security which would not be adjusted with the rent rather at the time of handing over possession, after the expiry of the tenancy period the entire security money would be refunded to the tenant. The said agreements also contended that at the time of handing over possession of the suit premises the tenant would hand over the receipts of all the paid up utility bills for Electricity, Gas, WASA, Telephone etc. in full which he consumed, to the landlord and thereby handover the possession of the suit premises without any encumbrances. But it is alleged by the plaintiff landlords that the defendant tenant defaulted in paying rent of the suit premises for the month of December 1996 when he paid the same on the 8th of December as such he became a defaulter and is liable to be evicted from the suit premises. It is further alleged that the defendant tenant did not pay the rent for the month of August 2003 till date nor he handover the possession of the same to the plaintiff landlords upon removing the unauthorized structures constructed thereon after the expiry of the tenancy on 31-12-1996 rather inspite of repeated intimations to vacant the suit premises as per agreement he continued to possess the same without paying rent and compensation to the plaintiff landlord. As such the plaintiff landlord, on 2-8-2003, issued a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act by registered post with A/D upon the defendant tenant which has been duly received by the defendant tenant on 6-8-2003. But the defendant tenant did not comply with the requests/directions made in the legal notice. As such the plaintiff landlord filed the present suit on 6-9-2003 for ejectment of the monthly tenant; for payment of the outstanding rent of Taka 49,28,000 for the suit premises from 1-1-1997 till September 2003 at the rate of Taka 2000 per day along with direction upon the defendant tenant to pay the utility costs which may be due and remove the unauthorized constructions made therein, for Khas possession in case the defendant after the decree, does not makeover the possession of the suit premises to the plaintiffs.

3. By amending the plaint it has been alleged that the defendant in violation of the terms of the agreement constructed Semi Pucca structures in the vacant Space, Unauthorizedly, and thereby the residential nature of the suit premises has been converted into commercial and, as such, the tenant is liable to be evicted from the suit premises upon removing the unauthorized constructions at his own cost for violation of the terms of agreement as provided in the terms of the said agreement. It is further contended that the tenant obtained order from the House Rent Controller in House Rent Case No. 12 of 1997 to deposit Taka 53,200 per month which is contrary to the agreement dated 22-1-1995 and, as such, the plaintiff preferred an appeal against the said order of the Rent Controller which is pending. It is alleged further that the defendant tenant did not pay the entire amount of rent as per agreement which is Taka 2,000 per day i.e. Taka 60,000 per month in the House Rent Controller. Thus apart from being a defaulter he is also liable to be evicted for violating the terms of agreement as provided under section 18 of the premises Rent Control Act, 1991. It is further alleged that the defendant tenant filed Title Suit No.38 of 1991 subsequently, remembered as TitleSuit No.157 of 1999 in the 3rd Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka against the plaintiff landlords, wherein he prayed for temporary injunction for restraining the landlords from evicting the tenant from the suit premises. Such conduct of the defendant, it is alleged, shows that he does not want to vacant the suit premises rather possessing the same illegally on different pretexts, Hence the suit.

4. The defendant tenant contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint contending inter alia that since long before, the predecessor of the defendant tenant having good relationship with the predecessor of the plaintiffs entered into two agreements for monthly tenancy of the suit premises on 12-1-1988; The rents were paid regularly. Thereafter the agreement being renewed from time to time after every two years the defendant tenant, is running the business of "Shapla Community Centre" in the suit premises; After the demise of both the original land lord and the original tenant the agreements were entered into and renewed from time to time between the present plaintiffs and the present defendant. For renovation of the community centre the defendant tenant spent Taka 75,00,000 and the tenant having paid rent regularly to the landlord within time he is not a defaulter. Pursuant to the good relationship between the families the tenant did not keep with him all the renewed agreements and the copy of all the rent receipt; after expiry of the lease deeds in question on 31-12-1996 the agreements were renewed pursuant to the discussions between them for the year 1997- 1998 and the defendant tenant, pursuant to such agreement as well as the discussions continued his business of running community centre in the suit premises. But when the landlord did not adjust the rent for the month of December 1995 with the security money, kept in deposit with them, the defendant tenant paid the rent of the said month on 8-12-1996. Subsequently, having failed to get the agreement renewed on requests the defendant tenant a legal notice upon the plaintiff landlords on 26-12-1996 through his Advocate and the plaintiff landlords having received the said notice did not reply to the same, as such another legal notice was issued by the defendant, which returned undelivered. However, the defendant tenant continued paying rent up to December 1996 which the landlord received upon issuing rent receipts. But however, when the defendant tenant wanted to pay rent for the month of January 1997, the plaintiff landlords refused to receive the same with intention to make the defendant tenant a defaulter. Understanding the said intention of the landlords, the tenant, on 8-1-1997 sent Taka 52,000 by Money Order to the plaintiff landlords which the plaintiffs, on 15-1-1997 refused to accept and the said refused having been received on 21-1-1997 by the tenant, House Rent Case No. 12 of 1997 was filed before the House Rent Controller for depositing the rent and since then the tenant had been depositing the rent regularly in accordance with law. The House Rent Controller by his order dated 17-1-2000 allowed the case of the defendant tenant and directed him to deposit Taka 53,200 as rent with the House Rent Controller regularly. It is further contended by the defendant tenant that he was compelled to file Title Suit No. 34 of 1997 (subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 157 of 1999 of the 3rd Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka) and obtained an ad interim order of injunction therein which is still pending. Thus the tenant is not a defaulter in the eye of law and he is running his business in the suit premises ad earning his livelihood through the said business. In case the defendant is evicted from the suit premises he will be in grave trouble as such the suit should be dismissed.

5. Considering the pleading of both the parties, the learned Joint District Judge framed as many as seven issues including the issue as to whether the defendant having not paid rent is a defaulter, whether the defendant constructed any unauthorized structures and running the business of Shapla Community Center; whether pursuant to the agreement the defendant tenant is liable to pay Taka 2000 as compensation on the expiry of the agreement, whether the tenant is liable to be evicted for violating the terms of the agreement; whether the plaintiff is entitled to get relief as prayed for on evicting the defendant tenant upon removing the unauthorized structures thereon' and recovery of arrear rent including compensation.

6. The plaintiffs in support of their claim adduced two witnesses including plaintiff No.3 (a) as PW 1 and the learned Advocate who issued the legal notice as PW 2. On the other hand, the defendant tenant adduced himself only as DW 1. The plaintiff landlords in support of their case made out in the plaint filed four exhibits including two agreements in question dated 22-1-1995 (Exhibit X, XI = 4, 4(ka), the legal notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act (Exhibit 2 series) along with notice of RAJUK and the Works Department addressed top the plaintiff (Exhibit 3 to 3 (gha). On the other hand, the defendant tenant filed three Exhibits namely the judgment of the House Rent Control Case No. 12 of 1997 passed on 17-1-2000 (Exhibit "Ka"), order No.9 dated 9-6-1997 passed by in Title Suit No. 34 of 1997 subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 157 of 1999 showing granting of injunction against the plaintiff landlords (Exhibit "Ka") and the legal notice dated 30-7-2003 issued by Mr Md Nurul Islam, Advocate on behalf of the plaintiff landlords upon the defendant tenant along with the registered receipt with AID (Exhibit "Ga", which has also been marked as Exhibit 2 series).

7. Upon considering the pleadings and the evidences on record, both oral and documentary, the learned Jude held that the suit is maintainable, the same is not barred by limitation, the defendant tenant as DW 1 having admitted that the rent for the month of December was paid on 8-12-1996, which is beyond the time fixed in the agreement and the rent for the month of January 1997 having paid on 25-1-1997 and the rent for the month of August 2003 having not at all being paid till date he has become a defaulter. Apart from this, upon examining the payment receipts as appears in the record of House Rent Control case No. 12 of 1997 the Court further held that the defendant tenant did not pay rent for the month of January 1997, February 1998, August 1998, December 1999, February 2001 within the stipulated period of first week of the month, as contemplated in the agreement, as such he has become a defaulter. It is further held that in violation of the terms of the agreements dated 22-1-1995 the defendant tenant constructed unauthorized structures and had been running the business of "Shapla Community Centre"; and the defendant tenant, pursuant to two agreements dated 22-1-1995 is liable to pay Taka 2000 as compensation, for each day's overstay in the suit premises after 31-12-1996; the Court also found that since the defendant tenant violated the terms of the agreement as such he is liable to be evicted. Accordingly the tenant defendant having not vacated the suit premises after the expiry of the agreement, he is liable to be evicted upon removing the unauthorized structures constructed therein with compensation and the plaintiff is entitled to get the arrear rents from the defendant for the period of his stay in the suit premises after 31-12-1996. With all these findings the learned Judge decreed the suit and directed the defendant to vacate the suit premises with 30 days upon removing the unauthorized structures situated thereon and also directed the defendant tenant to pay Taka 2000 per day i.e. Taka 60,000 per month and upon deducting Taka 53,200, which is being deposited with the Rent Controller, every month, from the said amount of Taka 60,000 the Court held that the remaining amount of Taka 6,800 is required to be paid from the date of expiry of the agreement till August 2008 i.e. 140 months which amounts to Taka 9,52,000 as compensation. The Court further deducted the security amount of Taka 2,08,000 from the said amount of Taka 9,52,000 and accordingly directed the defendant tenant to pay Taka 7,44,000 to the plaintiffs land lords. The defendant tenant has further been directed to pay the utility bills for the use of Electricity, WASA, GAS, Sewerage, telephone, etc, from 22-1-1995 till August 2008 and hand over the paid receipts to the plaintiff landlords in default the plaintiff be entitled to get the decree executed through Court. Hence this appeal.

8. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant appellant (tenant) at the very outset admitted that the question for determination in this appeal is whether the appellant is a defaulter as defined under the provision of the Premises Rent Control Act and/or he is entitled to get protection under the said Act. In this respect he submits that after the determination of the tenancy when the tenant remains in possession he becomes a "statutory tenant" as such he cannot be evicted as a default if such tenant continues paying rent regularly within the stipulated time of 15 days of the month following as provided in the statute. Relying on the case of Maria Keshi D' Rozaria vs Hassan Movies Ltd, reported in 41 DLR (AD) 35 submits that the facts of the said case and the facts of the instant case being almost similar the defendant appellant is entitled to get, the benefit of the said decision and, as such, he being a statutory tenant under section 2 (8) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1963 which is similar to section 2 (Umma) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991, he is entitled to get protection of the Act. Thus he submits that since, after the expiry of the agreement on 31-12-1996 the tenant had been paying rent with the Rent Controller within 15th day of the month following, as provided under section 18 (5) of the Act, 1991, the defendant appellant is not a defaulter as such is not liable to be evicted on such ground. He next submits that the learned Judge of the trial Court was wrong in calculating the rent for the scheduled premises, to be paid by the defendant appellant (tenant) after the expiry of the agreements, by deducting Taka 53200 (the rent deposited with the Rent Controller) from Taka 60,000 the compensation money @ of Taka 2000 per day, inspite of the fact that the same is admittedly the compensation money for' each day's possession. Thus the direction to pay Taka 7,44,000 upon deducting from the total amount of rent paid to the House Rent Controller and also upon deducting the security money, kept with the landlords is also illegal and liable to be set aside. He submits that the compensation can never be regarded as rent and if the defendant appellant is liable to pay the compensation then the plaintiff can recover the same in accordance with law, if necessary, by filing a separate suit But under no circumstances the compensation can be considered as rent and, as such, the direction in that regard is illegal and liable to be set aside. Lastly, Mr Alam frankly admits that till 31- 12-1996 the agreements were in force and the ten- ant, according to the terms of the said agreement, was liable to pay rent within the "first week" of every month, but it appears, that the rent for the month of December 1996, the last month of the tenant period, was not paid within time as per agreement rather the payment was made out of time by only one day. According to him since the defendant never defaulted in paying rent during the tenancy period and subsequently. as he is depositing the same with the House Rent Controller regularly according to law, the conduct of the defendant appellant is very clear and. as such, he should not be evicted from the suit premises on the ground of default. Rather, relying 011 the decision of Kalu Mondal vs Begum Fazilatun Nessa, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 53 he submits that the defendant's clear conduct should be taken into consideration and the delay of only one day in paying rent only for the last month of the tenancy period should be considered leniently and on enquiry, as contemplated in section 18 as to whether the tenant was entitled to the benefit of protection from ejectment at the instance of the landlord due to non-payment of rent, becomes all the more necessary when the tenant comes with a positive case, supported by evidence, that due to some kind of abnormal situation supervening at the relevant time it was beyond his control to pay rent and, as such, the tenant be allowed to remain in the suit premises.

9. On the other hand, Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the respondent-landlords, relying on the age old principle "once a defaulter always a defaulter" which has been approved by all the superior Courts of the sub-continent and by now has become a unique method for evicting a tenant, submits that since the defendant tenant as DW 1 admitted that the rent for the month of December 1996 was not paid within the stipulated period of the first week of the said month, he has become a defaulter in the eye of law and liable to be evicted accordingly. About the contention of Mr Alam as to payment made only a day beyond the time specified in the agreement', MrRahman submits that the same is no basis as the principle is very clear i.e. once the tenant defaults in paying rent, no matter by one day or more, he becomes a defaulter and, as such, becomes liable to be evicted from the suit premises anytime subsequent thereto. Mr Rahman next submits that apart from being a defaulted for the month of December 1996 the defendant appellant in his cross examination further admitted that the rent for the month of January 1997 was sent by money order on 8-1-1997 beyond time though after the expiry of the tenancy agreement which was not renewed or extended any further after 31-12-1996, and, as such, the defendant appellant again became a defaulter for nonpayment of rent for the month of January 1997. In support of his contention he relied on several decisions amongst which the case of Bulbul Begum vs Mohd Sanwar Belal, reported in 8 MLR (AD) 193; Nurul Islam vs Md Ali Hossain Miah being dead his heirs Amir Hossain and others, reported in 50 DLR (AD) 114; Boshir Ahmed, vs Ayub Ali Mollah reported in 19 BLD 537 are notable. Thus once a tenant becomes a defaulter under no circumstances he can get protection under the law from eviction on any ground not even in a case of adjustment of the rent from the security or advance kept with the landlord at the time of commencement of the tenancy, The payment of salami or advance in excess of one month's rent is strictly prohibited under section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act which is recoverable from the landlords on an application by the tenant to the Rent Controller within six months of marking such deposit/payment. Thus Mr Rahman submits that under no circumstances, the tenant can take a plea of adjustment of rent from the said security money or advance and thereby save him from being a defaulter and evicted. In support of this view Mr Rahman relied in the case of Md Mushtaque Hossain vs Md Shahjahan Miah reported in 10 MLR (AD) 139 = 57 DLR (AD) 60, Mostak Hossain Chowdhury vs Hosne Ara Salam, reported in 8 MLR (AD) 124; Md Jashimuddin vs Mrs Nurjahan Begum reported in 14 BLD 528; Mymensingh Arya Darma Gnan Prodaini Sava vs Rabindra Nayaan Paul reported in 56 DLR 47;

10. Mr Khalilur Rahman next contended that even acceptance of rent subsequent to the month of default will not protect the tenant and that will not act as an waiver of claiming the tenant a defaulter: nor acceptance or payment of rent in lump will save the tenant from the mischief of the law making him a defaulter. In reply to Mr Alam's submissions as to the defendant appellant is neither a "tenant by holding over" nor "by sufferance" rather a "tenant under the statute", Mr Rahman submits that the term 'statutory tenant' has been imported from the Transfer of Property Act. Section 116 of the said Act provides as to holding over. According to him the agreement has expired on 31-12-1996 on the basis of its term and admittedly the defendant appellant tenant was in possession of the suit premises after 31-12-1996 and he was depositing rent on the basis of rate fixed by the agreement, in the House Rent Controller and, as such, he is accepting part of the agreement. Again when the defendant appellant retains possession and the respondent landlords having issued notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and thereby directing the tenant to vacate the suit premises in 2003 the tenant's possession in the suit premises from 1-1-1997 till September 2003, in some respect, can be construed to be "with the assent of the landlords, impliedly not expressly", to such continuance of possession. As such the tenant after 31-12-1996 continued the tenancy by "holding over". Once the tenant posses the suit property by holding over the terms and condition of the agreement automatically comes into operation and the tenant again becomes liable to pay the rent on the basis of the terms of the agreement as fixed by the parties to the agreement. In this respect he relied on the case of Siddik Ali being dead his heirs Afia Rahman, vs Nurun Nessa Khatun , reported in 43 DLR (AD) 3. On these contentions Mr Rahman submits that the appellant again became a defaulter in not paying the rent to the House Rent Controller within the first week of the month concerned. Accordingly, he submits that the trial Courtrightly held that not only for the month of December 96 and January 1997 but the tenant also became a defaulter for nonpayment of rent of subsequent months of February '98, August, 98, December 99, February' 2001 and, as such, he is liable to be evicted from the suit premises. Apart from these Mr Rahman specifically submits that after receiving the notice dated 30-7-2003 under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act, on 6-8-2003 the rent for the month of August 2003 has not been paid by the defendant appellant till date thus there has been no illegality in holding that the tenant is a habitual defaulter and, as such; cannot get any protection under section 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991 and is liable to be evicted from the suit premises.

11. In addition Mr Rahman, upon drawing our attention to section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Act, submits that even then the tenant violates any of the terms of the agreement he is liable to be evicted even if he is not a defaulter. In this respect he submits that the defendant appellant in his evidence admitted that in violation of the agreements he constructed Semi Pucca structures unauthorizedly and without permission from the landlords and he did not pay the utility charges, e.g. WASA, Telephone, Gas in accordance with the terms of the agreements and did not return the copy of the bills to the landlords. Thus he having violated the terms of the agreement and having not fully paid the rent with the House Rent Controller the defendant appellant has become a defaulter and, as such, he is a tenant ejectable at the instance of the plaintiff landlords.

12. Heard the learned Advocates of both the parties and perused the record. From the facts and circumstances stated hereinabove and the submissions of the learned Advocates it appears that admittedly the appellant, since his predecessor's time was a tenant under the predecessor of the respondent. Subsequently, the tenancy agreements were executed afresh between them on 22-1-1995 under agreement that the tenancy period would expire on 31-12-1996 and under no circumstances the period would be extended any further. It was also agreed that the tenant will vacate the premises immediately after 31-12-1996. In case the tenant fails to vacate the same he shall pay Taka 2,000 to the landlord, as compensation for each days of overstay till vacating. Further the parties agreed to pay rent of Taka 52,000 within the first week of every month. Under such circumstances we find that the matter in controversy in this suit/appeal is very simple i.e. whether the defendant appellant, being a tenant under the plaintiff respondents, is a defaulter by any means at any time during the subsistence of the tenancy agreement or subsequent thereto and whether he is entitled to got protection under section 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Act and whether he violated the terms of the agreements and, as such, liable to be evicted? However to answer the question raised section 18( I) and 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Act are required to be looked into in this respect.

13. Upon reading the aforesaid provisions of law it is clear that the provisions are equally safe- guarding the interest of both landlord and the tenant meaning the landlord cannot evict the tenant if the tenant performs his part of duties as incorporated in the agreement including paying the entire rent within the time as specified in the agreement and comply with the other terms of the same as specified therein. In the instant case since a specific date has been fixed, mutually, by the parties in the following manner : “প্রতি মাসে অগ্রিম ভাড়া চলতি মাসের প্রথম সপ্তাহের মধ্যে দ্বিতীয় পক্ষ প্রথম পক্ষকে প্রদান করবেন।” the tenant is to pay the rent accordingly and the time fixed in the law (section 18(5) (Ka)) does not require to be called into and in case the tenant fails to pay accordingly, he becomes a defaulter. It is the specific case of the plaintiff landlords that the defendant tenant did not pay rent for the month of December within time which from the written statement as well as from the cross examination, appears to have been admitted. In his cross examination, the defendant tenant, as DW 1, admitted that ‘১৯৯৬ ইং সালের ডিসেম্বর মাসের ৮ তারিখের মধ্যে দেই।’ So from his own admission it is found that the tenant admitted that although the time specified in the agreement for payment of rent was first week of that month but he did not pay rent for the month of December within that time. The tenant whose default has been established by his own admission, he is not entitled to get any statutory protection against eviction. This view finds support in the case of Binning and Co vs Nasirabad Properties Ltd (40 DLR (AD) 89). The duty is always upon the tenant to take care that he does not become a defaulter. Thus the finding of the trial Court as to payment of rent for the month of Deember'96 is beyond the stipulated period of the agreements for which the tenant cannot avoid the mischief of law and since he is admittedly a defaulter in paying rent, at least for one month during the tenancy period he, under the statute, is nor entitled to get protection of law as provided under section 18(5)(ka) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991' is found to be in accordance with law.

14. Relying upon the case of Kalu Mondol (46 DLR (AD) 53) Mr Alam tried to make out a case that the delay of only one day in respect of payment of rent for the last month of the tenancy period should be taken into consideration with a lenient view and the tenant should get the benefit of abnormal circumstances prevailing then, which was, beyond his control for which the rent for that month could not be paid in time. We have gone through the said decision and we find that the facts and circumstances of both the cases are quite different. In the case referred above the tenant could not pay the rent within time because of the situation prevailing then due to war of liberation which was beyond the control of the tenant and the Court having taken a lenient view of the prevailing situation that 'the condition like war of liberation is beyond the control of the tenant', as an 'exception' to the statute for which the tenant should not be found to be a defaulter in not paying rent within time. But the situation in the case in hand is quite different. There is no such material on record to prove that the situation in the present case falls within the purview of 'exception' as determined in the Kalu MandaI's case referred by Mr Alam. Thus similar view cannot be taken in the present case. As such the submission of Mr Alam is not all sustainable.

15. It is enough, for the purpose of this case, but since some other questions, such as whether the tenancy after the expiry of the agreements is a tenancy by "holding over" or "by sufferance" or a "statutory tenancy", whether Taka 2000 to be paid for each day's possession after the expiry of tenancy period on 31-12-1996 can be adjusted with the rent and/or whether security can be adjusted with the rent and/or whether the unpaid utility bills can be claimed as rent and whether for violation of the terms and conditions of the agreement the tenant is liable to be evicted from the suit property under section 18 of the Act have been raised, we need to look into the said questions. There are series of decisions wherein all these questions have been answered. In the case of Continental Corporation (Pvt) Limited vs Al-Haj Md Ismail, reported in 16 BLD (AD) 285 = 48 DLR (AD) 90 it has been held that the unpaid utility bills cannot be construed as part of the rent rather the landlord could complain of such breach of agreement if such bills were not paid but nonpayment or non depositing the WASA charges along with the rent would not make him a defaulter for nonpayment of rent or non making a valid deposit. It has further been held by the apex Court that 'the WASA charges was not part of rent and deposit made as in the instant case was not a complete or valid deposit. In this respect the landlord may have alternative way of recovering the same'. Similar is the case in this appeal as to nonpayment of utility bills.

16. Next comes the question as to whether the payment of Taka 1000 in such deed (i.e. Taka 2,000 for the entire suit premises) for each day's possession, after the expiry of the agreement can be treated as rent and accordingly whether the trial Court was justified in calculating and directing the defendant tenant to pay Taka 7,44,000, upon deducting the amount deposited with the House Rent Controller and also from the security money, for 140 months after the expiry of the agreement. In this respect the relevant portion, as to payment and security deposit in clause 8 and clause 3 and 4 respectively, of the agreement dated 22-1-1995 are required to be looked into. Clause 8 runs as follows:

“৮। আমি দলিল দাতা ২য় পক্ষ সম্পাদিত ভাড়াটিয়া চুক্তি পত্রের বলে ২ (দুই) বৎসরের জন্য অর্থাৎ ১-১-৯৫ তারিখ হইতে ৩১-১২-৯৬ ইং তারিখ পর্যন্ত ভাড়া নিয়াছি। আমার ভাড়া নেওয়া উপরোক্ত বাড়ি ভাড়া মেয়াদান্তে তথ্য ৩১-১২-৯৬ ইং তারিখের বাড়ীর মালিক মেজর (অবঃ) এম, এ, হামিদ সাহেবকে কিংবা তাহার ওয়ারিশ জনাবা মাহজাবিন মাসুদ বাশারেকুল হামিদকে খাস দখর বুঝাইয়া দিব এবং ইহাতে কোন প্রকার অনাথা হইবেনা। যদি কোন কারণে আমি আমার ভাড়া নেওয়া উক্ত  বাড়ি ৩১-১২-৯৬ ইং তারিখের পরে বাড়ির মালিকের খাস দখর বুঝাইয়া দিতে ব্যর্থ হই তাহা হইলে আমি প্রতিদিনের দখলের জন্য বাড়ির মালিকে দৈনিক ১,০০০ (এক হাজার) টাকা হিসাবে দিতে বাধ্য থাকিব। আমি আরো অঙ্গিকার করিতেছি আমার ভাড়া নেওয়া উপরোক্ত বাড়িতে আমি যে অতিথি আপ্যায়নের যে সকল নির্মানাদি করিয়াছি তাহা আমি ২য় পক্ষ নিজ খরচে অপসারণ করিয়া নিব এবং অপসারণের কার্য্য ১লা জানুয়ারী ১৯৯৭ তারিখ হইতে আরম্ভ করিব।”

Clause 3 and 4 run as follows:

৩। ২য় পক্ষ ১ম পক্ষকে ৪ (চার) মাসের সমপরিমান ভাড়ার টাকার অর্থাৎ ৪৮,০০০ (আট চল্লিশ হাজার) টাকা জামানত বা সিকিউরিটি হিসাবে প্রদান করিয়াছেন এবং প্রথম পক্ষ এতদ্বার্থে উহার প্রাপ্তি স্বীকার করিতেছেন। রশিদের মাধ্যমে স্বীকার করিয়া ২য় পক্ষকে রশিদ প্রদান করিবেন।

৪। ২য় পক্ষ ১ম পক্ষকে মাসিক ১২,০০০ (বার হাজার) টাকা হিসাবে অগ্রিম মাসিক ভাড়া প্রদান করিবেন কিন্তু জামানত বা সিকিউরিটি টাকা হইতে কোন কর্তন করা হইবে না। মেয়াদ শেষে নতুন করিয়া কোন ভাড়াটিয়া চুক্তি সম্পাদন করা হইবেন না। চুক্তির মেয়াদ শেষে ২য় পক্ষ ১ম পক্ষকে তফলিশ বর্ণিত বাড়ির দখল বুঝাইয়া দেওয়ার সময় উক্ত জামানতের টাকা ১ম পক্ষ ও ২য় পক্ষকে এককালিন সর্ব সাকুল্যে টাকা ফেরত দিবেন। দ্বিতীয় পক্ষ চুক্তি মেয়াদের মধ্যে বাড়ী ছাড়িয়া দিলে ১ম পক্ষ সিকিউরিটির টাকা ফেরত দিতে বাধ্য থাকিবেন।”

17. Reading the aforesaid clauses of both the agreements, which are same, excepting the amount of security in both the deeds, it appears that the said amount of Taka 1000 in each deed, is compensation for possessing the suit premises for each day after 31-12-1996 and security during the tenancy which is to be refunded after the expiry of the tenancy. In this respect the trial Court in its judgment found and directed as follows:

“অত্র আদেশের পরবর্তী ৩০ (ত্রিশ) দিনের মধ্যে বিবাদীকে বাড়ি ভাড়ার অতিরিক্ত ক্ষতিপূরণ বাবদ দৈনিক ২.০০০ (দুই হাজার) টাকা হারে মাসিক ৬০,০০০ (ষাট হাজার) হইতে বাড়ি ভাড়া নিয়ন্ত্রকের দপ্তরে জমা কৃত ৫৩,২০০ বাদে মাসিক ৬,৮০০ টাকা হারে চুক্তির মেয়াদ এর পরবর্তী সময় হইতে আগষ্ট/০৮ পর্যন্ত ১৪০ (একশত চল্লিশ) মাসের ক্ষতিপূরণ বাবদ ৯৫২,০০০ (নয় লক্ষ বায়ান্ন হাজার) ���াকা হইলে, তাহা হইতে সিকিউরিটি বাবদ জমাকৃত ২,০৮,০০০ (দুই লক্ষ আট হাজার) টাকা বাদে ৭,৪৪,০০০ (সাত লক্ষ চুয়াল্লিশ হাজার) টাকা পরিশোধের নির্দেশ দেওয়া গেল।

18. From the above it is clear that the learned Judge rightly held that this payment of Taka 2000 per day is in addition to the rent and since there is no determination of rent between the parties under section 14 of the Premises Rent Control Act after the expiry of the agreement, the settled principle of law is the agreed rent which was being paid by the defendant tenant to the landlord till the tenancy was terminated the same shall prevail in the absence of any further determination and that shall be the rent for the purpose of section 18 and 19 of the Act. Thus the calculation and finding of the trial Court as to payment of Taka 9,52,000 on the basis of Taka 6,800 per month for 140 months upon deducting Taka 53,200 from Taka 60,000 and further deducting Taka 2,08,000, the security money, from Taka 9,52,000 and thereby the direction to pay Taka 7,44,000 as arrear rent up to August 2008 is not in accordance with law and thus the same is liable to be set aside. The landlord respondent is liable to get the arrear rent from the tenant (defendant appellant) But for recovery of the compensation at the rate of Taka 2,000 per day in addition to the rent for overstaying in the suit premises after the expiry of the tenancy is the matter to be sorted out by the appropriate prayer in an appropriate case. In the instant case it does not show that the plaintiffs prayed for payment of compensation amount at the rate of Taka 1000 in each deed, for each days over stay. Moreover, reading clause 3 and 4 of the agreements it appears that the deeds specifically spelt out that the security money of Taka 48000 and Taka 1,60,000 (in two deeds) are to be refunded on expiry of the tenancy. Apart from this the law is also very clear on this issue. Session 10 of the Act clearly debars claiming or making any deposit/advance/security more than the amount equivalent to one month's rent and section 14 provides for refund or adjustment of such deposit within six months from the date of making such payment on an application by the tenant. Thus the trial court, although observed the payment of Taka 2000 as "compensation in addition to the rent" but deducting the same from the rent already paid by the tenant with the Rent Controller and further deducting the same from the security money is beyond the principle laid down by the apex Court in the cases reported in 10 MLR (AD) 139, 8 MLR (AD) 124 and 56 DLR 47 referred above, and, as such, the decision in this respect being not proper is liable to be set aside.

19. In respect of the question as to whether the tenant is a tenant by 'holding over' or 'by sufferance' or 'a statutory tenant' we hold that as the defendant/appellant had been found to be a defaulter on admission the question of the nature of tenancy as to "holding over" or "sufferance" or statutory tenant" is no required to be discussed or determined in this case though the tenant is possessing the suit premises, after the expiry of the tenancy, with the implied assent of the landlords, and, as such, the terms and conditions of the agreements automatically became operative and having not paid the rents to the Rent Controller admittedly within the first week of every month after the expiry of the agreements on 31-12-1996 he becomes a defaulter. Once the tenant is found to be a defaulter during the tenancy period, it is immaterial to determine whether he has also defaulted on subsequent occasions. The 41 DLRs case, facts of which are not similar to those of the present case, and many other cases have categorically spelt out and set down the principle for determining the nature of such tenancy, depending on the facts and circumstances of each case, and consequences thereof.

20. Lastly, whether the defendant appellant tenant violated the terms and conditions of the agreement and thereby made himself liable to be evicted from the suit premises.

21. It is alleged in the plaint that the tenant constructed tin-shed structure in the vacant portion of the suit premises for entertainment of guests without prior consent of the plaintiff-respondent landlords and thereby made himself liable to be evicted from the suit premises under sub-section 1 of section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991. In this respect apart from the undertaking made by the tenant in clause 8 of the agreements as to removal of the structures by 1-1-1997, he, in his cross-examination as DW 1 admitted as follows:

“আমার শেষ চুক্তি হয় ১৯৯৫ ইং সনের জানুয়ারীতে। শেষ চুক্তিতে আমি স্বীকারকরি খালি জায়গায় নির্মিত স্থাপনা অনুমতি ব্যতীত করেছি এবং চুক্তির মেয়াদ শেষ হওয়ার পর আমরা তুলে নিয়ে যাব।”

<u>22. So, from the above it appears that the tenant appellant admitted that he constructed the tin-shed structures in the vacant space of the suit premises without prior permission or consent of the plaintiff landlords and, as such, he admitted that he. violated the terms of agreements and thus acted contrary to section 108(p) of the Transfer of Property Act which makes him liable to come within the mischief of section 18(1)(Ka) of the Premises Rent Control Act, and binds himself to vacate the suit premises for which he is not entitled to get any protection of law from eviction even if he is not found to be a defaulter in payment of rent. Under such circumstances the tenant cannot avoid eviction under section 18(1)(ka) of the Act 1991 for violating the terms of the agreement.</u>

23. Considering the facts and circumstances stated hereinabove and the decisions referred to by the parties and also on the basis of the principle laid down in the case of Md Nasiruddin vs Md Mizanur Rahman, Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1300 of 2006 (BSCD 2008 page 121) "Even the tenant cannot resist h is eviction if he is found defaulter for one month only and the Premises rent Control Act requires that the tenant must pay the monthly rent in terms of section 18 within the prescribed period to get protection from eviction and not other- wise," we are of the view that the defendant appellant tenant has been proved to be a "defaulter" on his own admission, for nonpayment of rent for the month of December 1996 and also guilty of "violating the terms of the lease agreements" admittedly by constructing structures on the vacant apace of the vacant space of the suit premises and, as such, is not entitled to get any protection from eviction under section 18(1) and 18(5) of the Act. In this respect we find substance in the submissions of Mr Rahman. Thus the defendant appellant tenant is liable to be evicted. Accordingly, the findings of the trial court, complained of herein in this appeal, is hereby affirmed. But so far the calculation to pay Taka 7,44,000 by the trial court, we are of the view that since compensation or security cannot be adjusted with the rent, hence the aforesaid direction of payment is wrong and, as such, the same is liable to be set aside.

24. For the reasons and discussions made hereinabove the appeal is allowed in part. The defendant tenant is a defaulter and guilty of violating the terms of the agreement as such liable to be evicted from the suit premises. The defendant appellant tenant is accordingly directed to vacate the suit premises within 30 days, upon removing the unauthorized structures situated on the suit premises in default the plaintiff respondent will be at liberty to get the decree executed in accordance with law. But the finding calculation and direction of the Trial Court to pay Taka 7,44,000 to the landlords being not in accordance with law the same is set aside. However, the plaintiff respondent landlords are entitled to withdraw/receive the rents deposited with the House Rent Controller since January 1997 till vacating the suit premises in accordance with law.

25. The connected Civil Rule No. 709 (F) of 2009 is hereby discharged. The ad interim order granted earlier in the Rule is also vacated.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.
