case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 3rd day of April, 2004 passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 229 of 2003 heard analogously with cross First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 294 of 2003 arising out of Arbitration Case No. 296 of 2000).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim, J: The Appeals, by leave are directed against the judgment and order dated 3-4-2004 by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 229 of 2003 heard analogously with Cross-First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 294 of 2003 arising out of Arbitration and Joint District Judge, Dhaka dismissing the appeal and allowing the Cross-Appeal with cost and sending the case back on remand to the Arbitrator for assessment of compensation afresh of the appellant's land acquired from date of service of notice on 30-10-1965.

2. The appellants filed the case stating, inter-alia, that the appellant made written bainanama on 3 1-10-1963 with the original owners for purchase of 16.65½ acres of chala land of CS Plot Nos. 44, 45, 46, 49, 77, 80, 76, 75, 81, 40, 48 and 70 of Ranabhola Mouza presently under the Police Station Uttara at a consideration of Taka 46,500 and took over possession. On that basis a regular sale deed (Exhibit 56 Cha) was executed and registered on 9-5-1969 on receipt of the full consideration money. Thereafter, the appellants raised its entire purchased land and developed it and converted the same into bhiti land. The aforesaid bhiti land with an area of 11.5750 acres of CS Plot Nos·. 45, 46, 48, 49, 70 and 76 along with running 8 industrial units set up by the appellants at a huge cost was purportedly acquired by the respondents under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 in Special LA Case No. 8 0f 1964-65 for setting up a rehabilitation zone for rehabilitation of the persons affected by the Scheme of Uttar a Model Town. No notice was served on the appellants. Possession of the land was taken over in 1972 after demolition of eight units of running industries there on. The appellants were paid. an amount of Taka 1,34,177 for the land, Taka 8,83,110.78 for the structures and Taka 2,913.24 for the trees standing on a portion thereof on the basis of provisional estimate on rough and ready calculation as per provisions of section 93(B) of the Town Improvement Act, 1953. That the respondents while taking-over physical possession of such a big area of bhiti land after paying a very small amount of money on rough and ready calculation started delaying the process of acquisition for years together in spite of repeated written representations to complete the same and to pay the compensation according to law but in vain. Of late, the appellants were forced to file Writ Petition No. 3828 of 1992 before the High Court Division for a direction either to release the land or to complete the process of acquisition early and to pay compensation. After hearing both sides, a direction was given on 2-8-1994 to the respondents to complete the process of acquisition within a period of six months from the date. Even the respondents did not comply with the aforesaid direction. Contempt Petition No. 13 of 1995 was started and a proceeding was drawn up against the respondents. By this time the process of acquisition was completed hurriedly by publishing it in the official gazette on 31-8-2000 as contemplated under section 93A(4)(h) of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and final award was made on 9-10-2000 by the Deputy Commissioner after about 35 years for a total amount Taka 10,10,257.49 paisa per acre. Thereafter, three separate notices (Exhibit 46) under section 7(aa) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 were issued asking the appellants to receive the balance amount. The appellants, not being satisfied with the amount of compensation offered on the basis of the aforesaid final award, filed an application before the learned Joint District Judge and Arbitrator, Dhaka as per provisions of section 7(aaa) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. It may be mentioned that under the provisions of section 93A(5)(b)(I) of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 an aggrieved person may also file similar application to the Arbitrator. In the instant case since the notices for receiving compensation were issued under section 7(11) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948, so the appellants filed the aforesaid application under section 7(aaa) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. Moreover, provisions of both the Acts are pari materia applicable so far it relates to assessment and payment of compensation. Arbitration Case No. 226 of 2000 was started on the said application in which the appellants claimed (a) Taka 115,75,00,000 as compensation for 11.5750 acres of bhiti land (b) Taka 57,87,50,000 as statutory compensation of 50% (c) Taka 3,22,05,000 as recurring loss for permanent acquisition of (d) Taka 50,00,000 for severance cost (e) Taka 80,000 for cost of structure (f) Taka 2,00,000 for tress i.e. in al Taka 178,50,16,000.

3. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed separate written objection denying the claim of the appellants asserting that the final assessment as has been done by the Deputy Commissioner is correct. By judgment and order dated 15-1-2003, the Joint District Judge and Arbitrator allowed Taka 4,52,75,612.50 as compensation for 11.5750 bhiti land 15% statutory interest Taka 67,91,341.87 paisa i.e. total Taka 5,20,66,954.37 paisa minus previously taken Taka 1,39,768.12 paisa balance Taka 5,19,27,186.25 paisa. It was submitted before the High Court Division that the Joint District Judge, and Arbitrator while assessing compensation for the appellants 11.5750 acres of bhiti land after due and proper appreciation of materials on record particularly Exhibit 53(Ka) by mistake referred chala land in some places and illegally rejected appellants claim for potential earnings there from for the last 35 years amounting to Taka 32,28,000 at the rate of Taka 40,00,000 per year and (II) severance cost of Taka 50,00,000 on the basis of materials on record particularly Exhibit 56. Besides, the Joint District Judge and the Arbitrator in making final assessment erroneously considered the average value of lands of the period from 1972 to 2000 instead of the period from 1988 to 2000 from such gazette notification.

4. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and award the appellants filed First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 229 of 2003 before the High Court Division on 20-4-2003. The respondent No.2 tiled a Cross Miscellaneous Appeal No. 294 of 2003 against the said judgment and award. Both the appeals were heard together, By judgment and order dated 3-4-2004 the High Court Division, after hearing, dismissed the First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 229 of 2003 filed by the appellants and allowed Cross-Miscellaneous Appeal No. 294 of 2003 filed by the respondent No.2 with cost and after setting aside the judgment and award of the Joint District Judge and Arbitrator, sent the case back on remand to the Joint District Judge and Arbitrator for assessment of compensation afresh on the basis of value of similar land with similar advantages during 24 months proceeding the date of service of notice on 30-10-1965. .

<u>5. Leave was granted to consider the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellants that" the impugned judgment and order dismissing the appellants appeals and allowing the respondent No. 2's cross-appeal with cost and sending the case back on remand for assessment of compensation afresh of the acquired land during twenty-four months preceding the date of service of notice on 30-10-1954, is not legal and the same is against the settled principles of law as laid down in the decision reported in 23 DLR (SC) 25. 27 DLR (AD) 65 and 29 DLR (SC)110; that the High Court Division while observing that period of such requisitioned property shall end with the publication of notification in the official gazette under section 93A(5)(h) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 and such requirement was mainly intended to bring to an end to the requisitioned proceedings and has got nothing to do with the mode and manner of determination of the price of acquired land, misinterpreted the relevant provisions of law and came to a decision contrary to the settled principle of law as enunciated by this Court reported in 23 DLR (SC) 25 and 29 DLR (AD) 110; that the High Court Division failed to appreciate and consider properly that the Joint District Judge and the Arbitrator while assessing compensation of the appellants 11.5750 acres of bhiti land at Taka 5,20,66,954.37 paisa on these basis of materials on record, particularly Exhibit 53(Ka) the registered deed dated 10-9-1999 has taken into consideration the proximity in between the average value of the land with similar description and similar advantages in the vicinity during 24 months preceding the date of Gazette Notification dated 31-8-2000 and the service of notice dated 18-1-1966 under section 5(1 a) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 at Taka 10,50,000 per acre which is in conformity with the decision of reported in 42 DLR (AD) 99.</u>

6. Mr Rafiqul Islam, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellants, submitted that the impugned judgment and order dismissing the appellants' appeals and allowing the respondent No. 2's Cross- Miscellaneous Appeal with cost and sending the case back on remand for assessment of compensation afresh of the acquired land during twenty-four months preceding the date of service of notice on 30-10-1965 is not legal and the same is against the settled principles of law; that. the period of such acquisitioned property shall end with the publication of notification in the official gazette under section 93A(5)(h) of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and under section 5(7) of (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 and such requirement was mainly intended to bring an end to the requisitioned proceedings and has got nothing to do with the mode and manner of determination of the price of acquired land, misinterpreted and mis-appreciated the relevant provisions of law and came to a decision contrary to the settled principles of law as enunciated by the highest Court; that the learned Joint District Judge and the Arbitrator while assessing compensation of the appellants 11.5750 acres of bhiti land at Taka 5,20,66,654.37 paisa on the basis of materials on record, particularly Exhibit 53(Ka) the registered deed dated 10-9-1999 has taken into consideration the proximity in between the average value of the land with similar description and similar advantages in the vicinity during 24 months preceding the date of gazette notification dated 31-8-2000 and of the service of notice dated 18-1-1966 under section 5(1a) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 at Taka 10,50,000 per acre; that the appellants received the part amount of compensation money on the basis of rough and ready calculation with objection and in his deposition as PW 1 categorically stated that he received the amount with objection, the High Court Division is not justified in taking evasive view on that point: that out of, total 16.65½ acres of appellants land only 11.5750 acres was acquired in Special LA Case No. 8 of 1964-65 and the fact was corroborated by evidence both oral and documentary; that while deciding to send the case back on remand to the learned Joint District Judge and the Arbitrator for assessment of compensation afresh as stated earlier the High Court Division failed to consider that the respondent took more than 35 years to complete the process of acquisition in the instant case.

7. Mr TH Khan, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondents, submitted that the determination of compensation price on the date of publication of notice finally acquiring the land in 2000 is against the law; that the Deputy Commissioner correctly determined the price on the average of 24 months' price preceding the date of service of initial, notice for acquisition whereas the learned Arbitrator erroneously determined the price prevailing in 2000 when the notification finally acquiring the land was published in the gazette on 31-8-2000; that acquisition and requisition in accordance with law is lawful even if payment of compensation is delayed: that the law requiring the Government to publish a notification in the official gazette that the Government has decided to acquire the requisitioned property and with such publication, the requisitioned property shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances; that the period of such requisition of such property shall and is the same as provided in section 93A(5)(h) of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 and section 5(7) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. Such notice was mainly intended to bring an end to the acquisition proceeding and has got nothing to do with the mode and manner of determination of the price of acquired land; that the perfection of requisition and acquisition of properties by the Government is not dependent upon payment of Compensation as far as possession thereof is concerned with the publication of the requisition notices in the gazette, the land or properties so requisitioned or acquired become vested in the provincial Government and compensation is paid in terms of the law either at ordering the requisition of properties or thereafter, but the vesting of the properties in the Government is not contingent on payment or non- payment of the compensation. The learned Counsel further submitted that under section 5(7) of the Act, 1948 the Provincial Government shall publish in the official gazette a notice to the effect that the Provincial Government has decided to acquire the requisitioned property; that determination of the price of the land by the learned Arbitrator was imaginary, baseless and against the law and such assessment could not be sustained in the facts and circumstances of the case; that the Deputy Commissioner determined the price of the land on the average of sales of similar land in the area. After the final award was given, very small amount was due to appellants for which the grievance of the appellants has got no basis. Finally, the learned Counsel submitted that the facts of the cases cited by the appellants are distinguishable and are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant cases and the High Court Division acted lawfully and in accordance with law in dismissing the appeals while allowing the cross-appeals with cost.

8. It appears from the record that the Deputy Commissioner determined the price of land on the average of sales of similar land in the area from 1963 at Taka 1,39,768.12 out of which the appellants already received Taka 1,34,177. Price of the structures through a joint inventory was determined at Taka 38,67,153.07 of which the appellants received Taka 8,63,110.78 and price of trees etc. was assessed at Taka 3,336.42 of which the appellants received Taka 2,913.24. After the final award was given, very small amount was due to appellant, for which grievance of the appellants has got no basis. It further appears that the Deputy Commissioner determined the price on the average of 24 months price preceding the date of service of initial notice for acquisition. The Arbitrator determined the price on the average of the same as determined by the Deputy Commissioner and that available in 2000 when the notification finally acquiring the land was published in the gazette. The appellants claim compensation at the rate of price on the date of publication of the notice finally acquiring the land in 2000. Under the pari materia of law for the purpose of acquisition, the price of the acquired land is to be calculated on the basis of the price of similar land with similar advantage during twenty four months preceding the date of service of initial notice for acquisition.

9. At the present, the Rule is changed for determination of the price on the basis of twelve months average preceding the date of publication of initial notice .for acquisition. Under all the provisions, the price of the land is to be determined with reference to the date of service and/or publication of the initial notice for acquisition. By Ordinance XIII of 1963, 'five years' average was substituted to 'twenty-four months.'

10. In the case of Bangladesh vs Abdul Khaleque 29 DLR (SC) 110. the Arbitrator assessed the compensation applying the Rule of two years average available under the Ordinance III of 1965 promulgated on 22-3-1965 but made retrospective with effect from 15-8-1963.

11. This Division framed the question for consideration as follow;

"What will be the law for the assessment of compensation for lands acquired either under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 or under section 5 of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 in view of the amendment of the former Act by Ordinance III of 1965, and the latter by Ordinance, XIII of 1963 and both Ordinances came into operation of 15-8-1963, the former retrospectively and the latter prospectively."

12.	This Court held that

"The sub-section clearly says that the step so taken and notice given is barely a proposal to acquire. Sub-section (6) provides for the decision of the Government to acquire, and sub- section (7) for the publication of the Government's decision, and the vesting of the property in the Government under the Act. Therefore, the property is acquired when the gazette notifications published under section 5(7) of the Act and the law in force on that day regarding the principles and manner of payment of compensation shall be governing law."

13. From plain reading of section 5(7) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 compensation is to be assessed when property is to be acquired under-section 5(7)or when the dispute about the compensation is referred to the Arbitrator in the case reported in 23 DLR (AD) 25.

<u>14. A notice under section 5(1) is only first step in the acquisition of a property. The Government may decide not to acquire the property on the report of the authorised officer and accordingly, no right or obligation arises due to issuance of a notice declaring merely the intention of Government to acquire any requisitioned property and accordingly no right or obligation is created by issuance of such notice. Thus, forming definitely the intention of the Government to acquire the property upon issuance of a notice under section 5(7) published in the official gazette definitely demonstrated that the property stood acquired and vested in the Government only when the question of assessment of compensation for the purpose arises. Thus, compensation should be assessed in accordance with state of law as it prevails when the property thus stands acquired.</u>

15. A requisitioned property before it stands acquired is to pass through various stages as set out in different sub-sections of section 5 when the gazette notification is published under sub-section 7 of section 5 of the Act and the law in force on that day is a date regarding the principles and manner of payment of compensation shall be the governing law. It has been held in the case of Bangladesh vs Abdul Khaleque reported in 29 DLR (SC) 110 that "We think, that on a true construction of the principal law of section 7, the governing date will be when the property stands acquired. Section 7 clearly says that on the requisition or acquisition of the property, the compensation in the manner indicated in the section shall be paid." On 15-8-1963 Ordinance XIII of 1963 was promulgated introducing twenty-four months average in place of gazette notification dated 30-3-1914 under section 5(7) of the Act was published on 9-4-1964 and the Supreme Court held that the value of compensation is to be assessed as the law stands when the property was acquired.

16. In the said decision it was held that "we, therefore, accept the decision of Sharafatullah's case to the extent it says that the compensation should be assessed in accordance with law as it prevails when the property stands acquired, but not the two other suggested dates." The said decision, thus, resolved the controversy as to the date which will govern the assessment of compensation.

17. In the case of Abdul Gafur Khan vs Bangladesh reported in 42 DLR (AD) 99 by this judgment the compensation as awarded by the Arbitrator has challenged the enhancement which was made by the Arbitrator in accordance with law. Although they differ as to which is the appropriate law governing the subject. The fact of the case was an area of 9.09 acres of land including tank was requisitioned under section 3 of the Emergency Requisition of Property. Act and possession was taken on 8-3-1961 for construction of WAPDA Colony. Subsequently, the said land was acquired on 1st November, 1968. The Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi, assessed compensation at Taka 41,053.03 paisa, the rate of which comes about Taka 4,500 per acre. The land owners did not accept this assessment on the ground that it was very inadequate and brought the matter to the Arbitrator appointed under the Act. Before the Arbitrator, the Government produced some sale deeds of years 1958-1961 in order to show that the average value of similarly situated lands in the neighborhood was Taka 6,000 (six thousand) per acre; whereas the land owners produced some sale deeds of the year 1968 showing per acre value of land in the vicinity at Taka 60,000 (sixty thousand). The Arbitrator did not accept either of the two widely divergent claims and fixed valuation at Taka 20,000 (twenty thousand) per acre and on that basis made an award for Taka 2,52,361. The owners filed an FMAT No. 242 of 1979 and the single Judge of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment took the average value of land during the period between year 1961 in which the land was finally requisitioned, and the year 1968 in which the land was finally acquired and on that basis fixed compensation at Taka 30,000 and on that basis fixed per acre. Accordingly, the learned single Judge of the High Court Division raised the assessment from. Taka 2,52,361 to 3,50,000.

18. In the appeal the learned Advocate for the appellant though submitted that the appellant who took leave to appeal was that the period of twenty- four months should precede the date of acquisition i.e. 1st November, 1968, but the Appellate Division held that this contention is palpably wrong being contrary to the statutory provision of law. In view of the law the Government in that case contended that the twenty-four months should precede the date of requisition but the land owners' contention was that twenty-four months should precede the date of acquisition. In the instant case though the notice for acquisition under section 5(a) was served in 1962 the land was actually acquired in 1968 i.e. after the expiry of 6 years when the value of the land increased to a great extent. The Government did not explain why the notice was served in 1962 but acquisition was made in 1968. The said decision proceed to hold that "although there is no particular period within which a requisitioned land is to be acquired for the notice for acquisition has been served, yet when the value of the land was increasing but that of money was decreasing the compensation to be paid now on the valuation of the year, 1962 would cause substantial injury to the land owner. There should be some proximity between the date of notice for acquisition and that actual acquisition. Be that as it may, the point of law now taken during the hearing of the appeal before us was not raised. The learned single judge of the High Court Division missed the appropriate law for laches of the Government; but valuation at Taka 30,000 per acre is found to have met the ends of justice, fairness and equity in this case in the circumstances as shown above.

19. In the instant case, the Deputy Commissioner determined the price of the land on the average of sale of similar land in the area from 1963 to 1965 at Taka 1,39,768.12 for the total land acquired. Following the aforesaid decision, particularly the decision in the case of Abdul Gafur Khan vs Bangladesh 42 DLR (AD) 99 we have noticed the gap between the notices of acquisition in 1963 and the final order of acquisition under section 5(7) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, On 2000.

20. Thus, we found that the amount assessed for compensation for the land was at shockingly low price according to the valuation of 2000 when the land stood acquired causing substantial injury to the land owner. The acquisition Authority lost sight of proximity both of the notices and the date of actual acquisition and even the High Court Division missed the appropriate part of laches of the Government in finally publishing the gazette acquiring the land in 2000 and the valuation of land in 1963 being negligible whereas the value of land unbelievably increased in 2000 than when the land in question stood requisitioned.

21. It appears from the judgment of Arbitrator i.e. Joint District Judge, Arbitration Court, Dhaka, fixed the value of the land at Taka 78,12,500 adding 25% more than the 'chala' land for 'nal' land and arrived at a finding that per acre of 'chala' land at Taka (78,12,500 + 10,500) ./. 2 = 39,11,400 and accordingly fixed the schedule land of 11.5750 acres of Taka 4,52,75,612.50 and together with 15% statutory compensation amounts of Taka 67,91,341.87 totaling 5,20,66,954.37 out of which the petitioner has already withdrawn Taka 1,39,768.92 remaining Taka 5,19,27,185.45.

22. The High Court Division, however, held that the appeal of the appellant was dismissed allowing the cross-appeal of the respondent-Government setting aside the impugned order of the Arbitrator and sending back the case on remand for assessment of compensation afresh of the land acquired on the basis of value of similar land and with similar advantage during twenty-four months in the light of its observations within a period of three months from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment.

23. It appears that the initial notice of acquisition was issued in the case on 30-10-1965 and the Deputy Commissioner determined the price of the value on the average sale during twenty-four months preceding the date of service of notice for acquisition at Taka 10,500.00, the total price of the land being at Taka 1,39,768.12, out of which the appellant already received Taka 1,34,177.

24. In the decision reported in 42 DLR (AD) 99 discussed above though the land was acquired under section 5(1)(a) in 1963 but finally such acquisition under sub-section 7 of section 5 was published by the Government in 1967.

25. In the said cited decision, thus, the acquisition was made in 1963 but the final gazette notification was published in 1967, considering the proximity of the date and for the ends of justice the Court fixed Taka 30,000 as the proper value for the acquired land. Following the principle decided in the said decision, in the instant case though the land was initially acquired in 1965 but the gazette notification under sub-section 7 of section 5 was published in 2000 with rise in the land value and the depreciation of the money value meanwhile and the deliberate laches of the Government to issue the final order, we are of the view that the valuation at Taka 80,000 (eighty thousand) per acre is found to meet the ends of justice, fairness and equity resulting in substantial justice in this case.

26. The amount of compensation regarding the trees, houses and structures taken over earlier were determined during the period of such takeover and accordingly, paid and, as such, no fresh assessment for the same as to the value of the trees, buildings and the structures at the relevant time do not arise in the fact and circumstances of the case. With this finding and observation we disposed of the appeal and sent the same to the Arbitrator for assessment of compensation in the light of our finding above for the land actually acquired in the case as early as possible.

Accordingly, the appeal is disposed of directing the Arbitrator to determine the trial involved in acquisition for assessment of compensation at Taka 80,000 per acre without any order as to costs.

End.

Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Farah Mahbub J: This Rule under Article 102 of the Constitution has been issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to implement the recommendation of the "Sick Industry Rehabilitation Cell" dated 29-1-1992 (Annexure B) and why the respondent No.5 should not be directed to take steps to get adjournment of the Mortgage Suit No. 71 of 1995 pending in the Court of Subordinate Judge (now the Joint District Judge), 1st Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong till final decision of the Reconciliation Committee as notified in the Bangladesh Gazette dated 4-2-1997 by the respondent No.2, Banking Division (Annexure E) and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. To appreciate the points that have been canvassed before us, it will be convenient to narrate briefly, the material fact in chronological order.

3. The petitioner company being registered with the Registrar of Joint Stock Company under the Companies Act, 1913 was engaged in manufacturing different categories of steel materials including erection and construction materials of all descriptions. However, the project financing was done by the respondent No.3, Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha. The respondent No.4, Investment Corporation of Bangladesh, made the bridge financing and respondent No.5, Arab Bangladesh Bank Limited through respondent No.6, its branch office, participated in the working capital financing of the project. It is the claim of the petitioner company that due to natural calamity which took place in the year 1991 and also due to the adverse impact of free market economic policy adopted by the then government rendered the petitioner company a sick project. At that juncture the government vide gazette notification dated 15-6-1991 (published on 11-7-1991) Annexure 'A' to the writ petition, constituted a high powered "Cell" with the administrative heads of different ministries, and other institutions run by the government with a view to identify the sick industries, the causes for its becoming a sick project and to give guidelines of the possible remedial measures in each case. Pursuant to the aforesaid notification the Member Secretary of the সুপারিশ বাস্তবায়ন কমিটি”, vide letter dated 29-9-1992 Annexure 'B' to the writ petition, with a copy to the petitioner company requested the respondent Nos. 3, 4 and 5 to provide required assistance to the petitioner company in the light of recommendation given thereto. But without paying any heed to the said letter of recommendation the respondent bank namely, Arab Bangladesh Bank Limited instituted a Mortgage Suit being No. 71 of 1995 on 13-9-1995 in the court of Subordinate Judge (now the Joint District Judge), 1st Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong against the loanee, the petitioner company as defendant for recovery of loan amounting to Taka 3,40,94,500.93 (Taka three crore forty lac ninety- four thousand five hundred and paisa ninety three) only, vide Annexure C to the writ petition. Ultimately, the defendant-petitioner company filed written statement in order to contest the suit on 16-3-1997, vide Annexure 'C' to the writ petition. Meanwhile, the respondent "No. 1, the Finance Ministry, Banking Division by publishing another gazette notification dated 6-3-1997 constituted a "Reconciliation Committee" consisting of five members to resolve the disputes out of court where the suit is pending and the bank concerned has been given the discretion to decide the issue in question upon considering the recommendations of the said "Committee". However, if disagreement occurs the concerned bank or the financial institution is to send the respective proposals to the Banking Division, Ministry of Finance for final decision and till then, the pending suits shall be kept in abeyance. In view of the said notification vide Annexure E, the petitioner company made several representations to the respondent bank but in vain. Hence, finding no other alternative, the loanee as the petitioner preferred the instant application under Article 102 of the Constitution in the nature of mandamus directing the respondent bank to implement the recommendation given by the said Committee, vide Annexure B to the writ petition.

4. Ms Hosne Ara Begum the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner company has put forward a three-fold argument on behalf of the petitioner company. She has contended in the first place that in view of Article 152 of the Constitution the Gazette notification, vide Annexure 'A', by which a high powered cell being constituted to identify the sick industries, its causes for being sick and to give recommendation for effective solution to the problem lying therewith, is a notification, and has the force of law for having been published in the Bangladesh Gazette by the order of the President. Hence, recommendation given by this "Cell" or 'Committee' vide letter dated 29-9-1992, Annexure B, in favour of the petitioner Company shall be incumbent and binding upon the respondent Nos. 5 and 6. In support of the said contention the learned Advocate has referred the case of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Establishment vs Shafiuddin and others reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 and the case of Jihad Ahmed and others vs Bangladesh Power Development Board and others reported in 52 DLR (AD) 75. In this connection referring to the case of Rony Twines Ltd vs Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Finance reported in 14 BLT 276 the learned Advocate further contends that in the said case one of the benches of this Division while making the Rule absolute observed, "Vide Annexure A to the Writ Petition a Special Committee was constituted by the Ministry of Finance which was duly notified in the gazette. Being a financial institution the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha has no way to bypass or avoid the instructions, directives, policy guidelines in respect of financial management issued by the Ministry of Finance. Hence, recommendation of the Special Committee of the Finance Division of Ministry of Finance is binding upon Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha". In coming to the said findings the High Court Division considered the case of Quaderia Publications Limited and others vs Sonali Bank passed in Writ Petition No. 1370 of 1991 which was affirmed by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 511 of 2000. In the present case as well, the learned Advocate submits, a "Committee" has been constituted under the order of the President and has been published in the Bangladesh Gazette, hence, recommendation given by the said "Committee" in the light of the above decisions is to be construed as "having the force of law" and is binding upon the respondent Bank.

5. The second contention raised by the learned Advocate is that the respondent bank instead of complying with the said recommendation dated 29-9-1992, vide Annexure' B' instituted a mortgage suit which is wholly illegal and without lawful authority.

6. The third and last contention being posed by the learned Advocate is that as per Rules of Business being promulgated under the authority envisaged under Article 55(6) of the Constitution of Bangladesh the executive is empowered to take decision or formulate policy in order to run the administration of the Government functionaries. In that view of the matter since the executive has constituted a "Reconciliation Committee", vide Annexure E, to resolve the dispute of those sick industries it has become an incumbent duty on the part of the financial institution to keep the pending case in abeyance till financial decision is taken by the Banking Division, Ministry of Finance.

7. Before parting with her submission the learned Advocate submits that the notification dated 15-6-1991 issued by the order of the President, published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 11-7-1991 has conceived and created a vested right to give effect to the recommendation being given by the said "Cell" 'vide' Annexure B for having the force of law in view of Article 152 of the Constitution and accordingly, she submits that the Rule should be made absolute by giving direction to the respondent bank to implement the recommendation given in favour of the petitioner company.

8. Mr Shahnawaz Akhand, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent Nos. 5 and 6, submits that the constitution of high powered "Cell" to identify the sick industry and ways for effective measures for their rehabilitation are merely matters of policies taken by the executive, the Government for rehabilitating the ideritified sick industries. The said "Cell" being constituted by the executive order under the Rules of Business for formulation of policy guidelines its recommendation cannot be held to have the force of law and have no binding effect upon the respondent bank only for the notification being issued by the order of the President and for having been published in the Bangladesh Gazette.

9. The learned Advocate next submits that admittedly the petitioner company took loan from the respondent bank. Hence, in default the bank in its turn has the right to recover the said dues in accordance with law. However, on the prayer of the petitioner-company the respondent bank has re- scheduled the loan amount on a number of occasions and the petitioner company in response to it has accepted the said re-schedulement but failed to fulfil its terms. In consequence, finding no other alternative the respondent bank instituted the mortgage suit in accordance with law on 13-9-1995. But even after more than ten years it failed to reach its finality by adjudication due to the dilatory tactics of the petitioner company.

10. Mr Akhand lastly, on drawing our attention to the Annexure "E" to the writ petition, submits that by gazette publication dated 6-3-1997, a "Re-conciliation Committee" was constituted headed by different government functionaries with a view to resolve the dispute out of Court and so has arisen between the identified sick industry and the respective bank. Keeping in view the said scheme of re-conciliation or mediation the legislature subsequently has incorporated different provisions of law in the remedial statute, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 as were not available in the earlier repealed statute, the Artha Rin Adalat, Ain, 1990 and would now be applicable in the petitioner company's case while adjudicating the respective mortgage suit. Thereby it has given the petitioner company ample opportunity to resolve the dispute with the respondent bank within the ambit of the said Ain, 2003 even after conclusion of execution proceeding. Accordingly, the learned Advocate prays that the present Rule having had no merit for consideration should be discharged with costs.

11. Mr Md Sham sur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the Respondent No.3 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition, submits that he has nothing further to add on point of law as has already been placed before this court by the learned Advocate for the respondent Nos. 5 and 6 except on bringing notice to Article 7(2) of the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha Ordinance, 1972 he submits that in view of the said provision of law the respondent No. 3 considered the recommendation of the "Cell" in its meeting held on 18-3-1993 vide Annexure 1 to the affidavit-in-opposition and extended re-scheduling facilities to the petitioner company in the shape of waiver of 75% simple interest and 100% penal interest but the petitioner company did not avail the said facility. Further, on 6-4-1998 the respondent No.3 allowed waver of 100% simple interest and 100% penal interest as evident from Annexure 1 (a) to the affidavit-in-opposition. But the petitioner company did not fulfil the conditions of the said waiver facilities extended to the petitioner company by the respondent No.3, the BSRS.

12. The question which now centres for disposal is, whether the notification issued by the .order of President dated 11-7-1991 Annexure A is "law" within the meaning of Article 152 of the Constitution and whether the recommendation dated 29-9-1992, Annexure B, given by the said "Cell" constitution under the said notification could be regarded as "having the force of law" in order to regulate the court's proceeding started under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990.

13. In the present case, admittedly a high powered "Cell" represented by different ministries and other government functionaries was constituted by the order of the President vide notification No. Shim/Shibi-1/2M-47/91/195(15) dated 15-6-1991 and the same was published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 11-7-1991 at page 183 (Annexure' A') in the following manner:

15. Now, the proposition being posed by the petitioner company is, whether the notification dated 11-7-91, Annexure' A', having been published in the Bangladesh Gazette by the order of the President and the "Cell" being constituted thereby is a statutory committee and its recommendation can be considered as having the force of law and is binding upon the respondent Nos. 5 and 6, the Arab Bangladesh Bank Ltd. or not.

16. However, as per Article 152 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh "law" means any Act, Ordinance, order, rule, regulation, by-law, notification or order legal instrument, and. any custom or usage, having the force of law in Bangladesh."

17. The above Article of the Constitution defines the terms "law" and "having the force of law in Bangladesh." The said definition is enumerative rather than substantive i.e. it mentions some of the normal forms in which the law finds its expression. In other words, the said Article speaks for both statutory law and custom or usage having the force of law in Bangladesh. In case of statutory law, it can be made either directly by the legislature or by the order subordinate authorities under the delegated law making powers. This delegated legislation appears under various names like ordinance, orders, regulations, notifications and by-laws mentioned in Article 152 of the Constitution. This list is not exhaustive because delegated legislation may appear under other name also. However, the term "notification" which is relevant for disposal of the present Rule, may be of two kinds. Most government orders are notified in gazette for public gaze only. All of them may not be treated as law. Only such notifications have the mandate of law which are species of subordinate legislation passed by a body having the authority to promulgate them and which lay down the rules of conduct for persons in the community to obey. But there may be notifications which lay down no rule of conduct. For example, all appointments and transfers of officers are notified through notifications and these are merely executive orders for the purpose of information to the public and do not lay down any rule of conduct to be followed by persons in the community.

<u>18. It is, therefore, clear that in order that a notification or order to have the mandate of law it is required to be passed by a body authorised by law for such purpose, and it is only then it will be enforceable by courts and other authorities.</u>

19. Let us now examine the notification in the present case on the basis of the above noted observations. The notification dated 11-7-91 says that for rehabilitation and to make refunctional the sick industries of the country a "Cell" has been constituted with nine members of different minis- tries and other government functionaries and its functions would be:

(1) To determine the sick industries in different sectors of the country;

(2) To find out the sick industries and its causes for being sick in the light of the said definition; and

(3) To submit report to the Ministry of Industry after formulating recommendation for effective solution to the respective problem in .each case.

<u>20. The said notification was published in the Bangladesh Gazette by the Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Industry as per order of the President. Subsequently, the said "Cell" or Committee gave recommendation in favour of the petitioner company on 29-9-92 stating, inter alia, শিল্প প্রতিষ্ঠানটিকে প্রয়োজনীয় সহায়তা গ্রহণের জন্য অনুরোধ করা হইল” On a plain reading of the same it transpires that in effect the said notification has been sued by a committee constituted by order of the President with a view to formulate policy which will enable to rehabilitate and recharge the sick industries in co-operation with the respective financial institutions which is neither the product of the Constitution nor the statute known as "Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990. As such, it cannot be considered as law, as argued by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, the loanee. However, the learned Advocate also tried to have a shelter under the provisions laid down in Article 55(6) of the Constitution since such notification, published in the Bangladesh Gazette, is found to have been made by the order of the President. But unfortunately, we are unable to accept this contention since the provision of Article 55(6) stands for rule making power of the President for the allocation and transaction of business of the Government which is available in the very preface of the Rules of Business in the following language:</u>

<u>"In exercise of the powers conferred by Article 55(6) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and in supersession of all previous rules and orders on the subject the President is pleased to make the following rules for allocation and transaction of business of the Government".</u>

21. As such, the Rules of Business only stands for transaction of the day-to-day business of the Government, which also deals with allocation of business amongst different Ministries and Divisions. But it does not empower the President or Government to frame Rules to regulate the court's proceeding which has been initiated under the enacted law. Therefore; any direction, recommendation or instruction made thereunder for the guidance of any other authorities is not meant to be enforceable under any legal obligation as has also been observed in the case of State of West Bengal vs Anwar Ali reported in AIR 1952 (SC) 75.

<u>22. Moreover, the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the recommendation given by the "Cell" has the force of law since the constitution and functions of the said "Cell" have been published in the official gazette by the order of the President bears no substance because the words "having the force of law" employed in Article 152 of the Constitution only qualify custom or usage for putting' the word "and" and a comma before it in order to disjunct other statutory law. To have this view we have relied upon the Oxford English Grammar, published in the year 1996 at page 530 which quotes thus:</u>

<u>"If two main clauses are linked by co-ordinating conjunction, a separating clause is generally used before the conjunction "and". For the said reason two clauses of Article 152 of the Constitution have been made disjunctive by conjunction "and" and by placing a comma before it. Further, it will be more clear if we quote our constitutional provision laid down in Article 152 of the Constitution in "Bangla" which runs thus:</u>

<u>আইন“অর্থ কোন আইন, অধ্যাদেশ, আদেশ, বিধি, প্রবিধান, উপ-আইন, বিজ্ঞপ্তি ও অন্যান্য আইনগত দলিল এবং বাংলাদেশে আইনের ক্ষমতা সম্পন্ন যে কোন প্রথা বা রীতি:</u>

23. Moreso, it will be relevant to mention that the title of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 (Act IV of 1990) projects the specific object of such an enactment in the following language :

আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক ঋণ আদায়ের জন্য বিশেষ বিধানে প্রণয়ন কল্পে প্রণীত আইন”।

24. With such a specific title Act IV of 1990 is found to have been promulgated where section 4 stands to constitute Artha Rin Adalat in order to adjudicate the suit filed by the "financial institution" as defined in section 2 of the said Ain. Even power and jurisdiction of such Adalat has also been specifically mentioned in section 5 of the said Ain which runs as follows:

৫। অর্থ ঋণ আদালতের ক্ষমতা ও এখতিয়ার—

(১)	অন্য কোন আইনে যাহা কিছু থাকুক না কেন, আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের ঋণ আদায় সংক্রান্ত যাবতীয় মামলা অর্থ ঋণ আদালতে দায়ের করিতে হইবে এবং উক্ত আদালতেই উহা নিষ্পত্তি করা হইবে।

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, কোন আইন দ্বারা কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান প্রতিষ্ঠা করা হইয়া থাকিলে এবং উক্ত আইনে উহার ঋণ আদায়ের জন্য কোন বিশেষ বিধান বা পদ্ধতি থাকিলে সেই বিধান বা পদ্ধতি এই ধারার বিধান দ্বারা ক্ষুন্ন হইবে না।

(৮) অর্থ ঋণ আদালত একটি দেওয়ানী আদালত (Civil Court) বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908) এ দেওয়ানী আদালতের যে সকল ক্ষমতা ও এখতিয়ার এই আইনের বিধান সাপেক্ষে অর্থ ঋণ আদালতেরও থাকিবে।

(৫) এই আইনে ভিন্নরূপ কিছু না থাকিলে, অর্থ ঋণ আদালত উহার কার্যক্রম পরিচালনার ব্যাপারে Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908) এ দেওয়ানী আদালতে কার্যক্রম পরিচালনা সম্পর্কে যে বিধান করা হইয়াছে উহা অনুসরণ করিবে।”

25. The above mentioned Ain has been repealed and replaced by Act VIII of 2003 which has also been named as অর্থ ঋণ আদালত আইন, ২০০৩”. The provisions as to definitions laid down in section, 2, 4 & 5 being more or less identical, we find it needless to discuss more about its application on the face of the provision laid down in section 60 of Act VIII of 2003.

<u>26. From the above provisions of law it is apparent that the legislature has created no scope for forming any committee by the order of the President whose recommendation will go to regulate the Adalat's proceeding in any manner. In fact, the legislature under section 14 of the Ain, 1990 and under section 58 of the Ain, 2003 has only given the government a power to frame rules for the purpose of fulfilment of the object of the Ain. Since no provision of the above notification is found to have been incorporated in the Ain to constitute any committee or cell and to abide by the recommendation given by the same, it bears no binding force to the court in any way.</u>

27. However, as to the case of Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin and others reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 , on perusal it appears that it has no manner of application in the present case as it involved notifications issued by the President as to terms and conditions of service of the employees of the Republic of Bangladesh under the proviso to Article 133 of the Constitution. The same view is also applicable in the case of Jihad Ahmed vs Bangladesh Power Development Board reported in 52 DLR (AD) 75. While examining the case of Shafiq Ahmed vs Registrar, Trade Marks reported in 47 DLR 309 it transpires that a notification being SRO No. 708(k)64 dated 17-9-1-964 was challenged as redundant for non-user of the same. The said notification was found as having the mandate of law for the simple reason that the said SRO, the Statutory Rules and Orders, has legislative sanction. But in the instant case, the constitution of the said Committee is not the product of law though it was published in the official gazette by the order of the President.

28. Moreover, in the case of Rony Twines Limited reported in 14 BLT 276 the High Court Division while giving binding effect to the recommendation made by the Special Committee has not given any observation in the light of Article 152 of the Constitution. Moreso, the observations made by the apex court in the case of Professor Abdur Rahim reported in 7 BLT (AD) 313 was not considered while making the aforesaid Rule absolute. The High Court Division in Rony Twines Case simply considered the point that the BSRS is a product of a statute and as per Article 7(2) of BSRS Order, 1972 in the discharge of its function the general policy and guideline given by the government shall be incumbent and binding upon the BSRS. On the other hand, in Quaderia Publication s Case the Appellate Division while mandating the views of the High Court Division that the petitioner Company has acquired a vested right on the basis of Bangladesh Bank memo mainly considered the ground of discrimination under Article 27 of the Constitution. Keeping this view in mind and facts and circumstances of these cases as referred above by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, it can be discerned that those are not identical to the facts of the present case, hence, cannot be applicable.

29. Moreso, the official letter dated 29-9-1992 vide Annexure 'B' which has been issued by the Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Industry and ex-officio Member Secretary of the said সুপারিশ বাস্তবায়ন কমিটি” addressed to other financial institutions and the respondent banks, might have, without statutory backing, persuasive authority over the latter but they are not obliged under the law to give effect to the said recommendation given' to them in the said letter. This view of ours has also been mandated by our apex court in the case of Professor Abdur Rahim Khan and others vs Bangladesh and others 7 BLT (AD) 313 by observing that recommendation of a cabinet committee cannot be enforced through a writ for the simple reason that it is not law.

30. However, it is now a settled principle of law that Article 102 of the Constitution can be invoked only where the petitioner's right has undisputedly accrued under the Constitution or under any other legal instrument and such right has not been given effect to. In other words, the petitioner is being deprived of the benefit of such right. The aforesaid letter dated 29-9-1992, Annexure 'B' to the writ petition, is not a legal instrument creating legal right for the petitioner for waiver of 100% interest and other benefits as has been observed above. It only lays down the policy of the government making recommendation for waiver of such interest without creating any legal right.

31. In view of the above observations it can clearly be found that there is nothing enforceable in this notification which is nothing more than constituting a "Cell" by an executive act or order to formulate certain policies which in our opinion, is not a law within the meaning of Article 152 of the Constitution and cannot go to regulate the proceedings of the Court or right of the banks or the financial institutions established by law.

<u>32. Now, as to the "Re-conciliation Committee" being constituted under the notification dated 6-3-1997, vide Annexure-E to the writ petition, it appears therefrom that its prime object was to resolve the dispute speedily out of Court where litigation is pending for disposal against the respective sick industries. If its recommendation or proposal is not accepted by the respective Bank or financial institution it shall forward the same to the Banking Division, Ministry of Finance for final decision and till final decision is not given the suit filed by the financial institution shall be kept in abeyance. In the present case, the mortgage suit was instituted against the petitioner company on 13-9-1995 under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 and the petitioner company entered appearance and filed written statement on 16-3-1997. In the said Ain, (the Ain of 1990), though there was no express provision for amicable settlement of disputes besides adjudication of the claim of the respondent bank but by virtue of section 5 of the Ain, 1990 the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure were made applicable so far those are not inconsistent with that of the provisions of the Ain, 1990. In the present case the said Ain has been repealed and has been substituted by the Artha Rin Adaiat Ain, 2003 where the legislature, keeping in mind the said concept of amicable settlement for speedy recovery of the loan amount, has particularly incorporated a separate chapter, namely Chapter V, with the heading বিকল্প পদ্ধতিতে বিরোধ নিস্পত্তি” wherein the statute has incorporated two mechanisms, one is section 21 for "settlement conference" and the other is section 22 for "Mediation". To avail this opportunity the respective parties are to follow the procedure laid down in sections 23, 24 and 25 of the Ain, 2003. Moreso, during the pendency of the execution proceeding under section 38 of the Ain 2003 and even after completion of judicial proceeding under section 45 of the Ain, 2003 the respective contending parties can go for resolving the dispute amicably out of Court. Hence, it cannot be said that the petitioners have been left out without any forum to place its grievance in accordance with law. Moreso, the Artha Rin Adalat being a creature of the statute (Act IV of 1990 and Act VIII of 2003) it cannot go beyond it nor can it be regulated by other notification which is not, at all, related with the adjudication of the suit rather, it was made for other purposes as discussed above.</u>

33. In this regard it is relevant to observe that, by and large the Court is to assume the role of sole expositor of parliamentary enactments. Judges are not legislators, their creative power is very much limited by existing legal material and to proceed at their commands. It would be nothing less than corrupt use of power if the Court or any other authority goes on ignoring the provisions of enacted laws in order to show an unregulated benevolence to any admitted defaulter on the basis of a recommendation of the committee, formulated by the Government overshadowing the provision of the enacted laws. It is to be borne in mind that express intention of the legislatures through statute can only guide the Court and procedure laid down therein can only regulate its proceeding but none else. Since formation of such "committee" referred above for special purpose cannot be considered as part of the statute, as such, it can neither regulate the Court's proceeding nor it can create any scope for adjournment of the pending suit being Money Suit No. 71 of 1995 as alleged by the petitioners rather, it should proceed in accordance with law.

34. Considering the observations and the findings made hereinabove, we are of the view that this Rule bears no merit for consideration. Accordingly, it is liable to be discharged.

35. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

The stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

End.
