full_judgment:
Abdul Awal J : This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 9-11-2009 passed by the learned Additional District judge, 2nd Court Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 230 of 2009 should not be set-aside and/or such order or further or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Opposite- party No.1 Sonali Bank Limited filed Artha Rin Suit No. 131 of 2003 on 26-4-2003 against the opposite-party No.4 and another impleading them as defendants for realization of TK. 47,40,875 (forty seven lakhs forty thousand eight hundred seventy five) contending, inter alia that one Saleha Khatun, who is now dead, and her son Abdul Latif took loan to complete the under construction building of Saleha Kahtun by mortgaging the schedule land including the structures thereon. The said suit was decreed ex parte on 27-9-2003.

3. Thereafter, an Execution Case bearing No. 355 of 2004 was started on 1-6-2004 pursuant to the execution case the executing Court invited tenders in respect of the schedule land to sell the same in auction. The tender notice was published in 'The Daily Protham Alo' and 'The Dainik Sangbad' on 13-8-2005, but no bidder was participated. Then, the decree-holder bank made a prayer to the executing Court on 8-1-2006 to issue certificate under section 33(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. Accordingly, a certificate under the said section was issued on 9-1-2007. On the basis of the said certificate the decree-holder bank invited tenders from the intending bidders for auction sale of the schedule property. The tender notice was published in 'The Daily Janakantha' on 23-4-2009, and on 28-4-2009 some officials of decree-holder bank along with some other persons went to the schedule property when they disclosed that they would take over the possession of the same as it was sold on auction. Following the invitation of tender the scheduled property was sold on auction and to that effect a deed was registered on 29-6-2009.

4. The petitioner along with three others filed an application on 4-5-2009 under Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the executing Court to release the schedule property, in question. The said petition was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 27 of 2009. At the time of filing of the application a bond for 10% of the decretal amount was filed. The decree-holder bank appeared and contested the miscellaneous case. After hearing the parties the miscellaneous case was dismissed by an order dated 20-7-2009.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order, the petitioner along with others preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Dhaka. The said appeal was registered as Miscellaneous Appeal No. 230 of 2009. Thereafter, the said miscellaneous appeal, on transfer was disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka, who after hearing the parties dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and order of the trial Court. Against the said judgment and order the instant Civil Revision has been prepared.

6. Mr. SB Bhandari, learned Advocate appeared along with Mr. Shah Md. Munir Sharif for the petitioner while Mr. Moudud Ahmed, learned Advocate appeared along with Mr. Raziuddin Ahmed, Mr. KP Bhowmik and Mrs. Khalifa Shamsun Nahar appeared for opposite-party No. 1 and Mr. Md. Hefzul Bari, learned Advocate appeared for opposite-party No.2.

7. Mr. SB Bhandari submits that the impugned judgment and order is erroneous. He submits that the petitioner along with three others preferred Miscellaneous Case No. 27 of 2009 as third party under section 32(2) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 by furnishing 10% bond to the decretal amount. He submits that the deposit of 10% bond by the petitioner did not take into consideration by the appellate Court and the trial Court as well. His submission is that the petitioner was not aware as to the filing of the Artha Rin Case No.131 of 2003 and the Execution Case No. 355 of 2004 prior to 28-4-2009 when some officials along with two others persons went to the schedule property disclosing the suit property was going to be sold in auction. Immediately, they Miscellaneous Case No. 27 of 2009 on 4-5-2009 without any delay. His submission is that the impugned judgment and order is illegal. Therefore, it is liable to be set-aside.

8. Mr Moudud Ahmed submits that the impugned order was once challenged in Writ Petition No. 7932 of 2009 and it was decided in a judgment and order dated 24-11-2004 delivered by a writ of this Court. Against the said judgment and order the writ petitioner preferred a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 199 of 2009 before the Appellate Division and the same has been disposed of as 'no order'. Mr Ahmed further submits that since the impugned judgment and order was thrashed out in a writ petition this revisional application does not lie and it embraces the doctrine of res judicata. He submits that as soon as the certificate under section 33(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 was issued, the function of the executing Court comes to an end. His further submission is that Artha Rin Suit was filed in the year 2003, but the petitioner as third party filed the Miscellaneous Case No. 27 of 2009 in the year 2009. In this respect he argues that the Court will help the vigilant but not the indolent. His last submission is that the impugned judgment and order passed by the lower appellate Court being based on law should not be interfered with by this Court.

9. We should confine ourselves within the ambit of the impugned order i.e. whether the impugned order passed by the appellate Court below is based on legal evidence or not. Before to discuss the merits and demerits of the impugned order we would like to narrate the facts of the case, in brief, though these are not that much relevant for the disposal of the Rule.

10. Saleha Khatun, mother of the petitioner, took loan of Taka 1,40,000 (one lakh forty thousand) by mortgaging the schedule property from the opposite party No. 1 bank in order to complete her under construction building. Her son Abdul Latif stood guarantor of the loanee. A mortgage deed was registered on 14-7-1991 in favour of the opposite party No. 1 executed by Saleha Khatun. The loan amount was to repay within fifteen years from the date of taking loan.

11. A counter-affidavit was filed by the opposite party No. 1 and in the said counter-affidavit a registered deed has been annexured-4 which is auction purchased deed. In this deed it is found that Saleh a Khatun took loan of Taka 19,00,000 (nineteen laks) for construction of her residential building. The difference of amount of loan between the mortgaged deed and the auction purchased deed could not be ascertained since no sanction letter or its subsequent enhancement letter was laid before us.

12. At the time hearing it comes to our notice that during pendency of Artha Rin Suit No. 131 of 2003 Saleh a Khatun died. The ex parte decree was obtained on 27-9-2003 against a dead person. The heirs of Saleha Khatun were not substituted before obtaining ex parte decree. On the death of Saleha Khatun heirs became owners of the schedule property. The petitioner, Abdur Rashid, Nazma Ahmed Shamima Begum including opposite-party No. 4(Abdul Latif) are the heirs of late Saleha Khatun. They were not made parties in the Artha Rin Suit No. 131 of 2003.

13. Now, let us go to the impugned order dated 9-11.2009 which arose out of an application filed by the petitioner and 3 others as third party in Execution Case No. 355 of 2004 for releasing the schedule property. In the said application it has been stated that a bond for 10% of the decreetal amount was furnished as required under section 32(2) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. But it appears that the said application was rejected both by the trial Court and the Court of appeal below on the ground that 10% of the decreetal amount was not deposited by the petitioners of the said application with a further finding that the petitioners filed bond with a promise to pay which is not permitted by law.

14. It is, however, apparent on the face of the record that at the filing of the Miscellaneous Case No. 27 of 2009 an order sheet was initiated with the following words and sentences:

“৪-৫-২০০৯ রেজিস্ট্রী ভূক্ত করা হউক। ইহা একটি দে:কা:বি: আইনের ২১ আদেশ ৫৮ নিয়ম তৎ সহ অর্থ ঋণ আদালত আইন ২০০৩ এর ৫৭ ধারা মোতাবেক দরখাস্ত। দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষ হলফনামা, নতুন ও কালতনামাসহ রোজাদি সহ নোটিশ ও ডাক নোটিশ দাখিল করিয়াছে। দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষ বগু দাখিল করিয়াছে।দরখাস্তকরী পক্ষ ফিরিস্তি যোগে দরখাস্তের ফটোকপি দাখিল করিয়াছে। দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষ দরখাস্ত ক্রমে দেঃ কাঃ বিঃ আইনের ২১ আদেশ ৫৮ নিয়ম তৎসহ অর্থ ঋণ আদালত আইন-২০০৩ এর ৫৭ ধারা মোতাবেক অর্থজারী মোকদ্দমা ৩৫৫/০৪ থেকে তফসিল ভূক্ত সম্পত্তির অবমুক্তির আদেশ দানের জন্য প্রার্থনা করেন। দেখলাম। ২৬-০৫-০৯ তাং রক্ষণীয়তা শুনানী।”

15. The order sheet of the trial Court itself shows that the petitioners filed bond at the time of filing of the application as third party. Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 was amended in the year 2007 vide Artha Rin Adalat (Amendment) Ordinance, 2007 (Ordinance No. XXXIX of 2007). In the amendment, section 32(2) was replaced as under:

“(২) উপরোক্ত মতে দাবী পেশ করিবার ক্ষেত্রে, দরখাস্তকারী, ডিক্রীকৃত অর্থের, অথবা ডিক্রীকৃত অর্থের আংশিক ইতিমধ্যে আদায় হইয়া থাকিলে, অনাদায়ী অংশের, ১০% এর সমপরিমাণ জামানত বা বগু দাখিল করিবে, এবং অনুররূপ জামানত বা বগু দাখিল না করিলেও উক্ত দাবী অগ্রাহ্য হইবে।”

16. Order No. 14 dated 4-5-2009 clearly shows that the petitioners at the time of filing of Miscellaneous Case No. 27 of 2009 necessary bond as required under the law was duly filed. The filing of the bond is made in accordance with the amended section 32(2) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain.

17. Mr Moudud Ahmed during his submission cited a decision reported in 15 MLR (AD) 20 wherein it has been held that-

"when the decree was put into execution and the auction of the mortgaged property held at the instance of the decree-holder bank, the auction sale was confirmed by the Court and the decree-holder bank already withdrawn the bid money resulting in the completion of the execution proceedings."

18. The above decision is distinguishable with that of the present one. On the present case the tender was initially invited by the Court from the intending bidders for selling the schedule property in auction through newspapers but no bidder participated in the bid.

Thereafter, at the instance of the decree-holder bank, a certificate was issued under section 33(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 giving title and enjoyment of the schedule property to the decree holder. The decree-holder bank then invited tenders and sold the schedule property in auction in their private capacity and that was not confirmed by the Court whereas in the cited decision the auction purchase was held through Court and was confirmed by the Court. Furthermore, in the cited case no third party was involved as is in the present case. In the cited decision the decree-holder bank itself came to the executing Court for setting aside the auction sale on the ground that the schedule property was sold at a shockingly low price but in the present case there was no such allegation or the decree-holder bank did not come to the executing Court for such setting aside the auction sale. In the present case auction sale was made between the two private parties and such sale was not confirmed by the Court.

19. It is apparent that the certificate was issued on 9-1-2007 and the decree-holder bank made an advertisement for the sale of the schedule property in auction on 23-4-2009. Consequent to the auction sale, a deed was registered on 29-6-2009. Thereafter, the decree-holder bank filed an application to the executing Court to get the possession of the schedule property. If, according to Mr Mudud Ahmed, the execution case comes to an end with the issuance of a certificate by the Court how the decree-holder bank goes to the executing Court after 9-1-2007? Therefore, we are unable to agree with the submission of Mr Moudud that with the issuance of certificate under section 33(5) by Artha Rin Adalat the execution case comes to an end.

20. Mr Moudud Ahmed further raised a point for res judicata. It is true that the impugned judgment and order was challenged in Writ Petition No. 7932 of2009. In the said writ petition the impugned order was affirmed by a judgment dated 24-11-2009 delivered by a Division Bench (Writ) of this Court. In this regard the decision reported in 15 BLT (AD) 237 may be referred to. In that it has been held that "the impugned order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in a proceeding under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not amenable to writ jurisdiction and the same can, in an appropriate case, be dealt with by a civil Court". It has further been held that "the order passed in exercise of power under the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be challenged under Article 102(2) of the Constitution." Therefore, the objection raised at to the res judicata has no substance. Mr Ahmed further argued that the Court cannot help the indolent but the vigilant. It is true that Artha Rin Suit was filed in the year 2003 and ex parte decree was passed in late 2003. Subsequently, execution case was started and the schedule property was advertised for auction sale in the two daily news-papers. The plea of petitioners was that prior to 8-4-2009 when some officials along with some order persons went to the schedule property and disclosed to them that the schedule property was going to be sold on auction. This plea of the petitioners, at this stage, we cannot brush aside. The petitioner along with three others filed an application on 4-5-2009 without delay and it was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 27 of 2009. In such view of the matter the petitioners cannot be held to be indolent.

<u>21. It is our view that the execution case does not come to an end with the issuance of a certificate under section 33(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. Rather, it remains alive till the possession of the property alleged to have been sold in auction, was handed over to the auction purchaser. This finding gets support from a decision reported in 15 BLT at page 425 wherein has been held that-</u>

<u>"sub-section 7 of Artha Rin Adalat envisages vesting of ownership of the property of the judgment debtor upon the decree-holder. The said vesting of ownership includes delivery of possession of the property. Without the delivery of possession, the execution case cannot be disposed of.</u>

22. It appears that the instant revisional application is vehemently opposed by the decree-holder bank though the schedule property was sold in auction and a deed alleged to have been registered in favour of a auction purchaser on 29-6-2009 at a price of TK 40,00,500 (forty lakhs five hundred) and the decree-holder bank withdrew the money. The auction purchaser did not come to the Court to be added as party and to place his case. The petitioner alleges that the auction purchaser is a name lender only and the opposite party No.1 is behind the scene.

23. In the circumstances as stated above it is held that the Miscellaneous Case No 27 of 2009 was filed in accordance with law. Therefore, the impugned judgment and order so passed by the Court of appeal below and the trial Court can be maintained. As such, it is liable to be set aside.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute. There being no order as to costs. The impugned order dated 9-11-2009 passed by the learned Additional District judge, 2nd Court Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Appeal No 230 of 2009 is here by set aside.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition For leave to appeal No. 751 of 2005
lawyer:
Md Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Petitioners. 
M Nurul Amin, instructed by AKM Shahidu Huq Advocate-on-Record------- For the Respondent.
parties:
Dalimon Nessa Bewa and other------- Petitioner
Vs.
Md Hasmat Ali  ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim, J : This application under Article 103 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is directed against the judgment and order dated 14-3-2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2467 of 2002 making the Rule absolute and set aside the judgment and decree dated 20-4-2002 passed by the Additional District Judge, 2nd Court Tangail in Title Appeal No. 124 of 1998 reversing those dated 10-5-1998 passed by the Sub-Judge, 2nd Court, Tangail, in Partition Suit No. 124 of 1987.

2. Plaintiff instituted partition suit No. 124 of 1987 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Tangail praying for a preliminary decree for partition of 3.60 acres of land appertaining to CS Khatian No. 50 of Mouza Chakra under Police Station-Madhupur, District-Tangail stating, inter alia, that the said land belonged to Madary Sheikh who transferred the entire land by an oral gift in favour of Sonajan. Madary Sheikh has no male issue. Sonajan was married to Jinnat Sheikh and the latter was taken as domesticated son-in-law. During CS operation the suit land was recorded in the name of  Madary Sheikh but in the possessor's column the name of Jinnat Sheikh was wrongly recorded, Sonajan died leaving behind her husband Jinnat Sheikh and one son Ahmed Sheikh. Jinnat Sheikh transferred 1.05 acres of land in favour of the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 Jinnat Sheikh took second wife. Thereafter, Jinnat Sheikh died leaving behind his second wife, three sons named Ahmed Sheikh, Kasem Sheikh and Jasimuddin and three daughters named Kamala, Rahima and Jarina. Thereafter, Ahmed Sheikh died leaving behind the plaintiff No.3 to be his wife and the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 to be his sons and one daughter named Ambia. Ambia sold her share in favour of the defendant No. 4. This is why the plaintiff inherited 3.06 acres of land and claimed partition but the same was refused and, as such, the suit

3. The defendant Nos. 1-5 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to Madary Sheikh who transferred the entire land by an oral gift in favour of Jinnat Sheikh and handed over possession. During CS operation that suit lands were correctly recorded in the name of Jinnat Sheikh being possessor. SA record was also prepared in the name of Jinnat Sheikh Jinnat Sheikh died leaving behind 3 sons named Ahmed Sheikh. Kasem Sheikh and Jasimuddin and three daughters named Kamala, Rahima and Jarina. Thereafter, Jasimuddin died leaving behind defendant No.1 to 5 to be his heirs.

4. Mr Md Aftab Hossain,Advocate-on- Record appearing for the petitioners, Submits that the High Court Division has not applied his judicial mind that the trial Court decreed partition suit in part and the lower appellate Court being the final Court also decreed the suit in part in respect of 3.60 acres of the disputed land in favour of the plaintiff- appellants but the High Court Division was pleased to go beyond the pleading of parties and misreading, misinterpreting and misapplying the Exhibit Ka (1) and Exhibit Ka (2) and even without touching the evidence of a single PW and DW regarding adverse possession made the Rule absolute to the serious prejudice of the petitioner occasioning a total failure of justice; that in view of pleading of parties, nature and character of the present partition suit, evidence both oral and documentary and findings of Courts below including the lower appellate Court, the High Court Division without application of judicial mind to the Exhibits Ka(1) and Ka(2)1 that exhibits has no nexus to the facts and Circumstances of the case and without discussion and analysis and giving any reason whatsoever relying on the principle enunciated in the case of Malik Din vs Md Aslam reported in 21 DLR (SC) 94 (Judgment, inter-parties), 1988 BLD (AD) 14 (Res judicata) has abruptly reached the conclusion of making of the Rule absolute to the serious prejudice of petitioners denying justice; that the High Court Division has not applied judicial mind that the lower appellate Court has not given any reason whatsoever for reversing the judgment of the trial Court and such judgment being not a proper judgment of reversal to the serious prejudice of the petitioners occasioning a failure of justice the High Court Division has not properly exercised jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure to achieve justice in the case of petitioners.

5. Mr M Nurul Amin, learned Advocate, appearing for the respondent, submits that the appellate. Court in the finding portion of Exhibit Ka (2) has held that "The defendants have examined 3 witnesses in all. CS record reveals that Jinnat Sheikh was in exclusive possession of the suit land and thus the heirs of the Jinnat Ali being in exclusive possession mutated their names in the landlord sherista and had been paying rent in their names.

<u>6. From the evidence of PW1 it is clear that the heirs of Jinnat Ali had never admitted the plaintiff as their co-sharers since the publication of their name in CS record i.e. 40 years back and that J innat Ali and his sons are in possession as sole owner to the knowledge of the plaintiff. From the evidence on record and from the facts and circumstances of the case, it is found that the defendants have been in possession of the disputed land for more than 12 years as of right and by asserting hostile title against the plaintiff or their predecessor and that there was a complete ouster and thus the right, title and interest of the plaintiff which they alleged had acquired in the properties had been lost by adverse possession and accordingly, it is found that the decision of the Subordinate Judge is justified.</u>

7. In view of the above, we find no substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners.

Accordingly, the leave petition is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Revision No. 3814 of 2006 with 4743 of 2007.
lawyer:
Ibrahim Mollah with Alamgir Hossain, Advocates----- For the Petitioners in CR No.3814 of 2006. 
Ekramul Hoque for Shafquat Hussain----- For the Petitioner in CR No.4743 of 2007. 
SH Md Nurul Huda Jaigirder----- For Opposite Parties in both Revisions.
parties:
Lila Begum and others ----- Petitioners
vs
Faruque Meah and anr ----- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
The above numbered 2(two) revisions arise out of the same judgment and decree dated 13-2-2006, passed by the Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Sylhet, in Title Appeal No. 72 1994, reversing those dated 30-3-1994, passed by the Assistant Judge, Balaganj, Sylhet, in Title Suit No. 02 of 1984.

2. The said 2(two) revisions were preferred by (two) sets of petitioners who were defendant in the original suit.

3. The plaintiff instituted the suit for partition being Title suit No. 122 of 1965 in the Second Court of the Munsif, Sylhet. On transfer to the Court of Assistant Judge Balaganj, Sylhet it was renumbered as Title Suit No. 2 of 1984. The plaintiff's claim in brief, Sukur Mahmood, was the owner of the suit land along with other lands. While he had been enjoying and possessing the suit land died leaving behind four sons namely Asadullah, Asimullah, Reasatullah and Samedullah along with 3(three) daughters namely Astora Banu, Kastura Banu and Mastura Banu. After death of Sukur Mahmood the suit land devolved upon his said sons and daughters. Amongst them Asadullah transferred his interest in the suit land to his wife Setara Bhanu by executing a registered kabala dated 23rd Ashar, 1314 BS and handed over possession. Asadullah died leaving behind his wife the plaintiff No. 1 Setara Banu and 2(two) sons the defendant Nos. 50 and 51 namely Abdur Noor and Abdur Rouf. After death of Asadullah his brother Asim Ullah gifted his share to his only son Kalamdar and adopted daughter Syeda Bhanu in equal shares. Thereafter, Kalamdar died leaving behind his wife Badrun Nesa, mother Ayesha Khatun and uncle Reasat Ullah. In the meantime Astura, Kastura and Mastura died leaving behind their respective successors. The plaintiff No. 1 again married with Reasat Ullah who transferred his share to her in lieu of moharana by executing a registered Kabala dated 17th Ashwin 1328 BS and handed over possession. Reasat Ullah died leaving behind wife the plaintiff No. 1, son the plaintiff No. 2 and daughter the plaintiff No.3. On death of Reasat Ullah the plaintiffs became owners of a share measuring in total 5 acres 11 gonda 3 kora, 1 (one) kranti of the land left by Kalamdar and Reasat Ullah and the plaintiff Nos.2 and 3 got 1 (one) powa, 3(three) gonda 2 (two) kranti share in the land left by Reasat Ullah. In total, the plaintiffs became successor; and possessors of the share measuring 7 (seven) acres, 3 (three) gondas 1 (one) karal(one) kranti in the suit land.

4. The defendants contested the suit by filing different written statements. The defendant Nos. 1- 25 in their written statement stated that Samedullah died leaving behind 3 (three) daughters. The defendant Nos. 3-6 and 7-12 are the heirs of Astura Banu, defendant Nos.12-15 are the heirs of Kastura Banu and the contesting defendant Nos. 1-25 claimed share in respect of 4 anna 7 gondas and I (one) karasaham in the suit land. In their written statement they stated that the suit suffers from defect of parties and all the properties have not been included in same hotchpotch. Asadullah did never execute any deed of gift and the alleged deed of gift is forged. Asadullah died leaving behind only son Kalamdar and wife Ayesha, Kalamdar died leaving behind wife BadrunNessa and mother Ayesha, Kalamdar transferred his property to his wife Badrunnessa alias Samsun Nessa. Syed Yakub Ali purchased the same in benami of Sunahar and Sajed Jaigirder and thereafter Syed Yakub Ali transferred the same to defendant Nos. 37 by executing a registered kabala. In this manner they accrued 8 annas share in the suit property and they have been enjoying and possessing the same. Ayesha gifted some land out of the Suit property to Jarid Chowdhury and they also prayed for saham. The defendant No. 43 claimed that his 2 (two) bothers Sori Mahmud and Ali Mahmud were owners of 7 powa, 1 jasti land in the northern portion of the suit property. Out of which Sori Mahmud transferred his share in favour of his wife Aptab Banu by executing a kabala who was succeeded by their only son Mazid Ullah who has been enjoying and possessing the same. Ali Mahmud gifted his share to Asim by executing a deed Kalamdar son of Asim and Ayesha wife of Saim sold and transferred their share to Jahiad Ullah by executing a registered kabala dated 16 Agrahyan 1337 BS. All the joint property have not been brought in the same hotchpotch.

5. The claim of the defendant Nos. 49-51 in brief that Asim Ullah transferred his entire share in the suit property by way gift to his son Kalamdar and adopted daughter defendant No. 49 Syeda Banu. Mastura Banu sold her share to Asadullah who gifted the same to defendant Nos. 50-51. They also prayed for their saham.

6. Defendant No. 54 Ayesha Khatun claimed her share stating that Asimullah did never execute any will and he did not transfer his share to Kalamdar and Syeda Banu by way of gift.

7. The defendant No. 56 claimed auction purchased land in the suit property.

8. After hearing the parties the learned Assistant Judge by the judgment and decree dated 30-3-1995 dismissed the suit.

9. On appeal, the judgment and decree of the trial Court were reversed and set by the impugned judgment and decree dated 13-2-2006 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Sylhet, in Title Appeal No. 72 of 1995.

10. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree 2(two) sets of defendants as petitioners preferred the above numbered 2(two) revisions and obtained the Rules.

11. In course of argument the petitioners of Civil Revision No. 3814 of 2006 filed an application under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil. Procedure to accept a kabala annexed to the that application as Annexure-A as additional evidence. Mr Md Ibrahim Mollah the learned Advocate appearing for them submits that they accrued right, title and interest in a part of the suit land by the said deed, regarding their such claim they made averments in their pleading but could not produce the document during the trial of the suit and hearing of the appeal. After preferring this revision they could manage a certified copy of the said deed and, as such, to adjudicate the dispute finally the said deed may be accepted as additional evidence, for that purpose the suit may be sent back on remand to the appellate Court after setting aside the impugned judgment and decree.

12. To oppose his such argument Mr SH Md Nurul Huda Jaigirdar, Advocate, appearing for the Plaintiffs/opposite parties submits that the documents submitted by the defendant-petitioners cannot be accepted as additional evidence at this stage to fill up the lacuna of defendants, as per the provision of law provides in Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure the additional evidence as placed by the petitioners cannot be accepted at this stage since the documents in question had not been mentioned in the written statement or in their oral evidence by the defendants, this sort of document cannot be considered in revisional stage.

13. Taking the floor again Mr Mollah further submits that Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides the scope to accept the additional evidence in appellate stage and the said provision of law is also applicable in the revisional Court. He also submits, that in the similar circumstances our Appellate Division expressed the view to accept the additional evidence even in revisional stage. In sup- port he cited the decisions in the cases of Meher Banuvs Abdul Barek and Muslim Bepari, reported in 13 BLT (AD) 177. Sana Mia Bepari vs Jamila Khatun, reported in 1988 BLD (AD) 141= 41 DLR (AD) 113 and Capital Properties Ltd. vs Bangladesh. reported in 11 BLD 523 = 44 DLR 308.

14. On perusal of the application and after hearing the learned Advocates it appears to me that the application filed by the petitioners as well as the Civil Revisions were not drafted properly, but under the provision of law the prayer made by the petitioners deserve consideration. Order XLI, rule 27 (1) and 27 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure are as follows:

"27-(1) the parties to an appeal shall not be entitled to produce additional evidence, whether oral or documentary, in the Appellate Court but if-

(a) the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has refused to admit evidence which ought to have been admitted, or (b) the appellate Court requires any document to be produced or any witness to be examined to enable it to pronounce judgment or for any other substantial cause, the Appellate Court may allow such evidence or document to be produced or witness to be examined.

(2) Wherever additional evidence is allowed to be produced by an appellate Court, the Court shall record the reason for its admission."

15. On perusal of the application it appears to me that sub-rule 1 (a) is not applicable in the instant case, rather the provision in sub-rule 1(b) is applicable. This Court in the decisions cited above decided that the provision of accepting additional evidence in appellate Court is also applicable in the revisional forum but such acceptance should be allowed after the assigning reason as per sub-section 1(b). The instant suit was nothing but a suit for partition and in absence of any share of any defendant/s there is no reason to impleade him/her/ them. as defendant/s in the suit. On perusal of the judgment of the Courts below it appears that the trial Court dismissed the suit but the appellate Court decreed the suit giving no saham to the petitioners through as defendants of the suit they cannot be sahamless, but the question remained whether their share/s had been transferred or not, and such question about transfer could be decided by the Court below. Annexure-A to the application filed by the petitioners is apparently a deed of transfer executed in favour of Mazid Ullah who is the admitted predecessor of the application of the said application, and regarding Mazid Ullah apparently they made, averments in their pleadings. Comparing schedule appended to the said deed with that of the plaint it appears that the land described in the schedule appended to the said deed is not beyond the area of the land described in the schedule appended to the plaint and, as such, this deed deserve consideration by the Court as evidence. Accordingly I am inclined to allow the said application and to send back the suit to the appellate Court on remand for hearing afresh after considering the said deed as evidence of the suit.

<u>16. In the result, both the Rules are hereby made absolute and the judgment and decree impugned in both the revisions are hereby set aside and the suit is hereby sent back on remand to the appellate Court for hearing afresh on consideration of the said deed as additional evidence, the parties will be at liberty to examine oral witness in support of against the said deed and they will be also at liberty to amend their respective pleading if necessary. However, the appellate Court is hereby directed to dispose up the appeal within 6(six) months from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment.</u>

17. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule in both the Revisions are hereby recalled and vacated.

18. Send down the LC Record immediately.

However, there is no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
AF Hassan Arif, Senior Advocate, (AQM Safiullah, Advocate with him), instructed by Md Ataur Rahman Khan, Advocate-on-Record-For the Appellants. 
Dr M Zahir; Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record-For the Respondents.
parties:
Ahmed Impex (Private) Ltd & others   ------ Appellants
Vs
Moqbul Ahmed being dead his heirs: Ferdous Ara Begum ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 13th August 1992 passed by the High Court Division in Matter No. 34 of 1989).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J : This appeal by leave arises out of judgment and order of the learned Company Judge dated 10-12-1989 in Matter No. 34 of 1989 allowing the appeal under section 38 of the Companies Act.

2. The short facts leading to this appeal are that Ahmed Impex Company (Pvt) Ltd which will hereafter be referred to as the company, was incorporated under the Companies Act 1913 as a private company limited by shares, the authorised capital of the company is Taka 20,00,000 divided into 20,000 shares of Taka 100 each. Its subscribed capital consists of fully paid up 600 shares of Taka 100 each.

3. The company when floated in the year 1978 had 5 share holders, present respondent No. 1 and his wife respondent No. 2 were two of the shareholders while the original respondent No. 2 Tofayel Ahmed, his wife petitioner No. 2 (respondent No.3) and his younger brother's wife respondent No. 4 were the other share holders, Excepting Tofayel Ahmed who was the owner of 200 shares all others held 100 shares each. Under the Articles of Association the Board of Directors of the Company was constituted by all the shareholders. Respondent No. 1 (Moqbul Ahmed), who happened to be the eldest brother of the said Tofayel Ahmed was appointed permanent Chairman of the company and Tofayel Ahmed became its Managing Director. In the year 1987 the said Tofayel Ahmed filed with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies a list of shareholders along with a summary of the shares capital and shares issued up to 15-7-1987 in which he showed himself to be the holder of 900 paid up shares, appellant No.3 as the holder of 200 paid up shares and his minor son, appellant No.5 as the holder of 100 paid up shares. The return further disclosed that the respondent No. I transferred his 100 shares to appellant No.3 and respondent No. 2 transferred her 100 shares to appellant No. 5 and the said transfers were registered on 3-1-1987. The names of the respondents were accordingly, excluded from the register of shareholders of the company.

4. The respondents now claim that neither respondent No. 1 nor respondent No. 2 transferred their shares to appellant No. 3 and appellant No. 5 and they are still lawfully holding the said 200 paid up shares in the company, but Tofayel Ahmed fraudulently omitted their names from the register of shareholders of the company. The company being a family concern the respondents reposed trust in Tofayel Ahmed, but he always kept them in dark about the affairs of the company. On 16-11-1986 Tofayel Ahmed obtained signatures of the respondents upon some blank forms, stamps and papers and also received their original share certificates representing that loan for the company was to be secured from the bank against the said papers. He also gave an undertaking in writing to that effect on that day by way of assurance for payment of the share of profits and also gave an undated cheque being No. 482621 for Taka 5,00,000 (Taka five lac) only in favour of respondent No. 1 giving out that there was an arbitration proceeding between the company and the Power Development Board in pursuance of which he expected to finalise the accounts and make all payments. In acknowledgment of the cheque respondent No. 1 granted a receipt which was counter-signed by Tofayel Ahmed. In the month of August, 1988 respondent No. 1 came to learn that the said Tofayel Ahmed by practicing fraud upon the respondents as well as the company and also acting contrary to his earlier promises and undertakings, converted the documents and papers containing signatures of the respondents into valuable security and got their 200 shares transferred in the name of his wife and minor son, appellant Nos. 3 and 5 respectively Respondent No. 1 thereupon asked Tofayel Ahmed on several occasions to return the papers including the share certificates, but he did not comply therewith. They also wanted to become parties in Title Suit No. 145 of 1988 of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which arose out of an award between the company and the Power Development Board. On the objection of Tofayel Ahmed, the then Managing Director, their prayer was, however, refused as the question whether the respondents continued to be shareholders of the company or not could be decided only by the company Court.

5. Shortly after the service of notice of the application under section 38 of the Companies Act, the original respondent No.2, Tofayel Ahmed died and in his place his wife, appellant No.2 became the Managing Director of the company. On behalf of appellant Nos. 1 and 5 and on her own behalf she filed an affidavit-in-opposition in which she denied the respondents claim and maintained that the respondents voluntarily transferred their shares to appellant Nos. 3 and 5. According to these appellants, the respondents on 16-11-1986 verbally agreed to transfer if an undated cheque for Taka 5,00 lac be given to them representing the value of their shares and claim on profits in the business of the company and they promised to return the cheque for the equivalent cash amount when the company would receive full amount of its claim from the Power Development Board. Accordingly, an undated cheque for Taka 5 lac was handed over to respondent No.1. But the respondents went on pressing Tofayel Ahmed for immediate payment of the cash consideration of their shares and claim on profit in the business of the company, the respondents eventually settled for cash of Taka 5.60 lac and transferred their shares to appellant Nos. 3 and 5 and resigned from the Directorship on 31-12-1986 upon receipt of the amount in cash. At that time they executed two instruments of transfer of shares in favour of appellant Nos. 3 and 5 and two receipts for the cash consideration and handed over their original shares certificates to appellant Nos. 3 and 5. They also wrote letters to the company relinquishing their directorship, and respondent No. 1 himself executed an acknowledgment dated 31-1-1986 for the receipt of the cash consideration upon a non-judicial stamp. In a meeting held on 3-1-1987 the Board of Directors; in presence of the respondents, approved the transfers and accepted the resignation of the respondents from directorship. As a result the respondents are no longer members of the company and they have no right to apply for rectification of the share register of the Company.

6. The application was contested by other respondents by filing affidavit-in-opposition, denying the allegations in the application. Thereafter, the respondents filed an application affidavit-in-reply reiterating the assertion in the petition. The High Court Division allowed the application whereupon leave was granted to consider:

"The learned Single Company Judge has erred variously in disposing of the matter. In that Exhibit A the undertaking was not scrutinised with a view to probing its genuineness in so far as it was signed by deceased Tofayel Ahmed on 16-11-1986 on a letter head which on the very face of it was a letter head used during the seventies. The elaborate pre-cautiousness of Exhibit A was not considered to determine whether it was subsequently created. Exhibit A was not considered in juxtaposition with a Exhibit A(1) also signed by deceased Tofayel Ahmed on 16-11-1986 on a fresh letterhead which was in use by the company in the eighties. The learned Company Judge did not ask itself as to why two different letterheads were used on the same date by late Tofayel Ahmed. When one letter head was in disuse and the other was in use. Mr Nurullah further submits that the debit vouchers Exhibits 1 and J were disbelieved on mere surmise and not on the evidence on record. He also submits that the learned Company Judge did not deal with Exhibit 3, a written statement filed by the appellants in a money suit, in which they clearly acknowledge on 10-6-1987 that they resigned from the directorship of the company and transferred their shares to others and had no connection with the company any more. Also he submits that the learned Company Judge did not correctly construe Exhibit 10a written objection filed by late Tofayel Ahmed on 16-3-1989 in the suit."

7. While substantiating the grounds on which the leave was granted, Mr Hasan Ariff, the learned Counsel appearing for appellants, submits that the learned Single Company Judge had erred as Exhibit A, the alleged undertaking, was not scrutinised and considered in juxtaposition with Exhibit A(1) with a view to probing the genuineness of the alleged undertaking as such as Exhibit A was allegedly signed by deceased Tofayel Ahmed on 16-11-1986 in a letterhead which on the very face of it was a letterhead used during the seventies whereas Exhibit A(1) was allegedly signed by deceased Tofayel Ahmed on the same date of 16-11-1986 on a fresh or different letterhead which was in use by the appellant company in the eighties but the Company Judge erroneously did not ask himself as to why two different letterheads were allegedly used on the same date by late Tofayel Ahmed when one letterhead was in disuse and the other was in use. The learned Counsel submits that the learned Company Judge had erroneously failed to consider the alleged undertaking Exhibit A for the purpose of determining whether it was subsequently created on the basis of evidence on record. The learned Counsel submits that the learned Judge had erroneously failed to consider nor did he even discuss that in Money Suit No.3 of 1987 of the Court of Subordinate Judge and Judge, Commercial Court No. 1, the respondents on 10-6-1987 filed a written statement, Exhibit 3, asserting that they no longer were the directors and shareholders of the respective shares to the appellant Nos. 3 and 5 which supported the case of the appellants that the respondents had no title to the shares concerned. The learned Counsel submits that the learned Company Judge fell in error in that he did not correctly construe Exhibit 10, the written objection filed by late Tofayel Ahmed on 16-3-1989 in Title Suit No. 145 of 1988 of the Court of Third Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. The learned Counsel submits that the learned Company Judge had failed to correctly determine the question of title to the shares in the appellant company in the stated circumstances of handing over of instrument of transfer of shares duly executed, delivery of the same with share certificate concerned, execution of letter of resignation from directorship of the appellant company, execution of debit vouchers acknowledging receipt of money against transfer of shares concerned in the appellant company at the instance of the respondents on the basis of proper appreciation of evidence on record.

8. Dr M Zahir, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondents, submits that the learned Judge of the High Court Division arrived at the findings that: "I am inclined to accept the evidence of petitioner's witnesses in preference to that of the respondent's witnesses and find that the petitioners did never transfer their 200 shares to respondent Nos. 3 and 5 as claimed and that the respondents fabricated Exhibits B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J and M to make an illegal gain" and allowed the case of these respondents for rectification of the share register of the company and this findings having been based on proper appreciation of materials on record and on sound reasoning need not to be interfered with. The learned Counsel submits that the learned Judge of the High Court Division upon considering the report of the handwriting expert (Exhibit N) found that all the signatures of these respondents appearing in the instrument of transfer of share are spurious and that the shares of these respondents have not been transferred inasmuch as no contrary material was produced by the appellants in support of their case for transfer of shares of these respondents, the judgment passed by the High Court Division need not to be interfered. The learned Counsel submits that the learned Judge of the High Court Division upon consideration the documents found that in Exhibits A and F, "there is big gap between the signature of the executing and the last line of the writings which is passed through with a ball pen, whereas the signature is by a fountain pen and none of the witnesses to the document is also examined. From the debit vouchers, Exhibit I and J, it is difficult to understand that the transferee had made the payment. These Exhibits show that the payment was in the Directors loan account of the company and accordingly, the High Court Division held that no transfer of shares of the company by these respondents had taken place and these findings having been based on sound principles of law ought not to be interfered. The learned Counsel submits that the learned Judge of the High Court Division found from Exhibit A that Exhibits B, D, E, F, G, I and J were handed over to Tofayel Ahmed on his assurance that those would be used as collateral security for raising loans for the company and for no other purpose, which Tofayel Ahmed manufactured as an instrument of transfer of shares of these respondents of the company and there being no document showing withdrawal and/or entry of payment of the amount, the learned Judge rightly held that there is no transfer of share of the company and accordingly, directed for rectification of share register and, as such, the impugned judgment need not to be interfered with.

9. The High Court Division found in support of the claim of the respondents that they had never sold their shares to appellant Nos. 3 and 5 and continued to be the shareholders and that their signature have been secured on certain blank forms, papers and stamps and also that Tofayel Ahmed received the original certificate representing them that it would use for the collateral purpose. The High Court Division arrived at a finding that:

" In support of the claim of the petitioners that first witness is petitioner No.1 himself. He admits the signatures marked B(1), D(2), E(2), F(1), G(1) and I(1) upon the alleged instrument of transfer of shares. (Exhibit B) the original share certificates (Exhibits D and E), the alleged receipt cum-declaration on a non judicial stamp (Exhibit F), letter of resignation from Directorship (Exhibit G) and debit voucher (Exhibit 1) respectively. He also admits the signature of his wife, petitioner No. 2 marked J(1) in the debit voucher (Exhibit J) but denies the signatures marked D(3) appearing in his name on the reverse side of the share certificate (Exhibit D) as also the signature marked L(\) upon an alleged minute of the Boards Meeting dated January 3, 1987. He further denies the signature marked C( I ), D(3), H(1) and I(2) upon the instrument of transfer of shares (Exhibit C), share certificate (Exhibit E), letter of resignation from Directorship (Exhibit H) and the Minutes of the Board's meeting dated January 3, 1987 respectively to be in the hand of petitioner No. 2. He also denies the signature of Tofayel Ahmed marked L(3) upon the said minutes of the Board's meeting as also the signature of Tanvir Ahmed upon the aforesaid instrument of transfer of share Exhibit C as regards the documents which contain the genuine signatures of the petitioners, he says that those were obtained by the then Managing Director of the company Tofayel Ahmed on 16-11-1987 representing that the same would be used as collateral security for raising loans for the company and those were blank at that time. On a reference to Exhibits B & C, he further says that the revenue stamps which now appear on the reverse side of the instruments, were not there at that time and those did not also contain the date 31 st day of December, 1986. According to him, every writing on the reverse side of the share certificates (Exhibits D and E) is antedated and forged. So far as Exhibit F is concerned, he states that it was absolutely a blank stamp and there was no signature of any witnesses thereon. As to Exhibit C he say that the writings on it are not his writings and the date appearing on top of it i.e. 31-12-1987, are also not his. He further says that the writing and the date appearing on Exhibit H are also false and that the writings, the dates and the amount of cash consideration, both in figures and in words, as appearing on the debit vouchers Exhibits 1 and J were inserted and the revenue stamps affixed subsequently. To support his statement that Tofayel Ahmed received the said blank forms, papers and documents on 16-11-1986 representing that those would be used as collateral security or raising loans for the company, he proves an undertaking in writing marked Exhibit A, it admittedly bears tile signature of Tofayel Ahmed. A suggestion was, however, given to him that it is not the actual undertaking given by Tofayel Ahmed on 16-11-1986 and it is written by petitioner No. 1 on an old signed paid of 1970. He also proves a copy of the receipt of an undated cheque for Taka 5,00,000 marked Exhibit A(1) and he claim that he gave it to Tofayel Ahmed who countersigned the same. He denies the counter-signature of Tofayel Ahmed upon A(1) is forged. The respondents cross-examined this witness at length but nothing could be elicited to show that these two exhibits are fabricated documents.

10. Exhibit A clearly supports the statement of this witness that he handed over the aforesaid

documents Exhibits B, D, E, F, G, I and J to Tofayel Ahmed on his assurance that they would be used as collateral security for raising loans for the company and for no other purpose.

11. The next witness for the petitioners is PW 2 Md Liaquat Hossain. He is a handwriting expert of the CID department. He compared the disputed signatures with the admitted signatures of those who purport to be their authors. HIS report IS marked, opinion as to the genuineness or otherwise of the signature Exhibit D(3) he opines that Exhibits C(1), E(3), H(1), I(1), L(2) and L(3) do not agree with admitted signatures of their respective authors. There appears to be no infirmity in the report. The evidence of PW 1 gets corroboration from his evidence."

12. The appellant however, sought to prove their case by three witnesses namely, respondent No.3 herself as DW 1, DW 2 Syed Badrul Alam, who allegedly paid them cash amount of Taka 5 60 000 and DW 3 Kawsar Ali Khan. DW 1 stated that:

In late 1986 they decided to purchase the shares of the petitioners and for that purpose they raised loan from her uncle DW 2 Syed Badrul Alam. The transfer took place on 31-12-1986 at her residence at Shantinagar. At the sitting her husband late Tofayel Ahmed, the petitioner, Nurul Huda, Kowsar Ali Khan, Hiralal, Ayub and Kuddus were present and her uncle brought Taka 5,60,000. The petitioners executed the forms of the instruments of the transfer of shares, Exhibits B & C, after those were duly filled in. Thereafter the petitioners handed over the share certificates, Exhibits D and E. The petitioners also signed Exhibits F, G and H in the same sitting. After receipt of Taka 5 60 000 petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 executed Exhibits I and J which were written by her husband, She does not, however, claim that petitioner No. 1 did not put any signature on the reverse side of the share certificate Exhibit D. She denies that Exhibits B, C, E, F, G, H, I and J were handed over to her husband for using as a collateral security.

13. She is sought to be corroborated by DW 2 Syed Badrul Alam. He happens to be her paternal uncle. He is, therefore, interested. His presence at the transfer of the documents proved in the case. He claims to have brought the entire cash amount of Taka 5,60,000 in a briefcase and seen the transaction of sale as also the payment of the money to the petitioners, but fails to produce any account books containing withdrawal and/or entry of payment of such a huge amount.

14. DW 3 admitted that Exhibit was not signed in his presence and accordingly, on consideration of the evidence on record found that the evidence of the above witnesses regarding the alleged signature yet consisting to the report of the handwriting expert and that Exhibit N is also contrary to the undertaking, Exhibit A even Exhibit F which is said to have been given by petitioner No. 1 in acknowledgment of his alleged receipt of the cash consideration for the sale ex facie shows that the writings over it were done upon a non-judicial stamp signed by petitioner No. 1 earlier. There is a big gap between the signature of the executant and the last line of the writings which is penned through by a ball pen, whereas the signature is by a fountain pen. Different typewriters were used for the writing. None of the witnesses to the documents is also examined. From the debit vouchers, Exhibits I and J it is difficult to understand that the transferee had made the payment. Those rather show that the payment was in the Director's loan account of the company. It further shows that it was signed by the then Managing Director as Accountant, although there was an account in the company. In Title Suit No. 145 of 1988 between Ahmed Impex (Pvt) Ltd vs Power Development Board the petitioners made a prayer for being added as defendants. From Exhibit 10 it appears that the Managing Director of the company Tofayel Ahmed opposed the prayer by filing a written objection on 15-3-1989. In that objection Tofayel Ahmed categorically stated that the petitioners decided to transfer their shares to respondent Nos. 3 and 5 and they sent two letters dated 31-12-1986 to the company tendering their resignation from Directorship and the same were accompanied by the share certificates. Had the alleged sale been effected and the instrument of transfer executed granting receipt of the cash consideration on 31-12-1986 I find no reason why those facts were not mentioned in the written objection.

It is again a claim of DW 1 that the disputed sales were approved by the Board of Directors of the company in a meeting held in presence of the petitioners on 3-1-1987. She proves the signature of the Chairman of the meeting in the minutes of the Meeting Exhibit L to be in her husband's hand. The signature along with the purported signatures of the petitioners were sent to the handwriting experts who opined that all the signatures are spurious. The entire Exhibit M thus seems to be a manufactured one.

In view of the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case I am inclined to accept the evidence of the petitioner's witnesses in preference to that of the respondent's witnesses and find that the petitioners did never transfer their 200 shares to respondents 3 and 5 as claimed and that the respondents fabricated Exhibits B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J and M to make an illegal gain. It is amply proved that the petitioners have fallen victims of fraud perpetrated on them by the Managing Director of the company."

15. We have ourselves perused the Exhibit A and other Exhibits and it appears that the money receipts Exhibits 3 and 3A though contained the signatures which were found to be forged by the handwriting expert were not signed on the stamps but the same is bank loan voucher signed by the Managing Director as accountant and admittedly written by the Managing Director. DW 2 though alleged that he has paid the amount in cash but has not produced any paper to show that he has paid the sum as alleged to the company. On the contrary, in order to support his contention he produced a receipt issued by the respondent No. 1 in his favour acknowledging the receipt of a loan of the Taka 80,000. It is not understood after receipt of so much amount of money totaling Taka 560,000 why the respondents took Taka 80,000 from DW 2, that also belies the transaction. There was, in fact, no payment of any loan by the company to Tofayel Ahmed or DW 1 inasmuch as although DW 2 stated that he has paid Taka 560,000 to Managing Director Tofayel Ahmed but no receipt acknowledging the alleged loan amount have been filed either by the Company or the Managing Director. DW 2 has sought to prove a money receipt of Taka 80,000 issued by respondent Md Moqbal Ahmed as loan. The receipt is dated 20-4-1988. It does not come to reason why a service holder by profession Moqbal Ahmed would take a loan of Taka 80,000 once he received a substantial amount of Taka 2,80,000 on 31-12-1986 as a sale proceed of his share in the company. Furthermore, this DW 2 though alleged that he has given a loan of Taka 560,00 to payoff Moqbal Ahmed and Ferdous Ara Begum by the company or Managing Director, nobody is coming up with any receipt showing loan from DW 2 on that account. So the loan of DW 2 to pay off Taka 560,000 to the defendants remains not proved in view of the Managing Director's own case that the company was not financially solvent to pay the account. From the above evidence and the facts and circumstances of the case it does not raise any confidence that the appellant has paid an amount of Taka 560,000 to the respondents as a consideration for their transfer of share in favour of defendant Nos. 3 and 5.

16. PW 1 stated that before a sitting on 16-11-1986 the Managing Director Tofayel Ahmed informed that the company was going through financial crisis and the management is badly in need of money and requested PW 1 to pay him some money and on his reply that he is not in a position to pay the money, the Managing Director informed about raising of money form outside and it is mutually agreed in a sitting on 16-11-1986 where the Managing Director requested the PW 1 to sign some blank papers, stamps and forms and to deposit original share certificates to raise fund. Accordingly, PW 1 executed certain blank forms, papers and stamps and handed over the signed original share certificates belonging to him and his wife for raising loan for the company as a collateral security upon Managing Director's executing an undertaking in writing. DW 1, however, has not denied the signature on Exhibit A but sought to explain the same saying that it is not an undertaking, the relevant letterhead of the company is prior to 1980 when the company was incorporated. The letterhead of Exhibit A(1) is of after 1980. Prior to 1980 while they were at Chittagong late Tofayel Ahmed (MD) used to give this kind of signed letterheads to the petitioner No. 1 (PW 1) for the purpose of office work of the company. Thus admittedly, Exhibit A bears the signature of the Managing Director Tofayel Ahmed and supports the evidence of PW 1 that he handed over the documents in Exhibits B, D, E, F, G, I and J to Managing Director duly signed on blank forms, papers and stamps to be used as collateral security for raising the loans required for the company. The High Court Division as well on consideration of the evidence on record arrived at the finding that Exhibit A was signed by Tofayel Ahmed giving an undertaking on receipt of the blank forms, stamps and papers from Maqbul Ahmed to be used as collateral security for raising fund for the company.

17. Next coming to Annexure 8 (Exhibit B) the alleged share transfer form of Maqbul Ahmed and Annexure 8(1) (Exhibit C) the alleged share transfer form of Ferdous Ara Begum, PW 1 in his deposition stated that the revenue stamps on Exhibits B and C were affixed subsequently and the same were not there when he handed over the blank signed instrument of transfer of shareforms and "since Exhibits Band C were handed over to the Managing Director as blank forms, the date 31 st day of December, 1986 were not written on those instruments at the time of handing over those instruments to the Managing Director Tofayel Ahmed on 16-11-1986. This date 31 st day of December, 1996 has been filled in later on". It further appears that on perusal of Exhibit D the share certificate of Moqbul Ahmed and Exhibit E the share certificate of Ferdous Ara Begum and their endorsements at the back of these certificates showing the date of transfer on 3-1-1987 whereas the instruments of transfer of shares were signed on 31-12-1986, Exhibit F acknowledging receipt of cheque for Taka 560,000 on transfer of shares by Maqbul Ahmed and resignation as the Chairman of the company, Exhibit G are dated 31-12-1986 and the alleged receipt (Debit Voucher) is also dated 31-12-1986 and curiously enough even on 3-1-1987 Maqbul Ahmed and Ferdous Ara Begum were shown as the Directors attending Board's meeting as such (this Exhibit 'L' has been filed by the company). DW 1 though asserted that Exhibit C1 were the signatures of Maqbul Ahmed and Ferdous Ara Begum respectively and signed in her presence and saw them signed but as the signatures are not denied the question is when and how these documents were signed. We have ourselves perused the aforesaid signatures. Exhibit F a typed acknowledgment by Md Maqbul Ahmed on a Taka 3 stamp. On perusal of the same it appears that the "Subject Transfer of shares" and in fifth line the words "as full and final settlement of our claims against surrender of our shares to our nominated persons" were typed by different machine or at least not simultaneous with other writings therein. The most curious thing is that had Md Maqbul Ahmed signed the same in the same siting after it is typed his signature would not have been towards the end of the stamp leaving a wide gap of about 2" below the writings on it, (between the content and the signature there is a unusual gap of more that two inches), which circumstance as well do not inspire any confidence in the authenticity of this document. Similar is the case with Exhibit G the alleged resignation dated 31-12-1986 of Md Maqbul Ahmed from the post of Chairman of the company. The gap in this Exhibit 6 between the content and the signature is more than 3 inches which apparently show that the document has been created with the signature of Md Maqbul Ahmed on blank signed paper.

18. Exhibit I and J are the alleged Debit Vouchers dated 31-12-1986 which the company alleged to be the money receipts by Md Maqbul Ahmed and his wife Ferdous Ara Begum being the full and final settlement of claims of their share value. The alleged receipt is named "Debit Voucher" and DR is "Director's loan Account" issued under the signature of Managing Director Tofayel Ahmed signing as Accountant but the content is "being full and final settlement of claims and share value of Mr Moqbul Ahmed and another one. Exhibit J is for Ferdous Ara Begum. It is thus apparent that contrary to the case of the appellants, the company is buying the shares of Maqbul Ahmed and Ferdous but the company under the law could not purchase those shares but the company's Debit Vouchers have been used as a money receipts for sale of shares in favour of Managing Director's wife and son. PW 1 has asserted that the revenue stamps appearing thereon were not there when they signed the blank forms. On perusal of the forms the truth of the deposition of PW 1 is apparent. It appears that the revenue stamps were subsequently affixed beside the signatures and ticked. If these were the money receipt against the share transfers any simple receipt acknowledging the receipt of the amount would suffice but the filling up of the 'Debit Voucher' of the company to use it as money receipts and the attending circumstances support the case of the respondents that these were fabricated and forged on signed forms.

19. Exhibit L is minutes of a Board's meeting of the company dated 3-7-1987 wherein Md Moqbul Ahmed and Ferdous Ara Begum as directors allegedly attended and signed but the Handwriting Expert has found these signatures to be spurious. We have ourselves as well verified the same and even by naked eyes while comparing the signatures with other standard admitting signatures it appears that the signatures appearing therein are forged and, as such, no reliance could be placed thereon.

20. The respondents have allegedly filed a joint written statement in (Exhibit 3) in Money Suit No.3 of 1986 on 13-6-1987 stating that:

“অত্র বিবাদীদ্বয়ের দাখিলকৃত এস্তেফাপত্র কম্পানির পরিচালক মণ্ডলী ১লা জানুয়ারি ১৯৮৩ সনের সভাই গৃহীত হয় এবং বিবাদীদ্বয়ের অংশ যথাক্রমে জনৈক তোফায়েল আহমদ ও মিসেস তাহমিনা বেগমের বরাবরে হস্তান্তরের অনুমতি দেওয়া হয় । অত্র বিবাদীদ্বয়ের এস্তেফা ১০ ইং জানুয়ারি  ১৯৮৩ ইং তারিখে বলবৎ ও কার্যকরী হয়। সুতরাং ১০-১-১৯৮৩ ইং তারিখের পর কম্পানির কোন কার্যকলাপ সম্পর্কে অত্র বিবাদীদ্বয় দায়ী নহে।”

21. The aforesaid statement in the written statement is opposed to the actual alleged transfer of share, dated 31-12-1986 in favour of Managing Director's wife and son and, as such, not true in order to rely upon those statements. PW 1 stated that those were filed by the Managing Director on their behalf as he used to manage the company. The statement finds support from the statement made in the written statement.

<u>22. Moreover, the PW 1 though was asked about the filing of the written statement in Money Suit No. 3 of 1986 but was not brought to his notice as to the content thereof in order to saddle the witness with the previous statement made therein and unless the witness is confronted with the said previous statement merely by asking the witness as to filing of the written statement would not bind him with the content thereof. Under section 155(3) of the Evidence Act the credit of a witness may be impeached by proof of former statement, oral or in writing, inconsistent with any part of his evidence which is liable to be contradicted, Since independent proof of a former inconsistent statement may be given, it follows that the PW 1 may in cross-examination be asked whether he has, on a previous occasion, made any statement concerning a fact relevant to the matter in issue, which is inconsistent with any part of his testimony given in Court and if he denies this fact, proof of it may be given to contradict him. In the instant case except asking the PW 1 about filing of the written statement, the content thereof with which the PW 1 presently making any inconsistent statement was not put to him in order to enable the respondents to explain the circumstances against him. In that view of the matter, the content of written statement though contradictory to the defendant's own case of transfer, could not be produced and relied in order to contradict PW 1.</u>

23. Before parting with, we have ourselves perused the documentary evidence produced in this case and considered the same with reference to the oral evidence on record and could not persuade ourselves in order to build up any confidence in support of the case of the appellants or in support of the submissions of learned Counsel for the appellants.

<u>24. The provision of section 38 of the Companies Act gives the Court a wide discretion to scrutinise any fraud, error or undue influence or misrepresentation in the matter of transfer of any share and grant relief commensurating with the appropriate possible relief contemplated under the said section.</u>

<u>25. Thus section 38 enables the persons mentioned therein the right to apply to the Court for rectification of the register of members where the name of a person is fraudulently or without sufficient cause entered in or omitted from that register. The instant case squarely fits in with the provision and the principle of law on the subject.</u>

<u>26. The finding arrived at by the learned Company Judge on scrutiny appear to be based on evidence on record, both documentary or oral, and we do not find any illegality or infirmity to interfere with the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division.</u>

27. In the result, we are in full agreement with the learned Judge of the High Court Division and accordingly, affirm the impugned judgment and order.

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

Rafique-ul Huq with M Moniruzzaman Khan, Marium Khan, Morshed Ahmed Khan, ASM Abdur Razzaque and Syed Aynul Kabir------ For the Petitioners.
