In assailing the findings and decisions of the High Court Division and the trial Court relating to the matter that weighed with the Courts, the learned Counsel has submitted that the courts being totally oblivious of the provision of the Act were in error in considering the matter of injunction in the background of the aspect that generally weighs with the Court in considering the matter of temporary injunction and granting an order of temporary injunction cannot be considered well founded since we have already mentioned that the law as in sections 3(1) and 3(4) of the Act barring the Court from granting an order of injunction is limited in application as to the arbitration being held in Bangladesh, but not as to matter restraining a particular party from proceeding with arbitration in foreign country in respect of a contract signed in Bangladesh.</u>

16. The learned Counsel for the respondent No.1 upon referring to the cases reported in 47 DLR (AD) 70, 49 DLR (AD) 46 and 5 MLR (AD) 45 has submitted that this Division has consistently refused to interfere with the order passed in respect of the interlocutory matter e.g. an order of injunction passed upon hearing both the parties, unless the discretion so exercised by the High Court Division in interlocutory matters is "wholly un judicially or is so palpably wrong that it shocks the judicial conscience." In the instant case from the judgment of the High Court Division, it is seen that the said Division while dismissing the appeal and thereby maintaining the order of temporary injunction passed by the trial Court has not committed an error of the kind calling for interference by this Division. In the background of the facts of the case and the materials brought on record, it can also be not said that the High Court Division and the trial Court exercised its discretion in the matter of granting temporary injunction wholly unjudicially or that the order so passed by the trial Court "is so palpably wrong that it shocks the judicial conscience." The learned Counsel for the respondent No.1 in support of his contention that with the termination of the contract, particularly because of the provision in section 2 Article 33.8 the provision in section 2 Article 30.2 i.e. referring dispute/difference between the parties to the contract to the arbitration became inoperative or ceased has referred to the unreported decision of this Division in CPLA Nos.73-75 of 1982, 32 DLR 94 and clause 67 of FIDIC. We are restraining ourselves from expressing any view on the subject since a petition filed by the defendants before the trial Court under section 34 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 awaits disposal and, in all probability, this question is likely to come up for decision before the trial Court. From the judgment of the High Court Division and the order of the trial Court granting temporary injunction it is seen that the matters that weigh with high court in considering prayer for temporary injunction those, after detailed discussions of the materials on record, have been found in favour of the plaintiff. The High Court Division while dismissing the appeal has directed the trial Court to dispose of expeditiously the petition filed by the defendant No.1 under section 34 of the Arbitration Act, 1940.

17. Learned Counsel for the respondent No.1 upon referring to the provisions of sections 379, 384 and 385 of the Companies Act, 1994 has submitted that the petitioners, particularly petitioner No.1, is not competent to proceed with petition for leave to appeal since petitioner No.1 has not been incorporated legally or that certificate of change in the Constitution of the Company has not been submitted before the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies within the time prescribed and, in support of the aforesaid contention the learned Counsel has referred to the decision in the case of Engineer Mahmudul Islam and others vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 55 DLR 171. We are refraining ourselves from expressing any view as to the aforesaid contention since without addressing the said contention the petition for leave to appeal can be disposed of Since the judgment of the High Court Division and the order of the trial Court appear to be reasonable one that the contentions as to maintainability of the suit as well as barring the Court from granting injunction In view of the provision of the Act and also the matter as to whether the agreement is a continuing one in spite of section 2 Article 33.8 or not made by the learned Counsels for the parties can very much be gone into at the time of disposing of the application filed under section 34 of the Arbitration Act, we do not find any reason to interfere with the judgment and order of the High Court Division.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 90 and 94 of 2000
lawyer:
Syed Ziaul Karim, Advocate instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioner (In both cases). 
Not Represented ----- Respondents (In both the cases).
parties:
Abu Siddique and anr ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Defence & ors ----- Respondent
case_source: (From the common Judgment and Order dated 22-3- 1999 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 4864 and 4863 of 1996).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: These two leave petitions have been filed by the writ petitioners of Writ Petition Nos. 4864 of 1996 and 4863 of 1996 against the common judgment and order of 22nd March, 1999 of a Division Bench of the High Court Division discharging the Rules. The writ petitions were filed challenging legality of the notices dated 5th November, 1996 and 6th November, 1996 in the respective writ petitions. The notices were issued under sections 94 and 160 CrPC by the District Anti-Corruption Officer, Dhaka, (respondent No.3 in the respective writ petitions) asking the respective petitioners to appear before him with the papers and documents in connection with an enquiry under the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 against them upon a complaint received by the Anti-Corruption Bureau.

2. The petitioners challenged the respective notices firstly, on the ground that the notice issued under sections 94 and 160 CrPC by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption were illegal, since in the absence of initiation of a case the Anti-Corruption Bureau, hereinafter in brief, the Bureau, is not authorised by law to issue the notice under the aforesaid sections of the CrPC. It was also contended that power under sections 94 and 160 CrPC could only be exercised by the Police Officer for the purpose of investigation where a case has been recorded and that the enquiry being not investigation, officers of the Bureau are not authorised to exercise power under sections 94 and 160 CrPC at the enquiry stage.

3. On consideration of the provision of section 3 of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957, hereinafter in brief, the Act, the High Court Division as to the contention of the writ petitioners as regard exercise of power under sections 94 and 160 CrPC by the officers of the Bureau in connection with enquiry in respect of a complaint arrived at the finding that the officers of the Bureau in connection with the enquiry of a complaint can very well issue notice under the said sections of CrPC and exercise the powers thereunder.

4. In support of the Rule obtained by the writ petitioners it was also contended that power to make enquiry by the Bureau is not available against a private person. The High Court Division upon placing reliance on the decision of the Appellate Division reported in 4 BLT (AD) 58 and that also upon a decision reported in 50 DLR 306 held that the contention of the petitioners is of no merit.

5. The other contention of the petitioner was that notices impugned in the respective writ petitions were violative of Article 35(4) of the Constitution. The High Court Division upon observing,

"It is only an accused in a trial who cannot be compelled to be a witness against himself. Therefore it is our considered view that a person cannot seek the protection of Article 35(4) when a notice is sent by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption under sections 94 and 160 CrPC. Section 3 of the Act which empowered an officer of Bureau of Anti-Corruption to serve notice under sections 94 and 160 CrPC only for the purpose of enquiry to determine the truth of the information received or as about offences connected with community interest, that is, offences in the schedule to the Anti-Corruption Act"

arrived at the finding that notices issued by the Bureau under sections 94 and 160 CrPC are not violative of Article 35(4) of the Constitution. The High Court Division while discharging the Rule has observed that "the officer of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption has the power to order and summon under sections 94 and 160 CrPC for the purpose of making a preliminary enquiry" and that the person who has been served with the notice under sections 94 and 160 CrPC would "have the right to know the nature of information and complaint the Bureau of Anti-Corruption has received so that he unknowingly does not make a statement to a question which might have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge". The High Court Division on consideration of the provisions of the Act, particularly provision of section 3 of the Act and the provision of sections 94 and 160 CrPC finally arrived at the finding that in issuing the notice under sections 94 and 160 CrPC by the Bureau asking the petitioners to appear before the specified officer of the Bureau in connection with an inquiry has committed no illegality.

6. Mr Syed Ziaul Karim, learned Advocate for the petitioners in the respective leave petitions upon referring to the provision of section 160 CrPC, submits that the notice issued by the Bureau under the said section was not legal since provision of said section is available to a police officer while making an investigation which presupposes pendency of a Case already initiated by lodging an information under section 154 CrPC. The submission of the learned Advocate is not legally well conceived one because of the provision of sub-section (2) of section 3 of the Act, empowering the officers of the Bureau to enquire into and investigate the offences described in the schedule attached to the Act. The provision of the said sub-section authorises the officers of the Bureau while enquiring into, and investigation of, the offences described in the schedule to make seizure, search and arrest of persons concerned in the said offences and that it is competent to exercise all other powers, duties, privileges and liabilities which the police officers of Bangladesh have in connection with the investigation of such offences.

7. In the background of judicial pronouncements the law is now at rest that in case of cognisable offences, receipt and recording of a first information report is not a conditions precedent to the setting in motion of a criminal investigation. The offences specified in the schedule are cognisable offences. The Bureau on receiving of .complaint or information as regard anyone of the offence specified in the schedule goes for enquiry into and 'investigation of such complaint to ascertain at the first truth of such complaint or information. The offences listed in the schedule being cognisable offence the enquiry into and investigation of the complaint or information without recording of case upon formal receiving and recording or First Information Report is permissible in law and that also legal. As per provision of sub-section (3) of section 3 of the Act, any officer of the Bureau is authorised to exercise, subject to any orders made by the Government, "any of the powers of officer-in-charge of police station in the area in which he is for the time being and. When so exercising such power shall", subject to any orders made by the Government, "be deemed to be an officer-in-charge of a police station discharging the function of such an officer within the limit of his station". This being the provision of law, officers of the Bureau are very much within the' bounds of law in serving notice under sections 94 and 160 of the CrPC and to exercise power thereunder.

<u>8. The other contention that action of the respondent No. 3 was violative of Article 35(4) of the Constitution is also of no substance since the notices impugned were issued in connection with an enquiry as regard the information received against the petitioners. The petitioners are not accused of any offence and, as such, protection under Article 35(4) is not available to them.</u>

9. Section 94 is in Chapter VII of the CrPC. The provision of the said section empowers or authorises the officer-in-charge of the police station to make direction to a person for the production of any document or other thing as considers necessary or desirable for the purposes of any investigation, or inquiry, under the Code before such officer, upon issuing notice in writing to the person "in whose possession or power such document or thing is believed to be, requiring him to attend and produce it, or to produce it, at the time and place specified in the notice or order.

<u>10. Section 160 CrPC is in Chapter XIV of Part- V of the CrPC. This part amongst others, also deals with the power of the police relating to investigation. As per provision of the said section any police officer while making an investigation under chapter XIV of Part V CrPC "may by order in writing require the attendance before himself of any person being within the limits of his own or any adjoining station, who from the information given or otherwise, appears to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case; and such person shall attend as so required". It has already been spelt out hereinabove that in case of cognisable offence receipt and recording of first information report is not a condition precedent to the setting in motion of a criminal investigation. That being the position in law the officers of the Bureau in connection with investigation of a complaint to ascertain truth thereof is authorised to issue notice under section 160 CrPC.</u>

<u>11. Provision of section 3(2) of the Act authorises the officers of the Bureau to inquire into and investigate the offences specified in the schedule to the Act and in doing so the officers have all the powers, duties, privileges and liabilities which the police officers of Bangladesh have in connection with investigation of offences. Under sub-section (3) of section 3 of the Act officers of the Bureau are authorised to exercise any of the powers of an officer-in-charge of the police station in the area in which he is for the time being enquiring into and investigation in the offence specified in the schedule and that while exercising the said powers he would be deemed to be an officer-in-charge of a police station discharging the function of such an officer within the limit of his station.</u>

In the background of the discussions made herein above we are of the view that High Court Division has committed no error of law in refusing to declare the impugned notices issued by the Anti-Corruption Bureau to the petitioners under sections 94 and 160 of the CrPC illegal. Accordingly, the petitions are dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Fazlul Karim,Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record------ For the Appellants.
Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate, (Probir Neogi, Advocate with him) instructed by Sufia Khatun, Advocate-on-Record------ For Respondent No. 1.
Not represented------  Respondent Nos. 2-22.
parties:
Abdur Rashid Sarker (Md) and others ------ Appellants
Vs.
Dines Chandra Das and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 19-11-1999 passed by (he High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 559 of 1997)
full_judgment:
MM Ruhul Amin J: This appeal, by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 19-11-1999 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 559 of 1997 making the Rule absolute.

2. Short facts are that the respondent No.1 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 394 of 1978 in the 2nd Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge); Gaibandha praying for pre-emption of the case land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. On transfer to the Court of the Senior Assistajrt Judge, Gobindaganj, the case was renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 38 of 1992. The pre-emptor asserts that he is a co-sharer in the case land and that the respondent No.1 sold the case rand to the appellants at a consideration of Taka 7,000 by registered kabala dated 26-1-1978 and that the pre-emptor has no land more than 10 bighas and accordingly, he is entitled to pre-empt the case land.

3. The pre-emptees contested the case by filing a written objection contending, inter alia that the case is barred by limitation and the same is bad for defect of parties, that the pre-emptor had knowledge of the sale as the sale took place with his consent and they have developed the case land at a cost of Taka, 5,000. Accordingly the pre-emptees Prayed for dismissal of the case.

4. The learned Senior Assistant, Judge on consideration of, the evidence on record found that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the case holding and the case is not barred by limitation and that the same is also not bad for defect of parties. The learned Senior Assistant, Judge also found I that the pre-emptees case that they made improvement of the case land at a cost of Taka 5,000 could not be proved, Accordingly, by judgment and order dated 26-6-1995 tile learned J Senior Assistant Judge allowed the Miscellaneous case.

5. The pre-emptees then preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 70 of 1995 before the learned District Judge, Gaibandha. The learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Gaibandha who heard the appeal concurred with the trial Court that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer, the case is not barred by limitation and that the pre-emptees could not prove their claim of Taka 5,000 as improvement cost. The learned Subordinate Judge further found that the pre-emption case is bad for defect of parties. Accordingly, by judgment and order dated 23-6-1996 the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal reversed the judgment and order of the trial Court and dismissed the Miscellaneous case.

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order, the pre-emptor moved the High Court Division and obtained the Rule.

7. The High Court Division relying upon a decision reported in 31 DLR (AD) 88 held that the pre-emptees did not disclose the names of those left out co-sharers and did not press the issue regarding the non-joinder of the co-sharers before the trial Court. Therefore, the pre-emption case could not fail on that account and accordingly, made the Rule absolute.

8. Leave was granted to consider the submission that the decision reported in 31 DLR (AD) 88 is no longer holding the field in view of the later decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 113 by which the Appellate Division, in fact, overruled its earlier decision and therefore, the High Court Division erred in law in allowing the prayer for preemption ignoring the special feature of the instant case that the non-joinder of certain co-sharers was admitted by the pre-emptor in his cross- examination during trial.

9. We have heard Mr Fazlul Karim, the learned Counsel for the appellants and Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel for respondent No.1 and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers.

10. It is not disputed that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding and the case is not barred by limitation.

11. The trial Court found that the case was not bad for defect of parties but the appellate Court held that the case was bad for defect of parties and accordingly allowed the appeal and reversed the judgment and order of the trial Court. The High Court Division reversed the Judgment of the appellate Court holding that the pre-emptees did not disclose the names of those left out co-sharers in reply to the interrogatories served upon them by the pre-emptor and also did not press the issue regarding the defect of party before the trial Court at the earliest opportunity. The High Court Division in this regard relied on a decision reported in 31 DLR (AD) 88.

12. It is on record that the pre-emptees raised the question of defect of parties in the written objection and accordingly, plaintiff served interrogatories upon the pre-emptees to supply the names of the necessary party. The pre-emptees supplied the names of necessary parties and they were impleaded by the pre-emptor in the case. But at the time of trial, during cross-examination of the pre-emptor by the learned Advocate for the pre- emptee, he disclosed the names of some persons who are' said to be necessary parties and accordingly, the appellate Court disallowed the case for defect of parties.

13. Mr Karim submits that impleading of necessary parties in a pre-emption proceeding is a mandatory requirement under section 96(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and non- disclosure of the names of the necessary parties by the pre-emptee cannot absolve the pre-emptor from complying with the mandatory provision of law regarding impleading necessary parties in a preemption case. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel relied on the decision in the case of Abdus Samad and others vs Md Shorab All and others reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 77 and also in the case of Jalaluddin Fakir vs Shajahan All Molla and others reported in 1984 BLD (AD) 27. In the case of Akhtarun Nessa and another vs Habibullah and others reported in 31 DLR (AD) 88 it was held that any objection as to omission of a necessary party must be taken at the earliest possible opportunity and such objection if not so taken, may be deemed to have been waived. In the case of Shahidur Rahman Molla vs Abdul Halim Molla reported in 1983 BLD 89, it was held that disclosure of the names of some persons who ought to have been impleaded in the proceeding would not make the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the Act bad on ground of defect of parties unless the pre-emptee opposite parties have raised the question of non-joinder of some co-sharer or contiguous tenant at the earliest opportunity before the trial Court. In that case, PW 1, in his cross-examination, disclosed the names of some contiguous tenants. In the said reported decision it was further held that the pre-emptee opposite parties having not raised the issue as to non-joinder in their objection, they cannot take advantage of any disclosure of such absence of any co-sharer at the trial and the trial Court as well was not required under the law to decide the question of non-joinder. In the instant case as we have indicated earlier in the written objection the pre-emptee raised the question of defect of party and the pre-emptor served interrogatory upon the pre-emptee to supply the names of the necessary party and the pre-emptee replied to the interrogatories by supplying some names and those persons were Impleaded by the pre-emptor in the preemption proceeding. The preemptor, in the instant case, however, in his evidence during cross- examination by pre-emptees lawyer disclosed some names who are said to be purchasers of land of the disputed jote. The High Court Division held that the disclosure of the names of persons in evidence for the first time by the preemptor will not defeat the right of pre-emption as the pre-emptees did not disclose these names at the initial stage of filing their written objection or even disclose the names in the reply to the interrogatories served upon them by the pre-emptor. The High Court Division also held that the facts of the case of Jalaluddin Fakir vs Shajahan Ali Molla and others reported in 1984 BLD (AD) 27 and the decision in the case of Abdus Samad and others vs Md Sohrab Ali and others reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 77 are distinguishable from the facts of the present case. In the case of Abdus Samad and others vs Md Sohrab Ali and others reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 77, it was held that on account of omission of necessary party a pre-emption case shall not be dismissed outright keeping in view the provision of Order I, rule 9, CPC inasmuch as non-joinder of a necessary party will not by itself defeat a suit/proceeding. The objection as to non joinder of necessary parties must be taken at the earliest opportunity by the defendant.

14. Mr Mahmudul Islam, on the other hand. cited the case of Motilal Sikder vs Benodini Dasi reported in 28 DLR (AD) 5. In that case, the case reported in 14 DLR 847 was discussed. In 14 DLR 847 it was held as under:

"In the case of pre-emption because of the special provision of the Act rights of the parties cannot be determined without considering the rights of others. The principles of Order 1, rule 9 of the Code cannot be made applicable. in the circumstances. It cannot be said that the tenants holding lands contiguous to the lands transferred are not necessary parties as they are persons whose presence is necessary for the proper constitution of the pre-emption application. Order 1, rule 9 of the Code does not apply when a cause of action arises against a number of persons jointly because when one of such persons is eliminated no cause of action subsists against others as in the suit for partition. In the case of the pre-emption under section 96 of the Act, the cause of action arises not only against the transferee but also against the co-sharers and other holders of contiguous lands."

15. In the case of Motilal Sikder vs Benodini Dasi it was held that it is difficult to place a suit for partition and a case for pre-emption on the same footing on the question of joinder of parties. In a suit for partition the co-sharers are necessary parties in the sense that in the absence of any such co-sharer the judgment which will be given in such a suit may be rendered infructuous at the option of the excluded party. It was further held that the question of parties in such a suit is considered entirely on a different footing, not because the provisions of Order 1rule 9, CPC or Order 1, rule 13, CPC are not applicable to such a suit but because the trial of such a suit is subject to another principle which is to the effect that no Court shall pass a decree which may be set at naught at the instance of a person who is not impleaded in the said suit. It does not however, mean that a suit for partition is beyond the pale of the procedural rules such as Order 1, rule 13 and Order VIII, rule 2, CP Code. Such rules are very much applicable in a suit for partition in the same way as in other classes of suits, and a party is precluded from taking at a late stage an objection as to defect of party of which sufficient notice has not been given to the other side, even in a suit for partition. It was held that a proceeding for pre-emption cannot be treated on the same level as a suit for partition.

16. He then cited the case of Abdus Samad & others vs Md Sohrab Ali and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 113 (same case has been reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 77). In that case the case of Motilal Sikder vs Benodini Dasi reported in 28 DLR (AD) 5 was discussed and it was held that in Motilal Sikdar vs Benodini Dasi an attempt has been made to lay down the principle that the provision as contained in sub-section (2) of section 96 is not mandatory but merely directory, in other words, no duty is cast upon the pre-emptor to implead all the parties who are, as contemplated under section 96, necessary parties. This view is more founded on the provision of procedure as provided under Order 1, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure than strict interpretation of the language of the section. In that case it was further held that the question of non-joinder of necessary party affecting framing of a pre-emption application is to be decided keeping in view the requirement of the different sub-sections of section 96 along with the provisions as contained in Order 1, rules 9 and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. because pre-emption proceedings being one of the proceedings as contemplated under section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the procedure of law in Order 1, rule 9 is applicable. On account of omission of necessary party, a pre-emption case shall not be dismissed outright keeping in view the provision of Order 1, rule 9, inasmuch as, non-joinder of necessary party will not by itself defeat a suit/proceeding. However, the special statutory provision in sub-section(2) of section 96 as to the necessary parties to be impleaded, is mandatory. In that case it was further held that the requirement of the statutory provision cannot be minimised by the procedural law as contains in Order I, rule 9, CPC. The special provision in sub-section (2) is not controlled by Order 1, rule 9, CPC which merely provides that a suit shall not be dismissed by reason of mere non-joinder of necessary parties. The objection as to non-joinder of necessary parties must be taken at the earliest opportunity by the defendant. Such objection provides an opportunity to the plaintiff to remove the defect by adding parties who were omitted. It was further held that if the pre-emptee or, for that matter, any of the parties disclose existence of a necessary party and furnishes the necessary particulars, but the pre-emptor still insists not to implead him as a party, consequence Oil adjudication is the same. Objection regarding non-joinder of necessary parties should be taken at the earliest opportunity, before' the trial, because an enquiry on this question may be necessary. Of course, in an appropriate case such objection may be allowed to be raised in the appeal. This may be done on the ground that the appeal is continuation of the suit or proceeding. But there is no scope for raising the question of defect of party on account of non-joinder of necessary parties, for the first time in revision. ln that case it was further held that the requirement as to making of parties is undoubtedly positive. It is the duty of the pre-emptor to implead the necessary parties and this requirement of law should be enforced keeping in view the provisions of Order 1, rules 9 and 10, CPC. If the pre-emptor, after getting an opportunity, fails to amend his application by impleading the necessary parties as pointed out by the pre-emptee. and on evidence if it is found that the application suffers from defect of parties, in that event the application cannot succeed and must be dismissed.

17. He next cited the case of Jalaluddin Fakir vs Shahjahan, AIi Molla and others reported in 1984 RLD (AD) 27 and submitted that in that case the pre-emptor did not take any steps to meet the objection of defect of parties raised in the written objection by serving any interrogatory upon the pre-emptee and that the law enjoins upon the pre-emptor to implead all the co-sharers as parties and, as such, the pre-emption has been rightly refused in the case. In that case, the case reported in 33 DLR (AD) 113 was considered.

18. in the instant case the pre-emptee raised the question of defect of party in the written objection and pre-emptor served interrogatory upon the pre-emptee to supply the names of the necessary parties who were left out. Accordingly, the pre-emptee supplied the names of necessary parties and those persons were impleaded as opposite parties in the pre-emption proceeding by the pre-emptor. Subsequently, during trial in the cross-examination of the preemptor by the pre-emptee the names of some persons were disclosed who according to the pre-emptee are necessary parties but they have not been impleaded and accordingly, the pre-emption application was disallowed by the appellate Court.

19. Thus, it is clear that those persons whose names transpired in the course of cross-examination of the pre-emptor by the pre-emptees were very much within the knowledge of the pre-emptees but the pre-emptees wilfully and purposefully did not furnish those names in reply to the interrogatory served by the pre-emptor upon him. If this practice is allowed to continue a pre-emption proceeding shall be an unending proceeding, for the pre-emptee in order to defeat the right of pre-emption would not disclose all the names in reply to the interrogatory served on him/ her by the pre-emptor and he would disclose some names during cross-examination obviously to make the pre-emption application bad for defect of parties.

20. We are of the view that if those left out persons were known to the pre-emptor from before, there was no reason for him to exclude those names as in that case his pre-emption case was liable to fail for defect of parties. A man of ordinary prudence would never do that.

<u>21. In view of the discussion made above we are of the view that objection as to defect of parties is to be taken at the earliest opportunity. In the instant case that has not been done. Moreover, the pre-emptees did not supply the names of the persons whose names he put to the pre-emptor during cross- examination in reply to the interrogatory served on him. Therefore, in our view, he was debarred from making such cross-examination regarding defect of parties and he was also debarred from raising the question of defect of parties at that stage of the proceeding after replying to the interrogatory served on him earlier.</u>

The appeal is, accordingly, dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

caseno: Appeal from original decree No.51 of 1969.
lawyer:
Abdul Hamid Chowdhury ------ For the appellants. 
Md. Yeasin—For Respdt. No.1.
Shamsur Rahman ------ For Respdt. Nos. 3(a) to 3(ka).
parties:
Muzaffar Ali Bepari & others  ------ Appellants. 
Vs. 
Abdul Baser and others  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Ahsanuddin Chowdhury, J.— In this appeal Mr. Md. Yeasin, the learned Advocate representing the plaintiff-respondent has raised a preliminary objection to the effect that on account of the death of appellants Nos. 1 and 6 whose heirs have not been substituted, the whole appeal has abated.

2. The circumstances under which this preliminary point has been raised may be stated as follows:

The plaintiff-respondent No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 13866 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca claiming a saham for 11.36 acres of land out of the suit and measuring 26.34 acres by virtue of his purchases on a number of sale deeds. The suit was contested by two sets of defendants, namely, 1, 2, 3 and 5 forming one set and 10 to 15, 17, 28 and 29 forming the other set. The suit was decreed in part on contest against the contesting defendants and ex parte against the rest in a preliminary form without, however, any order as to costs. The learned Subordinate Judge has found that the plaintiff-respondent by his purchases has acquired title in 6.80½ acres of land and has accordingly directed the partition of the suit property for allotting the plaintiff-respondent a saham for 6.80½ acres of land. Against this judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge the present appeal was filed by as many as 29 defendants. During the pendency of the appeal 3 appellants namely, appellant Nos.1, 6 and 9 died whereupon a Rule being Civil Rule No.169 (f)/72 was obtained from this Court for substitution of the heirs of those deceased appellants after setting side the abatement of the appeal which had already taken place, The Rule was heard by a division  Bench of this Court and the Rule was discharged on the findings that there was no sufficient cause preventing the petitioners in the Rule from taking necessary steps for the substitution of the heirs of the deceased appellants in time. It was, however, found that the heirs of the deceased appellant No.9 were already on record. Thereafter when this appeal was taken up by this Division Bench an application was filed under section 107 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and also read with Order 41, rule 20 and Order 1, rule 10 of the said Code playing for addition of the heirs of deceased appellants Nos. 1 and 6 as appellants in this first Appeal No.51 of 1969. But the prayer for substitution of the heirs of the deceased appellants 1 and 6 having been earlier refused by a Division Bench of this Court in the aforesaid Rule the petition for addition of those heirs in this appeal has been rejected by us. Consequently the question has arisen as to whether on account of non-substitution of the heirs of deceased appellants Nos. 1 and 6, the whole appeal has abated or it has abated in so far as the deceased appellant Nos. 1 and 6 are concerned.

3. On this point we have heard at length Mr. Md. Yeasin, who represents the plaintiff respondents Mr. Abdul Hamid Chowdhury learned Advocate who represented the appellants could not make his full argument on account or some difficulties on his part and on his behalf Mr. M.S. Rahman, the learned Advocate who represents defendant-respondents 3(a) to 3(k) has argued at length against the objection raised by Mr. Md. Yeasin.

4. Mr. Md. Yeasin has argued that the law has been well settled in respect of the parties to be made in the petition suit and the properties to be brought in the common hotch potch, that is to say, all the co-sharers in the property are to be made parties in the partition suit and the entire joint properties out of which a saham or sahaws are sought must be brought in the hotch potch of the suit and that the appeal being the continuation of the suit the same principle must apply in the appeal as well. He has thus submitted that in the present appeal the appellants 1 and 6 having died and their heirs having not been brought on record by way of substitution and the share or interest of the defendant-appellants having not been specified in the judgment and decree the whole appeal has abated. In support of his contention he has relied upon some decisions namely, 11 DLR, 441, 12 DLR, 363, 14 DLR, 471. The case of Iman Ali Halsana and others Vs. Furkun Ali Mondal & others reported in 11 DLR, 347 is the earliest decision of a Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court on the question of abatement. In this case the defendants were the appellants in a Second Appeal before the High Court of Dhaka. During the pendency of the appeal appellant No. 1 died and no step was taken to substitute his heirs A preliminary objection was taken to the effect that the appeal had abated.

<u>5. The appellant No. 1 having died during the pendency of the appeal and no step having heel taken to substitute his legal representative it was not disputed that so far as the appeal of appellant No. 1 was concerned, the appeal had abated. But the question arose whether according to the nature of the claim and according to the nature of the decree, on account of the failure to substitute the legal representative of appellant No.1, the entire appeal had abated. According to the view taken in that case, one of the tests as to whether an appeal as a whole has abated is as to whether if appeal succeeds there will be in existence two conflicting decrees. If such be the position then the appeal would not partially abate. It would abate as a whole. In the, case reported in (11 DLR 347 ) defendant Nos. 1 and 2 claimed or he co-sharers of the jama in suit, but nothing was said in the pleading if they held definite and specified shares in the lands appertaining to the Jama. The plaintiff got a decree in the suit. So far as the deceased-appellant No. 1 was concerned the decree would stand on account of abatement of the appeal consequent upon his death. If the appeal would succeed, in that event there would be two conflicting decrees, one of trial Court and the other of the Court of Appeal. So it was held that the entire appeal had abated. In that case the argument was advanced that Order 41, rule 4 of C.P.C. would govern the case but that contention was ruled out holding that Order 41, rule 4 cannot override or create exception to Order 22, rules 3 and 11. It was further observed that sub-rule (4) of rule 4 of Order 22 does not help appellants in a case where the appeal has abated as against legal representatives of a contesting defendant. In this case (11 DLR, 347) a number of decisions were considered and their Lordships are of the view that if the circumstances are such that the parties shares are not definite and specified in the land then on account of the death of one such contesting party whose heirs are not brought on record by way of substitution the whole appeal shall abate In the latter two cases, namely, 12 D.L.R. 363 Haji Asmat Ali Khan and others Vs. Municipal Commissioners of Madaripur Municipality and others and 14 D.L.R 471 Ahamedur Rahman and others Vs. Abdul Majid and others, the same view has been expressed by the Dacca High Court. It is thus obvious that the consistent view is that if the interest or share is not specified in respect of each of the parties in the suit and if death of any one of them occurs at the appellate stage and the heirs are not substituted then the whole appeal will abate if there is a chance of conflicting derees one of trial Court and the other of the Court of Appeal.</u>

6. On the other hand, Mr. Md. Shamsur Rahman, the learned Advocate has argued before us on behalf of 17 DLR (SC) 536 and 19 DLR (Dacca) 389. We are afraid that these two decisions render no support to the contentions raised by Shamsur Rahman who has tried to impress upon us that the appeal, if it has at all abated has abated only in respect of appellant Nos. 1 and 6 and it has not abated as a whole in the case of Wall and others Vs. Manik Ali and others reported in 17 DLR (SC) 536 the main contention on behalf of the appellants was that the share which the two plaintiffs Claimed in the property were ascertained or ascertainable and as such that appeal abated only in respect of the deceased plaintiff-respondent. This contention was not upheld because the share was neither ascertained nor ascertainable. In the present case also we do not find that the share which the defendants claimed in the property is ascertained or ascertainable on the evidence on record, In this connection the concluding order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge may be usefully quoted and it runs as follows :

"That this partition suit be decreed in part on contest against defendants 1-3, 10-15, 17, 18 and 19 and ex parte against the rest in a preliminary form without costs. The parties do effect partition by metes and bounds in respect of the plaintiff's share of land measuring 6.80½ acres within six months hence, failing which the plaintiff may apply to this Court for a final decree according to the provisions of the C.P.C. The plaintiff shall be given as far as possible a compact saham and the convenience of possession of the parties shall also be kept in view. In schedule 'C' of the plaint, plot No. 1882 (.82 acres) appears to have been inserted by mistake as this land is not show in the relevant Khatian No.1510 but is shown in Khatian No. 92 Let this clerical error in the plaint be rectified before drawing up of the decree."

7. It appears from the above quotation that it is only the plaintiff s share in the land measuring 6.80½ acres was found by the learned Subordinate Judge on the basis of the evidence that was adduced before him. The order is absolutely silent about the shares which each of the contesting defendants might have in the suit property, It is obvious that the shares of the contesting defendants or for that matter, of all the defendants have not at all been specified in the judgment of the Court nor their respective shares are ascertainable on the evidence which is on record. In this view of the matter the decision reported in 17 DLR and relied on by Mr. M. S. Rahman renders no support to the contention of the appellants, so also the case reported in 19 DLR shows that the plaintiff brought the suit for declaration of his title to and recovery of possession of the suit land against the defendants. Defendant No. 1 alone contested the suit. After a chequered career the suit was ultimately, dismissed by the First Appellate Court on the ground that the suit as a whole abated on account of the death of defendant No. 9 whose heirs had not been brought on record. In the Second Appeal preferred before the Dacca High Court, their Lordships observed as follows ;—

"Now in the instant case if a decree is passed as against the other defendants excluding defendant No. 9 or in other words, dismissing the plaintiff's suit as against defendant No. 9, and if the plaintiff there after wants to seek relief against the heirs of defendant No.9, he will naturally have to face some hurdles under the provisions of law; but the said decree can in no way be said to be an inconsistent one and the suit as against other defendants would be perfectly constituted in the absence of defendant No. 9."

8. It may be noted that the Second Appeal was allowed and the case was remanded to the First Appellate Court for disposal in accordance with law. The principle enunciated in this decision by their Lordships does not militate against the principle enunciated in the decisions reported in 11, 12 and 14 DLR already considered by us. It is, however, to be noted that whether an abatement of appeal on account of the death of one of the appellants or one of the respondents would affect the whole appeal or not would depend on the circumstances of each case. In the instant case the shares of the appellants being not specified, there is a chance of conflicting decrees, one of trial Court and the other of the appellate Court, if the appeal succeeds. Consequently the whole appeal has abated in view of what has been stated above and as such we do not propose to go into the merit of the appeal.

There will be, however, no order as to the costs in this appeal.

K. M. Subban, J.—I agree.

End.

full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J.-This appeal, at the instance of defendants. Nos. 1 to 5 arises out of a suit for partition which has been decreed in a preliminary form.

2. The plaintiff's case, in short, is that the property in dispute belonged to one Rajab Ali who died leaving two sons namely Jalal Baksh and Aziz Baksh and also a widow named Surati Bibi. Jalal Baksh the elder son was very clever and intelligent and used to manage the household. The younger brother Aziz Baksh was on the other hand illiterate and had to depend upon his elder brother who was entrusted with the management of all the affairs of the family. Taking advantage of the illiteracy of Aziz Baksh and his dependence upon him Jalal Baksh got 11 annas 4 gondas share of the suit land recorded in his name, -/2/- annas in the name of Surati Bibi and -/2/- annas 16 gondas only in the name of Aziz Baksh in the C.S. Khatian without the knowledge and consent of Aziz Baksh. The said entries in the records of rights in respect of the shares of Jalal Baksh and Aziz Baksh were wrong as the shares of the two brothers in the properties left by their father were equal. Surati Bibi having died subsequently, Jalal Baksh and Aziz Baksh inherited her share equally. On the death of Jalal Baksh his properties were inherited by his 5 sons namely Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 and seven daughters, namely, Defendant No. 6 to 9 and 11 Kulsum Bibi, predecessor of Defendant Nos. 11 to 15 and Batashi Bibi, predecessor of Defendant Nos. 16 to 18, all of whom thus jointly inherited -/8/- annas share of the suit land. Thereafter Aziz Baksh died leaving behind 4 sons namely plaintiff Nos. 1 to 4 wife plaintiff No. 5 and three daughters, plaintiffs Nos. 6 to 8 who jointly inherited the remaining -/8/- annas of the land in suit. The disputed land was never partitioned by metes and bounds and the principal defendants who are in possession of the major portion of the suit land and have sold away some of the lands did not agree to partition the ejmali land in spite of the interest made by the plaintiffs. It has been also alleged that the wrong entries in the C.S. records have since been corrected on the basis of an application made on behalf of the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs shares, totaling -/8/- as have been duty recorded in the new khatian after necessary correction. The proforma Defendants Nos. 20 to 26 are said to have purchased some of the lands in the suit. There was addition of a number of parties as defendants to the suit by the subsequent orders of the Court.

3. The suit was contested by Defendants Nos. 1 to 5 as well as by Defendant Nos. 27 to 48 and 50 to 61 who filed two separate written statements. Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 pleaded inter alia that the suit was not maintainable in the present form and was bad for defect of parties and misjoinder of parties and causes of action and alleged that the genealogy and the sequence of death as given in the plaint were incorrect and that the suit was barred by limitation and adverse possession. The main contention of the said Defendants as stated in their written statement was however that it was true that the suit properties did originally belong to Rajab Ali and that Rajab Ali died leaving behind not only two sons and a widow but also 6 daughters who inherited the suit property but that they being satisfied with the conduct of Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 and dissatisfied with the rude behavior and unkind treatment of Aziz Baksh, relinquished and gave up their -/8/8 gondas share of the disputed land in favour of Jalal Baksh and got the same recorded in the name of Jalal Baksh along with his own share to the knowledge of Aziz Baksh who raised no objection. Thereafter by amicable partition of the suit land by metes and bounds with his brother Aziz Baksh, Jalal Baksh possessed his -/11/4 gondas share of the suit land duly demarcated till his death. After the death of Surati Bibi the share of Jalal Baksh increased to /12/4 gondas share which was also duly demarcated. It is therefore alleged that the suit lands having already been partitioned amicably, there was no scope for further partition.

4. Defendant Nos. 27 to 48 and 50 to 61 who are the heirs of 5 daughters of Rajab Ali gave stated in their written statement that the other daughter of Rajab Ali, namely, Joytun Bibi, predeceased, her father and as such her heirs did not inherit anything in the properties of Rajab Ali, that their predecessors were in constructive possession of the disputed land through the plaintiffs and Defendants Nos. 1 to 5 and that they never made a gift of their share to Jalal Baksh who got the wrong C.S. records of right prepared fraudulently without the knowledge of his sisters.

5. Several issues were framed and the learned Subordinate Judge on a consideration of the evidence on record has come to the finding that the suit is not bad for mis-joinder of parties or causes of action nor for defect of parties and that the suit is maintainable in its present form. The learned Subordinate Judge has further held that the case made out in the plaint that Rajab Ali died leaving only two sons and a widow and no daughter is not correct and that he was survived by the 6 (six) daughters as contended by the contesting defendant Nos. 1 to 5 . On the question of the alleged gift and relinquishment of the shares of the sisters in favour of their brother Jalal Baksh, the learned Subordinate Judge has come to a definite finding on a consideration of the evidence on record and the circumstances of the case that 6 daughters of Rajab Ali did not gift away, relinquish or give up their shares of the suit land to Jalal Baksh and get the some recorded in the name of Jalal Baksh in the C.S. record. It has been further held on the basis of the said finding that the entries in the C.S. records of right regarding -/11/4 gondas share in the name of Jalal Baksh are wrong and have no basis whatsoever. On the question of the alleged amicable partition the learned Subordinate Judge has held on a consideration of the evidences on record that the suit lands were never mentioned by metes and bounds between Jalal Baksh and Aziz Baksh. With regard to the registered deed Ext. A evidencing an amicable partition as amongst the plaintiffs Nos. 1 to 4 the learned Subordinate Judge has held that the said document is not a legally valid one as other co-sharers were not parties to the same. The properties sought to be partitioned by the said document, according to the learned Subordinate Judge, are still joint and liable to be partitioned. On the question or the bar of limitation and adverse possession as has been pleaded by the contesting Defendant No. 1 to 5 the learned Subordinate Judge has come to the finding that 6 sisters of Jalal Baksh and Aziz Baksh used to possess the suit land constructively through their brothers by enjoying the usufructs of the joint lands or coming to their paternal house from time to time and therefore the question of limitation or of adverse possession does not at all arise in the present case.

6. On the basis of the said findings the suit was decreed in part and the plaintiffs and the defendants were found to be entitle to shares on the basis that on the death of Rajab Ali, his 6 daughters inherited the disputed proper ties left by him along with his two sons and the widow.

7. The present appeal has been filed by the contesting Defendants Nos. 1 to 5, the heirs of Jalal Baksh, disputing the corrective s of the aforesaid findings.

8. Mr. Jani Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants has challenged mainly the findings on the question of gift or relinquishment of the shares of the sisters in favour of their brother Jalal Baksh and also on the question of limitation and adverse possession.

9. On the question of the alleged gift or relinquishment of the sister's shares in favour of Jalal Baksh, the learned Advocate for the appellant has submitted that the appreciation of the evidence on record as has been made by the learned Subordinate Judge, is not correct because the learned Subordinate Judge, did not give adequate consideration to the admitted position that the predecessor of the plaintiffs had accepted the possession of Jalal Baksh of the larger share of the land which is consistent with the case of relinquishment as has been made out in the written statement of the contesting defendants Nos. 1 to 5. The learned Advocate has submitted that it is in the evidence of P.W. 1 and P.W. 3 that Aziz Baksh had possessionately in two plots out of the disputed plots representing his shares and the remaining plots were in possession of Jalal Baksh, which is, in accordance with the defence story of relinquishment. According to the learned Advocate, Ext. 4 which also shows that the plaintiff, the heirs of Aziz Baksh were is possession of only two plots gives support to the said story of relinquishment.

10. On a consideration of the evidence, however it appears that the sisters who used to live in the houses of their respective husbands admittedly used to come from time to time to the paternal house and take the usufructs of the lands and there is no reliable evidence to show that there was in fact any such gift or relinquishment made by the sisters in favour of the one of their brothers. It has been rightly pointed out by the learned Subordinate Judge that D.W. 2 Defendant No. 1 is not a really a competent witness because he has admitted that he does not remember anything about the preparation of the record of right as he was very young at that time. The alleged gift or relinquishment is said to have occurred before the preparation of the records of rights. D.W. 2 of course, has said that the sisters relinquished their interest in favour of their brothers but he does not recollect the name of any person who was present at the time when it was done. The evidence of D.W. 4 is absolutely hearsay and there is no other evidence on record in support of the case of relinquishment. If the story of relinquishment in favor of one of the two brothers were true, it is natural that there would have been some document to evidence the said fact. On the other hand, the evidence on record discloses that Jalal Baksh was literate and it was he who used to manage the affairs of the family, whereas Aziz Baksh was illiterate and their sisters were living away from the paternal house. In such a case it was not impossible for Jalal Baksh, if he wanted, to get the major share of the properties in question recorded in his favour to the exclusion of the daughters who were away and to persuade the younger brother to accept the said decision. We are, therefore of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge cannot be said to be wrong in dis-believing the story of gift or relinquishment alleged to be made by the sisters in favour of Jalal Baksh.

11. Mr. Jani Alam, the learned Advocate for the appellants has next contended that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in not holding that the contesting Defendants Nos. 1 to 5 had acquired valid tine with regard to -/11/- annas 4 gondas share by adverse possession. The learned Advocate has submitted that the record of right showing that Jilal Baksh was in possession of -/11/4 gondas share was a clear evidence of his assertion of hostile title and that the continuous exclusive possession of Jalal Baksh and his heirs in accordance with the entries in the records of right and non-participation in the rents and profits of the lands by the sisters of Jalal Baksh and or their heirs provides a sufficient basis for holding that the Jalal Baksh and his heirs have been exercising acts of possession in the major share of the properties to the exclusion of the other co-sharers in respect of the said share.

<u>12. It is now well-settled that the law as to acquisition of title by adverse possession in derogation of the right of a co-sharer or a stranger sets down two different standards of proof of such acquisition. There can be no acquisition of adverse possession against a co-owner until there is ouster or exclusion that is assertion of hostile title by a co-owner in possession against others and that to the knowledge of the latter. Unlike in the case of a stranger, mere exclusive possession by a co-owner is not sufficient to show his possession to be adverse against his co-owners, although such possession would be prima facie good evidence of adverse possession against a stranger. This is consistent with the principle that the possession of a co-owner is generally possession on behalf of other co-owners as well, and a co-owner out of possession is deemed to be in constructive possession of a property through the co-owner in possession thereof.</u>

13. It has however been contended before us that it has been held in some cases that there is another proposition of law recognized by the judicial authorities to the effect that non-participation in the rents and profits of a certain property by a co-owner for a considerable length of time may give rise to a presumption of ouster. Relying upon this principle the leaned Advocate for the appellants has submitted that exclusive possession of the joint lands by Jalal Baksh and his heirs to the extent of 11 annas 4 gondas share for more than the statutory period has, in their circumstances of the case, resulted in the extinguishment of the interests of the sisters of Jalal Baksh in the joint lands and acquisition of the said interests by him.

14. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has referred to several decisions namely the cases of Ayenenessa Bibi Vs. Sheikh Isuf and others reported in 16 C.W.N. 849, Krishna Chandra Das Vs. Puma Chandra as reported in 60 C.L.J. 232 and Ijjatullah Munshi Vs. Jabera Ali and others reported in 8 D.L.R. (Dhaka) 372. So far as the Dacca High Court case of Ijjatullah Munshi Vs. Jahur Ali and others is Concerned, it has been held in the said case that there must be not only an exclusive possession, but the possession must be under a claim of title to the whole estate, either brought home to the knowledge of other co-sharers or so notorious that their knowledge of such adverse claim may be presumed. This case is obviously not of much assistance to the learned Advocate. But so far as the two cases of the Calcutta High Court are concerned, they appear to lend some support to the contention of the learned Advocate but for a correct appreciation of the law of adverse possession as applicable to co-sharers we shall have to make appraisement of some of the important judicial authorities on this point.

15. The earliest case in which the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council had to deal with the question of exclusive possession of a co-sharer tenant in respect of a part of a joint estate vis-a-vis is his other co-sharers appears to be the case of Watson and Co. Vs. Ram Chand Dutt and others, L.R. 17 LA. 110 same case DLR. 18 Cual. 10. In that case, the Judicial Committee refused to issue injunction restraining Messers Watson & Co., who being co-owners were in exclusive possession and enjoyment of a joint plot of land from excluding the plaintiffs from the enjoyment of the said ejmali land and the following ,observations of the Judicial Committee is germane to the point :

"It seems to their Lordships that if there be two or more tenants in common and one (A) be in actual occupation of part of the estate, and is engaged in cultivating that part in a proper course, of cultivation as if it were his separate property, and another tenant in common (B) attempts to come upon the said part for the purpose of carrying on Operations there, inconsistent with the course of cultivation in which A is engaged and the profitable use by him of the said part, and A resists and prevents such entry, not in denial of B's title, but simply with the object of protecting himself on the profitable enjoyments of the land, such conduct in the part of A could not entitle B to a decree for joint possession."

In the next case before the Privy Council in which the position of a co-sharer in exclusive enjoyment of a ferry operating on ejmali lands and waters was analysed and the case of Watson & Co. Vs. Ram Chand Dutta and others, was considered is the case of Maharajah Sir Lachmenswar Singh, Bahadur Vs. Sheikh Monowar Hossain reported in L.R. 19 I.A. 48 same case ILR 19 Cal. 253. The concurring finding of fact made by the first appellate Court which, though differed from by the High Court, was accepted as conclusive by the Judicial Committee was to the following effect:

"The owner of Kamtowl Factory has been in exclusive possession of the profits of the ferry for a period extending over twenty years and there was no express permission on the part of the Defendants. The profits, as the books of the Defendants show were not inconsiderable, and I do not think that the plaintiffs of their own accord and free will allowed the Kuti to derive this profit. This possession by the Kuti must have been against the wishes of the Defendants and therefore adverse. There was no express trust and implied permission cannot, under the circumstances be inferred."

16. Lord Hobhouse, in delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee pointed out that the question whether possession was adverse or not was often one of simple fact but it might be also a conclusion of law or mixed question and referred to with approval, to an observation made by Mr. Justice Wilson in Mahomed Ali Khan Vs. Khajah Abdul Gunny, I.L.R. 9 Cal. 744 that many acts which would be clearly adverse and might amount to dispossession as between a stranger and the true owner of land, would between joint, owners naturally bear a different construction. The noble Lord then proceeded to make the following observation: 'Whether the facts found in this case would, as between strangers, raise the inference of adverse possession or of enjoyment of the ferry as an easement and as of right, is a question which need not be discussed. For the parties are co-owners, and the Defendant has made use of the joint property in a way quite consistent with the continuance of the joint ownership and possession. He has not excluded any co-sharer."

17. In one of the early Indian cases, namely Bandacharya Vs. Shriniwasacharaya (103) 5 Bom. L.R. 743, the question of exclusive receipt of profits by a co-sharer being evidence of ouster come for consideration and it was held relying upon the dictum laid down by Lord Denman in Culley Vs. Doedem Taylorson (1840) 11 A and E 1008:

"No doubt exclusive receipt of profits continuously for a long period may point to an ouster but the court must be satisfied that each taking of profits is an indication of a denial of rights in the other co-tenant to receive them".

17A. Sir Lawrence Jenkins, as the Chief Justice of the Bombay High Court had to deal with a similar question in a Second Appeal in the case of Gangadhar Vs. Paraihram (1905) I.L.R. 29 Bom. 340 and following the above mentioned case refused to interfere with a finding of ouster on the basis of the evidence of exclusive possession of a tenant-in-common for nearly 40 years, as it was impossible, according to the learned Chief Justice to say that there was no evidence in support of the said finding. As this decision has sometimes been cited in support of the proposition that mere non-participation in the rents and profits of a joint property for a long period may lead to a presumption of ouster the statement of law made by Mr. Justice Ashhurst in the case of Fisher and Taylor Vs. Prosser (1774) 1 Cowper 217 on which reliance was placed by the learned Chief Justice may be quoted as follows:

'Here is a possession of nearly 40 years without any claim by the lessors of the plaintiff to a share of the rents and profits, and without any acknowledgement of his right, by the other tenants in common. After so long acquiescence I think the jury was well warranted to presume anything in support of the defendant's title, and they might presume either an actual ouster or conveance."

17B. A few years later, Sir Lawrence Jenkins, while presiding over a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Ayennessa Bibi Vs. Sheikh Isuf (1912) 16 C.W.N. 849, had to consider a case in which the claim of the sister to a share in the joint property was resisted by her brother on the ground that the sister's right to her share had been extinguished by the exclusive possession of her brother. The concurrent findings of the courts below were set .aside and the High Court called for fresh findings on certain issues after laying down the following guide-line for the determination of the question whether there had been exclusion or ouster of a co-sharer :

"The circumstances that have to be taken into consideration appear to me to be these among others, the relationship of the parties, their position, the mode of life in the particular community to which the parties belong the character of the property and other circumstances of similar character. What has to be seen is whether having regard to the long possession and to all the circumstances, it can be said that there has been such an exclusive possession or perception of profits by the brother in this case as to afford an indication of a denial of the rights of the other co-tenants, and whether on the facts as found it would be right and reasonable to hold that there had been not only an exclusion of the other co-tenants but an exclusion so distant in date as to justify the view that there had been twelve years' adverse possession on the part of Defendant No. 1 at the time this suit was instituted".

It will be noticed that in all these cases, emphasis was more or less on the length of duration of the exclusive possession by a co-sharer of co-owner, and not upon his representative character. Although the learned Chief Justice referred to the relationship of the parties, their position and mode of life in a particular community, but the special position of a co-owner vis-a-vis other co-owners in respect of a joint 'property was not expressly mentioned. An inference as to ouster was according to the aforementioned decisions made dependent principally on the length of the period of exclusive possession of a co-sharer and the acknowledge of the co-sharer out of possession as to the hostile intent of the co-sharer in possession was not considered to be an important element for establishing such ouster.

18. In the case of Corea Vs. Appuhamy, (1912) A.C. 230, an appeal from Ceylone, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council threw new light on the law of adverse possession against a co-sharer by emphasing the following principle as recognized by Wood., V. C., in Thomes Vs. Thomas in 2 K & J 79 :

"Possession is never considered adverse if it can be referred to a lawful title".

18A. In Corea's case, one Elias Appuhamy, the owner of the property in suit died leaving a brother, Iseris Appuhamy and three sisters, and Iseris entered into possession of the said property claiming himself to be the sole heir. An action was raised by Corea after purchasing the share of the surviving sister as well as those of the heirs of the two other sisters against Iseris Appuhamy who was in exclusive possession.

19. Lord Macnaghten in delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee, in Corea's case analysed the nature of exclusive possession of Iseris Apphuhamy in the following words :

"On the death of Elias, his heirs had unity of title as well as unity of possession. Then comes the question, was the possession of Iseris adverse? The District Judge held that Iseris "entered in the character of sole heir or plunderer" "whichever it was", says the learned Judge, "so he continued and acknowledged no title in any one else. He has acquired a good prescriptive title." It is difficult to understand why it should be suggested that Iseris may have en Bred as "plunderer" Entering into possession, and having a lawful title to enter, he could not divest himself of that title by pretending that he had no title at all. His title must have enured for the benefit of his co-proprietors. His possession was in law the possession of his co-owners. It was not possible for him to put an end to that possession by any secret intention in his mind. Nothing short of ouster or some-thing equivalent to ouster could bring about that result."

In the light of the statement of law as quoted above, the Judicial Committee refused to make a presumption from Iseri's long-continued possession, which was undisturbed and uninterrupted, that there had been an ouster or something equivalent to ouster, although Iseris had been pretending all the time that he was the sole heir.

19A. The Judicial Committee followed the view taken in Corea Vs. Appuhamy, in the case of Muttunayagam Vs. Brito, (1919) A.C. 895 and citing the dictum of Wood V. C. in Thomas Vs. Thomas that possession is never considered adverse if it can be referred to a lawful title, held that the exclusive possession of the father who became joint owners with his children and had estrangement with the eldest son became of violent family quarrel, could not be adverse when no claim was made against the father during his life time by any of the children.

20. The Judicial Committee did not accept the evidence of mere uninterrupted sole possession of a joint property by a co-sharer as sufficient for inferring the said possession to be adverse also in the case of Hardit Singh Vs. Gurmukh Singh, 28 C.L.J. 437 same case A.I.R. 1928 P.C. 1 and Lord Buckmaster in delivering the judgment of the Committee observed:

"If by exclusive possession of joint estate is meant that one member of the joint family alone occupies it that by itself affords no evidence of exclusion of other interested members of the family. Uninterrupted sole possession of such property, without more must be referred to lawful title possessed by the joint holder to use the joint estate and cannot be regarded as an assertion of a right to hold if as separate so as to assert an adverse claim against other interested members."

It is interesting to notice that if Lawrence Jenkins, whose view as expressed in Gangadhar Vs. Parashyam, and Ayennessa Bibi Vs. Sheikh Isuf, are sometime cited in support of the proposition that uninterrupted exclusive possession may lead to an inference of ouster was a member of the Committee deciding this case.

21. In the case of Varada Pillai Vs. Jeevaratnammal reported in L.R. 46 I.A. 285 same case I.L.R. 43 Mad. 244 same case 24 C.W.N. 346 same case A.I.R. 1919 P.C. 44, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council had to examine again the question of possession of one of several co-owners being the possession of others and in explaining the limit of the said rule quoted the following passage from Colley Vs. Doe Lam Taylcirson, 11 A & E 1008 :

"Generally speaking, one tenant in common cannot maintain an ejectment against another tenant in common because the possession of one tenant in common is the possession of the other and to enable the party complaining to maintain an ejectment, there must be ouster of the party complaining. But where the claimant tenant it common has not been in participation of the rents and profits for a considerable length of time and other circumstances concern, the Judge will direct the jury to take into consideration whether they will presume that there has been ouster .....and if the jury find an ouster, then the right of the lessor of the plaintiff to an undivided share will be decided exactly in the same way as if he had brought his ejectment for the entirety".

21A. It may be noticed that in Varada Pillal's case it had not been necessary to apply the above quoted dictum as the person claiming adverse possession against her co-sharers had no interest in the land at the time when she was put into possession of the same by the two co-owners who wanted to invest full rights upon her and the possession which had been adverse against the said co-owners since the commencement of her possession did not cease to be so when on a subsequent date she inherited a moisty of the said land on the death of one of the said two co-owners. Nonetheless, the said dictum has sometimes been referred to in support of the proposition that mere non-participation in the rent and profits of a joint property for a long period is sufficient to lead to an inference of ouster. It is however pertinent to note what the court was considering in the Colley's case was the question of adverse possession against a tenant in common in an action of ejectment and it was pointed out there that in order to find ouster, in addition to non-participation other circumstances much concur and the matter was to be left to the jury to decide whether in the circumstances of the case, ouster could be presumed. This other circumstances points to the circumstances in which it is not possible to hold that the possession of one co-tenant is the possession of the other as has been stated in the first part of the passage, and is obviously referable to the state of mind of the person in exclusive possession as well as of the person against whom the adverse claim is sought to be made. The person in possession is to abandon his character of a co-sharer and this he cannot do, as was pointed out by the Judicial Committee in the case of Corea Vs. Appnhamy, by a secret intention in his mind. He can be shorn of his character which law attributes to him only if he gives notice of the change of his intention to the person most affected by it viz. his co-sharer on whose behalf he had been possessing all this time.

22. The Calcutta High Court has considered this question as to non-participation in the rents and profits of a joint property for a long time being the evidence of ouster in a number of cases, and the preponderant view expressed in the said cases some of which have been mentioned below following the various decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council referred to above, is that mere non-participation in the rents add profits of a joint property by a co-sharer for a long period would not be sufficient to give rise to the inference of ouster and that there is ouster only when there is an assertion of a hostile title by one co-sharer against the others to the knowledge of the lattet : Lokenath Singh Vs. Dhakeswar Prasad, 20 C.W.N. 51 same case 21 C.L.J. 253; Balaram Garin Vs. Shyama Charon, 24 C.W.N. 1057 same case 33 C.L.J. 344, Jagahnath Marwari Vs. Sm. Candni Bibi, 26 C.W.N. 65 same case 34 C.L.J. 432, Joy Narayan Sen Ukil Vs. Sri-kantha Roy, 26 C.W.N. 206 same case 33 C.L.J. 592: Jogendra Nath Vs. Rajendra Nath, 26 C.W.N. 890 same case A.I.R. 1922 Cal. 54, Moulavi Abdul Wahed Vs. Mohon Bashi Saha, 34 C.W.N. 246 same case A.I.R. 1930 Cal. 466; Jagidlsh Vs. Tayab Sardar, I.L.R. 61 Cal. 377 same case A.I.R. 1934 Cal. 644 and Nerasal Chandra Vs. Mohltosh 40 C.W.N. 777 same case A.I.R. 1936 Cal. 466

23. Sir Ashotush Mukherjee, the eminent Judge of the Calcutta High Court after making a review of all the previous decisions on this point, laid down the law in the case of Jagannath Maiwari Vs. Sm. Chandni Bibi in the following words at page 70 of 26 C.W.N. :

"The fundamental rule is that in order to establish adverse possession as between co-sharers, there must be evidence of an open assertion of hostile title by one of them to the knowledge of the others; mere non-participation in the profits by one party and exclusive occupation by the other is not conclusive."

23A. The learned Judge, after analyzing the nature of exclusive possession of a common property by a co-owner, proceeded to observe at page 71 of the said Report :

"In order to render the possession of one co-tenant adverse, to the others, not only must the occupancy be under an exclusive claim of ownership, in denial of the rights of the other co-tenants, but such occupancy must have been made known to the other co-tenants, either by express notice or by such open and notorious acts as must have been brought home to the other co-tenant's knowledge of the denial of their rights".

23B. In the case of Nirinal Chandra Vs. Monitosh, reliance was placed on behalf of one of the contending parties upon the passage from the judgment in Calley Vs. Deo d. Taylorson, as Us already been quoted at pages 26-27 of this judgment in support of the proposition that mere non-participation in the rents and profits by a co-sharer for a long period would constitute ouster and D. N. Mitter, J, in delivering the judgment in the said case made the following comment at page 787 of 40 C.W.N.

"This case does not support the broad proposition formulated that dispossession or non-possession for a considerable length of time is sufficient to give rise to an inference of ouster. The words which have been italicised, namely 'other circumstances concur are of very great materiality. It is a some-what dangerous doctrine to profound that mere non-participation of rents and profits of joint property by a co-sharer for a very long period would be sufficient to give rise to the inference of ouster".

23C. It seems to us that there had been a consensus of judicial opinion, so far as the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and the Calcutta High Court were concerned, as to the law of adverse possession against a co-sharer and knowledge of the non-possessing co-sharer as to the hostile intent of the co-sharer in possession was considered to be an essential element for establishing such possession to be adverse.
