24. This question came up for consideration before a Bench of the Supreme Court of India consisting of B. K. Mukherjee C. J., Venkatarama Ayyar and Imam JJ. in the case of Mohammad Baqr & others Vs. Naim-un-Nisa Bibi and others, A.I.R. 1956 S.C. 548 and the law was stated categorically by the said Bench in the following manner :

"The parties to the action are co-sharers, and as, under the law, possession of one-co-sharer is possession of all co-sharers, it cannot be adverse to them, unless there is a denial of their right to the knowledge by the person in possession, and exclusion and ouster following thereon for the statutory period."

24A. This question was considered by another Bench of the Supreme Court of India in the case of P. Laxmi Reddy Vs. L. Laxmi Reddy A.I.R. 1957 S. C. 314 same case P.L.D. 1957 SC. 251 (Ind) and Jagannath Das J. (Sinha and Imam JJ, concerning) made the following statement:

"Now, the ordinary classical requirement of adverse possession is that it should be nec vi nec clam nec precario (see. Secretary of State for India Vs. Debendralal Khan, 61 I.A. 78 same case A.I.R. 1934 P.C.23. The possession required must be adequate in continuity, in publicity and in extent to i show that it is possession adverse to the competitio (See Radhanoni Debi Vs. Collector of Khulna, 27 I.A. 136) But it is well settled that in order to establish adverse possession of one co-heir as against another it is not enough to show that one out of them is in sole possession and enjoyment of profits, of the properties. Ouster of the non-possessing co-heir by the co-heir in possession who claims possession to be adverse should be made out. The possession of one co-heir is considered in law, as possession of all the co-heirs. When one co-heir is found to be in possession of the properties it is presumed to be on the basis of joint title. The co-heir in possession cannot render his possession adverse to the other co-heir not in possession by an secret hostile animus on his own part in derogation of the other co-heir's title (see Corea Vs. Appuhamy (1912) A.C. 230). It is a settled rule of law that as between co-heirs there must be evidence of open assertion of hostile title, coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment by one of them to the knowledge of the other so as to constitute ouster. This does not necessarily mean that there must be an express demand by one and denial by the other."

24B. The learned Judge of the Indian Supreme Court, it will appear from the above-quoted passage, had no hesitation in pointing out that it was a settled rule of law that knowledge of the excluded co-sharer as to the adverse claim of the possessing co-sharer was an essential element of ouster, but he proceeded further to observe in the said case that there were cases in which it had been held that ouster could be inferred from "notorious exclusive possession" of a co-sharer" in assertion of hostile title" for a very considerable time and the excluded co-sharer did not take any step to vindicate his title and added that it was not necessary to decide whether that line of cases were right or wrong. It should, however, be noticed that the learned Judge was not referring while making the above-mentioned observation, to those cases which endorsed the view that mere exclusive possession by a co-owner for a very long periods and nothing more was sufficient to give rise to an inference of ouster. The line of case about the correctness of which the Indian Supreme Court appears to have refrained from expressing any definite view in the aforementioned case, were obviously, those in which there was exclusive possession in open assertion of hostile title and it was notorious for a considerable length of time. In these cases, it has been held that although there was no express notice the non-possessing co-sharer was presumed to have derived his knowledge from the notorious acts of the possessing co-sharer, which were done in open assertion of hostile title for a considerable length of time. In our opinion, the line of difference between these two classes of cases is very thin. In one class of cases there is positive evidence of the knowledge of the non-possessing co-sharer, but in the other class, the knowledge is inferred from certain circumstances.

25. Mr. Jani Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants has placed his reliance upon two cases of the Calcutta High Court, viz. Ayennessa Bibi Vs. Sheikh Isuf, 16 C.W.N. 849 and Krishna Chandra Das Vs. Purna Chandra Das, 60 C.L.J. 232, which have been mentioned above.

26. The decision in Ayennessa Bibi's case has been considered above and it has been noticed that the later decisions of the. Judicial Committee of the Privy Council have made it clear that the rule of law as to exclusive possession of a joint property by a co-sharer, as stated by Sir Lawrence Jenkins in the said case, has been too broadly stated. Sir Lawrence himself appears to have accepted this position when Lord Buckmaster laid down the law that uninterrupted sole possession of a joint estate by a co-sharer, without more, must be referred to his possession as a co-sharer, in the case of Hardit Singh Vs. Garmukh Singh, in the judgment delivered on behalf of the Judicial Committee of which Sir Lawrence was a member.

27. In the Single Bench decision in the case of Krishna Chandra Das Vs. Puma Chandra Das, Nasima Ali J of Calcutta High Court relying upon a decision of the Bombay High Court in the case of Coudbhai Mohammad Bhai Vohra Vs. Hasambhani Rahimtoola Vohra, 46 Bom. 213 took the view that sole possession by one tenant in common for a long period without a claim or demand by other tenants in common, was the evidence from which actual ouster of the other tenants in common might be presumed. This view is contrary to a long line of judicial decisions to which reference has already been made and the learned Judge of the Calcutta Nigh Court appears to have accepted the proposition of the Bombay case without examining the earlier decisions of the Judicial Committee and also of the Calcutta High Court itself.

28. The Dhaka High Court has considered this question in several decisions, of which reference may be made to the cases of Harun Mia Vs. Mir Maijuddin Ahmed Chowdhury and others, 4 D.L.R. 114, Bindu Bala De and another Vs. Rebate Mohan De and others, 4 D.L.R. 293, Maharaja Bhupendra Chandra Singha Sarma and others Vs. Sudhindra Chandra Singha and others, 5 D.L.R. 251, Sonaullah Howlader Vs. Apseruddin Bali and others 7 D.L.R. 514 and Ijjatullah Munshi Vs. Jahur Ali and others, 8 D.L.R. 732.

29. In these cases, the law of adverse possession against a co-sharer has been clearly laid down, more or less, in the same terms as in the most of the cases of the Calcutta High Court. The only case of the Dhaka High Court to which reference was made by the learned Advocate for the appellants, in support of his contention was the case of Ijjatullah Munshi Vs. Johurali and others, 8 D.L.R. 372, which obviously does not support the learned Advocate. The learned Advocate, however, might have cited the case of Bhupendra Chandra Vs. Shudhindra, 5 D.L.R. 251, with some plausibility, as there is a certain passage in the said judgment, which could have been referred in support of the proposition contended for on behalf of the appellants. After laying down what has been stated to be the true principle deducible from the authorities, that there cannot be adverse possession by one co-owner against others until i there is ouster or exclusion and that there can be ouster or exclusion only when there is an assertion of hostile 'We to the knowledge of the co-owner against when the claim is sought to be made; Guha J, in delivering the judgment of the Division Bench in the said case made the following observations :

"Another rule of law is now well established that where the tenant-in-common has not been in participation of the rents and profits for a considerable length of time and the "other circumstances concur" and the person claiming adverse possession possesses continuously for a long period without any claim or demand by any person claiming under the other tenant in common or where a tenant in common possesses for a statutory period without recognizing his other tenants -in-common and" the Court is satisfied" that such taking of profits is an indication of denial of rights in the other co-owners or tenants in common, the court may presume an ouster."

29A. In support of this proposition, several decisions of the Calcutta High Court, two decisions of the Bombay High Court and one decision of the Judicial Committee, most of which been considered by us earlier, have been mentioned. Although Mr. Justice Guha has made the above statement as if it were a different principle independent of the general principle of ouster of a co-sharer, and has included in the list of the decisions mentioned above the two judgments of Sir Lawrence Jenkins pronounced in the Gangadhas case (29 Bom. 300) and Ayennessa Bibi's case (16 C.W.N. 849), the judgment of Nasim Ali J in Krishna Chandra's case (60 C.L.J. 232) and that in Chand Bhai's ease (46 Bom. 213) which are sometimes cited in support of the extreme proposition that mere non-participation in the rents and prate of a joint property by a co-owner may give rise to an inference of ouster against him, the learned Judge has not, in our opinion, added the authority of the Court for such a proposition in the said passage. This is obvious from the fact that the learned Judge has included in the said list not only the Privy Council case of Varada Pillar but also the two cases of the Calcutta High Court, viz. Balaram Guria Vs. Shyama Charan, 24 C.W.N. 1059 and Nirmal Chandra Vs. Mohintosh, 40 C.W.N. 777 in which it was pointed out that more non-participation in the rents and profits by a co-owner could not be the foundation of a finding of ouster. Mr. Justice Mitter has expressed him-self rather strongly in Nirmal Chandra's case, by deprecating the proposition as a dangerous doctrine. It should also be noticed that the decision on the question of ouster of the co-sharers was rested in the said case of the Dacca High Court on a definite finding of their knowledge of the adverse claim.

<u>30. It is pertinent to mention that Sir Ashutosh Mukherjee, the learned Judge who delivered the judgment in Balaram Gunias case, 24 C.W.N. 1057, developed this point further in the case of Jagannath Marwari Vs. Sm. Chandi Bibi, and after propounding that a co-tenant's knowledge of the denial of his right is an essential element of adverse possession against the co-tenant, made the following observations :</u>

<u>"But the ouster of the other co-tenants in order to render the possession adverse, need not be violent or intimidating expulsion or repulsion, nor need the notice of the adverse holding be actually brought home to the other co-tenants by personal or formal communication It is sufficient if the contrary is not proved, that the circumstances show that such knowledge may be reasonably presumed".</u>

<u>30A. We may also profitably reproduce the enunciation of the law on this point made by M.N. Mukherjee, J, another distinguished judge of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Moulavi Abdul Wahed Vs. Mohan Bashi Saha, 33 C.W.N. 246, which is to the following effect:</u>

<u>"Exclusion or ouster involves not merely the act of the person ousting but the state of mind of the person ousted. Knowledge on the part of the latter, therefore, is essential. Such knowledge may be proved directly or inferentially on the principle of constructive notice. It may also be proved by show-in the co-sharer against whom possession bed sent notice of facts or sufficient information which would put a reasonable person on enquiry and on receipt of which a reasonably attentive person could not but realize that he was ousted."</u>

<u>30B. On a critical examination of the various judicial authorities on the question of this important branch of the law of limitation, we thus find that it is well settled that the knowledge of the non-possessing co-sharer as to the adverse claim of the possessing co-sharer is an essential element in making the latter's possession adverse against the former. We have noticed the distinguished views of the Judicial Committee and other learned Judges in this regard. An analysis of the relevant provisions of the Limitation Act also lead us to the same conclusion. Under section 28 of the Limitation Act a person's right to a property is extinguished at the determination of the period limited to him by the Limitation Act for instituting a suit for possession of the said property and under Art. 144 of the Schedule to the Act, the period of limitation is 12 years for instituting such suit and the said period of limitation starts running from the way "when the possession of the defendant becomes adverse, to the plaintiff". When a person without a claim of title gets into possession ousting a rightful person, there is no difficulty to determine the point of time when such possession becomes adverse to the latter, because possession is adverse from the very inception. But it is not so in the case of a co-sharer in exclusive possession of a joint property, because such possession is consistent with joint title and it becomes adverse only when the possessing co-sharer denies the title or right of the non-possessing co-sharer and a right to sue accrues to such non-possessing co-sharer. As has been pointed out in Corea's case, this cannot happen by a secret change of mind. The non-possessing co-sharer must know that there has been a change in animus and a right to sue the possessing co-sharer for recovery of possession has accrued to him. It appears to be an absurd proposition to contend that it does not matter whether the non-possessing co-sharer knows of the hostile intent of the possessing co-sharer or not a right to sue accrues to him and time starts running against him as soon as the possessing co-sharer conceives a malafide intention against his co-sharer within his mind or express it to some-body else. Without his knowledge with the result that the co-sharer out of possession ultimately loss his property without ever being given a chance to redeem the same. This view of law is certainly not in keeping with the principle of justice and good 'conscience and in an opinion the Legislative could not have enacted the said provision of the Limitation Act by attributing to it a meaning which has the effect of depriving a co-owner of his property without any conceivable lapse on his part. He should have been given an opportunity to know that rightful possession of his co-owner has become unlawful. As has been pointed out in the cases referred to above, the person concerned need not be notified or informed by an express notice, but it is sufficient if the circumstances show that such knowledge may be reasonably inferred.</u>

<u>31. If we analyse the evidence which has been adduced in this case in the light of the principle of law noticed above we have no manner of doubt that there is absolutely no evidence of any ouster or exclusion to the knowledge of the sisters who have been living away from the paternal house. Even according to the defence evidence the sisters had been visiting the paternal house from time to time and taking usufructs of the joint land. Having regard to the state of evidence as has been referred to above we have no hesitation to hold that the learned Subordinate Judge was correct in reaching the conclusion that there was no case of adverse possession defeating the claim of the co-sharers of the contesting defendants.</u>

32. Mr. Jani Alam, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants has next contended that having regard to the admitted position that a certain plot was said by Aziz Baksh to one Gadu and the said plot has again been transferred to one Asak Mondal who has been examined as D.W. 5 in this case, the Trial Court ought to have held that the suit being a partition suit was not maintainable in the absence of the said transferee. The learned Advocate has also submitted that admittedly one Abdur Rashid who happens to be a son of Defendant No. 25 is also a transferee of a part of the suit land from the plaintiff and the plaintiffs respondent took out a Rule in this Court being C.R. No. 1872 (f) of 1969 praying for a remand of the suit to the Trial Court to enable the plaintiffs to have a retrial of the suit after adding Abdur Rashid a party to the suit. The said rule, of course, has been discharged for non-prosecution as the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners of the said Rule has submitted that he had instruction not to press the said Rule. The learned Advocate for the appellant has contended that the said Abdur Rashid being admittedly a co-sharer in respect of certain plots in the suit, the suit is clearly not maintainable because of non-joinder of the said Abdur Rashid.

33. It may be pointed out that in the written statement no objection as to the defect of parties on the ground of non-impleading Asak Mondal or Abdur Rashid was taken. Although the general ground of defect of party was taken, the plaintiffs served a notice upon Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 with interrogatories for supplying the names of the persons who according to them were interested in the suit properties and should be impleaded. In answer to the said interrogatories Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 supplied certain names who according to them were interested in the properties in suit and therefore should be impleaded. After receiving the said names the plaintiffs added all those persons as patties defendants to this suit. But in the list given by the defendants the name of Asak or Abdur Rashid was not included. At the time of the hearing, however, evidence was led to the effect that there was a transfer of certain plot by Aziz Baksh to a certain person who again has sold it to Asak Mondal, although no registered deed has been put into evidence in support of the alleged transfer to Asak Mondal. It is not known whether he is in possession of any part of the disputed property on the strength of the said deed of transfer. As regards the transfer in favour of Abdur Rashid, it is the case of the plaintiff-respondents in their application in the Civil Rule referred to above that the said Abdur Rashid lives in joint mess with his father Defendant No. 25 and that on the idea that Defendant No. 25 is the real owner. Abdur Rashid was not impleaded as a party defendant.

34. Mr. Jani Alam the learned Advocate for the appellants has submitted that the partition suit is liable to be dismissed in absence of Asak Mondal and Abdur Rashid who are necessary parties and has relied upon a decision in the case of Churaman Mahto and others Vs. Bhatu Mahto and others reported in A.I.R. 1935 Patna 241 in which it has been held that in a partition suit no decree can be passed for partition in the absence of a single co-sharer.

<u>35. On the question of non-joinder of parties reference may be made to the provisions of Order 1 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil procedure in which it has been laid down that no objection on the ground of non-joinder of parties shall be given effect to unless it has been taken at the earliest possible opportunity and when such objection has not been so taken, it shall be deemed to have been waived. It is clear therefore that in view of the said provision the appellants are not entitled to raise the question of non-joinder of Asak or Abdur Rashid for the first time At the hearing of the suit when they have not taken such a plea at the earliest opportunity and have not included their napes in the list of the necessary parties supplied by theta while submitting answers to the interrogatories served upon them at the instance of the plaintiffs.</u>

<u>36. This question, however, is subject to another legal principle. It is not doubt true that the party to a suit shall not be allowed to agitate the question of non-joinder or mis-joinder of parties at a subsequent stage if such a plea has not been taken at the earliest opportunity. But there is also another principle which has received judicial recognition, according to which no court shall pass an infructuous decree. If it is found on a consideration of the evidence on record that a necessary party has not been impleaded in consequence whereof the decree which may be passed in the suit may be set at naught at the instance of the non-impleaded person, such a decree shall not be passed by a Court. This question was considered in a decision given by a Division Bench of this Court to which one of us is a party in the case of Asadunnessa and others Vs. Qumarazzaman and others, reported in 26 DLR (Dac.) at 363 in which the above mentioned principle of law, has been recognized.</u>

<u>37. In the present case, we are therefore to see whether there are sufficient materials on record from which we can say that a necessary party has really not been impleaded in the suit and that as such the decree which has been passed shalt be rendered in fructuous at the instance of such non-impleaded person. We have already noted that proper evidence in this regard has not been adduced in this case. None of the deeds of transfer on the basis of which the said non-impleaded persons namely Asak Mondal and Abdur Rashid have been produced it Court. In our opinion, oral evidence in support of a transfer which is made by a registered document is not proper evidence for proving the said act of transfer. In the absence of such a document it is difficult for us to hold that the said persons have acquired valid title to the disputed property in suit or any part thereof. Moreover, we are of the opinion that in any view of the matter the decree which has been passed in this partition suit cannot be rendered infructuous even if the said persons have some interest in any portion of the property in suit. According to the evidence which has been sought to be adduced in this respect the said persons have acquired, if at all, interest in some specific plots of the suit properties. The alleged transferees have not claimed any interest in the whole of the properties in the suit and as such they have no community of interest in the entire suit properties along with the others having interest therein. In the said circumstances it can at most be contended that any defect which may have crept in the frame of the suit because of not-empleading the said two persons having interest in the aforesaid two plots, the final decree which may be passed in this suit may be infructuous with regard to the said two plots only in which the said persons claim Some interest, but the rest of the decree will remain unaffected. Furthermore the said transferees may remain satisfied with the allotments which may be allocated to their predecessors in interest.</u>

38. Having regard to the said facts and circumstances of the case we, therefore do not think that the decree shall be set aside and the suit be remanded to the Trial Court for a fresh trial after impleading the said" persons in the suit as has been prayed for by Mr. Jani Alam, the learned Advocate for the appellant.

39. Mr. C.F. Karim, the learned Advocate for the respondent has relied upon a decision in the case of Mir Shariatuilah Vs. Abdur Rahman Bepary and others reported in 8 DLR 645 in support of his contention that the decree in question need not be set aside and the parties concerned may be asked to appear in the Court below for making appropriate prayer for their Saham at the time of the preparation or the final decree.

<u>40. In the present case, we think it is up to the said persons, if they are so advised, to press their claim with regard to their property at the time of the preparation of the final decree in the Trial Court. In view of the facts of the case, we are of the opinion that the decree need not be set aside on the ground of non-impleading the aforesaid Asak and Abdur Rashid. We, therefore, do not find any substance in any of the contention raised by the learned Advocate for the appellants.</u>

<u>The result therefore is that this appeal is dismissed with costs. There is a Civil Rule being C.R. No. 322 (f) of 1969 having been disposed of the said Rule is also discharged without any order as to costs.</u>

A.S. Faizul Islam Chowdhury, J.—I agree.

End.

lawyer:
Dr M Zahir; Advocate with Md Moazzem Hussain, Ziaul Hasan and KS Salah uddin Ahmed, Advocates------ For the Petitioner. 
Rafique-ul-Huq, Advocate with Kamal-ul Alam, Md Tosaddeque Hossain, Advocates------ For Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
New Zealand Milk Brands Ltd ------ Petitioner
vs
Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd & ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
New Zealand Milk Brands Ltd filed the instant application under section 46 of the Trade Marks Act, 1940 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") for rectification of the Register of Trade Marks by removal of registered trademark No. 62724 in Class 29 from the Register.

2. Rule was issued calling upon the respondent-opposite parties to show cause as to why the Register of Trade Marks should not be rectified by removal of the trademark No. 62724 in class-29 from the Register. By the same order the operation of registered trade mark No. 62724 in class-29 was stayed. Subsequently upon an application filed by the opposite party No.1, Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as opposite party No. 1 ") the order of stay was vacated. By a subsequent order of this Court dated 7-8-2004 the petitioner was directed to deposit Taka 1 lakh as security for costs, which has been complied with by the petitioner.

3. It is stated in the petition that New Zealand Milk Brands Ltd. ("the petitioner") is the successor-in-interest of Unilac Australia Pty. Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Unilac Australia") and Bonlac Foods Ltd. ("Bonlac"). The last mentioned two companies have been engaged in the business of manufacturing, importing and marketing of powder milk, butter oil, condensed milk, etc. in class-29 throughout the world with reputation for its unrivalled quality for about three decades. In order to distinguish their products, the predecessors-in-interest of the petitioner adopted a trademark consisting of the words "Red Cow" together with the device of a cow represented in a special and particular manner in the containers in a colour combination quite distinctive in its presentation. Due to the quality of the goods and the various promotional measures undertaken the trade mark "Red Cow" and the device of cow has become popular throughout the world as a product of quality. Unilac Australia submitted applications to the Trade Marks Registry under applications No. C2130 in class-29 on 24-10-1983, No. C2379 in class-29 on 10-9-1984 and No. 33421 in class-29 on 7-9-1991. The applications for registration of those trademarks were duly advertised in the Trade Marks Journal and, there being no opposition, were registered and subsequently renewed and are valid to date. Unilac Australia entered into an "Agency Agreement" dated 1st July, 1986 with Messrs Sanowara Corporation, represented by its Proprietor Mr Nurul Islam to promote, distribute and sell in Bangladesh products manufactured by Unilac Australia. Subsequently, Unilac Australia entered into another Agency Agreement with the said Sanowara Corporation in the year 1991 cancelling the previous Agency Agreement and stipulating some other conditions for the purpose of marketing the products under the brand "Red Cow". On 20-6-1989 Unilac Australia entered into a Joint Venture Agreement with Sanowara Corporation resulting in the formation of a company called Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd (the instant opposite party No.1). The Agency Agreement dated 1st July, 1991 was terminated on 7-3-2002; The present petitioner became proprietor of the trademarks No. C2130, No. C2379 and No. 33421 from 29-4-2002 by virtue of a Deed of Assignment dated 9-4-2002 executed by Unilac Australia Pty Ltd (Unilac Australia) and its sister concern namely, Bonlac Foods Ltd (Bonlac). It is contended by the petitioner that by virtue of the two Agency Agreements Sanowara Corporation and its other associate companies have been selling products of its predecessors-in-interest as selling agent and the shares of opposite party No. 1 are owned 51 % by Sanowara Corporation and 49% by Unilac Australia. It is contended that opposite party No: 1 secretly applied for and obtained registration of a trademark consisting of the words "Red Cow" and the device of the cow knowing that the petitioner is the lawful proprietor of the said mark. It is alleged that the registration of trademark under application No. 62724 for milk powder, filed by opposite party No.1, registered on 28-11-1999, is in complete derogation of the provisions laid down in sections 10(1) and 8( a) of the Act whereby registration of identical or similar trademarks is prohibited. It is contended that such registration by opposite party No. 1 is creating confusion amongst the traders and buyers about the true origin of the goods and it is also causing loss of goodwill and business reputation as well as the decline in turnover of the petitioner. The petitioner contends that only recently, when the petitioner applied through Form TM-24 on 8-6-2002 for registering its name as subsequent proprietor of the trademark "Red Cow", it came to know that the trademark "Red Cow" was also registered in the name of opposite party No.1 under the trademark No. 62724 dated 28-11-1999 in class-29, which is now impugned in the instant application. It is claimed by the petitioner that the entry relating to registered trademark No. 62724 in class-29 is an entry made without sufficient cause and is wrongly remaining on the Register and, as such, it is liable to be removed by way of rectification. It is claimed by the petitioner that opposite party No. 1 has obtained registration of the impugned trademark by suppression of material facts and by falsely claiming to be proprietor of the mark. The petitioner claims that the opposite party No. 1 is debarred under the law from making any claim over the trademark of the petitioner and the registration of the same trademark by opposite party No.1 has been obtained by exercising fraud upon the Trade Marks Registry and also upon the petitioner.

4. The application was opposed by Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd, (opposite party No.1) through Nurul Islam, its Managing Director by filing affidavit-in-opposition. It is contended therein that the registered trade mark No. C-2130 dated 24-10-1983 with the words "Red Cow" and the device 'Cow’' was registered by Unigate Pvt Ltd without exclusive right to Use the word and device of 'Cow'. They obtained another trade Mark No. C-2379 dated 10-9-1984 with the name "Red Cow" with the device of 'Cow'. It is claimed that Unigate did not obtain the exclusive right to use the words "Red Cow" with the device of 'Cow'. It is also mentioned that Unigate obtained registration of trade mark No. C-1491 dated 8-1-1981 in class-29 under the name and style "Red Cow" with the device of 'Cow'. The opposite party No.1 claims that the petitioner has suppressed all these facts and since the exclusive right over the trademark using the words "Red Cow" and the device 'Cow' was not given, Bonlac, a sister concern of Unigate, got registration of the word "RED COW FOLLOWUP". Hence, it is claimed that there is no prohibition for registration of the trade mark "Red Cow" with the device "Cow" under section 10 of the Act. It is further contended by opposite party No.1 that Unilac Australia never used the trademark in question and the petitioner has no market in this country of any goods using the trademark and since they have no reputation in the market, there is no possibility of any deception or confusion in the mind of public of this country. It is claimed that the petitioner, in a letter dated 12-10-1999, which is annexed as Annexure-II to the affidavit-in-opposition, 'approved' the registration of the impugned trademark by opposite party No.1. It is further con- tended that the petitioner is not the proprietor of the trademark's in question, but is a mere assignee, and therefore, has no locus standi to file the present application. It is also contended that the opposite party No.1 obtained the registration of its trademark on 28-11-1999 with the full consent of Unilac, which holds 49% of the shares in the opposite party No. 1 Company. It is further contended that the petitioner is not an aggrieved person within the meaning of section 46 of the Act and is not entitled to maintain the present application for rectification. On the other hand, opposite party No. 1 claims that the predecessor-in-interest of the petitioner never marketed any of their goods under the trademark "Red Cow" and' "Red Cow Follow up" in Bangladesh and hence, their application for registration for trademark No. C2130, C2379; C33421 were all obtained by practising fraud on the Trade Marks Registry. It points out that admittedly Unilac Australia entered into an Agency Agreement with Sanowara Corporation for the purpose of marketing its products in Bangladesh as from 1-7-1986 and, therefore, the claim by Unilac Australia in its application for registration of trademarks No. 2130 and 2379 that it had been using the trademark "Red Cow" for their products in Bangladesh since 1983, is false. It further points out that registration of the mark "Red Cow" having been obtained in 1983 and again in 1984, and subsequently through Bonlac in 1991, the petitioner has not come with clean hands and the instant application is an abuse of the process of the Court. It is further contended that the opposite party No. 1 is not a party to the alleged agency Agreement and that Sanowara Corporation and , Nurul Islam are different persons and the opposite party No.1 is not bound by the conditions stipulated in the Agency Agreement. It is also contended that the petitioner's predecessor-in-interest has been aware all along regarding the registration of the trademark by opposite party No. 1 and the matter was published in the Trade Marks Journal, which is a public notice, and no objection was ever raised and hence, the petitioner is estopped from filing the present application.

5. The petitioner then filed an affidavit-in- reply to the affidavit-in-opposition essentially reiterating its contentions made in the original petition. Additionally, it has been contended that the application for the registration of trademark of opposite party No. 1 has been registered in violation of Rules 23 and 24 of the Revised Trade Marks Rules, 1963 ("the Rules"). Also, it has been contended that the proviso in section 10(2) of the Act will not be applicable in the instant case, because the subsequent registration and use of the trademark by opposite party No. 1 has been proved to be dishonest and the registration of the impugned trademark has taken place in violation of Rules 23 and 24 of the said Rules and section 8(a), 10(1) and 14 of the Act.

6. It may be pointed out that in the supplementary affidavit on behalf of opposite party No. 1, filed as a supplement to the application for vacating the order of stay, Nurul Islam as Managing Director of Sanowara Dairy and Industries Limited who is also admittedly the Managing Director of opposite party No. 1, stated in paragraph 3 of the said supplementary affidavit dated 25-11-2002 that opposite party No.1 has been importing milk under the trademark "Red Cow" on the basis of an Agency Agreement entered on 1-7-1986 between Sanowara Corporation and Unilac Australia (Pvt) Ltd.

7. Mr Ziaul Hasan, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submitted that opposite patty No, 1, knowing fully well that the petitioner's predecessors-in-interest were the proprietors of the trade mark "Red Cow", fraudulently applied to register the very same trademark in its own name, falsely claiming to be the proprietor. He submitted that the selfsame Nurul Islam, who is the proprietor of Sanowara Corporation as well as the Managing Director of Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd, entered into the Agency Agreement on behalf of Sanowara Corporation admitting the petitioner's predecessor-in-interest as the proprietor of the trademark "Red Cow" in the year 1986 and subsequently, in the year 1999, falsely claimed himself to be proprietor of the same trademark. Learned Counsel pointed out that the claim by Nurul Islam in his affidavit that he had been importing milk under the trademark "Red Cow" since 1978 is palpably false since he entered the Agency Agreement much later, in 1986. Learned Counsel submitted that as the application filed by Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd is based on a false representation that it was the proprietor of the mark since 1990, the registration of that mark is liable to be expunged on that ground of fraud alone. In this regard, learned Counsel referred to the decision in the case of Societe de Fabrication et de Distribution de Parfumerie et Cosmetique (DIPARCO) Societe Anonyme vs Deputy Registrar of Trade Marks, Government of Pakistan and another reported in PLD 1979 Karachi 83. He further pointed out that the application for registration, which was filed on 28-11-1999 before the Registrar of Trade Marks, clearly shows interpolation of the date of the applicant's proprietorship in the trademark. That interpolation of the date not having been authorised, the application is liable to be expunged. Learned Counsel further submitted that the impugned trademark being exactly the same as that of the petitioner, undoubtedly, there is likely to be confusion in the minds of the public who are liable to be deceived as to the origin and manufacture of the product, which is violative of sections 8(a) and 10(1) of the Act. He submitted that in the interest of the public and for the sake of maintaining purity of the Register the impugned, trademark should be expunged. In support, he has referred to the decision in the case of Messrs Kanshiram Surinderkumar a Firm vs Messrs Thakurdas Deoonmal Rohire and others reported in AIR 1982 Bombay 505. Learned Counsel further submitted that the application having been received at a time when the same mark had already been registered earlier, the Registrar of Trade Marks failed in his duty under Rule 23 of the Rules in allowing the impugned trademark to be registered. In this regard, he has referred to the decision in the case of Md Abu Taher Sikder vs Registrar of Trade Marks and, another reported in 11 BLT 194. Referring to Annexure-M of the petitioner's affidavit-in-reply dated 12-6-2003, he pointed out that in Money Suit No. 13 of 2002, which was later numbered as Money Suit No. 20 of 2002, the plaintiff, Nurul Islam filed a money suit against Unilac Australia Pty Ltd. In that suit, the plaintiff filed an application for attachment, which is marked Annexure-N. In the prayer portion of the said application (Annexure-N) the plaintiff prayed for attachment of the trademark "Red Cow in Can" belonging to the defendant, namely, Unilac Australia Pty. Ltd. He submitted that the opposite party No. I thus admitted the proprietorship of the petitioner's predecessor-in-interest in the trademark "Red Cow in Can". Learned Counsel further submitted that the petitioner through its predecessors has been marketing  its goods  in the Bangladeshi, market since 1986 by virtue of the Agency Agreement  with Sanowara Corporation executed in 1986 and therefore, the claim of the opposite party No.1 that the petitioner does not market any goods under the trademark, is not true.

8. On the separate issue of registration on the basis of honest concurrent use, learned Counsel for the petitioner submitted that there cannot be any claim of registration by the opposite party No. 1 under section 10(2) of the Act since the user by the opposite party No. 1 cannot be said to be honest, inasmuch as his application for registration of the trademark itself is based on a false premise that he was the proprietor of the mark. Learned Counsel submitted that the registration Nos. 2130 and 2379 in the name of Unigate belong to one and the same entity and Unigate's name having changed to Unilac by submitting Form TM-33, the registering companies are not separate entities and, therefore, in the year 1999 only two registrations existed in the name of Unilac Australia having proprietorship over registered trademarks Nos. 2130 and 2379 and registration No. 33241 in the name of Bonlac Food Limited and, both the companies being sister concerns, it cannot be said that the trademark has become publici juris.

9. Mr Kamalul Alam, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1, submitted that the petitioner has no locus standi to file this application, inasmuch as he cannot be the assignee. He referred to section 34(2) of the Act and submitted that the associate trademarks of the petitioner have not been assigned and, as such, the assignment as a whole is imperfect. Moreover, he submitted, there is nothing to show that the products of the pre- decessors-in-interest of the petitioner bearing the trademark "Red Cow" have ever been marketed in Bangladesh and, as such, the registration of the trademark by the petitioner's redecessors-in-interest itself is a fraud on the Registry, In support of his submission, he has referred to the decision in the case of  Kohinoor Chemical Co (BD) Ltd vs Kohinoor Chemical Co Ltd and another reported in 1 BLC 245. He further submitted that the petitioner is not an aggrieved person and, as such, he cannot bring an application under section 46 of the Act. In support, he has referred to the decision in the case of Supermax International Private Ltd vs Samath Razor Blades Industries Ltd and another reported in 4 BLC (AD) 229. He further submitted that the petitioner has filed the instant application for rectification after three years of the registration of the impugned trademark and, as such, the application is barred under the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. In support of his submission, he referred to the decisions in the case of Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation and another vs Messrs Sattar Match Works and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 208 and National Match Works, Sivakasi vs ST Karuppanna Nadar (died) and others reported in AIR 1979 Madras 157. He further submitted that mere knowledge of the existence of a similar trademark does not prove dishonesty on the part of the applicant for trademark registration. In support, he has referred to the decisions in the case of Pakistan Soap Factory. Chittagong vs Chittagong Soap Factory, Chittagong & anr, reported in 22 DLR (SC) 400 and Messrs Surya Brothers vs Messrs Dada Soap Factory Ltd, reported in PLD 1971 Karachi 189. He pointed out that at the time when the trademark of the opposite party No. 1 was registered on 28-11-1999 there were three other registered trademarks comprising the same two words "Red Cow" and the device of a "Cow". He pointed out that trademark registration No. C-1491 obtained by Unigate on 8-1-1981, which has not been assigned to the petitioner, existed on the record and was extended up to 7-1-2003. At the same time, there existed the petitioner's predecessor's application No. C2130 dated 24-10-1983, which was initially registered by Unigate Australia Pvt Ltd and the name was subsequently changed on 21-10-1990 to Unilac Australia Pty Ltd. Also at the same time there was a trademark No. C33421 registered on 7-9-1991 by Bonlac Foods Limited and trademark No. C2379 registered on 10- 9-1984 registered by Unigate and subsequently, the name changed to Unilac on 21-10-1990. Learned Counsel submitted that all these trademarks comprising the words "Red Cow" and the device of a "Cow" were appearing in the Register of Trade Marks at the same time and, therefore, there is no reason why the application by the opposite party No. I should not have been registered. He submitted that the registration of the same mark under the names of three or more different entities makes the trademark publici juris and, therefore, there is no bar to registration of the same trademark of the opposite party No. 1. He submitted that the trademarks Nos. C2130, 2379 and 33421 have been assigned to the petitioner by Deed of Assignment dated 29-4-2002, but the registered trademarks No. C1491 and C1429 in the name of Unigate Australia Pvt Ltd, being associate marks, having not been assigned to the petitioner, the assignment is not complete and is, therefore, violative of the provisions of section 34(2). Thus the assignment being partial only, the petitioner has not acquired any right by the assignment and, therefore, has no locus standi to file this application. Referring to the Agency Agreement, learned Counsel submitted that Unilac Australia became proprietor of the trademark in 1990 and, therefore, could not have entered into the Agency Agreement in 1986 claiming itself to be the proprietor of that mark.

<u>10. I have considered the submissions of learned Counsel for both parties, perused the petition and the affidavit-in-opposition as well as the other supplementary affidavits filed in support both by the petitioner and the opposite party No.1. At the outset the provisions of section 46 of the Trade Marks Act 1940 may be reproduced:</u>

<u>46. "Power to cancel or vary registration and to rectify the register (1) On application in. the prescribed manner by any person aggrieved to a High Court or to the Registrar, the Tribunal may make such order as it may think fit for cancelling or varying the registration of a trade mark on the ground of any contravention, or failure to observe a condition entered on the register in relation thereto.</u>

<u>(2) Any person aggrieved by the absence or omission from the register of any entry, or by any entry made in the register without sufficient cause, or by any entry wrongly remaining on the register or by any error or defect in any entry in the register, may apply in the prescribed manner to a High Court or to the Registrar and the Tribunal may make such order for making, expunging or varying the entry as it may think fit.</u>

<u>(3) The Tribunal may, in any proceeding under this section, decide any question that it may be necessary or expedient to decide in connection with the rectification of the register.</u>

<u>(4) A High Court or the Registrar, of its or his own motion, may, after giving notice in the prescribed manner to the parties concerned and after giving them an opportunity of being heard, make any order referred to in sub-section (1) or sub-section (2).</u>

<u>(5) Any order of the Court rectifying the register shall direct that notice of the rectification shall be served upon the Registrar in the prescribed manner who shall upon receipt of such notice rectify the register accordingly."</u>

<u>So far as section 46(1) and 46(2) are concerned, the requirement is that an application under this section is to be filed by any person aggrieved. A person aggrieved can be described as one who will suffer as a result of the registration of the impugned trademark by way of diminution of his goodwill and business turnover. In the instant cases the petitioner has stepped into the shoes of Unilac Australia Pty. Ltd and Bonlac Foods Limited and has been assigned the trademarks of its predecessors-in-interestand, therefore, any activity from any third party, which detrimentally affects the business of the petitioner can be said to cause grievance and, therefore, makes it an aggrieved party. Learned Counsel for the opposite party No.1 argued that since the assignment was only partial it is incomplete and imperfect and, therefore, does not give any right to the petitioner by that assignment and hence it does not have locus standi to file the application. Section 34(2) of the Act. provides as follows:</u>

<u>"(2) Associated trademarks shall be assignable and transmissible only as a whole and not separately."</u>

11. The provision appears to be such that associated trademarks can be assigned as a whole and not in part. I understand that to mean that those marks which are associated with the principal marks have to be assigned along with the principal marks in order for the assignment to be complete, The purpose behind this provision of law is to prevent the associated mark being left behind, after transfer or assignment of the principal mark, thus resulting in the associate mark itself forming into a separate and distinct trademark. In the facts of the instant case, it appears that the associated mark, being registered trademark No. 1429, which is associated with trademark No. 2130, has not been assigned to the petitioner and hence, the assignment not being complete, on a strict legal construction, it has no locus standi to file this instant application.

12. Moreover, it appears that the predecessors- in-interest of the petitioner, namely Unilac Australia Pty Ltd and Bonlac Foods Limited, were at one time all in concert with opposite party No.1, inasmuch as they have been doing business together supplying the market in Bangladesh with milk powder under the various agreements into which they entered, in particular the Agency Agreement in this case, which dates back to 1986. It cannot be denied for one moment that Sanowara Corporation had knowledge of and admitted the proprietorship of Unilac Australia Ltd in the trademark comprising the words "Red Cow" and the device of "Cow". It is also evident that Nurul Islam, Managing Director of opposite party No. 1, in his affidavit dated 25-11-2002 admit- ted that opposite party No. 1 has been importing milk under the trademark "Red Cow" on the basis of the Agency Agreement dated 1-7-1986. At the same time, it cannot be denied that Unilac Australia being 49% shareholder in Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd had knowledge of the registration of the trademark by Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd. It is, therefore, crystal clear that so long as the parties were at par in business neither had any objection to the other using the same trademark, in the case of "Red Cow" with the device of "Cow". However, with the breakdown of relationship, and the termination of the Agency Agreement, the interests of the parties have been impinged and hence each one is trying to protect its own business interest at the cost of the other.

13. With regard to the concept of publici juris, Narayan on Trade Marks, Second Edition in paragraph 492. reflecting the decision in the wellknown case of Ford vs Forster (1872) 7 CH 611, wrote as follows;

"A word or device which was originally a trade mark, to the exclusive use of which a particular trader, or his successors in business, may have been entitled, may subsequently become publici juris and the exclusive right may be lost."

He goes on to say that if the mark has come to be so public and in such universal use that nobody can be deceived by the use of it, or can be induced from the use of it to believe that he is buying the goods of the original trader, the right to the trade mark must be gone. It is explained later in the same book in paragraph 496 that under the earlier UK Trade Marks Acts registration of identical or similar marks was allowed only up to a maximum number of three. Thus, if a mark was publicly used by more than three persons for the same or similar description of goods, before 13th August, 1875, it should be deemed common to the trade in such goods, i.e. the mark would become publici juris. Such provision was, however, dropped from the UK legislation since 1883 and corresponding provisions were not included in the Trade Marks Act, 1940.

In such view of the matter, the submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 that the trademark "Red Cow" with the device of cow has become publici juris is not sustainable. Moreover, on the face of the record, it is seen that Unigate Australia Pvt Ltd and Unilac Australia Pty Ltd. are one and the same entity, the former having changed its name to the latter. This is apparent from the submission of the form TM-33 in the year 1990. Thus the contention that at least three different entities registered the same trademark and all three registrations existed in the year 1999 is not borne out by the record. Furthermore, it is apparent that Unilac Australia and Bonlac Foods Limited are sister concerns and the mark is not common to the trade and used by the public at large. The reason behind the provisions for not allowing third parties to register the same trademark is so as to prevent confusion in the mind of the public and, in this case, it would be fair to say that Unilac Australia Pty Ltd and Bonlac Foods Limited, though two separate entities, are yet not third parties. The mark, therefore, cannot be said to be publici juris.

14. On the question of maintainability of the application for rectification, my view is that although the petitioner may be a person aggrieved in all practicalities, having stepped into the shoes of its predecessors-in-interest, in strict legal terms it does not have locus standi to file the application, as the assignment in favour of the petitioner was not in accordance with law. Moreover, the registration of the impugned mark was within the knowledge and assent of the petitioner's predecessors-in-interest and the latter, having been in business together with the opposite party No.1, there was no question of any grievance at the time of the impugned registration. However, the pertinent question is whether there is arty impediment in the impugned registered trademark remaining on the record. Section 46(4) of the Act gives this Court the power to pass an order in terms of section 46(1) and 46(2) of its own motion. The question would be, whether the registered trademark remains on the record without sufficient cause. In the course of hearing, the records of the impugned registered trade mark were transmitted by the Registrar of Trade Marks and the Same were scrutinised. the question of the claim to proprietorship of the mark was argued at length from the Bar. It appears from the application dated 28-11-1999 that the applicant therein, namely Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd. (opposite party No.1 ) claimed to be the proprietor of the trademark since 1990. It may be pointed out at this stage that the year "1990"; written on the application form, appears to have been interpolated and changed from 1998 without any endorsement or authorisation. Be that as it may, the Claim of the applicant is that it is the proprietor of the trademark comprising the words "Red Cow'; and the device of a "Cow". Turning back to the Agency Agreement dated 1-7-1986, it is clear that the agreement is 'between Unilac Australia Pty Ltd and Sanowara Corporation. That agreement relates to "Red Cow" branded products supplied by the principal, namely Unilac Australia Pty Ltd It is also clear from the agreement that Sanowara Corporation is the selling agent for the product in the Bangladeshi market. It is also apparent that the said agreement was signed On behalf of the agent by Nurul Islam. The argument put forward by the petitioner was that the selfsame Nurul Islam, who is the Managing Director of the opposite party No.1, cannot deny that the proprietorship of the trademark belongs to the predecessor of the petitioner, he laving entered into the Agency Agreement to market the products branded "Red Cow". It was argued that the opposite party No. 1 fraudulently claimed that the applicant was the proprietor of the trademark knowing that the petitioner was all along the proprietor of the mark.

15. The allegation of fraud is very serious indeed, and it is an established principle of law that fraud vitiates all, acts. We have held in the past, in the Trade Mark Application No.9 of 2002 that the practice of fraud will do away with the immunity given by section 24 of the Act. Similarly; it has been held in numerous cases that if fraud has been practised then the registration gained thereby will be expunged. In the case of Societe de Fabrication cited above, I Mahmud, J, referring to Kelry s Law of Trade Marks and Trade Names on the question of the expression "claimed to be proprietor", stated that if the applicant knew or the circumstances showed that he (the applicant for the registration of a trademark) was aware that another person is the proprietor of the Mark his claim to proprietorship would be false and his assertion in the application form would be regarded as a deliberate attempt on his part to deceive the Registrar and, if he succeeds in obtaining a registration, it would be liable to be expunged on the ground of fraud.

16. Let tis see whether in the instant case the opposite party No. 1 has taken recourse to fraud in obtaining registration of the trademark "Red Cow" with the device of a "Cow". In its application it quite categorically stated that it is the proprietor of the trademark, be it since 1990 or 1998 (as there is interpolation of the date. The Agency agreement dated 1-7-1986 and the subsequent Agency Agreement dated 1-7-1991 show that Sanowara Corporation agreed to act as the selling agent and market the product supplied by the principal (Unilac Australia Pty. Ltd) under the brand name "Red Cow". Although it is not clearly spelt out whether Unilae Australia Pty. Ltd. has proprietary right over the trademark "Red Cow" or is simply supplying products branded "Red Cow", of which the proprietary interest may belong to someone else, the fact re- mains that Sanowara Corporation and the signatory to the agreement on behalf of Sanowara Corporation, namely Nurul Islam, were fully aware that the brand name "Red Cow" did not belong to Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd. Thus to that extent the statement that Unilac Sanowara (BD) Limited has had proprietorship over the trademark since 1990 or 1998 is not a true fact. Moreover, it appears from Annexures-H, I and J that the tinned milk under the mark "Red Cow" with the device of "Cow" is a product from Australia supplied by Unilac Australia Pty. Ltd and Annexure] specifically shows that the packeting of the "Red Cow" branded milk powder was done by Unilac, Sanowara (BD) Ltd. for Bon- lac Foods Limited. This, along with the admission by Nurul Islam in Money Suit No. 20 of 2002 that the defendant, namely Unilac Australia Pty Ltd, owns the trademark "Red Cow in Can" and the admission in his affidavit dated 25-11-2002, mentioned above, is, in my view, clear indication that the trademark "Red Cow" did not belong to Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd. To that extent the registration has been obtained by fraud. For the same reason the trademark cannot be allowed to remain as a registration under section 10(2) of tile Trade Marks Act. Accordingly, it is my view that the registration obtained under trademark registration No. C-62724 in Class-29 dated 28-11-1999 is liable to be expunged.

<u>17. Furthermore, it is noted that the Registrar registered the trademark of opposite party No.1 when the trademarks of Unigate/Unilac Australia and Bonlac already legally and validly existed on the record. He has thus clearly fallen foul of the provisions of the Rules as well as. section 46(4) of the Act. From a perusal of the records relating to TM No. 62724 in Class-29, which is kept at the office of the Registrar of Trade Marks, it appears that after search Notice in Form TMR-12 was issued to the opposite party No. 1 indicating that three other marks of the same description had already been registered. In reply Nurul Islam, as Managing Director of opposite party No.1, sent an explanation along with a sworn affidavit to the effect that Unilac Sanowara (BD) Ltd had been preparing/ manufacturing/packeting and distributing and marketing Red Cow brand powder milk throughout Bangladesh since 1990. He attached the trade licences for Messrs Unilac Sanowara (Bangladesh) Limited since 1-9-1990. He also explained that the other registered and pending trademarks mentioned in the notice had no existence in the market. In the light of such a statement, the Registrar should have acted under the provisions of section 46(4) of the Act with a view, upon satisfaction of the allegation, to dealing with existing pending trademarks under section 46(1) and (2) of the Act. But his failure to do so before registering the impugned trade mark shows noncompliance of the Rules. For this reason also the impugned trademark is liable to be removed. It is noted also that the affidavit, which resulted in the impugned trade mark being registered, is itself palpably false since the Agency Agreements of 1986 and 1991 clearly show that. Unilac Australia Pty. Ltd. is the supplier of "Red Cow" branded products and Sanowara Corporation is the selling agent for the products in Bangladesh. Thus, the registration has taken place upon consideration of a statement which was patently a false representation. I would also add that this type of perfunctory compliance of the Rules by the Registrar of Trade Marks, ignoring the purpose of provisions of law in its totality, is highly deprecated. When search -is made under Rule. 23, those must be proper and meaningful and taken to their final conelusion. In the light of the allegation in the pending application, the Registrar should have suo moto taken action, in respect of the trade marks already registered, in accordance with section 46(4) of the Act.</u>

18. Finally, regarding the claim of the opposite party No.1 that the petitioner's predecessors trademarks, registered under application Nos. C-2130, C- 2379, were themselves based on false statements, suffice to say that those applications are not presently under consideration before this Court and refrain from passing any comment about those.

19. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without, however, any order as to costs. Registered trademark No. 62724 dated 28-11-1999 in class-29 is hereby directed to be expunged from the Register of Trade Marks.

20. Let a copy of this judgment be communicated to the Registrar of Trade Marks, who is directed to take necessary steps to effect rectification of the Register of Trade Marks in the light of this judgment in accordance with law.

21. The Bank Guarantee for Taka 1(one) lakh furnished by the petitioner in pursuance to this Court's order dated 7-8-2004 is directed to be returned to the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

Send down the Records of the Registrar at once.

End.

lawyer:
SN Goswami, Advocate with Afsana Begum, Advocates -----For the Petitioner. 
Md Golam Hossain Sarwar, Advocate -----For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Salima Akhter Niluma Banu ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Shahin Shakhider & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule, calls in question the legality and propriety of the judgment and decree dated 27-4-2005 passed by the learned District Judge, Joypurhat, in OC Appeal No. 1 of 2005 affirming those of dated 25-11-2004 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Joypurhat Sadar, Joypurhat, in Other Class Suit No. 58 of 2004, rejecting the plaint of the suit under Order VII, rule 11 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Short facts leading to this Rule are, that on 1-7-2004 the petitioner as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 58 of 2004 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Joypurhat, impleading the opposite parties as defendants for permanent injunction; restraining the defendant Nos. 1-3 from giving allotment to defendant Nos. 4 at the southern part of his plot No. 28/B of Joypurhat Housing Estate (briefly as Estate).

3. The plaintiff's case in short are that the plot No. 28/B was allotted, to him, accordingly on 10-5-1989 leased deed was registered in favour of him. Some portion of land at the southern part of his plot was fallen vacant, for beautification of the area but the defendants are trying to lease out the same in favour of the defendant No.4. Hence, the Suit.

4. Subsequently, the plaintiff filed two applications, one for amendment of the plaint and another for local investigation, fixing 25-11-2004 for hearing but on the same day defendant No.4 filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint stating that as per clause 14 of the terms and conditions of the Estate the suit is barred by law.

5. After hearing the learned judge of the trial Court by the order dated 25-11-2004 rejected the plaint.

6. On appeal, the learned District Judge by the judgment and decree dated 27-4-2005 passed in OC Appeal No. 1 of 2005 affirmed the order of the trial Court.

7. Feeling aggrieved the petitioner obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr SN Goswami, the learned Advocate appearing with Mrs Afsana Begum, the learned Advocate supports the Rule and submits that the plaintiff held the suit for permanent injunction not against any decision of the committee of the Estate. He adds that before rejection of the plaint he was not given any opportunity to file written objection, moreover, maintainability of the suit cannot be decided before framing an issue to that effect. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel refers the case of BADC vs Abedunnessa and others reported in 7 BLT 297 = 4 BLC 574, wherein it is held:

"In the present suit the Chairman is representing the corporation as the chief functionary and, as such, the objection that instead of the corporation itself the Chairman is made defendant in the suit, is a technical objection. It is posited here that the contention raised is a question of maintainability which does not come within the four walls of the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code and this question of maintainability can be agitated by the defendant at the time of hearing of the suit."

9. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and order.

10. Mr Golam Hossain Sarwar, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite No.1, opposes the Rule and submits that the opposite party No. 1 already constructed a building in the suit land which is a commercial space. He adds that after considering the materials on record, the courts below rightly rejected the plaint, which calls for no interference by this Court.

11. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels, I have gone through the revisional application as well as other materials on record and given my anxious consideration to their submissions.

12. Now, the question calls for consideration is, whether the plaint of the Other Class Suit No. 58 of 2004 was rightly rejected by the Courts below.

13. Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for the rejection of the plaint. For the convenience of understanding, the same reads hereunder:

"11-The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:

(a) where it does not disclose a cause of action:

(b) where the relief claimed is undervalued and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper in- sufficiency stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

(d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law,

Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty-one days."

14. On going through the materials on record, I find that the plaintiff filed the suit for permanent injunction. Both the courts below rejected the plaint mainly relying on clause 14 of the terms and conditions of the Estate. Clause-14, runs in the following manner:

"১৪ কমিটির সিদ্ধান্তের বেরুদ্দে কোন প্রকার আদালত করা যাইবে না”

15. The courts below failed to consider the other materials of the plaint, clause-14 must lie read along with other statements made in the plaint. The courts below misconstrued the principles laid down in Order VII, rule 11 of the Code, thereby came to an erroneous decision by rejecting the plaint.

<u>16. In the case of Secretary of State vs Mask and Co reported in AIR 1940 (PC) 105, 110, wherein it is held-</u>

<u>"It is settled law that the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts is not to be readily inferred but such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied. It is also well established that even if jurisdiction is so excluded, the Civil Courts have jurisdiction to examine into cases where the provisions of the Act have not, been complied with, or the statutory tribunal has not acted ill conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure."</u>

17. On critical analysis of the averments made in the plaint, I find that the same disclosed the basic requirements laid down in Order VII, rule 11 of the Code. The grounds taken and the submissions made by the learned Counsel for the opposite party No.1 may hold good at the time of trial after framing issue to that effect.

18. In the case of Sundar Ali being dead his heirs A Hannan and others vs Md Serajul Islam Sarker and others reported in 56 DLR (AD) 210 wherein it is held:

"For the ascertainment of the cause of action the Court is required to read the plaint in its entirety"

19. In the case of Abdul Malek Sawdagar vs Md Mahbubey Alam and others reported in 57 DLR (AD) 18 wherein it is held:

"The question whether the plaint is liable to be rejected being barred by law must be apparent from the statement made in the plaint itself and not from the written statement or any other material other than that has been put in the plaint."

20. In the case of Md Abul Khair vs Pubali Bank Ltd and another reported in 2001 BLD (AD) 32 = 53 DLR (AD) 62 wherein it is held:

"Where in a suit an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code is filed for rejecting the plaint on the ground that the averments made in the plaint do not disclose a cause or action for the suit, the Court is not called upon to decide the suit on merit on taking evidence. It is only the averments made in the plaint which are to be considered to come to a finding as to whether those disclose a cause of action. The Court while deciding such applications not permitted in law to travel beyond the averments made in the plaint.

21. Having regard to the facts the legal plea taken by the learned Counsel for the petitioner prevails and appears to have a good deal of force but I failed to discover any merit in the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the opposite party No.1

22. In view of the discussion made above and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above, I am of the view that the impugned judgment and decree suffers from legal infirmity which calls for interference by this court. Thus the Rule having merit succeeds.

23. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost The impugned judgment and decree dated 27-4-2005 passed by the learned District Judge, Joypurhat, in OC Appeal No. 1 of 2005 affirming those of dated 25-11-2004 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge; Joypurhat Sadar, Joypurhat, in Other Class Suit No. 53 of 2004, are hereby set aside. The other class suit No. 58 of 2004 will proceed in accordance with law.

24. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Joypurhat Sadar, Joypurhat is directed to dispose of the suit as early as possible preferably within 6(six) months from the date of receipt of this judgment and order.

Send down the records of this case at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mahmudul Hoque with Mohammad Ziaul Haque. Advocates-For the Petitioner. 
HN Nondy with Moqbul Ahmed, Advocates-For the Opposite Party No. 1
parties:
Afzal Khan (Md) ------ Petitioners
vs
Md Azmal Khan and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J : This Rule at the instance of defendant-petitioner is directed against the order No. 83 dated 29-7-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in partition suit No. 89 of 1996 allowing the application for additional statement and an application for amendment of written statement filed by the defendant 2 (hereinafter called the opposite party No.1) in the suit and by the same order rejecting an application filed by the present defendant-petitioner (hereinafter called petitioner) for expunging the deposition of opposite party No. 1 as outside of his original written statement.

2. The relevant facts, in short, are that the opposite party No.3 (hereinafter called the plaintiff) as plaintiffs instituted partition suit No. 89 of 1996 praying for saham of 1/4 share in the suit property according to partition deed No. 160 dated 23-12-1958. It is contended that on the basis of partition deed No. 160 dated 23-12-1958, the plaintiff got 1(c) schedule property in his saham, defendant Ibrahim got 4(B) schedule land, defendant Afzal Khan got 3(B) schedule land and defendant Azmal Khan got 5(B) schedule land as their respective share from the Suit property. Before the execution of partition deed dated 23-12-1958 suit land was rented to SVOC Petrol Pump and all the 4 brothers were enjoying possession according to their respective share through tenants. Subsequently, the schedule land was rerited by a tenancy agreement to Esso Standard Eastern Co. for constructing a petrol pump and after liberation the said petrol pump was transferred to Meghna Petroleum Co. Ltd, and thereafter, the plaintiff gave a power of attorney in favour of his brother opposite party No. 1 Azmal Khan to look after his share on his behalf. But subsequently, for certain misdeeds, the plaintiff having been dissatisfied with the opposite party No.1, requested Meghna Petroleum to execute a new tenancy agreement with him for 1/4 his share of the suit land and thereafter also served a notice through his lawyer after expiry of tenancy agreement dated 31-10-1990 and, in fact, no tenancy agreement was executed with him Accordingly, the plaintiff as owner of 1/4 share of the suit land has not been getting due share of the rent as heirs by, metes and bounds, so the plaintiff asked all other share holders to get the suit land divided for getting their due shares except the opposite party No. 1 as defendant No. 2 having been in advantageous position in joint ownership suit land denying to give their due shares. Hence the suit.

3. Opposite party No. 1 as defendant No. 2 appeared in the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegation and asserted that the plaintiff in collusion with defendant Nos. 1 and 3 instituted the partition suit in order to create problem to this defendant. It is further contended' that according to the partition deed dated 23-4-1956 the plaintiff and defendants were jointly managing their partnership business including petroleum business and thereafter in a meeting under the president ship of late Amanat Khan by agreement dated 1-9-1961, the plaintiff and defendant No.1 retired from the partnership business and transferred their capital share and interest in favour of the defendant-opposite party No.1 and in this way after execution of that agreement the entire ownership and management of the partnership business transferred to the opposite party No.1 and therefore he invested a huge amount of money for buying new pump and generator, etc. It has been further contended that the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1 and 3 are only entitled to get rent of the suit property as per tenancy agreement executed on 17-4-1968 with ESSO Standard Eastern Corporation but seeing progress in the business, the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1 and 3 have been hatching conspiracy to cause damage to the petrol pump business of the instant defendant-opposite party No.1.

4. After filing of the written statement dated. 27-7-1997 the trial of the suit started and thereafter at the belated stage the defendant-opposite party No. 1 filed the additional written statement on 10-4-2003 stating that the partition agreement dated 23-12-1958 regarding purchase of the suit land by a kabala dated 30-10-48 is false, baseless and collusive, etc. Furthermore, after having been examined by the trial Court the defendant-opposite party No. 1 filed another petition praying for amendment of his written statement under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure stating that due to ill health he ,could not properly advise his appointed lawyer about his fight, title and possession in the suit property and, as such, some material facts were not correctly stated in the written statement and therefore some mistakes are necessary to be amended in the interest of justice otherwise, he will suffer irreparable loss and injury.

5. Plaintiff opposed the prayer for amendment of the written statement on the grounds firstly, that after being examined by the trial Court the defendant No.1 (opposite party) cannot amend the written statement raising a new story which is apparently contradictory and inconsistent with his main written statement. Secondly, the application for amendment of the written statement is very belated one and an afterthought and the same having not been made bonafide should not be allowed.

6. On the other hand, the present petitioner as defendant No.1, filed an application praying to expunge to the statements as made in the deposition of defendant-opposite party No.1, inasmuch as in his testimony before the trial Court he deposed absolutely beyond the pleadings and introduced a completely new story.

7. However, after hearing the parties the learned Joint District Judge, Chittagong by a common order dated 29-7-2003 allowed the application for additional statement and prayer for amendment of the written statement filed by the defendant- opposite party No. 1 in the suit and rejected the application filed by the present petitioner for expunging the deposition of defendant-opposite party No. 1 as outside of his original written statement.

8. Being aggrieved by that order, the defendant-petitioner moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule.

9. Mr Mahmudul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioner, submits that the impugned order dated 20-7-2003 is a nonspeaking order and the learned trial Court without assigning any reason whatsoever allowed the application in a summary manner which is illegal and beyond the scope of law. The learned Advocate, referring to written statement, additional written statement and amendment petition (Annexure-A, B and C to the main Revisional Petition) filed by the defendant opposite party No.1, submits that the averments made in the written statement itself reflects the same is apparently inconsistent and contradictory with the additional written statements inasmuch as in the additional' statement the defendant-opposite party No. 1 falsely stated that the partition deed No. 160 dated 23-12-1958 is false, fraudulent, void and not acted upon and the same was not signed and executed by him etc. but in fact, he admitted the partition deed dated 23-12-1958 in his earlier written statement (Annexure-A) and hence' the order of allowing the additional written statements cannot be sustained in law.
