Mr Md Mahmudul Hoque, the learned Advocate, further submits that the learned trial Court failed to appreciate that the prayer for additional written statement and proposed amendment is a deviation from the earlier taken by the opposite party No. 1 in his original written statement, inasmuch as in his earlier written statement (Annexure A) he categorically admitted the partition deed No. 140 dated 23-12-1958 but in the proposed amendment a new story has been set up changing the main issues of the case at a very belated stage of the suit, which cannot be said to be just and necessary for the purpose of determining the real controversy between the parties and, as such, the learned Joint District Judge by passing the instant impugned order committed an error of law as well as facts in issues and resulted an error in its decision occasioning failure of justice which warrants interference by this Court. Finally, the learned Advocate most emphatically submits that the deposition made by the defendant-opposite party No.1, before the trial Court introducing a new story which is contradictory and inconsistent with his earlier pleadings but the trial Court overlooking this aspect mechanically rejected the petitioner's application for expunging the deposition of defendant-opposite party No.1, as outside of his written statement. In support of his submissions the learned Advocate has relied on some decisions reported in 46 DLR (AD) 130, 51DLR 420, 44DLR 69,34 DLR 278, 1992 BLD 591, 41 DLR 190, 15 DLR 315,46 DLR 273, PLD 1982 (Kar) 111, 46 DLR 57, AIR 1961 (Born) 136, AIR 1953 (Cal) 15.

10. On the other hand, Mr HN Nondy, the learned Advocate, has urged on behalf of the defendant-opposite party No.1 only two points. His first submission is that when an amendment is proposed by the defendant. In the instant suit it is only the plaintiff who can oppose the same, but in the instant case the proposed amendment is brought by one defendant which is opposed by the other defendant though not resisted by the plaintiff and law does not authorise a defendant to raise any such objection. He then relying on the decision reported in 49 DLR 315 submits that an amendment cannot be disallowed on the ground that if allowed it will take away the admission made by the party earlier ill his pleading:

11. We have heard the learned Advocate of both the side at length and persused impugned order and other tangible materials on record. It appears that the real question in controversy in the suit was for partition of the suit properties in between the co- sharers according to partition deed No. 160 dated 23-12-1958, whereas the issue raised in the amendment application is claiming exclusive title and possession in the suit property after denying existence of admitted partition deed dated 23-12-1958; It also appears that in this case the original written statement was filed much earlier i.e. on 27-7-1997, and after a long lapse of 6 years an application for amendment of the written statement was filed on 10-4-2003 and within that long 6 years PWs and DWs including defendant-opposite party No. 1 himself having been examined and cross- examined before the trial Court apparently a new story was attempted to be added in the additional written statement stating exclusive ownership, possession and control in the suit property by giving a go-bye to the earlier pleadings of joint property equally belonging to this petitioner and other opposite parties as per Partition Deed No. 160 dated 23-12-1958. As a matter of fact, no papers and documents were annexed with the additional written statement and the amendment application showing exclusive ownership of the defendant No.2 in the suit land. Furthermore, ongoing through the impugned order dated 20-7-2003 it appears that the learned joint district judge without assigning any reason whatsoever allowed the application for additional statement and prayer for amendment of written statement filed by the defendant No.2. Mr Mahmudul Hoque, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has cited a number of decisions as stated above, to show that the prayer for amendment of written statement and prayer for additional written statement should not be allowed, if it is found malafide, belated, inconsistent in character and that does not relate to the real point in controversy. In the case reported in 34 DLR 278 the governing consideration was that according to the provisions under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code the parties after filing their pleadings they will not be allowed to depart from the pleadings or raise any new allegation of fact inconsistent with the previous pleadings. The Court will not allow any party to blow hot and cold at the same time. In the case of Abul Kalam Azad vs Sunhar Ali reported in 46 DLR (AD) 130 it has been observed as follows:

"From the materials on record, it appears that the evidence on the side of the plaintiffs having been closed and all the plaintiffs' witnesses having been examined and cross-examined, a completely new story was attempted to be added in the additional written statement by giving a go-bye to the earlier case of monthly tenancy and in that place a case of permanent tenancy on payment of salami and making out a case of reconstruction of the premises incurring an expenditure of Taka 1,75,000 was attempted to be introduced. As a matter of fact, no papers and documents were annexed with this additional written statement showing payment of salami nor any tangible paper of expenditure of the reconstruction was filed. It appears that a new and vague story has been set up at a subsequent point of time only to save the monthly tenancy on the plea of permanent tenancy and to delay the disposal of the case. It also appears that the learned Single Judge failed to consider that contesting defendant No. 7 was not only the son of defendant No. 1 and nephew of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 but was also the constituted attorney of defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3. In the additional written statement also there is no averment that the defendant No. 7 was not aware of this now story of permanent settlement as set up or defendant Nos. 1-3 were not aware of the contents of the written statement filed in their behalf. On the materials on record the learned Single Judge ought to have held that the amendment of the written statement was not bonafide."

12. This view also finds support in the cases reported in PLD 1982 (Kar) 111, 46 DLR 57, AIR 1961 (Bom) 136, AIR 1953 (Cal) 15.

In the case of Abdur Rahman vs Sajjadur Rahman, reported in 51 DLR 420 it has been observed by this Court as follows:

"It appears from the application for accepting the additional written statement that the reasons set out therein are not substantiated by the facts incorporated in the additional written statement. Because the facts sought to be introduced to make out a defence were already there and within the knowledge of the defendants at the time when the written statement was filed in 1986. Moreover, the defendants are seeking to introduce a new and inconsistent defence and that too at a belated state. The defendants by filing their written statement on 20-6-1986 completely denied the existence of any agreement of sale by their predecessor-in-interest. Whereas in the additional written statement they admit the existence of the agreement of sale but disputes its genuineness and validity stating that the plaintiff created such agreement by obtaining signature of their predecessor-in-interest on blank cartridge papers on fraudulent misrepresentation of facts. Such defence sought to be introduced at a belated stage is absolutely an inconsistent and a new defence and is therefore, not permissible."

In the case of Major (Retd) M Afsaruddin vs Kamal Rahman reported in 41 DLR 190, wherein it has been laid down as follows;

"The governing consideration in an application to amend the written statement should be how far, if at all, the proposed amendment of the defence is necessarily evident that the Court has the positive duty to decide whether the proposed amendment is necessary to determine the real controversy between the parties. If that test is satisfied amendment should be allowed otherwise not."

This decision also finds support in the case of Bangladesh vs Md Aslam reported -in 1992 BLD 591,44 DLR 69 and 46 DLR273.

13. Mr Mahmudul Hoque, the learned Advocate, in course of argument, has taken us through the written statement and deposition of defendant-apposite party No. 1(Annexure-A & L-1) and submits that a party cannot adduce evidence unless he pleads his case in the pleadings. In this case there being no specific demand of the assertion of the plaintiffs with regard to their partition deed dated 23-12-1958 and joint ownership, of the suit property by way of inheritance in the written statement filed by the defendant opposite party No.1, but subsequently, shifting his earlier stand introduced a new story in his deposition before the Court denying the contention of the said partition deed dated 23-12-1958 but the plaintiff instituted the suit for partition according to the terms of registered partition deed dated 23-12-1958. and therefore, inconsistent and contradictory portion of testimony of the defendant opposite party No. 1 should be expunged. In support of this submission, the learned Advocate heavily relied on the decision reported in 38 DLR 39 wherein this Court observed as follows;

"Having regard to the facts, circumstances and in view of the discussions and provisions of law as noted above the said portion of the order No. 96 dated 11-9-1983 allowing the plaintiff to depose in support of his claim that introducing a new story is liable to be expunged and the exhibits marked on the same day which are 17 in number in support of the said claim of the plaintiff on 12-9-1983 are also liable to be kept out of consideration in the suit."

This view also finds support in the case of Shamsul Hoque vs Sarafat Ali reported in 46 DLR 57.

<u>14. We have considered the above submissions of the learned Advocates, examined the propriety of the impugned order vis-a-vis the law and the settled principles and it seems to us that in the facts and circumstances of the case the facts of proposed amendment of the written statement and the averments of the additional written statement is completely a new story and an afterthought and apparently the same is contrary to the earlier main written statement filed by the defendant-opposite party No. 1 and accordingly, we find substance in the submission of the learned Advocate that the opposite party No. 1 has attempted by the proposed amendment to introduce a new fact with malafide intention by which the nature and character of the suit or the pier ding will be changed or altered. To meet the first argument of Mr Nondy, it may be said, it is now well settled that a defendant can cross- examine another defendant who is hostile to the former. In the instant case by introducing a new case through the amendment has set up a case adverse to defendant No. 2. Therefore the defendant-petitioner has legitimate grievance and locus standi to oppose the amendment. Besides, in a partition suit all the parties stand at par and there is no distinction between the plaintiff and defendant and thus anybody adversely affected by the proposed amendment can oppose the same. There is no bar in law rather it is necessary in the interest of justice. In the second contention Mr Nondy has relied on the case reported in 49 DLR 315 wherein (one of us) My Lord Mr Justice Syed Amirul Islam was a party and in that case amongst others, it was decided that an amendment cannot be denied simply on the ground that if the same is allowed it will take away the admission made by the parties without anything more. The facts of the case are all together different from the facts of the instant case. In that case it was found as a matter of fact that the amendment was bonafide and Court allowed it in the interest of justice to settle all the controversies between the parties., Therefore, the principle laid down in that case is not attracted in the instant case, as we have already found that the proposed amendment is not a bonafide one and it is made to overreach. Malafide like fraud vitiates everything. Thus, the case does not, in fact, help Mr Nondy in any way.</u>

15. Normally the Court shall refuse to permit filing of an additional written statement at a very belated stage of the suit or when the case of the parties have been closed. A defendant is not allowed to introduce an inconsistent and new defence by filing additional written statement. Court has to carefully consider whether the statements made or the facts sought to be introduced at a belated stage by way of additional written statement was already there available or not. Such facts or statements which were already available at the time of filing written statement and the defendant was aware of that but failed to incorporate such facts the defendant shall be debarred from bringing such facts on record at a belated stage in the interest of justice. The defendant can raise all legal pleas which are legally permissible, consequential and necessary to meet the case set up in the plaint. Moreso, now it is well settled that the amendment of written statement can be allowed provided it is not malafide, belated and it relates to the point in controversy.

<u>16. Having regard to the foregoing discussions and observations, we are of the view that additional written statement filed on 10-4-2003 and an application for amendment of written statement filled on 10-5-2003 (Annexure B&C) by the opposite party No. 1 claiming his alleged exclusive title and possession in the suit land by Kabala dated 30-1-1948, denying the admitted partition Deed No. 160 dated 23-12-1958 to depart from earlier pleadings .incorporated by the opposite party No.1 (defendant No.2) in his original written statement dated 27-7- 97 with sole motive of harassing and causing financial loss to the, petitioner and other co-sharers by dragging the matter for an indefinite period and it also appears that the opposite party No. 1 (defendant No.2) in his deposition introduced a new and inconsistent story beyond his pleadings which is prohibited under the provisions of Order VI, rule 17 of the Civil Procedure Code. Moreover, on perusal of the said applications dated 10-4-2003 and 10-5- 2003 (Annexures B & C) filed by the opposite party No. 1 it becomes clear that a new claim and new allegations of facts, raised subsequently by the opposite party No. 1 are totally inconsistent with his earlier pleadings or a go-bye to his earlier pleadings/ case of joint property belonging to this petitioner and defendant-opposite parties equally by partition deed dated 23-12-1958. So, in the given facts and circumstances of the case and in view of the provisions of Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the uniform decisions of the highest Court as cited above, we are constrained to hold that the learned trial Court ought to have held that the additional written statement and the amendment petition (Annexures B & C) filed by the opposite party No. 1 (defendant No.2) are not bonafide rather malafide.</u>

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned order dated 29-7-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in partition suit No. 89 of 1996 is hereby set aside, so far it relates to the allowing of the applications dated 10-4-2003 for additional written statement and application dated 10-5-2003 for amendment of written statement and the application dated 3-5-2003 filed by the defendant-petitioner for expunging the examination in-chief of the defendant No.2 is allowed and the deposition beginning with the words; ৩০-১-৪৮ইং তারিখে and ending with the words, “পড়তে পারি না" quoted in the application dated' 3-5-2003, recorded beyond pleadings, is expunged.

18. The trial Court is directed to proceed with the trial of the suit as expeditiously as possible.

The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

End.

 Fida M Kamal, Attorney-General with Salauddin Ahmed, Additional Attorney-General -----For Respondent No.1 & 2.

As Amicus Curiae Fida M Kamal, TH Khan. Rafiq-ul-Huq, Khandakar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, M Amirul Islam, Dr Kamal Hossain, Dr M Zahir Mahmudul Islam and Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, A F Hasan Arif J.

Iqbal Hasan Mahmood alias Iqbal Hasan Mahmood Tuku ----- Petitioner 
Vs. 
Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: Above Rule Nisi was obtained by the petitioner for a declaration that the entire proceedings taken and continued in Special Case No.6 of 2007 arising out of Complaint Case No. 33 of 2007 in the 5th Court of Special Judge at the Parliament Building at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar at Dhaka under sections 165 and 166 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 were all without any lawful authority and, as such, of no legal effect.

2. The aforesaid case arises out of the complaint filed on 4-7-07 before the Senior Special Judge at Dhaka by one Md Nurul Amin, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, Large Tax Payers Unit (LTU) under sections 165 and 166 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984, in short, the Ordinance, read with Rule 15 of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, in short, Rules.

In the complaint, the allegations made are that,

i. in the assessment year 2000-2001 the petitioner did not disclose the investment of Taka 27,85,056.00 in the extension and renovation of the two-storied building to three-storied building upon an area of about 12.05 katha of land in 117, Asad Avenue at Dhaka and thereby, concealed the equivalent amount of income and thereby, evaded tax payable thereon;

ii. in the assessment year 2003-2004 the investment of Taka 9,26,345, which was the proportionate cost of expenditure of the inherited share of the petitioner in the extension of the paternal house property at Al-Mahmud Avenue at Sirajganj Town and the petitioner concealed said amount of investment in his return by concealing the particulars of investment and thereby, evaded tax payable thereon.

iii. in the assessment years 2003-2004, 20004-2005, 2005-2006 and 2006-2007 the petitioner invested Taka 50,81,150 by payment of instalments for the purchase of Plot Nos. 309 and 311 in Block-L of the Bashundhara Housing Project of the East West Property Development (Pvt) Limited, which he did not disclose and thereby, concealed the equivalent amount of income by concealing the particulars and thereby, evaded tax payable thereon;

iv. in the assessment years 1999-2000, 2000- 2001 and 2001-2002 the petitioner invested in Total Taka 47,50,000 for purchase of the saving certificates but did not disclose such investments and thereby, concealed the equivalent amount of income by concealing particulars and thereby, evaded tax payable thereon;

v. in the assessment year 2003-2004, the petitioner invested Taka 40,00,000 in fixed deposits and earned interest of Taka 10,35,111.11 thereon but did not disclose said investment and thereby, concealed the equivalent amount of income by concealing particulars of the investment and thereby, evaded tax payable thereon;

Vi. in the assessment year 2004-2005, the petitioner as a member of the Parliament purchased a luxury BMW car at a cost of Taka 47,76,906.42 but did not disclose such investment and thereby, concealed equivalent amount of income and thereby, evaded tax payable thereon;

Vii. having not disclosed particulars of the total balance of Taka 1,29,39,087 in different accounts operated in his name in different banks in the assessment years 1999-2000, 2000-2001, 2001-2002, 2002- 2003, 2003-2004, 2004-2005, 2005-2006 and 2006-2007 the petitioner concealed the undisclosed balance of Taka 1,05,43,495 in those accounts in the respective assessment years and thereby, concealed equivalent amount of income and evaded tax payable thereon; and

viii. having not disclosed the expenditures and source of Taka 41,15,984.77 transacted through 'the credit cards of different banks, in the assessment years 2001- 2002, 2002-2003, 2003-2004, 2004-2005, 2005-2006 and 2006-2007 the petitioner thereby concealed equivalent amount of income of said undisclosed expenditures and evaded tax payable thereon.

3. Upon the above allegations, it was asserted that having not disclosed the investment/earned income/expenditure amounting to Taka 3,80,14,048.30 in non-agricultural property, saving certificates, term deposits, interest on the term deposits, motor car, bank balances and credit cards in the income tax returns and wealth statements (asset and liability) of the assessment years 1999- 2000 to 2006-2007 (eight years) the petitioner concealed the particulars of income and evaded tax payable thereon and thereby, committed an offence under section 166 of the Ordinance read with rule 15 of the EP Rules.

4. Upon the aforesaid transactions it is also alleged in the complaint that the petitioner committed an offence under section 165 of the Ordinance for:-

ii. the assessment year 2000-2001 the petitioner filed false statements in the verifications of the wealth statement by not disclosing the .expenditure in the extension and renovation of the aforesaid house property at Asad Avenue;

i. in the assessment year 2003-2004 the petitioner submitted false particulars in the verifications of the income tax return and wealth statement by not disclosing expenditure and investment in the house property at Sirajganj;

iii. in the assessment years 2003-2004, 2004- 2005, 2005-2006 and 2006-2007 the petitioner did not disclose the payment of installments for purchase of Plot Nos. 309 and 311 of Bashundhara Housing Project and submitted false statements in the verifications of the respective income tax returns and wealth statements;

iv. the petitioner invested huge amount in the purchase of saving certificates in the joint names of his wife and him, but did not disclose said investment and source of money in the assessment years 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and 2001-2002 and submitted false statements in the verifications of the income tax returns and wealth statements;

v. in spite of huge investment in the fixed deposits the petitioner did not disclose such investment and source of money III the assessment year 2003-2004; and the interest earned on such fixed deposits in the assessment year 2006-2007 by filing false verifications in the income tax returns and wealth statements;

vi having invested huge amount of money in the purchase' of luxury BMW car the petitioner did not disclose such investment and/or source of money in the assessment year .2004-2005 in the income tax return and wealth statement by filing false statements in the verifications;

vii. in the income tax returns and wealth statements for the assessment years 1999- 2000, 2000-2001, 2001-2002, 2002-2003, 2003-2004, 2004-2005, 2005-2006 and 2006-2007 the petitioner concealed the particulars of the huge balance in the bank accounts operated by him in various banks and submitted false statements in the verifications of the income tax returns and wealth statements thereof;

Viii. in the income tax returns and wealth statements for the assessment years 2001- 2002, 2002-2003, 2003-2004, 2004-2005, 2005-2006 and 2006-2007 the petitioner did not disclose the expenditure carried on through the credit cards of different banks and the source of the money by filing false statements in the verifications in the income tax returns and wealth statements.

5. At the outset in the complaint, the complainant stated that the petitioner was a Member of 8th Parliament and a State Minister in charge of Ministry of Emergency, Electricity and Minerals for about four years. He was a tax payer of the Large Tax Payers Unit (LTU) with TIN: 766-100-0859. The income lax return of the petitioner for the assessment year 2006-2007 filed under section 82B of the Ordinance was accepted and payment of tax stood settled.

6. The petitioner is the director of the Apex Weaving and Finishing Mills Limited (TIN: 002-200-7676). Accordingly assessment of income of the petitioner was carried on under the section of the Large Tax Payers Unit since 2003-2004.

7. Before the complaint was made, the complainant obtained sanction of the National Board of Revenue, in short, the Board, vide a letter dated 28-6-05.

8. The complainant examined him upon solemn affirmation in support of the complaint. He stated that being a Member of the Parliament and one of the State Ministers of the Cabinet, the petitioner concealed particulars of income, expenditure and wealth repeatedly and submitted false statements and thereby, evaded tax. On 8-7-07 learned Senior Special Judge at Dhaka took cognisance of the offences under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance read with rule 15 of the EP Rules against the petitioner who was already in custody in connection with Mohammadpur PS Case No. 95(3)07 and Metropolitan Special Case No. 32 of 2007. The petitioner was shown arrested in the instant case and custody warrant was accordingly issued for his appearance.

9. On 10-7-07 the case was transferred to the aforesaid 5th Court of Special Judge at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka for Speedy Trial. Same date, the case record was received by the said Special Judge, 5th Court and registered as Special Judge No. 06 of 2007. On 15-7-07 charge was framed against the petitioner under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance. On 19-7-07 the trial of the case commenced. On 29-8-07 the depositions of the prosecution witnesses was completed and the above Rule was issued and further proceedings of the case stayed.

10. It is further stated in the writ petition that on 4-2-07 the petitioner was arrested by the law and order enforcing agency and on 5-2-07 a detention order was issued against the petitioner. He was detained in the Chittagong Central Jail. On 18-2-07 when the petitioner was in custody, the Secretary of Anti-Corruption Commission issued a notice under section 26 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 asking him to submit his and his family's wealth statements within seventy-two hours. As the petitioner was in custody, he asked his son Abed Hasan Mahmud to submit the wealth statements of his and his family members on his behalf to the Anti-Corruption Commission. Accordingly, on 25-2-07 said Abed Hasan Mahmud submitted a wealth statement on behalf of the petitioner.

11. Meanwhile, on 21-3-07, the Anti-Corruption Commission lodged a FIR being Mohammadpur PS Case No. 95(3)07. After investigation, a charge sheet being charge sheet No. 479 dated 28-6- 07 was submitted against the petitioner, his son said Abed Hasan Mahmud, wife Rumana Mahmud and daughter Sarah Hasan Mahmud under sections 26 and 27 of said Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 read with section 15(Gha)(5) of the EP Rules and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.

12. In the said charge sheet, it was alleged that by misuse of power and through illegal means the petitioner purchased saving certificates of Taka 83,71,600, made fixed deposits of Taka 40,00,000, bank balance of Taka 4,70,969, purchased BMW Jeep at Taka 47,76,906, payment of installments of Taka 74,08,300 for purchase of two plots of the Bashundhara Housing Project, the valuation of the house at 117, Asad Avenue at Taka 58,76,168, purchase of flat at Dhanmondi In the name of his wife at a price of Taka 11,50,000, deposit of share money of Taka 1,00,00,000 in the name of his wife in One Entertainment Limited (Channel-L), fixed deposit of Taka 55,052,540 in the names of his son and daughter, purchase of shares of Taka 9,85,000 in the name of his daughter, bank deposit of Taka 10,29,433 in the name of his daughter, in total acquired property worth of Taka 4,96,11,916 and thereby, committed offence punishable under section 27 of said Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and his wife, son and daughter abetted him.

13. It was also alleged that during investigation, it appeared from the record of the income tax that the petitioner in his own name earned in cash Taka 1,00,00,000 and invested Taka 6,99,15,200 in the purchase of shares, Taka 5,38,00,000 in the purchase of shares in the name of his wife and Taka 15,15,000 in the purchase of shares in the name of his son in total whitened black. money in total Taka 28,52,15,200.

14. On 17-9-07 as the issues raised or likely to be raised in the Rule appeared to be of great public importance, we needed assistance of senior members of the Supreme Court Bar and accordingly, sent requests to the following learned Senior Counsels to appear and assist the Court: in the case as Amicus Curiae:

a. 	Mr Fida M Kamal, Attorney-General

b. 	Mr TH Khan

c. 	Mr Rafiq-ul-Huq

d. 	Mr Khandakar Mahbub Uddin Ahmed

e. 	Mr M Amirul Islam

f. 	Dr Kamal Hossain

g. 	Mr Dr M Zahir

h. 	Mr Mahmudul Islam

I. 	Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan

J. 	Mr AF Hasan Ariff.

Of them Dr M Zahir appeared and begged to be excused on the ground that he found himself embarrassed in expressing any opinion on the issues that may arise in the Rule.

Mr Khandakar Mahbub Uddin Ahmed and Mr M Amirul Islam communicated that they were not physically fit to appear and assist in the technical issues of income tax laws.

Dr Kamal Hossain, Mr T H Khan, Mr Rafiq-ul-Huq, Mr AF Hasan Aritf, Mr Mahmudul Islam and Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan made their learned submissions both orally and in writing.

15. Mr Fida M Kamal appeared both as the Attorney-General as well as Amicus Curiae. Mr Salah Uddin Ahmed, learned Additional Attorney-General appeared and submitted on behalf of the respondent No.2, Bangladesh, Mr Ajmalul Hossain, QC led the Counsels for the petitioner while Mr Khan Saifur Rahman being specially appointed represented respondent No.3, the Board.

16. Mr Ajmalul Hossain challenged the sanction of the Board for prosecution for said offences, cognisance of offences by the senior special judge, framing of charges and continuance of the trial of the case against the petitioner under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance on various grounds.

17. He submitted that the petitioner is a regular tax payer since 1981. By an order of the Board dated 29-10-03, the petitioner as director of the Apex Weaving and Finishing Mills Limited was included as tax payer under the Large Tax Payers Unit (LTU), Dhaka and has been paying tax as such, since 2003-2004.

18. He submitted that the petitioner paid tax as determined during the assessment years 1980-1981 up to 2006-2007 in addition to the taxes paid by his various companies. No objection and/or notice was ever taken or issued for re-assessment of any income during this long time. Assessment of the income of the petitioner for all those years was never challenged. After declaration of emergency, the petitioner was arrested on 4-7-07 by the law and order enforcing agency and aforesaid case was initiated against the petitioner without any notice for the assessment of any income that escaped assessment in any assessment year under section 93 of the Ordinance. In the trial of the case, the investigating officer disclosed that the petitioner was singled out on the basis of newspaper reports published against him.

19. He took us through the Ordinance and placed the scheme under the Ordinance and submitted that the sanction as accorded under section 171 of the Ordinance was no sanction in the eye of law for non application of mind, was malafide, discriminatory, arbitrary in not giving any opportunity of hearing for composition of any offence under section 170 of the Ordinance and lastly, coram non-judice.

20. Reading the latter dated 28-6-07 of Mr Ahmed Ali, member of the Board, addressed to the Commissioner of Tax, LTU, Dhaka communicating sanction of the Board for prosecution and asking the concerned Deputy Commissioner of Taxes for taking steps, the letter of same date of said Commissioner of Taxes to the complainant Deputy Commissioner of Taxes asking him to take steps for prosecution, Annexure-'A' and 'B' to the writ petition and the minutes of the urgent meeting of the Board held same date on 28-6-07 at 4-00 PM with the Chairman Mr Badiur Rahman in the chair and in presence of eight Members of the Board Annexure-1 to the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of respondent No. 3, he submitted that in the said meeting the subject for prosecution of the petitioner along with two others were considered and sanction was accorded under section 169 of the Ordinance for prosecution under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance, which clearly disclosed that the Board had no materials before it for according sanction for prosecution of the petitioner.

21. He submitted that in the supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the respondent No.3, the Board, a letter dated 28-6-07 of the said Commissioner of Taxes addressed to aforesaid member of the Board was annexed as Annexure-5. In the letter, it is stated that a proposal of 3 pages, draft complaint of 10 pages and other papers of 70 pages, which were closely typed by computer in total comprises 83 pages were sent for sanction. Had the Board time to apply its mind to those papers, it could not have even finished reading the voluminous papers before the end of office working time on 28-6-07, which clearly shows that the sanction was accorded without examining any record in respect of the petitioner.

22. He submitted that how the petitioner who is one of the few Large Tax Payers in the country and all through paid tax could be singled out just on the basis of newspaper reports. In view of the prosecution commenced against him under the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 1947 and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, such prosecution of the petitioner nearly On the selfsame grounds of concealment of income was intended to single the petitioner out just to harass him. Prosecution under charge of corruption as well as evasion of tax on the same and similar transactions in the same Court must be held to be mala fide; motivated and illegal.

23. In view of the provisions of sections 169 and 170 of the Ordinance, he submitted that before initiating the prosecution, the petitioner deserved and was entitled to an opportunity for composition of any offence in respect of any demand that may be brought by the Board for evasion of tax. When the Ordinance was promulgated for the purpose of raising tax and punishing any evasion of tax which is ultimately determined on assessment, reassessment or fresh assessment, the Board was not at all justified in according sanction for prosecution for evasion of tax without giving any opportunity to the petitioner for composition of any offence.

24. He then, seriously pressed that sanction as was accorded by the Board was coram non-judice, for the Board, which accorded such sanction, was not constituted as per provisions of the President's Order No.76 of 1992. Elaborating, he argued, the chairman who presided over the meeting and signed ,as such, the sanction was not a member of the Board and such sanction on this count only becomes bad and invalid for being coram non-judice. Consequently, cognisance of the offences against the petitioner taken by the Special Judge under section 171 of the Ordinance upon such sanction and commencement and continuance of the trial, all became without jurisdiction and liable to be quashed.

25. He submitted that the initiation of the prosecution. Without serving any notice under section 93 of the Ordinance for re-assessment of the income that escaped assessment or without opening previous assessment of the petitioner for any assessment year was bad and unauthorised. Chapter XXI of the Ordinance cannot be conceived of independent and separate from the rest of the Ordinance and resorted to punish an assessee. He strenuously argued that the phrase "all the provisions of this Ordinance shall, so far as may be, apply accordingly" in sub-section (1) of section 93 of the Ordinance required of the income tax authority to proceed under section 93 for prosecution of any offence under Chapter XXI of the Ordinance.

26. He submitted that before a prosecution for any offence under Chapter XXI to be initiated, the natural justice required a notice to be served upon the assessee to re-open any of the final assessments to assess the income that escaped assessment. It cannot be conceived of that the Ordinance has authorised the Board or any of the income tax authorities subordinate to it to straightaway prosecute an assessee without giving him any opportunity to hear and/or seeking explanation for any evasion of tax.

27. He read the EP Rules, 2007, particularly rule 15, and submitted that during the emergency, the officers of the Anti-Corruption Commission and the law and order enforcing agencies were only authorised to make complaint under the Ordinance. During the drive against corruption under the emergency, the officers and staffs of the Board could not be relied upon for understandable reasons and they were therefore, not authorised to initiate or investigate any such case. Filling of the complaint on 4-7-07 by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes under rule 15 of the EP Rules who is not a member of law and order enforcing agency or officer of the Anti-Corruption Commission, entire proceeding initiated upon his complaint was illegal and without jurisdiction.

28. He submitted that in view of the provisions of section 171 the Special Judge is obliged to follow the procedure laid down under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 to try the offences under Chapter XXI as, if such offences were offences specified in the Schedule thereto but learned Special Judge, 5th Court was most illegally following the procedure laid down by the EP Rules, which made the trial vitiated.

29. He submitted that this Division has got ample jurisdiction no look into if any proceeding trial that is continuing before any Court subordinate to this Division is authorised by law and not vitiated for want of jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. If the proceeding trial is found to be without jurisdiction, this Division is fully empowered to declare such proceeding without jurisdiction and a nullity.

30. In support of his submissions, he cited [Hagi Ali Mohammad vs CIT: [1940] 08ITR 243; Rajmani Devi vs CIT: [J937] 5 ITR 631; Mohammad Hayat vs CIT: [1937] 5 ITR 159; Dhuni Chand Dhani Ram vs CIT: AIR 1926 Lahore 161; Nirmal Kumar Singh vs Secretary of State: 2 ITC 20; Kesaridas and Sons vs CIT: 2 ITC 213; Ram Pratap Sukh Dial vs CIT: 3 ITC 362; Harmukhrai Dulchand vs CIT: 3 ITC 198; Messrs Burn &Co. [J934] 2 ITR 30; Jawala Prasad Chobey vs CIT: [1935] 3 LTR 295; Maharaja Patiala vs CIT: [1943] 11 ITR 202; V Srinivas Naichen vs Agricultural Income-tax Officer: [1963] 47 ITR 122; P V Pai vs R L Rinawma, DCI: [1993] 200 ITR rt n ITO vs S K H abibullah: [1962] 44 ITR 809 SC; CIT vs Khemchand and Ramdas: [l938] 6 ITR 414 PC; American Express Bank vs Chairman, NBR: 54 DLR 06; P Jayappan vs S K Perumal: [1984] 149 ITR 697 SC; CIT vs Chowdhury Ramzan Ali and another: 34 DLR 278 AD; Dr. MO Ghani vs A N M Mahmood: 18 DLR 463 SC; Nagina Silk Mill vs ITO: 15 DLR 18 SC; Anisminic Ltd. vs Foreign Compensation Commission: [1969] 2 AC 147 HL at 195; MD Rupali Bank Ltd Tafazal Hossain: 44 DLR (AD) 260; Nazrul Islam Chowdhury vs State: 1999 BLD 18 AD; Nesar Ahmed vs Government of Bangladesh: 49 DLR (AD) 111 Suraj Mall Mobta and Co. vs AV Visvanatha Sastri and another: [1954] 26 1TR 01 SC] and Dhakeswari Cotton Mills Ltd vs CIT: [1954] 26 ITR 775 SC, which shall be considered at the time of consideration of the relevant issue.

31. Mr Salahuddin Ahmed, learned Additional Attorney-General, on behalf of the respondent No .2, submitted that re-opening of any previous assessment is not the only method for the Deputy Commissioner to prosecute any assessee for concealment of income and/or false statement in the verifications of the income tax returns under the Ordinance. Said Annexure-1 to the affidavit-in-opposition, the minutes of the meeting of the Board,even if do not show the reasons for sanction but the Board had all information regarding the assessments of the petitioner and accordingly, accorded the sanction. The discretion lies with the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes to choose the way he should follow and even after initiating the prosecution, the Deputy Commissioner may assess the income that escaped assessment and determine the tax payable thereon. Protection under due process principles however, cannot be denied to the petitioner even independent of the Constitution.

32. Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, learned Advocate on behalf of the respondent No. 3 also read the relevant provisions of the Ordinance and submitted that before the trial is concluded, this Division has got no jurisdiction under so-called jurisdiction of certiorari to intervene in the trial, which was about to be completed. As the trial was continuing on the basis of sanction of the Board, jurisdiction of the Special Judge to try such case could not be denied. The petitioner has got no right to prevent the commencement or continuation of any proceeding/trial under the Ordinance,

33. He submitted on the scope and extents of section 93 of the Ordinance from different angles of view. He submitted that prosecution of offences under Chapter XXI at the instance of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is independent of his discretion available under section 93 of Chapter IX of the Ordinance. It is for the Special Judge to decide whether the petitioner concealed any income and/or submitted false statements in the verifications in the return of various assessment years.

34. He forcefully submitted that there is no provision in the Ordinance requiring a proceeding to take for assessment before launching criminal prosecution and there is no bar put in by the Ordinance for simultaneous proceeding for assessment and prosecution of the offences under the Ordinance and therefore, there is no substance in the submission of the learned Counsel for the petitioner that without exhausting all the provisions relating to assessment including that of section 93 of the Ordinance no prosecution for the offences of concealment of income and making false statements could be available.

35. He submitted that the case of the petitioner is so grave that in the reasonable expectation of the income tax authority it could be taken to the Special Judge for trial for an exemplary fine against the petitioner in addition to punishment so that loss of revenue payable on both out of time and within time could be compensated in lieu of recovery.

36. He submitted that in case of concealment of income and submission of false statements in the verifications of the income tax return for the assessment beyond five years no notice under section 93 of the Ordinance could be served. But the prosecution for such concealment of income and submission of false statements in the returns for the assessment years beyond 5 years could be launched as there is no time limit for criminal proceeding.

37. He submitted that upon receipt of the information of concealment of income and submission of false statement in the verification in the returns for further assessment years in question the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes verified the tax record of the petitioner and prepared a draft complaint and presented it before the Board for consideration and sanction under section 169 of the Ordinance. After examination of the papers and the draft complaint, the Board found massive evasion of tax and in order to prevent such evasion it approved the draft complaint and issued sanction letter. At any point of time in the trial before the Special Judge the petitioner has got all opportunity to challenge the sanction and seek a decision of the Special Judge thereon. The petitioner did not challenge the jurisdiction of the Special Judge to entertain the complaint in taking cognisance of offences.

38. On composition of offence under section 170 of the Ordinance, he submitted that there is option and end of prosecution and use of such option depends on a citizen for expectation for the purpose, which is necessary for consideration. After the condition for prosecution under sub-section (2) was omitted there is no other condition precedent left for according sanction for prosecution under section 169 of the Ordinance.

39. He submitted that rule 15 of the EP Rules is enabling one for combating corruption but has not thrown for taking proper action. Here in the case, the petitioner was taken into custody by law and order enforcing agency and produced him time to time before the Court in the course of ongoing trial and to that extent of the above, rule 15 shall be applicable and relevant in the case.

He submitted that the case initiated under the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 read with section 5(2) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 is based on an offence for criminal misconduct against the petitioner. The said corruption case and the instant case do not constitute same offence, and section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 therefore, does not prohibit prosecution and punishment under two different Acts. Under section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 different prosecutions are permissible but award of punishment cannot be twice for the same offence. Section 26 therefore, does not have any manner of application in the instant case. In support of his submissions, he referred to P Jaydppan vs S K Perumal: [l984] 149 ITR 696 SC; P Jayappan vs S K Perumal: [1984] 149 ITR 692 (Madras); Telu Raungi Ram vs ITO: [1984] 145 ITR 11 and Vijay Kumar vs ITO: [1984] 150 ITR 126.

40. Numerous issues arose out of the conflicting submissions of the learned Counsels for decision. Of them the moot issue is, whether or not the trial of the petitioner under sections 165 and 166 is based on a valid complaint made under section 171 and on the basis of a valid sanction accorded under section 169 of the Ordinance and continuance of the trial of the petitioner in the Court of said Special Judge is permitted by law. Before we could answer the moot issue we need to answer the following issues:

(a) Whether in the facts and circumstances of the case the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes was authorised to straightaway make a complaint under section 171 of the Ordinance for prosecution of the petitioner under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance without taking a proceeding for assessment of income that escaped assessment for the relevant assessment years?

(b) Whether the sanction dated 28-6-07 accorded by the Board was valid and a sanction within the meaning of section 169 of the Ordinance for prosecution of the petitioner for said offences?

(c) Whether cognisance of the offences under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance read with section 15 of the EP Rules, 2007 by the Senior Special Judge at Dhaka just on the basis of said sanction was itself vitiated and vitiated the entire proceedings and trial of the petitioner before the 5th Court of the Special Judge? and

(d) Whether in the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of sections 169 and 170 of the Ordinance the petitioner deserved and/or was entitled to a hearing for composition of the offence(s) brought before granting sanction by the Board for prosecution? And

(e) Whether this Division is empowered to issue an appropriate declaration and/or direction under sub-article (2) of Article 102 of the Constitution in respect of the trial of offences under the Ordinance during the currency of emergency?

41. Before the issues are taken up for consideration, the scheme under the Ordinance must first be understood. In pursuance of the proclamation of 24th March 1982 and in exercise of all powers enabling him in this behalf, the President is pleased to make and promulgate the Ordinance, which came into source on the 1st July, 1984, to consolidate and amend the law relating to income tax. The law that was existing was the Income-tax Act, 1922 was repealed and replaced. The Income-tax Act, 1922 held the field of levy, collection and administration of the income tax up to 1961 in India when the Income-tax Act 1961 came into force there, up to 1979 in Pakistan, when the Income-tax Ordinance, 1979 was promulgated and up to 1984 in Bangladesh, when was replaced by said Ordinance.

42. The Ordinance comprises 187 sections, which are grouped under twenty-three chapters.

Chapter, I comprising sections 1 and 2 deals with title, commencement and definition of different terms. Chapter II comprising sections 3 to 10 relates to administration, which creates different income tax authorities with the Board at the top and the inspector of taxes at the bottom of the hierarchy. For formation of the Board, President's Order No. 76 of 1972 was promulgated. The Board is empowered to appoint Director General, Inspecting Commissioner (appeals), Commissioner, Joint Commissioner of Taxes, etc all other authorities under section 5 made subordinate to the Board. Sections 6 to 9 define respective jurisdiction of the income tax authority.

Chapter III comprising sections 11 to 15 deals with establishment of the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, exercise of power by such tribunal and regulating the procedures to be followed by such tribunal. Chapter IV comprising sections 16 to 19 BBB provides for charging income tax for any assessment at any rate or rates subject to the provision of the Ordinance. Chapter V comprising sections 20 to 43 has classified-income for the purpose of charging income tax and computation of total income under seven heads on the basis of different allowance and deduction. Chapter VI comprises sections 42 to 47 provides for exemption and allowances from tax. Chapter VII comprising sections 48 to 74 provides for payment of tax before assessment including deduction of tax under various circumstances. Chapter VIII comprising sections 75 to 80 relates to the return of income and statements of assets, liabilities and life style etc. Chapter IX comprising sections 81 to 94A provides for various kinds of assessment, which would be relevant for our purpose. Chapter X comprising sections 95 to 103A deals with the liability in special cases. Chapter XI comprising sections 104 to 107 providing special provision relating to avoidance of tax. Chapter XII comprising sections 108 to 110 required furnishing certain information. Chapter XIII regarding registration of form was omitted by the Finance Act, 1995. Chapter XIV comprising sections 112 to -122 describes the powers of the income tax authorities including the power to call for information, inspection, survey, search and seizure, retention of seized asset and application of retained assets, etc. Section 120 empowers the Inspecting Joint Commissioner to revise orders of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes. Chapter XV comprising sections 123 to 133 deals with imposition of penalty for omission and/or failure in maintaining accounts, in failing to file return, not paying advance tax, etc. Section 128 empowers the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes to impose penalty for concealment of income, furnishing inaccurate particulars of income or understated value of immovable property in connection with a view to evading tax, etc. Chapter XVI comprising sections 134 to 143 provides for recovery of tax determined in the assessment. Under the chapter, various modes are prescribed for recovery of tax determined. Section 134 provide that for the purpose of this chapter tax shall include any sum imposed, levied or otherwise payable under the Ordinance as penalty, fine, interest, fee or otherwise. Chapter.

XVII comprising sections 144 to 145 provides for double taxation relief and Chapter XVIII comprising sections 146 to 152 provides for refunds of the tax paid in excess. Chapter XVIIIA comprising section 152A to 152E relating to settlement of cases was omitted by the Finance Act, 2002. Chapter XIX provides for appeal before the Appellate Joint Commissioner or Commissioner (Appeals) and the Taxes Appellate Tribunal. Chapter XX comprising section 163 relating to protection of information declaring all particulars or information contained in any statement made, return furnished or accounts or documents produced under the Ordinance; any evidence given or affidavit or deposition made in the course of any proceeding; any record or assessment proceeding or any proceeding for recovery of demand confidential.

Chapter XXI comprising sections 164 to 171, which is very relevant for our purpose creating certain obligations, false statement in the verification of the income tax returns, concealment of income, etc as punishable offences. Section 169 provides for sanction for prosecution. Section 170 empowers the Commissioner to compound any offence punishable under the Ordinance either before or after the institution of the proceeding or prosecution for an offence. Section 171 empowers a Special Judge appointed under the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1958 to punish any offence under this chapter as if such offence were specified in the schedule to that Act. Chapter XXII comprises sections 172 to 184D providing for miscellaneous matters for correction of errors, computation of limitation, service of notice, bar of suits and prosecution, etc. Section 184 regarding restriction on registration of documents was omitted by Finance Act, 1992. Chapter XXIII comprising sections 185 to 187 empowers, inter alia, the Board to make rules and provides for repeal and savings. Section 187 empowers the government by notification in the official gazette to make such provisions as it think fit for removing any difficulty that may arise in giving effect to any of the provisions of the Ordinance. However, no notification shall be issued under this section after the thirtieth day of June, 1988.

43. The jurisprudence of income tax developed under the Income-tax Act, 1922 and its precursors, namely, the Income Tax Act (II) 1886, Income Tax Act 1898 and Super Tax Act 1970 is a common heritage for the people of the Subcontinent. Such jurisprudence mainly developed on the common law jurisprudence in the peculiar reality of this part of the world. Concepts of income, income tax, assessment, appeal, revision, offences, etc and the proceedings for assessment of income, recovery of tax and imposition of penalty and prosecution for offences for evasion of tax are though of universal application but carry special purport under the Ordinance.

44. Reading the entire Ordinance, it appears that the Ordinance was promulgated for replacing Income-tax Act, 1922 to update and consolidate the income tax law to raise revenue in the name of income tax for the Government. The income tax is a tax imposed on income. Income tax is popularly known as direct tax and forms major part of all other direct taxes and also substantial part of the revenue in the developed economies. If the entire provisions of the Ordinance are closely read, only objective to be achieved is assessment of the <u>Income chargeable to tax</u> and determination of the tax payable thereon. Penal provisions that are provided are intended to enforce payment of tax and discourage evasion thereof with the pain of going to the jail, which would be considered little later.

45. The proceedings for assessment of income are numerous depending upon the returns of income. Recovery of the tax determined upon such assessment is also varied. Proceeding for imposition of penalty and prosecution for the offences created under the Ordinance for certain failings in carrying out the obligations are also provided. The Ordinance is therefore, exhaustive in the sense that it is a complete code for the purpose of charging and collection of income tax and prevention of evasion of tax payable under the Ordinance, [The Commissioner of Income Tax vs Chowdhury Ramzan Ali and another: 34 DLR (AD) 278. It has defined the rights, obligations and remedy. Any expression or phrase used must be understood and construed in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance. In order to achieve the objective of the Ordinance all the Chapters are neatly woven into a whole.

46. Now let us examine the procedure the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes followed for seeking sanction of the Board and making the complaint for prosecution of the petitioner.

47. In the complaint it is stated that the assessment of income of the petitioner was completed and the tax determined thereon up to the assessment year 2006-2007 was finally settled. In the letter dated 30-9-07 sending the record comprising 148 pages and two page note sheets to this Division, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes stated that a separate file was opened in respect of evasion of tax by the petitioner. He then sought for approval of the Commissioner of Taxes for requisitioning the information under section 113(f) of the Ordinance on the above bank statements.

On 10-6-07 he also sent letters to the Cards Divisions of the Standard Chartered Bank, National Bank Ltd and Prime Bank requiring information.

52. What appears from the above facts is that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes opened a separate file for prosecution of the petitioner under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance for evasion of tax under command from the above. But he did not take any step for assessment of the income that according to him, escaped assessment in any assessment year in the past. He found in lump that the petitioner submitted false declarations in the income tax returns and concealed particulars of income in eight assessment years 1999-2000 to 2006-2207. He did not even try to ascertain the amount of income concealed in which income tax return for which assessment year and how the declarations in the verifications in the returns and wealth statements do relate to which assessment year. Omission appears to be deliberate since for such investigation upon receipt of any information of concealment of any income that escaped assessment in the past he was required to follow a particular procedure prescribed by the Ordinance. For the moment, it can safely be said that the procedure adopted by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes was actuated with the sole objective to prosecute the petitioner under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance, which was not authorised by the Ordinance.

53. If any information of concealment of income that was not disclosed in the assessment year in question reaches the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes during the course of the proceedings for assessment, under sub-section (2) of section 83 of the Ordinance he is required to ask the assessee for explanation or to produce evidence upon such concealment and then, upon consideration of the evidence or the explanation, if any, submitted by an order in writing assess the total income of the assessee and determine tax payable thereon and also communicate the order to the assessee within thirty days next following.

54. The issues raised also demand consideration of certain technical terms and concepts with reference to the relevant provisions of the Ordinance.

55. Under section 2(8) of the Ordinance the word 'Assessment' with its grammatical variations and cognate expressions includes reassessment and additional or further assessment. And under section 2(9) 'Assessment Year' means the period of twelve months commencing the first day of July in every year and includes any such period which is deemed under the provisions of the Ordinance to be assessment year in respect of any income for any period. Under section 2(35) 'Income Year', in respect of any separate source of income, means, inter alia, the financial year immediately preceding the assessment year and/or where the accounts of the assessee have been made upto date within said financial year and the assessee so opts, the twelve months ending on such date, etc. Financial Year has not been defined in the Ordinance. Section 3(19) of the General Clause Act, 1897 defines, 'Financial Year' as the year commencing on the first day of July and ending on the 30th June next.

56. From the above definitions of the 'Income Year' and 'Financial Year' what is to be remembered is that both financial year and income year mean the period of twelve months commencing the first day of July in every year preceding the assessment year. Let it be clarified by an illustration, if the assessment year 2007-2008 commenced first day of July 2007, the income year for such assessment year would be the financial year 2006-2007 that commenced on the first day of July, 2006.

57. Section 2(34) gives an inclusive definition of the word 'Income' as any income, profits or gains from whatever source received chargeable to tax under any provisions of the Ordinance under any head specified under section 20; and/or any loss of such income, profits or gains, etc.

58. The words 'assessment' and 'assess' are used in different places in the Ordinance with different meanings for different purposes. Under sub-section (2) of section 83 of the Ordinance, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is empowered to assess the total income after hearing and determine the tax payable upon such assessment within thirty days of such hearing or consideration of the evidence or materials produced in support of the return and communicate the order to the assessee within thirty days next following.

59. The proceedings for assessment of the total income of an assessee shall end in an order, which is simply known as assessment. This process is no doubt a quasi-judicial process. Such assessment is made appealable or revisable.

60. The concept of assessment developed in the sub-continent under the old law, the Income-tax Act, 1922. Assessment has to be construed in wider sense and means not only the computation of the income but also the entire process of computing income and the tax payable thereon, CIT vs Balkrishna Malhoka: [1971] 81 ITR 759. It also does not include the proceedings for recovery of tax or other proceedings under the Ordinance.

61. Distinction between regular assessment and reassessment or further assessment however subtle, but is of significance. Generally, regular assessment means the first or original assessment made by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes for a particular assessment year. Assessment of income that escaped assessment in any assessment year is generally understood as reassessment or further or additional assessment of such income. The assessment however, covers the proceedings for rectification, reassessment or revision. An assessment shall be final when it is finally disposed of in revision, appeal, or reference, if any, see Dhaka Vegetable Oil Industries Limited vs CIT 49 DLR (AD) 136 = 25 BTD (AD) 118. Such views find reflection by the Supreme Court of India in said Balakrishna Malhotra s case, as under:

"The income tax officer is duty bound to assess the total income of the assessee and to determine the sum payable by him on the basis of return under section 23 of the Act (the Income-tax Act, 1922) and the whole process of assessment may end with his order or may be revised by the higher appellate authority including the appellate Commissioner and Tribunal recognised by the Act".

62. Assessment is generally made on the return of income submitted by an assessee. Section 75 requires every person to file or cause to be filed with the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes a return of his income or the income of any other persons in respect of which he is assessable to tax under the Ordinance if his total income during the income year exceeds the maximum amount which is not chargeable to tax under the Ordinance or if he was assessed to tax for anyone of the three years immediately preceding that income year, etc. Such return shall be furnished in the prescribed form setting forth therein such particulars and information as may be required thereby including the total income of the assessee in case of a company by l5th day of July next following the income year and in all other cases by 30th day of September next following of the income year. Such return shall accompany in the case of an individual a statement in the prescribed form and verified in the prescribed manner giving particulars of his life style, etc and in the case of a company a statement of accounts audited by a chartered accountant. While section 77 empowers the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes to issue a notice in writing at any time after the expiry of the date specified in section 75 requiring any person or a company to file a return of the total income as provided ill that section, if, in the opinion of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes the total income of such person was, during the income year of such amount as to render liable to tax; .any company to file of its total income if it is not filed, Return shall be filed within such period not being less than twenty-one days as maybe specified in the notice or within such extended period if the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes may allow.

63. As already stated hereinabove. Chapter-IX deals with various kinds of assessment. Section 81 provides for provisional 'assessment, section 82 for assessment on current return section 82A for assessment under; simplified procedure,' 82B' for assessment on the- basis of 'return, section 82BB, newly inserted, for universal self-assessment, section 82D for spot assessment, section 83 for assessment after hearing that is regular assessment, section 83A to 83AAA for various self-assessments and section 84 for best judgment assessment, that is ex-parte assessment in the absence of title assessee by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes etc.

64. For the case at hand, the assessment under section 83 of the Ordinance would be relevant, which reads as follows:

83, Assessment after hearing-

(1) Where a return or revised return has been filed under Chapter VIII and the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is riot satisfied without requiring the presence of the person who filed the return or production of evidence that the return is correct and complete, he shall serve on such person. a notice requiring him, on a date to be therein specified, to appear before the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, to produce or cause to be produced before him or at his office, any evidence in support of the return.

(2) The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, after hearing the person appearing or considering the evidence produced in pursuance of the notice under sub-section (1) and also considering such other evidence, if any, as he many require on specified points, by an order in writing assess, within thirty days after the completion of the hearing or consideration vas the case may be, the total income of the assessee and determine, the sum payable by him on the basis of such assessment, and communicate the order to the assessee within thirty, days next following.

65. When the Deputy Commissioner of taxes is not satisfied with a return or revised return that is filed he is empowered to require presence of the person who filed the return or production of the evidence in support of the return as correct and complete. He shall serve on such person a notice requiring him to appear before him either in person or through an authorised representative on a date to be specified in such notice or to produce before him any evidence in Support of the return.

66. After hearing the person and/or consideration of the evidence produced in pursuance of the notice under sub-section (1) the Deputy Commissioner  of Taxes shall in writing assess the total income of the assessee within thirty days of the completion of hearing or consideration of the evidence produced and determine the tax payable on such assessment and communicate the order on the assessee within thirty days next following.

67. At the hearing after said notice if he requires any, other evidence he shall call for such evidence on the points specified, which is now being done by serving a notice under sub-section (2).

68. In such assessment, the total income received by the assessee under various heads of income in the particular income year is to be assessed: The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is however not authorised to assess the income of an assessee for more than one income year. So, the assessment of the total income is always meant for one assessment year only. He is further required to complete assessment of the total income and determine the tax to be payable thereon within thirty days of hearing or consideration of the evidence produced and communicate the order of assessment to the assessee within next thirty days. Under section 94 of the Ordinance, no assessment could be made after the expiry of six months from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable only subject to the period under, sub sections (a) and (b) of section 93(3) of the Ordinanee. In spite of such limitation, such assessment is always subject to correction, modification or revision in pursuance of the direction(s) that may be issued in revision under sections 120 and 121, appeal, under sections 156 and 159 and reference under section 161 to the High Court Division and appeal under section 162 to the Appellate Division.

69. Any such assessment if not revised under sections 120 and 121, modified, varied or set aside in appeal under sections 156 and 159 shall become final. Once the assessment becomes final that is conclusive in respect of all the particulars covered by such assessment including the total income and the tax payable thereon and the statements made in the verifications in the returns and binding upon all the parties for that particular assessment year. Under section 182 of the Ordinance, no suit shall lie in, any civil Court to, set aside or modify any assessment made under the Ordinance that is a final assessment shall remain final until and unless set aside or modified in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance. The principle that an assessment could be questioned only by the machinery expressly provided by the Act (the Income-tax Act, 1922) was laid down by the Privy Council in Raleigh Investment Co Ltd: 1947 ITR 332, And in Kelwa Devadattam vs Union of India: [1963] 49 ITR 165 (SC). the Supreme Court of India held-

"Liability to pay income tax arises on the accrual of the income, and not from the computation made by the taxing authority in the course of assessment proceeding; it arises at a point of time not later than close of the year of account."

70. In Dhaka Vegetable Oil Industries Ltd vs CLT: 49 DLR (AD) 136 = 25 BTD (AD) 118 our Appellate Division held

"The Income-tax Officer's duty to assess the total income of the assessee and to determine the sum payable by him on the basis of the return under section 23 of the Act is the whole process of assessment which may end with his order or may be revised by the higher appellate authorities including the Appellate Commissioner and the Tribunal recognised by the Income-tax Act Finality of assessment does not attain unless the case is finally disposed of by the appellate authority.

71. During the course of assessment, if any information reaches the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes that arty particulars of income were concealed or inaccurate particulars were furnished, he is empowered to require by notice of the assessee to file a return of his total income in the relevant income year as in section 77 or in respect of the income that appeared to him to have been concealed and after hearing and/or examination of the explanation; if any, produced he shall assess the total income of the assessee or determine the tax payable by him. If he is satisfied that the assessee deliberately concealed the income or furnished inaccurate particulars by false verification in the return he may also proceed, under section 128 for imposition of penalty and/or prosecute the assessee for the offences under Chapter XXI of the Ordinance with sanction of the Board.

<u>72. When any such information of income that escaped the assessment in any assessment year reaches the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, only course open to him is to proceed under section 93 of the Ordinance which reads as hereunder:</u>

<u>(2) No proceeding under sub-section (1) shall be initiated unless definite information has come into the possession of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes and he has obtained the previous approval of the Inspecting Joint Commissioner in writing to do so, except in a case where a return has not been filed under section 75 or 77.</u>
