73. Here, it may be mentioned that after five years, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes has got no power to open any assessment under the section. After five years the assessment of income for any assessment year shall become, closed for all purposes and the assessee acquired a vested right in such assessment, In Nagina Silk Mill vs Income-tax Officer: 15 DLR (SC) 181, the Supreme' Court of Pakistan held that "It is a well recognised principle of the law Of limitation that mice time begins to run from, a : specified date it cannot be interrupted or . extended unless the legislature intervenes and makes express provisions to the contrary.

Even if two interpretations are equally possible. the one that saves vested rights would be adopted in the interest of justice, specially where the court is dealing with a taxing statute.

74. In K M Sharma vs the Income-tax Officer: [2002] 254 ITR 772 at 777 the Supreme Court of India was of similar view that,

"A fiscal statute; more particularly a provision such as the present one regulating period of limitation, must receive, strict construction. The law of limitation is intended to give certainty and finality to legal proceedings and to avoid exposure to risk of litigation to litigants for an indefinite period on unforeseen events, Proceedings; which have attained finality under taxing law due to bar of limitation cannot be held to be open for revival unless the amended provision is clearly given retrospective operation so as to allow upsetting ,of proceedings, which had already been concluded and attained finality

<u>75. In such proceedings taken by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes all the provisions of the Ordinance shall, so far as the case may be, apply accordingly. Under the proviso to sub-section (1), the tax shall be charged at the rate or rates applicable for the assessment year for which the assessment is, made. The income that has escaped the assessment shall have to be assessed with reference to the relevant assessment year. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is, however, not empowered or authorised to assess the income of more than one income year that escaped assessment in more than one assessment year.</u>

76. Section 93 therefore provides for a detailed procedure for assessment of the <u>Income chargeable to tax</u> for any assessment year that has, escaped assessment. Such assessment may be reassessment or additional assessment of, the income that escaped assessment of, a particular assessment year. Such procedure is no doubt quasi-judicial. Whenever the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes gets any information of concealment of income or inaccurate particulars of income furnished or omitted or nondisclosure of any material fact for assessment, he is obliged under the Ordinance to proceed to assess the income of the assessee that escaped assessment in any assessment year. This Obligation or command under the Ordinance cannot be avolded or circumvented by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes to take other, proceedings; Moreover, whatever proceedings that are available under the Ordinance would follow only in course of such proceeding under the section on concealment of any income or furnishing inaccurate particular or omission of such income' that escaped assessment in any particular assessment year.

77. Now; letus consider the offences that are created, arid the procedure prescribed for prosecution of the offence sunder Chapter XXI of the Ordinance. It is better to quote the entire chapter, which is as under,

Chapter XXI Offences and Prosecution

164. Punishment for non-compliance of certain obligations-

A person is guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend toone year, or with fine, or with both, if he, without reasonable cause;

(a) fails to deduct [or collect] and pay any tax as required under the provisions of Chapter VII except advance payment, of tax or fails to deduct and pay tax as required under section 143(2);

(b) fails to produce, or cause to be produced, on or before the date mentioned in any notice under Chapter VIII, or under section 83, such accounts, documents or statements as are referred to in such notice;

(c) fails to furnish, In due time, the return of income which' he .is required to furnish under section 75, or by notice given under section 77 or 93;

(d) refuses to permit inspection or, to allow copies to be taken in accordance with the provisions of section;

(e) fails to afford necessary facilities or to furnish the required information to an income tax authority exercising powers under section 115; or

(f) refuses to permit or, in any manner obstructs the exercise of powers, under ,section 117 by an income tax authority.

165. Punishment for false statement in verification, etc.

A person is guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may , extend to three years but shall not be less than three months, or with fine, or with both if he

(a) makes go statement in any verification, etc. in any return or any other document furnished under any provisions of this Ordinance which is false;

(b) knowingly willfully aids, abets, assists or induces another person to make, or deliver a false, return, account, statement certificate or declaration under this, Ordinance or himself knowingly  and willfully delivers such false return, account, statement, certificate or declaration on behalf of another person;

(c) signs, and issues any certificate mentioned in the first or second proviso to section 82 which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true;

(d) refuses to furnish such information as may be necessary for the purpose of survey under section115.

166. Punishment for concealment of income etc.

A person is guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment which may extend to five years but shall not be less than three months, or with fine, or with both, if he conceals particulars, or deliberately furnishes inaccurate particulars, of his income.-

167. Punishment for disposal of property to prevent attachment-

The owner of any property, or a person acting on his behalf or claiming under him, is guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both, if he sells, mortgages, charges, leases or otherwise so deals with the property after the receipt of a notice from the Tax Recovery Officer as to prevent its attachment by that Officer.

168. Punishment for disclosure of protected information-

A public servant, or any person assisting, or engaged, by any person acting in the execution of this Ordinance, is guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, if he discloses any particulars or information in contravention of the provisions of section 163.

169. Sanction for prosecution.-

No prosecution for an offence punishable under any provisions of this Chapter shall be instituted except with the previous sanction of the Board.

[Sanction under sub-section (1) shall not be given in respect of an offence other than an offence under section 128, which consists of the same facts on which a penalty has been imposed under Chapter XV]

170. Power to compound offences;

The Commissioner may, either before or after the institution of any proceedings or prosecution for an offence punishable under this Chapter, compound such offence.

171. Trial by Special Judge-

(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), or in any other law for the time being in force, an offence punishable under 'this Chapter, other than an offence under section 168, shall be tried by a Special Judge appointed under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 (XL of 1958), as if such offence were an offence specified in the Schedule to that Act.

(2) A Special Judge shall take cognisance of, and have jurisdiction to try, an offence triable by him tinder sub-section (1) only upon a complaint in writing made, after obtaining the sanction under section 169, by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes-

(a) who is competent to make assessment under this Ordinance in the case to which the offence alleged to have been committed relates, and

(b) whose office is situated within the territorial limits of the jurisdiction of the Special Judge.

78. Section 164 makes non-compliance of certain obligations as are enumerated therein punishable offence. Section 165 makes making of any false statement in the verification of the return or any other document produced and section 166 makes concealment of particulars or deliberate furnishing inaccurate particulars of income punishable offences.

79. Section 165 deals with false statement in any verification in any return. While section 166 deals with concealment of particulars or deliberate furnishing inaccurate particulars of income. In both sections the words, "a person are used instead of an assessee not without any reason. Reason is not far away to find that in furnishing false statement in the verification in the return or document produced and concealment of particulars of income there may be involvement of any person other than the assessee himself and such person may be held responsible for abetment, aiding, assistance, incitement, endorsement execution of such return submitted or document produced.

80. In the above provisions, the words statement 'verification', 'return' and 'income' carry special meanings as is assigned to each of them by the Ordinance. All those terms/concepts relate only to the assessment of the total income of an assessee in question for a particular assessment year and determination of the tax payable thereon. The Ordinance has also created different taxing authorities to finally estimate the chargeable income and determine the tax payable thereon on clear understanding of those concepts with the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes at the bottom of hierarchy. No other authority could be conceived of the Ordinance, to deal with those terms/concepts. The special judge under section 171 of the Ordinance is empowered to try such offence(s) only on the basis of the complaint made by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes. More clearly statedin the absence of a complaint made by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes the special judge would have no jurisdiction to try any of the offences.

81. On behalf of the Board, Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, learned Senior Advocate, tried to make distinction between concealment of income, concealment of particulars or deliberate furnishing inaccurate particular of income.

82. Word concealment is defined in shorter Oxford English Dictionary, 3rd Edition, Volume I as follows:

"In Law, intentional suppression of truth or fact known to the injury or prejudice of another."

The word 'concealment' inherently carries with it the element of mens rea Mere fact that some figures or some particulars have been disclosed by itself, even if takes out the case from the purview of non-disclosure, cannot by itself take out the case from the purview of furnishing inaccurate particulars. Mere omission from the return of any item of receipt does neither amount to concealment nor deliberate furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income unless or until there is some evidence to show or some circumstances are found from which it can be gathered that the omission was attributable to an intention or desire on the part of assessee to hide or conceal the income so as to avoid the imposition of tax thereon; Cf. K C Builders vs Assistant CLT: (2004)2 SCC 731.

83. There could not be any occasion for concealing particulars or deliberate furnishing inaccurate particulars of income had there been no intention to conceal the income. Similarly, there could not be any occasion for making false statement in any verification in any return had there been no intention to avoid tax. The anxiety of the Board with regard to the distinction between concealment of income and furnishing false statement in the verification in the return or concealment of particulars or deliberate furnishing inaccurate particulars of income is therefore, of no significance.

84.Mr Khan Saifur submitted that in cases where opening of the assessment has become barred under sub-section (3) of section 93, there cannot be prohibition for prosecution for the offences under Chapter XXI of the Ordinance for concealment of income Or false statements in the verification in the return as there cannot be any limitation for criminal prosecution.

85. The offences created under Chapter XXI are fundamentally different in nature and scope from any other offences, say, created under the Penal Code or other special offences created by special laws. Under the criminal administration of justice, the prosecution can be set into motion, by the victim of such offence or any other person including a police officer who got the first information of the commission of an offence. But under the Ordinance, it is the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes who is only empowered to lodge a complaint for prosecution of such offence. No other authority below or above him is empowered to initiate the prosecution of such offence. This special requirement under the Ordinance makes all the difference. Because, it is the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes who is only entrusted with the assessment of income of an assessee and such offence could only be committed in respect of such assessment, not outside any proceeding for assessment. There could not be conceived of commission of any offence under the Ordinance save and except in connection with assessment or reassessment or fresh assessment of income:

86. It is therefore, not possible or permissible to tear the Chapter XXI off the Ordinance and use for prosecution for the offences enumerated therein like any offence of the Penal Code or any other special offences. We shall shortly deliberate on the connection of Chapter XXI for prosecution for an offence with the rest of the Ordinance.

87. Another pertinent aspect should not escape notice. No prosecution for such offences under Chapter XXI could be initiated without prior sanction of the Board under section 169. The Ordinance has empowered the Board as a statutory body to accord sanction. But on the other hand, the Commissioner is empowered under section, 170 of the Ordinance to compound any offence under .the chapter before or after institution of the-proceedings or prosecution for offence. Use of the words it the proceedings is not without any meaning or significance since-no word in a statute could be read superfluous and/or redundant. And such power to compound an offence has got no reference, to sanction. In our judgment; in the course of the proceedings for assessment of income when the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes decides to take steps for prosecution for an offence such steps may have been termed as the proceedings for an offence such proceedings shall then turn into a prosecution for an offence only after the sanction and cognisance.

88. Now, the question arises, why such plenary power to compound an offence is given to a petty office of the rank of the Commissioner, Intervention of a Court, more specifically the Special Judge, is not at all necessary. In any other criminal cases, either general or special, composition of an offence is not possible without the leave, of the Court. If such distinction is kept in mind, then the objective of the prosecution for an offence under the Ordinance shall become Clear, which is tax that evaded not jail that is the only objective of, the criminal prosecution for any offence of the Penal Code or any Special Law.

89. In order to prosecute any offence under Chapter XXI, it may again be noted, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes shall have, to find commission of such offence in the course of assessment of the total income under section 83 or of an assessment of the income that escaped assessment for any assessment year under section 93 of the Ordinance. Without taking any such proceedings for assessment of the income, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is empowered to make a complaint in respect of commission of any offence under the Ordinance.

90. It is true that there is no limitation for prosecution of any offence of the Penal Code or any other special or general penal law. But the offence (s) created under the Ordinance cannot be prosecuted if the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is not authorised to assess the income or reassess the income the escaped assessment for any assessment year, which has become final and closed, and/or reassessment of such income has become barred by special limitation. When the assessment of income becomes closed and time barred, commission of any offence of concealment of income or false statement in the verification in the return could not be conceived of the Ordinance. That is when the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is prohibited from examining any return for assessment of any income for a particular assessment year he cannot be authorised to consider the information of false statement in the verification or concealment of income for the purpose of prosecution only.

91. We have already found that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is empowered to assess the total income of an assessee under section 83 for one assessment year only or to assess the income that escaped assessment for any particular assessment year under section 93 of the Ordinance. As under the Ordinance, assessment of the income is permitted for one assessment year only so commission of any such offence of concealment of income or false statement in the return could be possible in respect of that particular assessment year only. In finding prima facie commission of any such offence he shall have to find exact sum of income concealed, exact particulars of income concealed or inaccurate particulars of income furnished for that particular assessment year. It is needless to say that such particulars could only be found in a proceeding for assessment of income. either under section 83 or 93 of the Ordinance. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is therefore, not authorised to make straight away complaint upon receipt of any information of concealment of income or false statement in thereturn. Similarly, he is not permitted to make a lump complaint for concealment of income or making false statement in the return in respect of more than one assessment year.

92. From day one we wanted to be sure that the prosecution for offence(s) under Chapter XXI of the Ordinance is possible just on the complaint lodged by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes. What disturbed us most, how it was possible for the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes to straightaway file a complaint for prosecution for concealment of income and/or false statements in the verification in the return without taking any proceeding for assessment of the income that escaped assessment for the relevant year(s) he complained of. What was the basis for his complaint?

93. Precisely such set of mind encouraged us to call for assistance of the learned senior lawyers of the Bar. The Bar appears to be sharply divided on the above issues. Mr Fida Kamal, Mr Salauddin Ahmed, Khan Saifur Rahman, Dr Kamal Hossain, Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiya and Mr Mahmudul Islam submitted that the prosecution for any of said offences is separate and independent of any other proceedings under the Ordinance and could be initiated by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes without taking any recourse to section 93. We were made to understand from their submissions that we should consider the Chapter XXI of the Ordinance and deal with it separately and independently as a chapter of any other penal law.

94. On the other hand, Mr Ajmalul Hossain, Mr TH Khan, Mr AF Hassan Ariff and Mr Rafiq-ul-Huq were assertive that no prosecution could be conceived of the Ordinance without taking a proceeding for assessment of the income that escaped assessment in any relevant assessment year after service of notice upon the assessee under section 93.

95. Learned submissions at the Bar, throw out the challenge to our face to examine if there is any nexus between the chapter IX, precisely section 93, and the prosecution of the offences under Chapter XXI of the Ordinance.

96. Confronted, it was disclosed on behalf of the Board that no such prosecution for offences of concealment of income or furnishing false statements in the verification in the return or document was ever initiated in this part of the world. Why then the time of emergency was so suited to them to flood the special Courts with such prosecution, it was further revealed that first, such a proceeding for assessment is time-consuming which may ultimately end up in an appeal before the Appellate Division. Second, no proceeding under section 93 for assessment of the income that escaped assessment beyond five years could possibly be resorted to None of the reasons however, appeared to be real or sanctioned by the Ordinance, which we shall scrutinise shortly.

97. In India, there is no dearth of cases we are tearing our hair for answers to find from. We shall consider some of the cases, which would definitely guide us to find the answers of the elementary questions facing us for the first time in our jurisprudence of income tax.

98. In G L Didwania and another vs ITO and another: [1997] 224 ITR 687 SC, in 1961 assessment was completed. Then, in the course of assessment of a firm the income tax officer found that the assessee concealed income out of said firm. Notice was issued and assessment was reopened. In 1969 the total income was reassessed for the said assessment year adding the income of the firm. In 1977 complaint was made and a criminal case initiated for concealment of income and making false declaration.

99. In appeal, the findings of the Income-tax Officer were set aside by the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal and addition of the income of the firm was deleted.

100. Whereupon, the application made by the assessee for dropping the criminal case on the basis of the decision of the appellate tribunal was first rejected by the Magistrate on the view that the prosecution has got a right to lead evidence in support of the complaint and the Court can come to the decision as to whether or not any criminal offence is made out. The order of the appellate tribunal could at best be taken as evidence. The application made under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against such order for quashing of the criminal proceeding was dismissed in limine by the High Court.

101. Relying upon its earlier decisions in Uttam Chand vs ITO: [1982 133 ITR 909 SC and P Jayappan vs S K Perumal, First ITO: [1984] 149 ITR 696, relied upon by Dr Kamal Hossain and Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, the Supreme Court of India quashed the proceedings on the following view,

"In the instant case, the crux of the matter is attracted and whether the prosecution can be sustained in view of the order passed by the Tribunal. As noted above, the assessing authority held that the appellant assessee made a false statement in respect of income of Young India and Transport Company and that finding has been set aside by the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal. If that is the position then we are unable to see as to how criminal proceedings can be sustained.

"The whole question is, whether the appellant-assessee made a false statement regarding the income which according to the assessing authority has escaped assessment. So far the issue is concerned the finding of the Appellate Tribunal is conclusive emphasis supplied by us.

102. In Commissioner of Income Tax vs Bhupen Champak Lal Dalal and another: [2001] 248 ITR 830 SC, an order of the High Court staying further proceedings before the Metropolitan Magistrate was challenged by the income-tax authority. Twelve criminal cases were originally lodged under the Income-tax Act, 1961 against the assessee for prosecution of the offences under the Act. Appeals were presented by the assessee against the assessments for different assessment years. Pending disposal of the appeals against assessments, the assessee prayed for stay of the criminal cases before the Metropolitan Magistrate. Magistrate granted limited stay staying framing of charge, discharge of the accused or acquittal of the accused until disposal of the appeals but ordered to continue recording evidence. Revision applications made against such limited order of stay before the Sessions Judge were rejected. Then, the High Court entertaining writ petitions issued Rule and also granted an ad-interim order staying the criminal proceedings.

103. Dismissing the leave petition of the Commissioner of Taxes, the Supreme Court of India appears to have laid down a guideline in matters of the proceeding for assessment of income vis-a-vis prosecution for offences as hereunder:

"However, a wholesome rule will have to adopted in matters of this nature where Courts have taken the view that when the conclusions arrived at by the appellate authorities have a relevance and bearing upon the conclusions to be reached in the case necessarily one authority will have to wait the outcome of the other authority.

When ultimately the result to come out of the proceedings before the appellate authorities would have a definite bearing on the cases alleged against the respondents, we find that the High Court is justified in granting the interim order it did and we do not think that such an interim order call for interference at our hand.

104. In recent case of K C Builders vs CIT: [2004] 2 SCC 731 treating the difference of income disclosed in the original return and revised return as concealed income, penalties were imposed by the assessing officer in respect of four assessment years. Appeal preferred there from was dismissed by the appellate authority. As per direction of the Chief Commissioner of Income Tax, four complaints were lodged for prosecution of the assessee, mainly under section 276-C of the Income-tax Act, 1961, for concealment of income to evade tax. In further appeal under said Act, the Appellate Tribunal found that there was no concealment and set aside the penalties. The reference of the revenue department was rejected by the High Court. Then, the revision application moved on behalf of the assessee for stay of criminal proceeding was rejected by the High Court. An appeal was taken there from to the Supreme Court.

105. Of various issues taken; moot issue was whether the criminal prosecution gets quashed automatically when the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal final Court on facts found that there was no concealment and such finding is binding upon the criminal Court.

The Supreme Court of India held, amongst others,

"......Originally the penalty cannot stand if the assessment itself is set aside. Where an assessment or reassessment on the basis of which penalty has been levied on the assessee has itself been finally set aside or cancelled by the Tribunal or otherwise, the penalty cannot stand by itself and the same is liable to be cancelled as in the instant case ordered by the Tribunal and later, cancellation of the penalty by the authorities."

......the finding of the Appellate Tribunal was conclusive and the prosecution cannot be sustained since the penalty after having been cancelled by the complainant following the Appellate Tribunal's order, no offence survives under the Income-tax Act and thus quashing of prosecution is automatic."

106. Even in the cases of P Jayappan vs S K Perumal: [1994] 149 ITR 696 (SC); Tip Top Plastic Industries P Ltd. vs ITO: [1995] 214 ITR 778 (Madras); N K-Mohan vs CAT [1992] 72 ITR 72 (Madras) and Dr Ms Dhowania vs Ragresree: [1992] 72 ITR 962 (Madras) relied upon by Dr Kamal Hossain for the propositions that the criminal case could proceed independent of the proceedings for assessment and that the prayers for quashing of such prosecution for offences in view of the proceedings for assessment under the Incometax Act, 1961 are liable to be dismissed. But the fact remains that in all the cases, the prosecutions for offences - were initiated in the course of the proceedings for assessment - of income and not straightaway like the case at hand. Besides, the above decisions of the Supreme Court of India finding a nexus between the proceedings for assessment of income and the prosecution for offence under the Income-tax Act, 1961 and holding that ultimate outcome of the proceedings for assessment of income shall bind the prosecution for such an offence, evidence that much water 'flowed down the Yamuna after the decisions cited at the Bar.

107. Not a single case could be cited at the Bar nor could we find a case, where a prosecution for any of the offences created by the income tax law anywhere received sanction and was launched straightaway on receipt of the information of concealment of income or false statement in the verification in the return of any assessment year.

108. From the above cases of the Supreme Court of India, what is clear is that every case of prosecution for offences created by the Income-tax Act, 1922 or the Income-tax Act, 1961 arose out of either an original proceeding for assessment of income or a proceeding for assessment of the income that escaped assessment in the relevant year(s) (as under section 93 of the Ordinance).There is although no bar in simultaneous proceeding for assessment of income or penalty and the prosecution of the offences for concealment of income or false statement in the verifications or documents produced. B4t the nexus between the proceedings for assessment and the prosecution for offences is now recognised. In the case of CIT vs Champak Lal Dalal a wholesome rule was laid down by the Supreme Court of India for guidance. Lastly, in the case of KC Builders vs CIT, it is emphatically ruled that the finding of the Appellate Tribunal was conclusive and the prosecution cannot be sustained since the penalty after having been cancelled by the complainant following the Appellate Tribunal's order, no offence survives under the Income-tax Act and thus quashing of prosecution is automatic.

109. Nexus between the proceedings for assessment of income or penalty and the prosecution for offences committed in the course of a proceeding for assessment of income is real. No prosecution for any offence of concealment of income or false statement could be conceived of the Ordinance independent of the proceedings for assessment of the total income or the proceedings for assessment of the income that escaped assessment in the relevant assessment year(s). More clearly, any prosecution for offences enumerated in Chapter XXI of the Ordinance must be founded in a proceeding for assessment of income of an assessee. Mere sanction cannot save such prosecution for offences of concealment of income or false statement from being vitiated at its commencement for having no foundation for the complaint.

110. Coming back to the facts of the case, we find, in the complaint dated 4-7-07, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes alleged that having not disclosed the investment/earned income/expenditure amounting to Taka 3,80,14,048.30 in non-agricultural property, saving certificates, term deposits, interest on the term deposits, motor car, bank balances and credit cards in the income tax returns and wealth statements of the assessment years 1999-2000 to 2006-2007 (eight years) the petitioner concealed the particulars of income and filed false statements in the verifications and evaded tax payable thereon and thereby, committed offences under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance read with rule 15 of the EP Rules.

111. He wanted to prosecute the petitioner for evading tax for concealment of income that escaped assessment in those eight assessment years and for filing false statements in the verifications in the returns of income. An offence either under section 165 or 166 of the Ordinance definitely relates to particular assessment year. But he did not or could not specify the particular assessment year in which false statement in the verification or particulars of the income were concealed or inaccurate particulars were deliberately furnished. Had he taken a proceeding for assessment of the income that escaped assessment according to his information then he could have found the assessment year in the return of which false statement was made or the income was concealed.

112. There could possibly be lodged one complaint in respect of such offence of concealment of income or furnishing false statements in the return for any particular assessment year. Lump complaint against the false statements and/or concealment of income in respect of eight assessment years is neither conceived of nor permitted by the Ordinance. Such complaint therefore does not disclose any offence either under section 165 or 166 of the Ordinance; Cj Kusum Products Ltd. vs ITO: [1980] 126 ITR 804; P Jayappan vs S K Perumal, First ITO: [1984] 149 ITR 696 (SC); Dr M S Dhowani vs J Ranganathan: [1992] 194 ITR 690; V Gopal vs A CIT [1994] 207 ITR 971and CIT vs Bhupen Champak Lal Dalal and another: [2001] 248 ITR 830 (SC). In each ofthe cases, it would be found that the proceedings for penalty or prosecution for any offence of concealment of income or furnishing false statement in the return was initiated in the course of assessment of income for every assessment year in question.

113. Moreover, when the assessments of income for the assessment years up to 2006-2007 became final and binding upon all the parties including the Board, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes was not permitted to complain about concealment of income by furnishing false verifications in the returns without opening such assessments in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance.

114. After receipt of the information from various agencies of concealment of income and/or furnishing false statement in the verifications of the returns for the assessment years in question, he was required to examine and proceed to assess the income that escaped assessment for the particular assessment year under section 93 of the Ordinance. He was duty bound to recover the tax, if any, evaded by such concealment or false statements, for which he was enjoined by the Board. Prosecution for any offence of concealment of income or furnishing false statement could only be resorted to in the course of such assessment of the income that escaped assessment. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes examined the information received and made a draft complaint for sanction for prosecution but deliberately abstained from taking any steps he was required under the Ordinance.

115. Under sub-section (3) of section 93 of the Ordinance, if he was sure that the information received was definite that the petitioner concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars thereof or failed to disclose all material facts necessary for assessment for such assessment years, he was required to proceed with approval of the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes by issue of a notice upon the petitioner to assess the income that escaped assessment for the assessment years in question.

116. Mr T H Khan took much pain to impress upon us that without proceeding under section 93 no prosecution for any offence-under Chapter XXI of the Ordinance could be launched. And before initiating such proceeding, a notice was mandatory for reopening the assessment(s). In support, he cited CIT vs Navinchandra: AIR 1961 SC 1717, CIT vs lshwar Singh & Sons: f1981] ITR 480; State of Assam vs Chaudhury: 76 lTR 706 SC and American Express Bank vs Chairman, NBR 54 DLR 6. With reference to the scheme of the Ordinance Mr A F Hassan Ariff also submitted that without exhausting the procedure laid down under section 93, no prosecution for such offences could be possible. Such prosecution could only be resorted to as a last measure for preventing evasion of tax.

117. The proceedings under section 93 to assess the income that escaped assessment for any relevant year is not only necessary for the recovery of the tax evaded, which is the only objective of the Ordinance to achieve but also essential for prosecuting an assessee for an offence under the Ordinance. The assessee could not be deprived of any of the remedies as prescribed by the Ordinance of revision, appeal and reference against any re-assessment or additional assessment of income such proceedings to assess the income may ultimately result in. Depriving the petitioner of the remedy available against departmental proceedings also appears to be deliberate and mala fide, which was not concealed on behalf of the Board.

<u>118. Furnishing false statement in the verification in the return for particular assessment year or concealment of particulars or deliberate furnishing inaccurate particulars of income for a particular assessment year makes one liable to be prosecuted for that particular assessment year only under section 165 or 166 of the Ordinance and complaint against such false statement and/or concealment of income shall have to be made for that assessment year only. And such complaint could only be made in the course of assessment of the income that escaped assessment in that particular assessment year in a proceeding taken under section 93. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes was therefore not authorised and/or permitted under the Ordinance to straightaway lodge a lump complaint in respect of eight assessment years on receipt of the information from various sources and such complaint must be held to be inherently invalid and vitiated.</u>

119. The reasons that have been revealed on behalf of the Board for not taking a proceeding under section 93 of the Ordinance make it further clear that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes deliberately wanted to circumvent the requirements under the Ordinance with the sole objective to seek quick conviction of the petitioner under the present situation that arose under the emergency and not to recover any tax that was evaded. Such course must be held to be not bona fide and actuated by certain objective, which is not permitted by the Ordinance.

120. Now, let us take up the issue of sanction, which according to the Board, was long debated at the Bar. Mr Ajmalul Hossain challenged the sanction on various grounds. He took us through the minutes of the meeting of the Board held on 28-6-07, Annexure-A to the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the Board and submitted that the sanction was accorded in haste, at rocket speed without any application of mind. He also submitted that the sanction was bad and illegal for being coram non-judice since the chairman who presided over the Board meeting was not a member of the Board.

121. Dr Kamal Hossain, Mr Mahmudul Islam and Khan Saifur Rahman in one voice submitted that the process of sanction is an administrative act and is not subject for judicial scrutiny. They also submitted' that whether the sanction was proper or valid or suffers from any defect that could only be determined at the trial on the evidence that could be adduced to satisfy the trial Court that all material facts were before the sanctioning authority, when sanction was accorded. In support Dr Kamal Hossain cited V Gopal vs Assistant CIT: (1994) 207 ITR 971 (Madras); M K Mohnot vs CCIT: [1992] 195 ITR 72 (Madras) and M K Gopalan vs State of Madhya Pradesh: AIR 1954 SC 362.

122. It appears from the record that the meeting of the Board was held on 28-6-07 at about 4-00 PM. On the same date, the Commissioner of Taxes sent a letter addressed to Mr. Ahmed Ali, Member (Tax Administration) of the Board for approval of the draft complaint prepared by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes under section 169 of the Ordinance. Along with the letter were attached a proposal comprising three pages, written-up draft complaint comprising ten pages and 'other enclosures comprising seventy pages in total eighty-three computer typed pages. In the meeting, matters regarding prosecution against the petitioner and two others were discussed. After elaborate discussion sanction was accorded under section 169 of the Ordinance for prosecution of the petitioner along with two others under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance: Same date said member of the Board communicated the sanction to the Commissioner of Taxes requesting him to direct the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes for taking steps upon such sanction. Same date the Commissioner of Taxes communicated the fact of sanction to the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes and asked him to lodge the complaint.

123. All communications, deliberations and according sanction for prosecution took place after 4-00 PM of the day that is 28-6-07. There was no bar for the revenue authority to work even after the office time that is after 5-00 PM in matter of urgency unless such endeavours are tainted by any bad faith. But the question raised, was it possible for the Board to consider in one meeting within such short a time eighty-three pages of papers in respect of the petitioner only and accord sanction for prosecution.

Besides, did the Board consider, in such short time, the following facts, circumstances and law. before according the sanction for the first time in its life,

a. when the assessments of income of the petitioner for the assessment years up to 2006- 2007 were final and conclusive, how then a complaint could be made under the. Ordinance for prosecution without any step for opening any of such assessments;

b. how one lump complaint against concealment of particulars or deliberate furnishing of inaccurate particulars of income or furnishing false statements in the verifications of the returns for eight assessment years for prosecution of offences under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance could be valid in law;

c. could the process of sanction circumvent the command of the Ordinance to assess the income that escaped assessment for the relevant assessment year(s) that came to the knowledge of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes from various sources to recover the tax that was evaded.

124. No answer could be found in the minutes of said Board meeting nor could any record be produced justifying such omissions. Such failure or omissions in considering the above facts and circumstances would invite the presumption that had those been considered, then, the Board could not accord the sanction.

125. It is true that the order of sanction is no doubt administrative in nature, not a quasi-judicial one nor a lis involved. But it cannot be gainsaid that the sanction to prosecution goes to the root of launching any prosecution of any offence under the Ordinance. Such sanction is intended to safeguard frivolous and vexatious prosecution. It also gives an opportunity to the authority concerned to decide in the circumstances of a particular case whether the prosecution was necessary in the greater interest of revenue.

126. It is therefore, now well settled that the sanctioning authority must have before it all the material facts and circumstances which prima facie establish the commission of the offence charged with and the sanctioning authority would apply its mind to those facts. The letter for sanction or consent for prosecution, and authorisation of prosecution must contain the facts constituting the offence; CJ Md Iqbal Ahmed vs Andhra Pradesh:

AIR 1979 SC 677,

127. In Mansukhlal Vithaldas Chauhan vs State of Gujarat: (1997) 7 SCC 622 (at para 19), the Supreme Court of India was of the following view:

"Since the validity of 'sanction' depends on the applicability of mind by the sanctioning authority to the facts of the case as also the material and evidence collected during the investigation, it necessarily follows that the sanctioning authority has to apply its own independent mind for the generation of genuine satisfaction whether prosecution has to be sanctioned or not. The mind of sanctioning authority should not be under pressure from any quarter nor should any external authority force be acting upon it to take a decision one way or other. Since the discretion to grant or not to grant sanction vests absolutely in the sanctioning authority, its discretion should be shown to have not been affected by any extraneous consideration. If it is shown that the sanctioning authority was unable to apply its independent mind for any reason whatsoever or was under an obligation or compulsion or constraint to grant the sanction the order will be bad for the reason that the discretion of the authority "not to sanction" was taken away and it was compelled to act mechanically to sanction the prosecution."

128. After such authoritative statement of the law on sanction by the Supreme Court of India, we do not need to consider the case of Gopal decided by a single Bench of the Madras High Court. Dr Kamal relied upon the following observation of the Supreme Court of India in M K Gopalan vs Madhya Pradesh: AIR 1954 SC 362 that

"the lacuna, if any, in the sanction of the kind contemplated in Gokulch and Dwarkadas vs the King: AIR 1948 PC 82 can be remedied in the course of the trial by specific evidence in that behalf."

129. In the case, it was argued that in the absence of any evidence the sanction was granted. But in the case at hand, the defects mentioned herein above and to be noticed hereinafter are of such fundamental nature that those could not be resolved at the trial of the case, even if it is found to be otherwise valid prosecution. Moreover, the special judge has got no jurisdiction to decide such facts and circumstances. Besides, the sanction lifts, the bar against the prosecution and an assessee has a right to know why and under what basis the sanction was accorded. 'Such reasons cannot be supplied afterwards at the trial by introducing evidence. In support of the submission that the sanction is not subject to judicial scrutiny no authority could be cited. Rather, such submission does not stand before the following authorities.

130. In Commissioner of Police, Bombay vs Gordhandas Bhanji: AIR 1952 SC 16 the Supreme Court of India answered the question in the following words,

"Public orders, publicly made, in exercise of a statutory authority cannot be construed in the light of explanations subsequently given by the officer making the order of what he meant. or of what was in his mind. or what he intended to do. Public orders made by public authorities are meant to have public effect and are intended to affect the actions and conduct of those to whom they are addressed and must be construed objectively with reference to the language used in the order itself." (underlined by us)

131. The Supreme Court of Indiastated the law in Mohinder Singh vs Chief Election Commissioner: AIR 1978 SC 851 in the following words,

"When a statutory functionary makes an order based on certain grounds, its validity must be judged by the reasons' so mentioned and cannot be supplemented by fresh reasons in the shape of affidavit or otherwise. Otherwise, an order bad in the beginning may, by the time it comes to Court on account of a challenge, get validated by additional grounds later brought out."

In order to appreciate the newer approach of Mr Rafiq-ul Huq .tothe constructions of sections 169 and 170 of the Ordinance, and the submission that an assessee deserves and is entitled to a hearing or an opportunity for composition of the offence that he may face before sanction is accorded for prosecution of such offence in the interest of revenue and justice, we should examine sections 169 and 170 closely, which we have already quoted them earlier and quote again,

169. Sanction for prosecution.-

No prosecution for an offence punishable under any provisions of this Chapter shall be instituted except with the previous sanction of the Board.

Sanction under sub-section (1) shall not be given in respect of an offence other than an offence under section 128, which consists of the same facts on which a penalty has been imposed under Chapter XV] omitted by Finance Act, 1999

170 Power to compound offences.-

The Commissioner may, either before or after the institution of any proceedings or prosecution for an offence punishable under this Chapter, compound such offence.

<u>139. If both sections are read together, it would be clear that the machinery of prosecution for an offence created by sections 164 to 168 of the Ordinance can only be set in motion by the Board by according sanction for such prosecution. But section 170 empowers the Commissioner only to compound any of the offences under Chapter XXI either before or after the institution of any proceedings or prosecution for an offence. Here use of the word 'proceedings' in the plural sense and 'prosecution' in the singular sense appears to be not without any significance. It is well settled rule of interpretation of any section of a statute that no word in any section could be thought to be redundant, superfluous or carrying no intention or meaning. Rather, every word should receive proper attention for harmonious interpretation of the intention of the legislature.</u>

140. On the basis of such principle of construction, the words 'any proceedings' shall mean and include each and every proceeding that are available under the Ordinance. Such proceedings may also include a regular proceeding for assessment of the total income under section 83 or a proceeding for assessment of the income that escaped assessment in any relevant assessment year(s) under section 93 of the Ordinance. In the course of such proceeding, a prosecution for an offence punishable under sections 164 to 167 may crop up, not outside any such proceeding.

141. The power of the Commissioner to compound any offence at any stage of such proceedings or even during the trial of a prosecution for an offence is plenary. No leave of the Court or permission of the Board, which sanctioned the prosecution for any offence, is necessary. Such power of composition would not be seen in any other procedure for prosecution of an offence under any other penal law. The purpose/intention is clear to keep the revenue authority at the helm of the scheme of the Ordinance for the interest of revenue only.

142. Both Mr Khan Saifur Rahman and Dr Kamal pressed hard to make us understand the consequence of the omission of sub-section (2) of section 169 of the Ordinance and submitted that after such omission, the obstacle in the way to sanction for prosecution of any offence was removed. In our considered view, such omission would not make any difference or make the Board free of the obligation originally expected of or imposed upon it in the making of its decision for sanction.

143. Now, let us face the question raised, whether in the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of sections 169 and 170 of the Ordinance the petitioner deserved andlor was entitled to a hearing or composition of the offence(s) alleged before according the sanction by the Board for prosecution? Mr Rafiqul Huq also urged that even where there is no provision for notice, it is in the interest of national revenue to give an opportunity of hearing to a potential assessee for composition of any offence before according sanction for prosecution on the basis of development of the jurisprudence for fair and transparent dealing with the tax matters.

144. In Suraj Mall Mohta and Co vs A B Visvanakh Sastri and another: [J954] 26 ITR 01 at page 11, the Supreme Court of India was, inter alia, of the view in case of evasion of income tax that,

"It is clear that if persons dealt with by the impugned Act are deprived of substantial and valuable privileges, which they would otherwise have if they were dealt with under the Indian Income-tax Act, in that situation it is no defence to say that the discriminatory procedure also advances the course of justice. The matter has to be just from the point of view of the ordinary reasonable man and not from the point of view of the government. The ordinary reasonable man would say, when the stakes are heavy and serious charges of evasion of income tax was made against him, why one person similarly placed should have the advantage substantially of the procedure prescribed by the Indian Income-tax Act, while another person similarly situated be deprived of it."

145. In Indian jurisdiction, in such proceedings for penalty or prosecution for concealment of income or false statement in the verifications, the Supreme Court of India gradually started to read the principles of natural justice too in the tax laws in allowing an opportunity or hearing to an assessee.

146. In CB Gautam vs Union of India: [1993] 199 ITR 530 SC at page 553, validity of Chapter XXC inserted in the Income-tax Act, 1961 by the Finance Act, 1986 was challenged by way of a writ petition in the Delhi High Court: The case Was transferred to the Supreme Court of India as a test case. By such new provisions ofthe chapter, appropriate authority was empowered to compulsory purchase of immovable property as a punitive measure where said authority takes the view that there was undervaluation of the property in an agreement for sale with a view to, avoid tax. An order of the appropriate authority under such provisions for purchase of the property in question was served on 15 December, 1986 upon the purchaser-appellant.

147. The issue raised was whether the provisions of Chapter XXC were bad in law as there was no provision for giving the concerned parties an opportunity of being heard before an order could be passed under the provisions of section 269UD of the said Chapter for purchase by the Central Government of an immovable property agreed to be sold in an agreement of sale.

148. In relying upon its earlier decisions, namely, Union of India vs J N'Sinha: [1971] 1 SCR 791,= AIR 1971 SC 40, Kraipak vs Union of India AIR 1970 SC 150and Vargese (K P) vs ITO: [1981] 131 ITR 597, the Supreme Court of India allowed the writ on the view that,

"It must, however, be borne in mind that Courts have generally read into the provisions of the relevant sections a requirement of giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard before an order is made which would have adverse civil consequences for the parties affected. This would be particularly so in a case where the validity of the section would be open to a serious challenge for want of such an opportunity.

...we are clearly of the view that the requirement of a reasonable opportunity being given to the concerned parties, particularly the intending purchaser and the intending seller,must be read into the provisions of Chapter XXC. In our opinion, before an order for compulsory purchase is made under section 269UD, the intending purchaser and the intending seller must be given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against an order for compulsory purchase being made by the appropriate authority concerned."

In Union of India vs ca. J N Sinha: AIR 1971 SC 40 at 42=[1971] 1 SCR 791, the Supreme Court of India held,

"The rules of natural justice are not embodied rules nor can they be elevated to the position of fundamental rights. The aim of the rules of natural justice is to secure justice or, to put it negatively, to prevent miscarriage of justice. As observed by this Court in Kraipak vs Union of India: AIR 1970 SC 150, 'the aim of rules can operate only in areas not covered by any law. They do not supplant the law but supplement it. It is true that if a statutory provision can be read consistently with the principles of natural justice, the Courts should do so because it must be presumed that the Legislatures and the statutory authorities intend to act in accordance with the principles of natural justice. But, if, on the other hand, a statutory provision either specifically or by necessary implication excludes the application of any or all the rules of principles of natural justice then the Court cannot ignore the mandate of the Legislature or the statutory authority and read into the concerned provision the principles of natural justice. Whether the exercise of a power conferred should be made in accordance with any of the principles of natural justice or not depends upon the express words of the provision 'conferring the power, the nature of the power conferred, the purpose for which it is conferred and the effect of the exercise of that power."

In Olga Tellis vs Bombay Municipal Corporation: [1985] Suppl 2 SCR 51 at 89=AIR 1986 SC 180, the Supreme Court of India held,

"The ordinary rule which regulates all procedure is that persons who are likely to be affected by the proposed action must be afforded an 'opportunity of being' heard as to why that action should not be taken. The hearing may be given individually or collectively, depending upon the facts of each case. A departure from this fundamental rule of natural justice may be presumed to have been intended by the Legislature only in circumstances which warrant it. Such circumstances must be shown to exist, when so required, the burden being upon those who affirm their existence."

In S L Kapoor vs Jagmohan: AIR 1981 SC 136, the Supreme Court of India reiterated that "Therefore, merely because facts are admitted or are indisputable it does not follow that natural justice need not to be observed. The order of superseding the New Delhi Municipal Committee was held to be vitiated by the failure to observe the principleaudi alteram partem.

In Institute of Chartered Accountants of India vs L K Ratna : [1987] 133 ITR 01 SC, in connection with a proceeding for misconduct of member of the institute, the Supreme Court of India held that the principles of natural justice must be read into the unoccupied interstices of the statute unless there is a clear mandate to the contrary.

149. Such principles of giving an opportunity of hearing as enunciated and followed by the Supreme Court of India not only before according the sanction but also before initiation, of the prosecution for any offence of concealment of income are also being followed in .different High Courts in India, namely, in Kusum Products Ltd vs S K Sinha: [1980] 126ITR 804, Shree Singhvi Brothers vs Union of India: [199.1J 187ITR 219; P V Pai vs R I Rinawma, DCIT: [1993J 200 ITR 717; Universal Supply Corporation vs State of Rajasthan: [1994J 206ITR 322 and Tip Top Plastic Industries P. Ltd. vs ITO: [I995J 214 ITR 779.

150. In P V Pai vs R I Rinawma, DCIT: [1993] 200 ITR 717 at page 729, a Division Bench of the Karnatak High Court took the view that,

"If the provisions of section 279 of the Act are read in totality together. with the-provisions of section 278 regarding abetment of assessee or a person abetting the commission of the offence under section 276C, the intention of the legislature becomes clear, namely, to give an opportunity to the assessee or the person charged with abetment to satisfy the sanctioning authority about his bona fides or about the circumstances under which certain 'statements were made. As far as compounding is concerned, the same may be made either before or after institution of the proceedings. Therefore, an assessee may be anxious to offer composition even before prosecution to save himself from 'disgrace and ignominy of the prosecution.

Therefore, simply because there is an opportunity to compound after the prosecution is launched, it, does not necessarily follow that such opportunity: should be denied before the prosecution is launched. The stage at which such offer may be considered could be. at the time the sal1ctioning' authority considers according of sanction to prosecute.

151. Our jurisdiction did not lag behind. In Sk Ali Ahmed vs Secretary of Ministry, Home Affairs: 40 DLR (AD) 170 at 173, our Appellate Division approving 'the opinions of other apex Courts on the application of the principles of natural justice held,

"in all proceedings by whomsoever held, whether judicial or administrative, the principles of natural justice have to be, observed if the proceedings might resultin consequences affecting 'the person or property or other right of the parties concerned. This rule applies even though there may be no positive words 'in the statute or legal document whereby the power is vested to take such proceeding, for in such cases this requirementis to be implied into it as the minimum requirement of fairness."

152.Under section 169 or 170, there is no express requirement to give notice or an opportunity of hearing to the assessee before according-sanction for initiating a criminal proceeding or prosecution for any offence under Chapter XXI of the Ordinance. But if such notice is given or opportunity is offered, the revenue department would have an opportunity to check frivolous, vexatious and unnecessary prosecution being initiated and could save valuable time and money in prosecuting a lengthy litigation. Question is as to whether such course would be advisable in the interest of revenue, whether it would fit in with the scheme of the Ordinance. If the principles of natural justice of hearing the delinquent prior to the sanction for prosecution of any offence within the unoccupied interstices of sections 169 and 170 of the Ordinance are read, would it not advance the justice?

153. In our view, such an opportunity of prior hearing if given to a potential assessee or person would make the entire proceeding more transparent and fairer. And the Board would have the chance to compound the offence that might be initiated if the assessee is desirous so to do. Absence of such attitude and mind of the Board would not help enhance augment the revenue of the nation, which would be clearer in our deliberation, a little later.

<u>157. Section 3 of the Ordinance enumerated the classes of income tax authorities with the National Board of Revenue at the top. Clause (a) of article 2 of said Order defines the Board as the National Board of Revenue constituted under the provision of the Order and the Government as the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.</u>

<u>Article 3 of the Order reads as follows:</u>

<u>(i) as soon as may be after commencement of this Order the government shall constitute a Board to be called the National Board of Revenue.</u>

<u>(ii) The Board shall consist of such number of members as may be appointed by the Government.</u>

<u>(iii) The Government shall appoint one of the members of the Board to be its Chairman.</u>

<u>(iv) The Board shall subject to the control of the government exercise such powers and perform such duties as may be entrusted to him by the Government or by or under any law.</u>

<u>(v) Without prejudice to the provision of clause (4), the Board shall exercise all the powers and perform all the duties, which immediately before the commencement of this Order, were being performed by the Central Board of Revenue constituted under the Central Board of the Revenue Act, 1924 (Act IV of 1924); by any government or under any law.</u>

<u>158. Under clause (3) of article 1 the Order came into force at once and shall be deemed to have taken effect on the 16th December, 1971. <u>159. Article 3 clearly empowers the Government to constitute a Board to be called the National Board of Revenue comprising such number of members as may be appointed by the government. The Government shall then appoint one of the members as the Chairman of the Board. So, the Chairman must first be appointed a member of the Board. No one could be conceived of being appointed chairman who is not a member of the Board. His existence outside the Board cannot be conceived of under such Order. If the Board is not so constituted in accordance with the provisions of article 3 of the Order only legal consequence that would follow is that any power exercised and any duty performed by such Board would be vitiated for being coram non judice.</u>

160. In the Federation of Pakistan vs Sayeed Ahmed: PLD 1974 SC 151 at page 168, in respect of coram non Judice decision the Supreme Court of Pakistan held,

"Indeed, malafide, acts stand on the same footing as acts done without jurisdiction. Similarly, coram non judice also stands on the same footing because these words would literally mean that they have been done by an authority or body exercising judisial or quasi-judicial powers whichwas not properly constituted even under the law under which it was set up and that its decision is not a decision of a competent authority."

Our Appellate Division approving such view in Khondker Ehteshamuddin @ Iqbal: 33 DLR (AD) 154 held,

"Of course when, a Martial Law Court or Tribunal has acted without jurisdiction or such Court or Tribunal is not property constituted, that is to say, is coram non judice or has acted malafide, the power of the superior Courts under Article 102 of the Constitution in an appropriate case may be invoked."

161. In the case of Nur Mohammad vs M Ahmed: 39 DLR (AD) 1 the Appellate Division followed such view on coram non Judice.

Rights enumerated under Articles 27, 31 and 35 of the Constitution are now accepted to be essential rules of due process in USA and the rule of law and natural justice in the common law countries. The rule of law and the principles of natural justice are now universally accepted as minimum standard to follow in the administration of justice in the trial of any case. No tribunal or Court of law could be conceived of working and/or discharging its obligations in the administration of justice without following such rules or principles. Otherwise, the proclamation of emergency would mean a licence for such authority or tribunal in dealing with the life, liberty or property of the citizens.

209. It would be difficult to find out a nation that never faced a state of emergency in its history. The need to declare a state of emergency may arise from situations as diverse as an armed action against the state by internal or external elements, a natural disaster, civil unrest, an epidemic, a financial or economic crisis or a general strike. The implementation of emergency law invariably leads to restrictions on normal economic, civil or political activity and rights in order to address the extra-ordinary circumstances that have given rise to the emergency situation. Certain restrictions may be fully justified. At the same time, there is a danger at a government will take advantage of a state of emergency to introduce unwarranted restrictions on human rights and civil liberties, to neutralise political opponents, to postpone elections, or for other self-serving purposes that would be more difficult to pursue under normal circumstances. It is also in the experience, in some country there has been tendency to maintain state of emergency for years or even decade long after the original reason for its proclamation has disappeared.

210. The experience of the American people in facing emergency one after another has got no comparison. Bush administration after September 11, 2001 declared state of war against the rest of the world, which is still continuing. In prosecuting such war, the USA captured and detained more than five hundred people from all continents as enemy combatants in Guantanamo Bay in its military base in Cuba for more than five years denying them all rights, basic or humane, available under various international treaties and conventions. The detainees were long denied access to the American judicial system.

211. On February 19, 2002 Asif Iqbal and Shafiq Rasul of British citizenship, and David Hicks of Australian citizenship made a petition for a writ of habeas corpus that is release from unlawful imprisonment and access to lawyers of their choice to have private and unmonitored conversations and ceasing interrogations until the completion of the trials.

212. The District Court dismissed the petition. The Court of Appeal affirmed the lower Court's decision on the view that there was no US Court that had jurisdiction over Guantanamo Bay. Then, the case reached the US Supreme Court. The sole question before the Supreme Court was, whether the foreign nationals in Guantanamo Bay might invoke the habeas corpus jurisdiction at all. Either US citizenship or Court jurisdiction was necessary for this invocation, and since the detainees were not citizens, US Court jurisdiction over Guantanamo Bay was at issue. According to the US treaty with Cuba over Guantanamo Bay, the US has "complete jurisdiction" over the base, but Cuba has "ultimate sovereignty." The government alleges that the fact that the treaty says this implies that the Courts have no jurisdiction; the detainees argue that regardless of what the treaty says, the US has full legal control in the area and should have jurisdiction.

213. In a landmark 6-3 ruling on June 28, 2004, the US Supreme Court established that the US Court system has the authority to decide whether foreign nationals (non-US citizens) held in Guantanamo Bay were rightfully imprisoned. Justice John Paul Stevens wrote the majority opinion and was joined by Sandra Day O'Connor, David Souter, Ruth Bader Ginsburg, and Stephen Breyer, with Anthony Kennedy concurring. Justice Antonin Scalia filed a dissenting opinion and was joined by William Rehnquist and Clarence Thomas. The claimant whose name the case bears, Shafiq Rasul; was released before the decision was handed down, Rasul vs Bush, 542 US 466 (2004).

214. Same date, the Supreme Court of USA also decided the case of Hamdi vs Rumsfeld. After the Congress passed a resolution-the Authorisation for Use of Military Force (AUMF)-empowering the President to "use all necessary and appropriate force" against "nations, organisations, or persons" that he determines "planned, authorised, committed, or aided" in the September 11, 2001, al Qaeda terrorist attacks, the President ordered the Armed Forces to Afghanistan to subdue al Qaeda and quell the supporting Taliban regime. Petitioner Hamdi, an American citizen whom the Government has classified as an "enemy combatant" for allegedly taking up arms with the Taliban during the conflict, was captured in Afghanistan and presently was detained at a naval brig in Charleston, SC.

215. Hamdi's father filed a habeas petition on his behalf under 28 USC 2241, alleging, among other things that the Government held his son in violation of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. Although the petition did not elaborate on the factual circumstances of Hamdi's capture and detention, his father asserted in other documents in the record that Hamdi went to Afghanistan to do "relief work" less than two months before September 11 and could not have received military training.

216. The Government attached to its response to the petition a declaration from Michael Mobbs (Mobbs Declaration), a Defence Department official. The Mobbs Declaration alleged various details regarding Hamdi's trip to Afghanistan, his affiliation there with a Taliban unit during a time when the Taliban was battling US allies, and his subsequent surrender of an assault rifle.

217. The District Court found that the Mobbs Declaration, standing alone, did not support Hamdi's detention and ordered the Government to turn over numerous materials for in-camera review. The Fourth Circuit reversed, stressing that, because it was undisputed that Hamdi was captured in an active combat zone, no factual inquiry or evidentiary hearing allowing Hamdi to be heard or to rebut the Government's assertions was necessary or proper, Concluding that the factual averments in the Mobbs Declaration, if accurate, provided a sufficient basis upon, which to conclude that the President had constitutionally detained Hamdi, the Court ordered the habeas petition dismissed.

218. The appeals Court held that, assuming that express congressional authorisation of the detention was required by 18 USC 4001(a)-which provides that "[n] citizen shall be imprisoned or otherwise detained by the United States except pursuant to an Act of Congress" the AUMF's "necessary and appropriate force" language provided the authorisation for Hamdi's detention. It also concluded that Hamdi is entitled only to a limited judicial inquiry into his detention's legality under the war powers of the political branches, and not to a searching review of the factual determination's underlying his seizure.

219. The Supreme Court vacated the judgment and remanded the case.

220. Justice O'Connor, joined by Chief Justice, Justice Kennedy and Justice Breyer, concluded that although the Congress authorised the detention of combatants in the narrow circumstances alleged in this case, due process demands that a citizen held in the United States as an enemy combatant be given a meaningful opportunity to contest the factual basis for that detention before a neutral decision maker.

221. In the recent case of Hamdan vs Rumsfeld, D/D 29-6-06, pursuant to said Congress' Joint Resolution authorising the President to use all necessary and appropriate force against those nations, organisations, or persons he determines planned, authorised, committed or aided the September 11, 2001, al Qaeda terrorist attacks (AUMF), US armed forces invaded Afghanistan. During the hostilities, in 2001, militia forces captured petitioner Salim Ahmed Hamdan, a Yemeni national and a former driver for Osama bin Laden and turned him over to the US military, which, in 2002, transported him to prison in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. Over a year later, the President deemed Hamdan eligible for trial by military commission for then unspecified crimes. After another year, he was charged with conspiracy "to commit......... . offences triable by military commission."

222. In habeas and mandamus petitions, Hamdan asserted that the military commission lacks authority to try him because

(1) neither congressional Act nor the common law of war supports trial by this commission for conspiracy, an offence that, Hamdan says, is not a violation of the law of war; and

(2) the procedures adopted to try him violate basic tenets of military and international law, including the principle that a defendant must be permitted to see and hear the evidence against him.

223. The District Court granted habeas relief and stayed the commission proceedings, concluding that the President's authority to establish military commissions extends only to offenders or offences triable by such a commission under the law of war; that such law includes the Third Geneva Convention; that Hamdan is entitled to that Convention's full protections until adjudged, under it, not to be a prisoner of war; and that, whether or not Hamdan is properly classified a prisoner of war, the commission convened to try him was established in violation of both the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ), 10 U.S.C. $801 et seq., and Common Article 3 of the Third Geneva Convention because it had the power to convict based on evidence the accused would never see or hear. The DC Circuit reversed. Although it declined the Government's invitation to abstain from considering Hamdan's challenge, of: Schlesinger vs Councilman, 420 US 738, the appeals Court ruled, on the merits, that Hamdan was not entitled to relief because the Geneva Conventions are not judicially enforceable. The Court also concluded that Ex parte Quirin, 317 US I, foreclosed any separation-of- powers objection to the military commission's jurisdiction, and that Hamdan's trial before the commission would violate neither the UCMJ nor Armed Forces regulations implementing the Geneva Conventions.

224. The Supreme Court reversed the judgment, and remanded the case. What demands attention of all of us is the observation of the Court that even assuming that Hamdan is a dangerous individual who would cause great harm or death to innocent civilians given the opportunity, the Executive nevertheless must comply with the prevailing rule of law in undertaking to try him and subject him to criminal punishment.

Dr Kamal Hossain referred to the case of A1 Capone and filed reported photo clippings of the incarcerated political leaders including those of the former prime ministers and asked us to pay due regard in the judicial review to the fundamental principles of state policy and national policy objectives in respect of ongoing trials against corruption. But he could not cite a single authority to support his view that during emergency in the trials of cases against corruption, the-rule of law or due process must be sacrificed.
