We are therefore, convinced to say that the language of justice shall be the same in war, emergency or peace in the judicial review that every prosecution or trial shall pass the test of the rule of law and the principles of natural justice.

226. The rule of interpretation of suspension of some of the rights in emergency legislation does not allow reading any abridgment of the powers of the superior Court save any express provision. Legislation suspending any fundamental right must receive strict construction. Constitution needs to bend for accommodation of the emergency measures for the safety otherwise it would break down. The elasticity of constitutional law has decisive implications for the scope of constitutional rights during emergency. Civil liberties must vary with the threat level. The need to strike a balance between the interests in liberty with the safety of the country is of paramount interest for the nation. With the change in the threat level the emergency starts ceasing its efficacy; Cf CIT vs Gulistan Cinema Co: 28 DLR (AD) 14 (para 12) and Super. &Remembrancer vs Jobed Ali: 26 DLR (AD) 1 (para 22).

227. In Jamil Huq and 11 others vs Bangladesh: 34 DLR(AD) 125, our Appellate Division held that,

"It is well settled that in a democratic country with an independent judiciary, the jurisdiction of the superior Courts are not to be interpreted to have been taken away, and if it is so intended, it may be done by the appropriate legislation or constitutional authority by express words and not by implication.

228. Civil liberties depend in large scale on national security in a broader sense. Tax evasion was not a source for declaration of emergency. Such malady is at best sui generis-it fits legal category neither of "war" nor of "crime". In this twenty-first century, it is therefore risky to think any abridgment of the rule of law or the principles of due process or natural justice in the prosecution or trial of an assessee like that of the petitioner in a petty case of evasion of tax, which entails maximum punishment of five years. Even notoriety of an offence cannot deny a fair trial to an offender by internationally recognised tribunal and standards of procedure.

229. Dr Kamal Hossain also submitted that in view of equally efficacious remedy provided by law, meaning section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a writ petition under Article 102(2) was not maintainable since such right is not available under Article 102(2) of the Constitution during the emergency.

<u>230. How the emergency affects the right of a citizen arraigned in a criminal case during emergency has already been answered. But the remedy as claimed under section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is 'equally efficacious' is not supported by any authority. Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure gives no new power to this, Division what it does not already hold nor does it create a right of a citizen. The power conceived of under said section is inherent with this Division. Rather, by an obstante clause, "nothing in this Code" shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent power of this Division to make such order as may be necessary, amongst others, to prevent abuse of process of any Court or otherwise to secure ends of justice. The power that is inherent with this Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not denied' under Article 102(2) of the Constitution for issuing certain direction or declaration where the facts and circumstances demand. Such power that is exercised in wider perspective under the authority of the Constitution, the supreme law of the land under which said Code of Criminal Procedure is allowed to be followed in investigation and prosecution of the criminal cases, is more efficacious.</u>

231. In Haryana vs Bhajan Lal: (1992) SUPP(1) SCC 335, a case of political corruption against Bhajan Lal who was a Minister in 1977 when Devi Lal was the Chief Minister of Haryana. Bhajan Lal was the Chief Minister from 1982 to 1987. At the time of initiation of the criminal proceeding against corruption he was State Minister of Environment and Forest, Government of India. On the complaint of a political rival, Dharampal a case was registered under sections 161 and 165 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 on November 21 of 1987. Bhajanlal challenged the investigation on the basis of such FIR by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India which is similar to our Article 102.

232. In dismissing the petition on the ground of disclosure of a prima facie case in paragraph 102, the Supreme Court of India put the interpretations of the powers of quashing under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, our section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure vis-a-vis Article 226 of Indian Constitution.

"102. In the backdrop of the interpretation of the various relevant provisions of the Code under Chapter XIV and of the principles of law enunciated by this Court in a series of decisions relating to the exercise of the extraordinary power under Article 226 or the inherent power under section 482 of the Code which we have extracted and reproduced above, we give the following categories of cases by way of illustration wherein such power could be exercised either to prevent abuse, of the process ,of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, it may not be possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined and sufficiently channelised and inflexible guidelines or rigid formulae and to give an exhaustive list of myriad kinds of cases wherein such power should be exercised,

(a) Where the allegations made in the first information report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused,

(b) Where the allegations in the first information . report and other materials, if any, accompanying the FIR do not disclose a cognisable offence, justifying an investigation by police officers under section 156( 1) of the Code except under an order of a Magistrate. within the purview of section 155(2) of the Code.

(c) Where the uncontroversial allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused. (d) Where the allegations in the FIR do not constitute a cognisable offence but constitute only a non cognisable offence, no investigation is permitted by police without an order of a Magistrate as contemplated under section 155(2) of the Code.

(e) Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.

(f) Where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any of the provisions of the Code or the concerned Act (under which a criminal proceeding is instituted) to the institution and continuance of the proceedings and/or where there is a specific provision in the Code or the concerned Act, providing efficacious redress for the grievance of the aggrieved party.

(g) Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge."

In the recent case of State of Orissa vs Debendranath Padhi: (2005) 1 SCC 568 (para 29 at 581) the Supreme Court of India again ruled that,

"Regarding the argument of the accused having to face the trial despite being in a position to produce material of unimpeachable character of sterling quality, the width of the powers of the High Court under section 482 of the Code and Article 226 of the Constitution is unlimited where under in the interests of justice the High Court can make such orders as may be necessary to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice within the parameters laid down in State of Haryana vs Bhajan Lal: 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335.

233. In American Life Insurance Company vs Dacca Municipal Corporation: 31 DLR (AD) 276 and Kh Ehteshamuddin Iqbal: 33 DLR (AD) 154 our Appellate Division also held that when a tribunal has acted without jurisdiction or in excess of jurisdiction, the High Court Division can intervene.

<u>234. Such interpretation of the powers of this Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure vis-a-vis Article 102 of our Constitution would, we hope, set at rest the controversy that was raised. What can be done under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot be denied to be done under Article 102 of the Constitution to prevent the abuse of the process of a Court of law or to secure the ends of justice.</u>

<u>235. The process of a Court of law is most sacred. If abuse or misuse of any process of a Court of law is brought 'to the notice in a properly constituted petition under Article 102(2) of the Constitution, this Division is not permitted to shy away and to show the petitioner the provisions of section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.</u>

<u>In the case at hand, it is already found that cognisance of the offences under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance as taken mostillegally on an incompetent and unauthorised complaint and invalid sanction of the Board and trial commenced and 'continued' upon such illegal and void cognisance. To prevent persistent abuse of the process of the Court of the special judge, this Division is obliged arid duty bound to intervene matter what was the stage the trial reached and cannot allow further continuance of the trial of the case for the ends of justice.</u>

<u>236. With regard to the anxiety of Mr Ajmalul Hossain for double-jeopardy for prosecution and trial of the petitioner under the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, the Emergency Powers Rules, 2007 and the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 in Speciai Case No. 5 of 2007 and again under sections 165 and 166 of the Ordinance in Special Case 06 of 2007 on the same allegations under section 26 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 it must be stated that when an act or omission constitutes an offence under two or more enactments, then the offender shall be liable to be prosecuted and punished under either or any of those enactments, but shall not be punished twice for the same offence.</u>

237. In the words, "the act or omission constitutes an offence under two or more enactments" in section 26, the emphasis is given not on the facts alleged in the two complaints but on the ingredients which constitute the two Offences for which one is charged with. Secondly, the trial under two enactments is not barred but what is barred is the punishment of the offender twice for the same offence; Cf State of Bombay vs S L Aple: AIR 1961 SC 578 at 583=(1961) 3 SCR 107•and t S Baliah vs T S Rangachari, ITO, Central Circle: AIR 1969 SC 701=(1969) 3 SCR 65.

238. Upon the deliberation as hereinabove, the conclusions arrived at are as follows:

i. Of the proceedings conceived of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984, the proceedings for assessment of the total income under section 83 or for assessment of the income that escaped the assessment for any relevant assessment year under section 93, and the proceedings for imposition of penalty for concealment of income or furnishing inaccurate particulars of income under section 128 or the prosecution for any offence under Chapter XXI for concealment of income or false statement in the verifications are 11, no doubt, permitted to be initiated and continued separately and independently of each other. But such proceedings for imposition of penalty or prosecution for any such offence shall ultimately abide by the outcome of the proceedings for assessment of the total income or the income that escaped assessment.

ii. Any complaint under section 171 by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes must be founded in either of the proceedings for assessment of the total income under section 83 or for assessment of the income that escaped the assessment for any relevant assessment year under section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984.

iii. No complaint alleging concealment of income or false statements in the verification in the return under Chapter XXI of the Ordinance could be permitted to be lodged and/or taken cognisance of in respect of more than one assessment year within the meaning of section 2(9) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. In the instant case, the lump complaint dated 4-7-2007 for prosecution of the petitioner for concealment of income and/or furnishing false statements in the verification under sections 165 and 166 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 in respect of eight assessment years and having not been based on any proceedings for assessment of income is incompetent, unauthorised and vitiated.

iv. If sections 169 and 170 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 are read together, then, there would be left no option for the National Board of Revenue but to accept the jurisprudence as developed in other jurisdiction that transparency, fair play and justice demand an opportunity should be given to a potential assessee before or during the process of according sanction for prosecution of any offence under Chapter XXI of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 to compound such offence that he may be likely to face.

v. Sanction dated 28-6-07 as was accorded by the National Board of Revenue was bad, illegal, mala fide, and arbitrary, and not a sanction within the meaning of section 169 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. Over and above, the sanction was coram non judice since it was accorded by the National Board of Revenue with Mr Badiur Rahman as its Chairman, who presided over the Board meeting and signed on behalf of the Board was not a member of the Board, which was not constituted in accordance with the provisions of the President's Order No. 76 of 1972.

vi. Cognisance of so-called offences under sections 165 and 166 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 read with rule 15 of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 by the Senior Special Judge by his order dated 8-7-2007 on the basis of an illegal, mala fide and coram non judice sanction was equally illegal, without jurisdiction and vitiated.

vii. Framing of the charges by the 5th Court of Special Judge at the Parliament Building at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar in Dhaka under sections 165 and 166 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 upon such invalid, illegal and void cognisance, and commencement and continuance of the trial of the petitioner in Special Case No. 6 were all serious abuses of the process of the Court.

viii. proclamation of Emergency on 11th day of January, 2007 for internal disturbances and promulgation of the Emergency Powers Ordinance, 2007 on the same date suspending enforcement of the fundamental rights under Part III of the Constitution, do not ipso facto abridge the jurisdiction of this Division, in anyway, to issue appropriate direction and declaration under sub-article (2) of Article 102 of the Constitution.

239. For the reasons aforesaid, commencement and continuance of the trial of the petitioner in Special Case No, 6 of 2007 in the 5th Court of Special Judge at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka must be held to be serious abuse of the process of the Court and vitiated from its very inception for want of valid sanction under section 169 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 and cannot be allowed to continue any further for the ends of justice.

240. Before parting with the case, we must record our deep gratitude to the assistance rendered by the learned senior members of the Bar from both sides of the aisle in their earnest efforts and taking out time from their busy schedule otherwise it would be not so easy for us to arrive at the above conclusions.

241. In the result, the Rule is made absolute with cost.

It is hereby declared that the entire proceedings in Special Case No.6 of 2007 arising out of Complaint Case No. 33 of 2007 now pending for trial of the petitioner, Iqbal Hasan Mahmood alias Iqbal Hasan Mahmood Tuku under sections 165 and 166 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 before the 5th Sher-e-Bangla-Nagar in Dhaka, which commenced and continued without any lawful authority and, as such, of no legal effect and is, accordingly, quashed for the ends of justice.

Send down the records and communicate at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam with M Enayetur Rahim, Obaidul Hasan Shaheen, Md Shahidul Islam, Md Khairul Alam, Md Jahangir Alam, ARM Hasanuzzaman and Sonali Haider, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners. 
TH Khan with Fida M Kamal, Md Idris Khan, Nawshad Zamir; Mahfuza Begum Shathika Hossain, AHM Kamruzzaman, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties.

full_judgment:
This Rule has been issued at the instance of the defendant-petitioners on an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the order dated 20-10-03 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dinajpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 66 of 2003 allowing the application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure restraining the defendants from holding election of Dinajpur Bar Association on the basis of the amended Constitution of the said Association by reversing the Order No.4 dated 20-9-03 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Dinajpur in Other Suit No. 142/03 should not be set aside.

2. The facts leading to issuing the Rule, in short, inter alia, is that the opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit No. 142 of 2003 on 17-9-03 in the Court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Dinajpur against the defendants-petitioners for a declaration that the decision dated 14-9-03 relating to amendment of the Constitution of Dinajpur District Bar Association is illegal void without Jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiffs and for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from giving effect and confirming of the said amendment and for a mandatory injunction directing the defendants for holding election of the Bar Association on the basis of the original Constitution. On the same day they filed an application under Order XXXIX, rules I and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for a temporary injunction restraining the defendants from holding a meeting on 17-9-03 to give effect and confirming of the amendments of the Constitution dated 14-9-03 during pendency of the suit and for a temporary ad interim mandatory injunction against them to hold election of the Association for the year 1410 BS on the basis of the original Constitution and as per direction of the High Court Division passed in its judgment and order dated 6-7-03. The plaintiffs in their application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure stated, in short, inter alia, that the plaintiffs, the President and members of the Executive Committee of Dinajpur Bar Association for the year 1409 BS., during their tenure constituted a 16 member Sub-Committee for amendment of the Constitution of the Samity to meet the long standing necessity and demand of the Bar. The Sub-Committee after hard toil and great efforts prepared a draft recommendations of the amendment under the supervision of plaintiff No.1 which was finally approved on 20-4-2003 by the Sub-Committee under his Presidentship and as 2/3rd majority of the members of the Samity was necessary to finally adopt the same as per Constitution, a meeting was called on 8-5-03 but could not be held due to conspiracy of some interested and vested quarters. Thereafter, on the expiry of the period of the Executive Committee, an ad-hoc Committee (consisting of the defendants) was formed illegally at the instance of the said quarter as per provision of Article 109 of the Constitution of the said Samity. One Mustafizur Rahman, an Advocate and two other members of the Samity brought Other Class Suit No. 43 of2003 in the Court of the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dinajpur on 17-5-03 against the present plaintiffs and 10 others for a declaration that the period of the Executive Committee for the year 1409 BS having expired it is a non-existent committee and cannot function as such. They also filed an application under Order XXXIX, rules I and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for an ad interim injunction restraining them from functioning as such in any way and conducting any meeting of the Samity or utilising its fund including holding of election, etc. and the learned Joint-District Judge accordingly, restrained them by his order dated 25- 5-03 allowing the application. The present plaintiff No. 1 who was the President of the said Executive Committee and defendant No. 1 in said Other Class Suit No. 43/2003 and others being aggrieved by the aforesaid order of temporary injunction/preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 288 of 2003 in the High Court Division in which Civil Rule No, 305(fm)/03 was issued which was disposed of along with the appeal vide its judgment and order dated 6-7-03. In the said judgment and order the High Court Division directed the ad-hoc Committee formed on 14-5-03 to function as ad-hoc Committee and to hold election as per decision of the ad-hoc Committee within 45 days from the date of receipt of the judgment and discharged the Rule and dismissed the appeal accordingly.

3. The plaintiffs of present Other Class Suit No. 142/2003 further alleged in their application under 0rder XXXIX, rules I and 2 that the defendants (the ad-hoc Committee) held a meeting on 14-9-03 and amended the Constitution of Dinajpur Bar Association, 1979 adopting the draft recommendations of the said Constitution Amendment Sub-Committee without requisite 2/3rd majority of the members of the Samity and by showing false and forged signatures of the members in Resolution Book and is going to hold election on the basis of the amended Constitution in violation of the judgment and order of the High Court Division passed on 6-7-03. On the said application filed on 17-9-03 the learned Senior Assistant Judge issued a notice upon the defendants to show cause within 3 days as to why a temporary injunction should not be passed restraining them from holding election on the basis of the amended Constitution and refused to issue mandatory injunction as prayed. The defendants-petitioners appeared before the Court on 20-9-2003 in compliance of the notice and prayed for time for filing written objection. The Court allowed the prayer and also passed another order on the application of the plaintiffs filed in the morning directing the defendants to file Notice and Resolution Books which the defendants complied on the same day with an application for safe custody of those books. The plaintiffs filed another application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 of the Code in the afternoon at 2-50 PM praying for issuing temporary ad interim mandatory injunction upon the defendant-petitioners, but the Senior Assistant Judge rejected the said petition and also rejected the prayer of the plaintiffs to take notes of the resolution book and allowed the application for safe custody of those books filed by the defendants. Having been aggrieved by the said order dated 20- 9-03 the plaintiff-opposite-parties preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 66/03 before the learned District Judge, Dinajpur and again filed an application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for issuing temporary injunction and for temporary ad interim mandatory injunction against the defendant-petitioners. The defendant-respondents appeared in the appeal and filed written objections denying the material averments of the plaintiffs made in the said application and giving a chronological statement of fact. and events with dates of the formation and functions of the ad-hoc Committee including the date of receipt of the information of the judgment of the High Court Division received from the trial Court, facts and events of the Samity with date leading to amendment of Constitution, formation of election commission, declaration of election schedule and of the application filed by plaintiffs to remove the Chief Election Commissioner. The learned Additional District Judge heard the said application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 on transfer and passed the impugned order dated 2-10-03 granting temporary injunction against the defendants- respondents restraining them not to hold election of Dinajpur Zilla Ainjibi Samity for the year 1410 BS on the basis of the amended Constitution till hearing of the Miscellaneous Appeal and also passed a temporary ad interim mandatory injunction directing them to hold election on the basis of the Constitution of the Samity as it was on 6-7-03, the date of passing the judgment and order by the High Court Division.

4. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned order dated 2-10-03 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dinajpur the defendants as petitioners obtained the present Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

5. It may be stated here that although the first part of the above impugned order relating to temporary injunction passed against the defendants has been mentioned in the Rule and the 2nd part relating to the temporary ad interim mandatory injunction has inadvertently been missed in the prayer of the petitioners in their application under section 115(1) of the Code as well as in the Rule, but both the parties have battled mainly on the same at the time of hearing. Both the parties fiercely battled each other on the propriety of passing the temporary ad interim mandatory injunction and this Court has duly considered the same being competent to do so as per provisions of section 115(1) of the Code as it was at the time of issuing of the Rule and also in view of the ruling in the case between Safaruddin and others vs Fazlul Haque, reported in 49 DLR (AD) 151.

6. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Advocate, appeared for the defendant-petitioners along with Mr Enayetur Rahim and others while Mr TH Khan, the learned Advocate, appeared for the opposite parties along with Mr Fida M Kamal, Mr Nawshad Zamir and others.

7. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, took me through the application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the plaintiffs, the written objections filed by the defendants, the documents and papers enclosed with the application under section 115(1) of the CPC marked Annexures A-E including the judgment dated 6-7-03 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Rule No. 305(fm)/03 arising out of FMA No. 288 of 2003, counter-affidavit filed by plaintiff-opposite-parties, affidavit-in-reply filed on behalf of the petitioners including several documents annexed thereto and the impugned order. assailing the impugned judgment and order, he submitted that by making specific findings that the amendments are illegal, violative of Articles 109 and 110 of the Constitution, the signatures in the Resolution Book are false and forged, the amendments are not binding and acceptable, etc., the learned Additional District Judge has, in fact, disposed of the suit and the appeal on merit by the impugned order passed in interlocutory matter and has thus erred in law resulting in an error in the decision of the case occasioning failure of justice. He further submitted that the petitioners (ad-hoc Committee) has done nothing except completing the formalities in adopting the recommendations of the Constitution Amendment Sub-Committee admittedly constituted by the plaintiff No.1 himself as convener and the draft recommendations prepared under his supervision were also approved by the Sub-Committee in a meeting held under his Presidentship which the ad-hoc Committee adopted at the request and demand of the members of the Bar Association in a properly called and attended General Meeting of the general members of the Bar held on 14-9-03 with over 2/3rd majority and there was no illegality in holding the meeting or lack of quorum of the meeting adopting the amendments. He added that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 himself as President of erstwhile Executive Committee of the Samity for the year 1409 BS did everything as aforesaid to bring about amendment of the Constitution of the Samity and also admittedly called a general meeting of the Samity to adopt those amendments in vain but he is now reprobating the same which is unfair and he cannot do so at the same time.

8. It is contended by him that the appellate Court below wrongly found that the ad-hoc Committee amended the Constitution in violation of provisions of Articles 109 and 110 of the Constitution of the Samity inasmuch as there is no provision in the whole of the Constitution, 1979 of the Samity including the provision of Article 37 barring the ad-hoc Committee or authorising any particular Committee to amend the Constitution. Mr Alam asserted that the petitioners rightly amended the Constitution adopting the recommendations made long ago by the Sub-Committee and constituted Election Commission which already declared the schedule of election of the Samity to hold election within 45 days as directed by the High Court Division in its judgment dated 6-7-03. He further argued that the amendments of the Constitution having been adopted in a meeting held on 14-9-03, the appellate Court. below has erred in law in passing the temporary ad interim mandatory injunction directing to hold election as per unamended Constitution restoring the situation which was not in existence on the date of passing of the impugned order on 20-9-03. It is also contended by Mr Alam that the ad-hoc Committee did nothing of its own or at its initiative to amend the Constitution but has only performed the formalities to implement the desire of the general members of the Samity and has thus committed no wrong or illegality or violation of any provision of the Constitution of the Samity. It is also argued by him that although the appellate Court below in its impugned order restrained the defendant- respondents (petitioners) to hold election for the year 1410 BS on the basis of the amended Constitution till hearing of the Miscellaneous Appeal, but it has erred in law in directing them by its ad interim mandatory injunction to hold the election of the Samity on the basis of unamended Constitution by which it has, in fact disposed of the appeal on merit and the same is thus liable to be set aside. He also submitted that the appellate Court below has infringed the order of the High Court Division dated 6-7-03 by issuing temporary injunction restraining the defendant-petitioners from holding election as per its decision as directed by the said order. He also argued strongly that the present suit is a private suit instituted by 3 individual learned members of the Bar and not a representative suit representing the Dinajpur Bar Association and nothing has been stated in the plaint or in the application for injunction nor the appellate Court below found in its impugned order as to how the plaintiffs or any member of the Bar has been aggrieved or injured and will suffer irreparable loss and injury if the injunction is not granted. In support of his submission Mr Alam has cited a number of decisions in the cases between the National Bank of India vs Yakub Mia, reported in 7 DLR 606; Abdul Barek Mia vs ABM Serajul Islam, reported in 20 DLR 501; Md Ashid Mia vs Province of East Pakistan, reported in 22 DLR 694; Khondker Monjur Morshed vs Executive Committee (NB), reported in 28 DLR 449; Abdul Jalil vs Abu Bakar Siddique, reported in 35 DLR (AD) 42; Bangladesh Muktijoddha Kalyan Trust vs Nurul Hossain, reported in 44 DLR 22; Ministry of Communication vs Md Ferozur Rahman, reported in 45 DLR 762; Abul Hayat Sarker vs MA Reza, reported in 47 DLR 170; Chairman, Bangladesh Oil and Gas vs Md Abul Kashem, reported in 47 DLR 413; Babul Kanti Das vs Abul Hashem, reported in 47 DLR (AD) 6; Anwarul Hakim vs Ramiz Ali, reported in 47 DLR 531; Anwara Begum vs Shamsun Nahar Begum, reported in 49 DLR 364 and Fulbaria Adarsha Market Dokandar Malik Samity vs Fulbaria Adarsha Markel Khatigrastha Dokandar Kalyan Samabaya Samity and others, reported in 53 DLR 220.

9. On the other hand, Mr TH Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties, submitted in support of the impugned order reading the findings of the appellate Court below that it has rightly passed the impugned order finding a good prima facie and arguable case and he cannot further' improve the case of the plaintiff-opposite-parties. better than the findings of the appellate Court below.  He also contends that the ad-hoc Committee constituted under Article 109 of the Constitution adopted amendments of the Constitution in violation of the provision of Articles 109 and 110 of the Constitution of the Samity and the function of the ad-hoc Committee was to hold election as per original Constitution according to the Order dated 6-7-2003 of the High Court Division and not to amend the Constitution. Mr Fida M Kamal. the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of Mr TH Khan for the opposite parties on 17-1-2004 (the date set for judgment), added repeating the findings of the appellate Court below that it has granted the injunction vide his impugned order on finding a strong prima facie arguable case and irreparable loss to be suffered by the plaintiffs if the defendants are not restrained from holding election on the basis of amended Constitution. He further submitted that the ad-hoc Committee took charge and started functioning on and from 9-7-2003 and amended the Constitution without any authority and without 2/3rd majority of the members of the Samity. He also contended that a discretionary interim relief granted by the lower Court subject to final order passed in the suit on consideration of the materials before it should not be interfered under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure in its revisional jurisdiction and as such, it would be proper to direct the trial Court to dispose of the main suit expeditiously, etc. In support of his submission, Mr Fida M Kamal has referred the decisions of the cases between Mansur Ahmed vs Kalipada Chattapadhyaya and others, reported in 11 DLR 1032; Abdul Jalil Munshi and another vs Abu Bakar Siddique, reported in 35 DLR (AD) 42; Amirul Huq Shameem and others vs AKM Shamsuddin and others, reported in 49 DLR 77; Md Ashid Ali vs Province of East Pakistan and others, reported in 22 DLR 694; Kalur Hat KC Bilateral School vs Sabbir Hossain Chowdhury and others, reported in 52 DLR 102 and The National Bank of India Ltd., Narayanganj vs Yakub Mia, reported in 7 DLR 606.

10. Perused the revisional application, the counter-affidavit, the affidavit-in-reply, the Annexures, the impugned order and other materials on record of the case and heard the learned Advocates of both the sides at length.

11. For the convenience of understanding the instant dispute, it is necessary to state the background of the case, in short, that one Mostafizur Rahman and two other learned members of the said Bar filed Other Class Suit No. 43/2003 in the Court of Joint District Judge, Sadar, Dinajpur for declaration that the Executive Committee consisting of defendants 1-11 of the suit for the year 1409 BS is a non-existent committee and is unable to function on the expiry of the period for which they were elected and obtained an order of injunction from the trial Court restraining them from functioning as such. In that suit the trial Court also passed an order of temporary injunction restraining the present petitioners (ad-hoc Committee) from functioning and running the affairs of the Bar although the ad-hoc Committee was not made defendant in the suit. In an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 288 of 2003 filed in this Court by the defendants of that suit against the said order of injunction a Civil Rule bearing Civil Rule No. 305(FM)/2003 was issued and the same along with the appeal was disposed of by a Division Bench of this Court vide judgment and order dated 6-7-2003. In that judgment it was held and directed that:

"The suit relates to a Bar Association and therefore, the ad-hoc committee which has not been challenged anywhere' as constituted under Article 109 of their constitution should be allowed to hold election without any further delay and the appellants committee having served for more than one year has no locus standi to continue any more. In such circumstances the impugned order does not call for any interference by this Court excepting part II of the order which restrained the ad-hoc Committee from functioning and holding election.

In the result, this appeal is dismissed and the ad interim order earlier passed by this Court is vacated. The ad-hoc Committee as formed on 14th of May 2003 is authorised to function as ad-hoc Committee and to hold the election as per decision of the ad-hoc Committee within 45 days from the date of receipt of this judgment. The connected Rule is accordingly, discharged."

13. The petitioners were informed the details of the judgment by the trial Court on 2-9-2003 after the Court received the judgment on 27-8-2003. The above order of the High Court Division clearly empowered the ad-hoc Committee formed under the provision of Article 109 of the Constitution of the Samity on 14-5-03 to function as ad-hoc Committee and to hold the election as per its decision within 45 days from the date of receipt of this judgment. In the meantime being informed of the above judgment of the High Court Division by Mr Enayetur Rahim, the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs of that Other Class Suit No. 43/2003 when the ad-hoc Committee took steps for appointment of Auditor which is a condition precedent to hold election, a learned Senior member who was the Government Pleader opposed the same giving out that no such step should be taken by the ad-hoc Committee before receiving the judgment of the High Court Division as it is evident from Annexure H. It appears from Annexure 1 that in a subsequent meeting one Mr Md Mozharul Islam, a learned Member of the Bar, mentioned that the approved draft amendments of the Constitution has been lying long for adopting the same which should be adopted in a General Meeting and requested the ad-hoc Committee to convene a General Meeting to that effect. Accordingly, the petitioners convened a general meeting- on 14-9-03 and adopted the recommendations of the Sub-Committee duly approved by the Sub-Committee on 20-4-2003 under the President- ship of Mr Khatibuddin Ahmed, President of District Bar Association, Dinajpur, the present plaintiff-opposite party, No. 1 and plaintiff-opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 were the members of that Sub- Committee. The approved proposed amendments of the said Constitution of the Samity has been enclosed with affidavit-in-reply of the petitioners and marked as Annexure-F which shows that the proposed amendments were made under the supervision of the present plaintiff-opposite party No.1 who was President of the Bar at that time and the same was also approved by the Sub-Committee under his Presidentship which has been adopted without any addition or alteration by 2/3rd members of the Bar Association in a General Meeting held on 14-9-03 convened by the petitioners. Thereafter, the petitioners formed an election commission on 17-9- 03 which declared election Schedule vide Annexure-D to hold election on 10-10-2003 within 45 days as directed by the High Court Division. It appears from Annexure D 1 that said Mr Khatibuddin Ahmed, the plaintiff No. 1 and few others including other 2 plaintiffs made an application on 20-9-03 to the defendant petitioner No. 1, the President of the ad-hoc Committee to remove the Chief Election Commissioner and appoint some other Advocate to the said post and still brought the present suit on 17-9-2003.

14. The trial Court having refused to grant temporary injunction on an application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 filed' by them on the same date and again having refused to Issue ad interim temporary mandatory injunction on 20-9-2003, the plaintiff-opposite-parties filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 66 of 2003 before the learned District Judge, Dinajpur and again filed aforesaid application for temporary as well as temporary ad interim mandatory injunction under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2. The same was transferred to the Court of the learned Additional District Judge. The learned Additional District Judge by his impugned order allowed the application and granted temporary injunction as well as temporary ad interim mandatory injunction against the defendant- petitioners clearly and specifically finding that the ad-hoc Committee has no power to amend the Constitution under Article 109 of the Constitution of the Samity, that the amendments made by the ad- hoc Committee are illegal and not binding upon the plaintiffs as those were made illegally and in violation of the provisions of Articles 109 and 110 of the Constitution. The appellate Court below further found that the amendments were made without quorum being not supported by 213rd members of the Samity as required under Article 110 and that the same has been passed by showing false attendance by forging the signatures of the members of the Bar and, as such, the said amended Constitution should be treated as illegal and not acceptable in law, etc.

15. Castigating the above findings, Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, categorically submitted that by giving above findings the appellate Court has granted entire relief to the plaintiffs in interlocutory matter on merit pending hearing of the suit. Neither Mr TH Khan nor Mr Fida M Kamal, the learned Advocates for the petitioners, could controvert the same. On the other hand, Mr Khan submitted that he cannot make out a better prima facie case for the plaintiffs than found by the appellate Court below as quoted above. The above findings of the appellate Court definitely touches the merit of the case and amounts to a judgment on merit pending disposal of the suit. The appellate Court has virtually left nothing to decide in suit on merit. The impugned order shows that it has made specific findings that the amendments were adopted without quorum of 213rd majority, that the signatures of the members of the Bar as shown in the Resolution Book are false and forged, etc. The appellate Court below gave its above findings on disputed and controversial issues involved in the suit pending hearing, on the affidavits filed by some members of the Samity and without taking any evidence which is thus, not sustainable in law. Those findings also tantamount to disposal of the suit on merit in interlocutory matter. Mr Fida M Kamal has submitted that a discretionary order in terms of temporary injunction granted subject to final order passed in the suit should not be interfered in revisional jurisdiction. But the impugned order shows that the appellate Court below has left nothing but passed a final order in discretionary manner. The decision he referred in support of his above submissions, as reported in 11 DLR 103 in the case between Mansur Ahmed vs Kalipada Chattopadhyaya and others, I have no reason to disagree with the principle enunciated in the said case. But the learned Counsel has missed the sentence at para 8 of the decision that" No Court should go into the merit of the suit in which temporary injunction is prayed for", and at paragraph 9 that "It is a discretionary power of the Court to grant or not to grant injunction. If the Court exercises its judicial discretion, the High Court is not to interfere under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure." Mr Kamal has missed words that "No Court shall go into the merit of the suit" and the words that "if the Court exercises its judicial discretion". In the instant case the appellate Court below has passed the impugned order on merit of the case which does not come within the principle of a 'judicial discretion'. Hence this decision is not of any help to him. The other decisions referred by him are also of no help in the facts of the case.

16. Mr Khan as well as Mr Kamal, the learned Advocates for the petitioners, have also failed to show that the present suit is a representative suit filed on behalf of the members of the Dinajpur District Bar Association nor they have been able to show as to how the plaintiffs or any other members of the said Bar Association have been aggrieved or injured by the amendment of the Constitution adopting the recommendations already made and approved by a Sub-Committee under the supervision and presidentship of plaintiff No. 1. There is also nothing either in the plaint or in the application for injunction as to how the plaintiffs or for that matter any member of the Bar shall suffer irreparable loss if the injunction was not granted nor there is any finding in the impugned order that the balance of convenience was in favour of the plaintiffs making them entitled to get an order of injunction in any form

<u>17. The plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 has admitted in his application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 that the recommendations for amendment of the Constitution was made by a Sub-Committee constituted by the executive committee of which he was President and those were also approved by the Sub-Committee under his Presidentship and he took the initiative unsuccessfully to adopt those amendments. It also appears from Annexure D1 that all the three plaintiffs are the signatories in that letter in which they requested the President of the ad-hoc Committee to remove the Chief Election Commissioner. From all these facts, apparently admitted and prima facie true from the Annexures which has not been controverted by the opposite parties, that the plaintiffs were very much a party to entire initiative and process of amendment of the Constitution and also took the initiative to adopt the same. It is thus the decision of the plaintiffs which has only been implemented by the petitioners as a matter of formalities without any addition or alteration. The plaintiffs thus being a party to the same should not be allowed to blow hot and cold at the same time as per settled principle held in the case between Nur Banu vs Nur Mohammad and others, reported in 35 DLR (AD) 182, where it has been held that a party should not be allowed to approbate and reprobate at the same time. The conduct of the plaintiffs-opposite-parties appears unfair and mala fide. They also failed to show, even prima facie, that they have been prejudiced injured or in any way aggrieved by the amendment of the Constitution. Order of injunction, in whatever form, is an equitable relief and in order to invoke the same, an aggrieved plaintiff must come bona fide with clean hands with a prima facie case of h is loss and injury showing that if an injunction is not granted he/they will be prejudiced and suffer irreparable loss and injury or his right will be throttled. An order of mandatory injunction or mandatory ad interim injunction is an extremely harsh and highly discretionary order passed at the discretion of the Court to restore a situation existing on the date of filing of the suit or occurred after filing of the suit arid in breach of any order of the Court. Such order cannot be passed to restore or bring back a situation which was not in existence on the date of filing of the suit or of passing of such an order on fulfilling the above conditions. But in the instant case none of the above conditions was existing at the time of filing of the suit or of passing the impugned order.</u>

18. On perusal of all the Articles of. the Constitution of Dinajpur Bar Association 1979, nowhere I found in any of the Articles of the Constitution that any Committee has been so authorised specifically to amend the Constitution except Article 110 which said that "The provision of any of these articles may be amended, altered or modified at any time in an ordinary General Meeting by a majority of two-thirds of the total number of members of the Association." On the other hand, Article 109 says "Nothwithstanding anything contained in this Constitution, in case of any emergency or when the Executive Committee itself becomes non-existent or functus officio or unable to function due to unavoidable circumstances, eleven members at the least may convene a general meeting of the Association which shall have the power to form an ad-hoc Committee consisting of three members of whom one shall act as President and another as Secretary as decided by the General Body for running the affairs of the Association for such period as may be fixed by the General Body."

19. In Article 109 the ad-hoc Committee has been authorised to run the affairs of the Association for such period for which they were formed without any restriction on their function and authority. The power and function of the Executive Committee has been set in Article 37 of the Constitution and there is also nothing to show that Executive Committee can amend the Constitution. The present scenario arose out of amendment of the Constitution by the petitioners (ad-hoc Committee) after the High Court Division passed its judgment and order on 6-7-2003. In the said judgment the High Court Division clearly authorised the ad-hoc committee "to function as ad-hoc Committee and to hold election as per decision of the ad-hoc committee within 45 days from the date of receipt of the judgment" which clearly indicates that the Committee will hold election as per its decision and no restriction or limitation was imposed on the functions and activities of the ad-hoc Committee.

20. In view of what I have discussed and considered above, I am of the opinion that the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dinajpur has grossly erred in law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned order which is not sustainable in law and is liable to be set aside. I find substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners and find merit in the Rule.

21. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 20-10-03 passed by the appellate Court below in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 66 of 2003 is hereby set aside.

22. The orders of both temporary and ad interim mandatory injunctions granted by the appellate Court below are hereby vacated.

23. The relevant findings of the appellate Court below touching the merit Of the suit contained in its impugned judgment and order as mentioned above having already been set aside, those shall have no bearing in any manner whatsoever on the merit of the case at the time of trial of the suit and the trial Court is at liberty to decide the suit on merit independently and freely in accordance with law on the evidence adduced by the parties, if any.

Send down the copy of this judgment and order to Courts below at once.

End.
